topics.name: Aksum
topics.scope: The ruined capital of the ancient Kingdom of Aksum in northern Ethiopia, famous for its field of giant carved stone pillars (stelae). T1: the stelae are single towering stones carved to look like multi-storey tower-houses, complete with false doors and rows of false windows -- the tallest standing one shows about thirteen 'floors'. T2: the Obelisk of Axum, 24 m tall and 160 tonnes of one solid stone, was looted by Italian troops on Mussolini's orders in 1937, stood in Rome for decades, and only returned to Aksum in 2005 (re-erected 2008) -- invert: the stolen-and-returned stone is the hook, the place is the answer. T3: DINNER TEST -- the Great Stele, 33 m and roughly 520 tonnes, is the largest single block of stone humans have ever TRIED to raise; it lies shattered where it fell, probably collapsing during the very attempt to stand it up. T4: the stelae marked the graves of Aksum's kings, and Aksum was a trading empire rich enough to mint its OWN gold coins -- one of the first states on Earth to do so, ~3rd century AD. T5: under King Ezana (~330s AD) Aksum became one of the first kingdoms anywhere to adopt Christianity, and Aksum's Church of St Mary of Zion claims to guard the Ark of the Covenant to this day (label as sacred CLAIM held on faith).
topics.source: Wikipedia 'Obelisk of Axum' & 'King Ezana's Stele'; UNESCO WHC list/15 (Aksum); SFU Museum of Archaeology (Aksumite Stelae). (Grokipedia 403; corroborated via these.)
topics.framing_note: Voice: the Great Stele's 'largest stone humans ever attempted' is the invert-the-wonder hook -> the answer is that it FELL and shattered during erection (T3 dinner-test). Accuracy rail: keep the three stelae straight -- standing Ezana's Stele 21 m, looted-and-returned Obelisk of Axum 24 m/160 t, shattered Great Stele 33 m/~520 t; do NOT conflate them. Stance: present Aksum as a FULL civilization (monumental engineering, its own coinage), never 'primitive'; RESPECT the Ark-of-the-Covenant claim on its own terms -- attribute it as a belief, no smug secular dismissal and no asserting it as proven. Distractors: other tall monuments/obelisks (Egyptian obelisks, Cleopatra's Needle) keep all four live.
topics.history_overlap: Ezana's adoption of Christianity is a candidate history-bank episode; keep the geography answer a PLACE-fact about Aksum (the stelae, the coins, the St Mary of Zion site), not a biography of Ezana.

topics.name: Cape Town & Table Mountain
topics.scope: A city wedged between the Atlantic and a flat-topped mountain at the southern tip of Africa. T1: Table Mountain has a summit as flat as a tabletop, and a low cloud regularly pours over its edge and hangs there like a white 'tablecloth.' T2: that tablecloth forms when the moist south-east wind -- nicknamed the 'Cape Doctor' because it sweeps the city's air clean -- is forced up the slope and cools into cloud (invert: 'why does one mountain wear a permanent cloud?' -> the rising wind). T3: DINNER TEST -- the mountain is the heart of the Cape Floral Kingdom, the SMALLEST but richest of Earth's six great plant kingdoms; Table Mountain ALONE holds around 2,200 plant species -- more than the whole of Britain -- most of it a shrubland called fynbos. T4: the flat summit is ancient -- its sandstone was laid down roughly half a billion years ago, before animals had crawled onto land, and hundreds of millions of years of erosion planed the top dead flat. T5: HONEST HISTORY -- from the summit you look out to Robben Island in the bay, the prison island where Nelson Mandela was held about 18 of his 27 years before walking free in 1990.
topics.source: Wikipedia 'Table Mountain'; Britannica 'Table Mountain'; Table Mountain Aerial Cableway info guide (geology & fynbos). (Grokipedia 403; corroborated via these.)
topics.framing_note: Voice: open on the flat-topped mountain wearing a cloud (T1 picture); the Cape Floral Kingdom's richness (more species than all of Britain) is the dinner-test payoff (T3), with Robben Island the honest-history close (T5). Accuracy rail: teach 'fynbos' and 'floral kingdom' before testing; the sandstone is ~450-510 My old -- say 'roughly half a billion years,' don't overstate a single crisp number. Lane border: the Cape Floral Kingdom is the PLACE's biome/earth-fact (geography); do NOT drift into one plant's or animal's biology (that's the animal/plant lane) -- keep the answer the place-superlative. Stance (VISION-MANDATED on T5): present Robben Island / Mandela plainly and with dignity. Distractors: other flat-topped or floristic-rich places (Roraima tepui, mesas, the Cerrado) keep all four live.
topics.history_overlap: Mandela's imprisonment on Robben Island is a candidate history-bank episode; keep the geography answer the PLACE (the island visible from the summit, the prison), not a full biography of Mandela.

topics.name: Gondar
topics.scope: A former imperial capital in the Ethiopian highlands, nicknamed the 'Camelot of Africa.' T1: Gondar is startling because it is full of real stone CASTLES -- towers, battlements, and turrets -- looking like a slice of medieval Europe dropped into the Ethiopian mountains. T2: Emperor Fasilides built the first castle around 1636 and made Gondar Ethiopia's permanent capital, ending centuries of moving royal camps; the whole royal compound, Fasil Ghebbi, sits behind a 900-metre wall (invert: 'why did Ethiopia's emperors build a European-looking fortress-city?' -> Fasilides settling a fixed capital). T3: DINNER TEST -- the ceiling of Debre Berhan Selassie church is covered edge to edge with the winged faces of about 80 cherub angels, all gazing down at once -- one of the most famous painted interiors in Africa. T4: nearby, Fasilides' Bath -- a stone pool -- is filled just once a year for the Timkat (Epiphany) festival, when thousands of pilgrims plunge into the blessed water to renew their baptism.
topics.source: UNESCO WHC list/19 (Fasil Ghebbi, Gondar Region); ICCROM (Debre Berhan Selassie angel ceiling); Brilliant Ethiopia (Gondar). (Grokipedia 403; corroborated via these.)
topics.framing_note: Voice: lead on the surprise of stone castles in the Ethiopian highlands (T1); the 80-angel-face ceiling is the dinner-test payoff (T3). Accuracy rail: attribute the castle-founding to Fasilides ~1636; give the ceiling's angel faces as ~80 (the commonly cited count) without over-precision, and note the church itself is 17th-18th century. Stance: RESPECT the Timkat plunge as a living sacred rite, described on its own terms. Distractors: other fortified royal/monastic sites (Lalibela, Fasil vs Kuskuam, Ethiopian vs European castles) keep all four live.

topics.name: Gorée Island
topics.scope: A small rocky island off Dakar, Senegal, a memorial of the Atlantic slave trade -- HONEST HISTORY. T1: Gorée's pink-and-ochre House of Slaves (Maison des Esclaves) has a narrow 'Door of No Return' opening straight onto the open Atlantic -- the world's best-known memorial to the transatlantic slave trade. T2: DINNER TEST / the honest debate -- Gorée is a powerful SYMBOL, but historians disagree how many enslaved people actually shipped from this specific island: some Senegalese scholars say vast numbers passed through, while historian Philip Curtin argued the figure was far smaller (a few hundred a year at most), with most captives in the region leaving from busier river-mouth ports on the mainland (label DISPUTED, present BOTH honestly). T3: the island itself was fought over and traded between the Portuguese, Dutch, English, and French because its little harbour guarded the sea route around West Africa -- its real value was its POSITION on the Atlantic corner of the continent. T4: today Gorée is a UNESCO site and a place of pilgrimage and reconciliation -- presidents, popes, and Nelson Mandela have stood at its door -- and the memory it carries matters regardless of the exact count.
topics.source: Wikipedia 'House of Slaves'; History News Network 'The Myth of Gorée Island'; Philip Curtin, 'The Atlantic Slave Trade: A Census' (1969); UNESCO WHC (Island of Gorée). (Grokipedia 403; corroborated via these.)
topics.framing_note: Voice: the honest historians' debate IS the ladder's dinner-test payoff (T2) -- present it truthfully from BOTH sides, neither erasing the memorial's meaning nor overstating the island's actual shipping volume. Stance (VISION-MANDATED): honest-both-ways on the slave trade; the anchor stays the PLACE (the island, the House, the Door, its strategic harbour). Accuracy rail: label the numbers DISPUTED explicitly -- attribute the millions-claim to Senegalese memorial tradition and the far-smaller estimate to Curtin; do not present either as settled. Distractors: other slave-trade sites / Atlantic forts (Elmina, Cape Coast Castle, Bunce Island) keep all four live.
topics.history_overlap: The transatlantic slave trade is a major history-bank topic; the geography lane keeps the PLACE (the island, the memorial house, the harbour's strategic position), not the trade's overall history.

topics.name: Harar
topics.scope: An ancient walled Muslim town on a plateau in eastern Ethiopia, a tangle of alleys inside a stone ring. T1: Harar Jugol is a whole town wrapped in a 5-metre stone wall pierced by just five gates, and inside it packs 368 narrow twisting lanes into barely one square kilometre. T2: Harar is counted by many Muslims as Islam's FOURTH-holiest city (after Mecca, Medina, and Jerusalem) -- inside its walls stand 82 mosques, three of them from the 10th century, and over 100 saints' shrines (invert: 'why is this tiny Ethiopian town so sacred?' -> the fourth-holy-city status). T3: DINNER TEST -- every night a 'hyena man' sits just outside the wall and hand-feeds strips of meat, sometimes mouth to mouth, to wild spotted hyenas that trot in through drainage holes in the wall -- a tradition running back generations. T4: Harar's tall old houses have brightly painted, basket-hung interiors (Harari architecture), and the town has long been a famous highland trading and coffee-growing centre on the caravan route to the coast.
topics.source: UNESCO WHC list/1189 (Harar Jugol, the Fortified Historic Town); Museum of Wander (Harar); Dawan Africa (Harar as Islam's fourth holy city). (Grokipedia 403; corroborated via these.)
topics.framing_note: Voice: the nightly hyena feeding is the dinner-test payoff (T3) -- lead with the scene of a man hand-feeding wild hyenas at the town wall. Lane border: the hyenas are an ANIMAL aside -- keep the answer the PLACE-tradition (the walled town where men feed wild hyenas by hand), NOT the hyena's biology or behavior (that belongs to the animal bank). Accuracy rail: '82 mosques / 102 shrines / 368 lanes / five gates' are UNESCO's figures; the fourth-holiest-city status is a widely held claim -- attribute it, don't assert it as universal. Distractors: other walled old towns / holy cities (Fez medina, Kairouan, old Sana'a) keep all four live.

topics.name: Kano
topics.scope: One of the oldest cities of West Africa, a Hausa trade capital in northern Nigeria. T1: Kano is ringed by ancient mud CITY WALLS, raised and extended over centuries (from around the 11th century) to guard a great trans-Saharan trade town at the desert's southern edge. T2: DINNER TEST -- the Kofar Mata dye pits, dug around 1498, are the OLDEST indigo-dyeing pits in Africa still in use: deep clay pits of near-black blue dye where cloth has been coloured by hand for over 500 years (invert: 'where has the same blue dye been made in the same pits for five centuries?'). T3: Kano's Kurmi Market, founded in the 15th century, was one of the great markets on the southern edge of the Sahara, trading indigo cloth, leather, and goods carried by camel caravan across the desert.
topics.source: Wikipedia 'Kofar Mata Dye Pits' & 'Kano'; Kohan Textile Journal (522-year-old dye tradition); Google Arts & Culture (Kano tie-and-dye). (Grokipedia 403; corroborated via these.)
topics.framing_note: Voice: the 500-year-old indigo dye pits are the dinner-test payoff (T2) -- lead with 'where has the same blue dye been made in the same clay pits since ~1498?'. Lane: indigo dyeing is a CRAFT/industry genuinely born and sustained in THIS place (a made-here creation -> geography), and the answer stays a place-fact (the Kofar Mata pits, the walls, Kurmi market) -- do not stray into textile chemistry. Accuracy rail: the pits date to ~1498 ('over 500 years'); the walls are centuries-long constructions, not a single build date. Distractors: other ancient West African / Hausa trade cities & crafts (Timbuktu, Katsina, Benin City walls, Djenné) keep all four live.

topics.name: Lagos
topics.scope: Africa's largest city, sprawled across islands and a lagoon on Nigeria's Atlantic coast. T1: Lagos is not built on solid ground but spread across ISLANDS, sandbars, and a huge coastal LAGOON -- its very name comes from the Portuguese word for 'lakes/lagoons.' T2: DINNER TEST -- in the Makoko district a whole neighbourhood of wooden houses stands on tall STILTS above the lagoon water, reached only by canoe, earning it the nickname 'the Venice of Africa' (invert: 'why do thousands of people live in houses standing IN the water?'). T3: long barrier islands and sand spits shield the city from the open Atlantic; the Yoruba original name for the place is Èkó, older than 'Lagos.' T4: Lagos was Nigeria's capital until 1991, when the government built a brand-new planned capital, Abuja, in the country's centre -- yet Lagos stayed the country's crowded economic heart, one of the fastest-growing megacities on Earth (roughly 15-20+ million people).
topics.source: Wikipedia 'Lagos' & 'Makoko'; Britannica 'Lagos'; BlackPast (Abuja becomes capital, 1991). (Grokipedia 403; corroborated via these.)
topics.framing_note: Voice: lead on the city built ON water -- islands and lagoon (T1); the Makoko stilt village is the dinner-test payoff (T2). Accuracy rail: the population is genuinely uncertain -- say 'roughly 15-20+ million' as a range, never a false-precise figure; the capital moved to Abuja in 1991. Keep answers place-anchored (the lagoon, the stilt village, the name Èkó, the capital move) -- avoid a bare 'largest city in Africa' superlative-pick as the answer. Distractors: other coastal/water-built or fast-growing cities (Venice, Ganvié stilt village, Abuja, Kinshasa) keep all four live.

topics.name: Stone Town, Zanzibar
topics.scope: The old Swahili-coast trading town on Zanzibar island, a maze of coral-stone alleys off the Tanzanian coast. T1: Stone Town is famous for hundreds of hand-carved wooden DOORS -- heavy, studded with brass spikes, each carved with symbols of the owner's trade, faith, and status. T2: DINNER TEST -- the brass spikes were copied from India, where such studs were meant to stop war ELEPHANTS from battering doors down; Zanzibar has no war elephants, so on the island they became pure decoration and a badge of wealth. T3: Zanzibar's Omani sultans made the island the world's leading CLOVE grower -- the 'Spice Island' -- and even shifted their capital here all the way from Arabia (invert: 'why would a sultan move his capital from Arabia to a small African island?' -> the spice/trade wealth). T4: HONEST HISTORY -- Stone Town held East Africa's largest slave market; today an Anglican cathedral stands on that exact site, its altar set where the whipping post once was, above preserved underground holding cells. T5: the House of Wonders (Beit-al-Ajaib) was the first building in all of East Africa to get electric light and an elevator.
topics.source: Wikipedia 'Stone Town'; Siyabona (Stone Town architecture / Zanzibari doors); UNESCO WHC (Stone Town of Zanzibar). (Grokipedia 403; corroborated via these.)
topics.framing_note: Voice: the war-elephant door studs are the dinner-test payoff (T2) -- lead with 'why are these African doors covered in spikes?' and let the India/war-elephant origin be the reveal. Lane border: CLOVES here are a place CROP and the reason the island became a trade capital (geography), NOT a cooking ingredient -- keep the answer the place-fact ('Spice Island' / capital moved here), don't drift into recipes. Stance (VISION-MANDATED on T4): present the slave-market history honestly and plainly, cathedral-over-market as the sober reversal. Accuracy rail: the door-stud/war-elephant origin is a well-attested tradition -- fine to state as the doors' Indian-influence origin. Distractors: other Indian Ocean / Swahili trade towns (Lamu, Mombasa, Kilwa) keep all four live.
topics.history_overlap: The East African slave trade is a candidate history-bank topic; keep the geography answer the PLACE (the market site, the cathedral built over it), not the trade's full economic history.

topics.name: Amritsar — the Golden Temple in its sacred pool
topics.scope: The holiest shrine of the Sikhs, in the Punjab city of Amritsar, India. T1: the Harmandir Sahib sits on a marble island in the middle of a great square pool, a golden shrine you reach by a single causeway across the water (answer: the temple in the pool). T2: its upper storeys and dome are sheathed in real gold — about 400 kg of gold leaf that blazes in the pool's reflection at sunrise (answer: the gold covering — invert with 'why does the water seem to catch fire at dawn?'). T3: the pool itself is the Amrit Sarovar, the 'pool of nectar' that gives the city its very name; pilgrims bathe in water believed to heal (answer: the sacred nectar-pool). T4: the temple has a door on EACH of its four sides — deliberately open to people of every direction and every caste — and its entrance sits BELOW street level, so everyone must step DOWN, in humility, to enter (answer: the four open doors / step-down humility — DINNER-TEST payoff). T5: its free community kitchen, the langar, seats anyone — rich, poor, any faith — on the floor as equals and serves around 100,000 free meals every single day (answer: the world's largest free kitchen).
topics.source: Wikipedia (Golden Temple, Amrit Sarovar); Britannica; Incredible India. Verify on Grokipedia first at build time.
topics.framing_note: PLACE ladder, the Golden Temple/Amritsar named in every stem. Distractors = other real gilded/sacred sites (Kyoto's Kinkaku-ji, Bangkok's Wat Phra Kaew, the Shwedagon, Varanasi's temples). Invert — lead with the pool 'catching fire' at dawn → the gold. Dinner-test payoff = the four open doors / the langar feeding 100,000 a day. LANE BORDER: the langar is a CULTURAL-CREATION/equality fact of the PLACE — keep the answer the KITCHEN-and-equality wonder, not a dish (dishes are COOKING-bank). VISION: sacred Sikh site on its own terms.
topics.history_overlap: The 1984 Operation Blue Star is charged modern history — out of lane; keep every answer on the shrine, the pool, the doors and the langar.

topics.name: Bukhara — the Silk Road 'museum city'
topics.scope: A sacred caravan city in Uzbekistan whose old town survives almost intact. T1: the Kalyan minaret has loomed over Bukhara since 1127 — about 46 m of patterned brick that called the faithful to prayer (answer: the minaret; teach 'minaret'). T2: legend says when Genghis Khan rode in to raze the city he tilted his head back to see the tower's top and his hat fell off; awed, he ordered it spared — the one thing left standing, later nicknamed the 'Tower of Death' for the criminals thrown from it (answer: Genghis spared the tower). T3: the Samanid Mausoleum, a perfect brick cube from the 900s whose woven brick patterns shift with the sun, survived the Mongols only because centuries of flood-silt had BURIED it — the raiders never found it (answer: the tomb saved by being buried in sand — DINNER-TEST payoff). T4: the Ark of Bukhara, a mud-brick citadel raised on the rubble of its own earlier selves, was the fortress-palace of the emirs for over a thousand years (answer: the Ark citadel). T5: Bukhara keeps the whole Silk Road pattern — a domed covered bazaar, caravanserais, and the four-turret Chor Minor gate — earning the name 'museum city' (answer: the intact old town / Chor Minor; teach 'caravanserai').
topics.source: Wikipedia (Kalyan Minaret, Samanid Mausoleum, Ark of Bukhara, Bukhara, Chor Minor); people-travels.com; Atlas Obscura. Verify on Grokipedia first at build time.
topics.framing_note: PLACE ladder, Bukhara named in every stem. Distractors = other real Silk Road towers/tombs (Samarkand's Registan, Khiva's Kalta Minor, the Gur-e-Amir). Invert the wonder — lead with 'the hat that fell' and 'the tomb saved by sand,' never 'What is the oldest mausoleum?'. Accuracy rail: the Genghis-hat detail is LEGEND (flag it), but the sparing of the minaret and the silt-burial of the Samanid tomb are real. Teach 'minaret'/'caravanserai' before testing.

topics.name: Delhi — the city of seven cities
topics.scope: India's layered capital, rebuilt on the Yamuna plain again and again. T1: the Qutb Minar, begun in 1199, spirals 72.5 m into the sky in red sandstone and marble — the tallest brick minaret in the world (answer: the Qutb Minar). T2: beside it stands a 7-metre iron pillar forged about 1,600 years ago in the Gupta age that has barely rusted — its iron holds just enough phosphorus to grow a thin, self-healing protective skin (answer: the rust-free iron pillar; the phosphorus/misawite film is the mechanism — DINNER-TEST payoff). T3: the Quwwat-ul-Islam beside the Minar was India's first mosque — and its carved columns were reused from 27 demolished Hindu and Jain temples, still plainly visible in the stone (answer: the first mosque, built from temple stones — state honestly). T4: Humayun's Tomb (1560s) was India's first great garden-tomb, a red-sandstone mausoleum set in a four-part charbagh, its double dome linking Samarkand's Gur-e-Amir to the Taj Mahal (answer: the first garden-tomb / the dome lineage; teach 'charbagh'). T5: Shah Jahan's Red Fort (Lal Qila, 1648) once held the jewelled Peacock Throne, and its marble Hall of Private Audience is inscribed 'If there is a paradise on earth, it is this, it is this, it is this' — a canal called the 'Stream of Paradise' once flowed through its palaces (answer: the Red Fort / the paradise couplet). Frame: Delhi is nicknamed the city of 'seven cities' for its stacked ruined capitals.
topics.source: Wikipedia (Qutb Minar, Iron pillar of Delhi, Qutb complex, Humayun's Tomb, Red Fort); Britannica; UNESCO WHC #232/#233. Verify on Grokipedia first at build time (esp. Red Fort couplet + Peacock Throne).
topics.framing_note: PLACE ladder, a Delhi monument named in every stem. Distractors = other real Indian monuments (Agra Fort, Fatehpur Sikri's Buland Darwaza, Lahore's Badshahi Mosque). Invert — lead with 'a 1,600-year iron pillar that won't rust' → answer the phosphorus self-healing film (put the mechanism in the ANSWER, never the stem). Dinner-test payoff = the rust-free iron pillar. HONEST-BOTH-WAYS rail: the first-mosque-from-temple-stones rung states the spoliation plainly, no polemic and no smug framing. Keep the Peacock-Throne rung on the throne-as-place-treasure.
topics.history_overlap: Nader Shah's 1739 sack (the Peacock-Throne looting) and the 1947 Independence-Day flag-raising are history-bank episodes — keep the Red Fort answers on the place and its treasures, not the invasion or independence narrative.

topics.name: Fatehpur Sikri — the abandoned red city
topics.scope: The perfect Mughal capital Akbar built and then walked away from, near Agra. T1: Fatehpur Sikri is a whole imperial city of red sandstone — palaces, courts and a great mosque — that Akbar raised in the 1570s and abandoned within about 15 years (answer: the abandoned 'ghost' capital). T2: it was left empty mainly because it ran out of WATER — the rocky ridge simply could not keep the growing city supplied (answer: water shortage — invert with 'why abandon a brand-new capital?'). T3: its gateway, the Buland Darwaza, soars about 54 m — often called the 'highest gateway in the world' — built to mark Akbar's Gujarat victory (answer: the giant victory-gate). T4: the Panch Mahal is a five-storey open pavilion of columns that shrinks tier by tier like a wedding cake — a 'wind-catcher' raised to trap the breeze in the summer heat (answer: the five-tier wind palace). T5: Akbar built here to honour the Sufi saint Salim Chishti, who had foretold he would finally get a son — the saint's delicate white marble tomb still sits inside the mosque courtyard (answer: the saint's tomb / why he built here).
topics.source: Wikipedia (Fatehpur Sikri, Buland Darwaza, Panch Mahal); UNESCO WHC #255; Grokipedia (Panch Mahal page). Verify on Grokipedia first at build time.
topics.framing_note: PLACE ladder, Fatehpur Sikri named in every stem. Distractors = other real deserted/Mughal sites (Mandu, Hampi, Delhi's Tughlaqabad, Agra Fort). Invert — lead with 'a flawless new capital emptied in 15 years — why?' → the water answer. Dinner-test payoff = abandoned-for-water. Teach 'Sufi' lightly. Akbar's court religious debates here are HISTORY — keep answers on the BUILDINGS and the water/place-fact.

topics.name: Jaipur — the Pink City and its stone sky-machines
topics.scope: A planned royal city in Rajasthan, laid out on a grid in 1727 by the astronomer-king Sawai Jai Singh II. T1: Jaipur's whole old town is washed a single terracotta pink, earning it the name the 'Pink City' (answer: the Pink City). T2: it was painted pink in 1876 to welcome one royal guest — the visiting Prince of Wales, later Edward VII — because pink was the colour of hospitality (answer: painted for a royal visit — invert with 'why is a whole city one colour?'). T3: at the Jantar Mantar, Jai Singh built astronomy instruments as BUILDINGS you climb — the Samrat Yantra is a stone sundial about 27 m tall that tells the time to roughly two seconds (answer: the giant climbable stone sundial). T4: the Hawa Mahal, the 'Palace of Winds,' is a five-storey honeycomb facade pierced by 953 tiny latticed windows so royal women could watch the street unseen while breezes cooled the rooms (answer: the 953-window palace). T5: above the city, Amber (Amer) Fort mirrors itself in Maota Lake, and its own Sheesh Mahal blazes with mirror-work that lights the whole hall from a single flame (answer: Amber Fort / its mirror hall). Frame: the grid plan by Vidyadhar Bhattacharya made Jaipur one of India's first fully planned cities.
topics.source: Wikipedia (Jaipur, Jantar Mantar Jaipur, Hawa Mahal, Amer Fort); Rajasthan Tourism; BBC Sky at Night. Verify on Grokipedia first at build time.
topics.framing_note: PLACE ladder, Jaipur or its monument named in every stem. Distractors = other real Rajasthan/Indian sites (Udaipur's lake palace, Jodhpur the 'Blue City,' Jaisalmer the 'Golden City,' Delhi's Jantar Mantar). Invert — lead with 'a 27 m sundial accurate to 2 seconds' → answer 'a sundial.' Dinner-test payoff = the climbable giant sundial and the 953 windows. Settled wonder — vision not engaged; no food/animal drift.

topics.name: Khiva — the walled desert city
topics.scope: A fortified oasis town in Uzbekistan, the last caravan stop before the Karakum desert crossing to Persia. T1: Khiva's inner town, the Itchan Kala, is wrapped in mud-brick walls about 10 m high — a whole walled city you can still walk inside (answer: the walled inner town). T2: the fat, stubby Kalta Minor minaret glows solid turquoise from base to top — it is UNFINISHED: its khan died in 1855 and it froze at about 29 m instead of becoming Central Asia's tallest tower (answer: the unfinished minaret — invert with 'why is the gorgeous tower so SHORT?'). T3: inside the Djuma (Friday) Mosque a forest of more than 200 carved wooden columns holds up a flat roof, some pillars over a thousand years old (answer: the wooden-column forest). T4: Itchan Kala was the FIRST place in all Central Asia named a UNESCO World Heritage Site, in 1991 (answer: first Central-Asian World Heritage site). T5: Khiva's skyline of minarets, madrasas and palaces is so perfectly preserved that the whole town looks frozen in time (answer: the 'time-frozen' old town).
topics.source: Wikipedia (Khiva, Itchan Kala); UNESCO WHC #543; Advantour. Verify on Grokipedia first at build time.
topics.framing_note: PLACE ladder, Khiva/Itchan Kala named in every stem. Distractors = other real walled/desert Silk Road towns (Bukhara, Samarkand, Merv). Invert — the Kalta Minor rung leads with its beauty and asks why it is so SHORT (answer: the khan died, it was never finished). Dinner-test payoff = the unfinished squat turquoise minaret. Khiva's slave-market past is at most a light factual mention — keep every answer on the PLACE/architecture.

topics.name: Lahore — the Mughal city of mosque and garden
topics.scope: The Mughal heart of the Punjab, in present-day Pakistan. T1: the Badshahi Mosque, built by emperor Aurangzeb in 1673, is a vast red-sandstone mosque whose courtyard holds tens of thousands of worshippers — for three centuries the largest mosque on Earth (answer: the Badshahi Mosque). T2: across from it the Lahore Fort hides the Sheesh Mahal, a 'palace of mirrors' whose walls and ceiling are set with thousands of tiny mirror-tiles that turn a single candle into a galaxy (answer: the mirror palace). T3: Shah Jahan's Shalimar Gardens step down the land in three terraces threaded with hundreds of fountains — a Persian charbagh, a four-part 'paradise garden' fed by a canal dug for miles (answer: the terraced fountain garden; teach 'charbagh'). T4: the fort's outer 'Picture Wall' is a giant mosaic of glazed tile showing elephants, camels and polo games — one of the largest tiled murals in the world (answer: the Picture Wall). T5: the nearby Wazir Khan Mosque (1634) is so densely covered in fresco and 'kashi' tilework it is called 'a jewel on the palm of Lahore' (answer: the tiled Wazir Khan mosque).
topics.source: Wikipedia (Badshahi Mosque, Lahore Fort, Shalimar Gardens Lahore, Wazir Khan Mosque); UNESCO WHC #171; Britannica. Verify on Grokipedia first at build time.
topics.framing_note: PLACE ladder, Lahore in every stem, each answer a concrete Lahore monument. Distractors = other real Mughal works (Delhi's Jama Masjid/Red Fort, Agra Fort, Kashmir's Shalimar). Invert — lead with 'one candle becomes a galaxy' for the Sheesh Mahal. Teach 'charbagh'/'minaret' before testing. Dinner-test payoff = the mirror palace. LANE BORDER: Lahori food is COOKING-bank — do NOT seed a dish rung; keep answers on mosque/garden/fort.

topics.name: Lhasa — the Potala Palace above the roof of the world
topics.scope: The sacred capital of Tibet, set on a plateau about 3,650 m up in the Himalaya. T1: the Potala Palace climbs 13 storeys up the Red Hill above Lhasa, a white-and-crimson fortress of more than 1,000 rooms — for centuries the winter home of the Dalai Lamas (answer: the Potala Palace). T2: it stands at roughly 3,700 m on Marpo Ri ('Red Hill'), its top some 300 m above the valley floor — one of the HIGHEST palaces on Earth (answer: the world's highest palace / its dizzying altitude — invert with the number as hook). T3: the 5th Dalai Lama began the present palace in 1645; the outer shell took just three years but the painted, gilded interior took 45 more (answer: the 5th Dalai Lama's palace). T4: at the city's heart the Jokhang Temple is the holiest shrine in all of Tibetan Buddhism — pilgrims prostrate full-length again and again toward its doors (answer: the Jokhang, the holiest temple). T5: around the Jokhang runs the Barkhor, a pilgrim circuit walked always CLOCKWISE by a slow river of pilgrims turning prayer wheels (answer: the Barkhor pilgrim circuit).
topics.source: Wikipedia (Potala Palace, Jokhang, Barkhor, Lhasa); Britannica; New World Encyclopedia. Verify on Grokipedia first at build time.
topics.framing_note: PLACE ladder, Lhasa/the Potala named in every stem. Distractors = other real high/holy places (Bhutan's Tiger's Nest, Ladakh's Thiksey, Nepal's Boudhanath, Machu Picchu). Invert — lead with '3,700 m up, 13 storeys, 1,000 rooms' → the Potala. Dinner-test payoff = the world's-highest-palace altitude rung. VISION RAIL: respect the sacred site on its own terms; state Tibet as timeless geographic fact (a high-plateau Himalayan capital) and DO NOT editorialize on the China–Tibet political dispute.
topics.history_overlap: Tibet's 1950 annexation and the Dalai Lama's 1959 exile are history/current-events — keep every answer on the buildings and the plateau, not the political dispute.

topics.name: Samarkand — the Registan and Timur's Blue City
topics.scope: The turquoise-domed capital Timur (Tamerlane) built in today's Uzbekistan, the grand crossroads of the Silk Road. T1: three towering madrasas (Islamic colleges) frame the Registan, Samarkand's great plaza whose name means 'sandy place' — the answer is the Registan (teach 'madrasa'). T2: on the Sher-Dor madrasa's portal two great cats chase white does under a rising sun-with-a-face — startling because Islamic art usually avoids living creatures; 'Sher-Dor' means 'lion-bearing' (answer: the forbidden living-creature mosaic). T3: Timur's own tomb, the Gur-e-Amir, is crowned by a ribbed, melon-shaped azure dome that became the model later copied at Humayun's Tomb and the Taj Mahal (answer: the fluted turquoise dome / the dome lineage). T4: Ulugh Beg, Timur's astronomer-grandson, sank a 40-metre stone arc — the Fakhri sextant — into a Samarkand hillside and catalogued over 1,000 stars and the length of the year so precisely his figures stood until Tycho Brahe (answer: the giant buried sextant / observatory). T5: when Soviet scientist Mikhail Gerasimov opened Timur's grave on 20 June 1941, a warning was said to read 'whoever disturbs my tomb unleashes an invader worse than I' — two days later Hitler launched Operation Barbarossa (answer: Gerasimov's 1941 exhumation — flagged as LEGEND/coincidence). Also: the Bibi-Khanym mosque, raised so hugely and hastily from India-campaign loot that it began crumbling within decades; the Shah-i-Zinda 'avenue of tombs' tiled in every shade of blue.
topics.source: Wikipedia (Registan, Gur-e-Amir, Curse of Timur, Ulugh Beg Observatory, Bibi-Khanym Mosque); centralasia-travel.com; St Andrews MacTutor (Ulugh Beg). Verify on Grokipedia first at build time.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led PLACE ladder: Samarkand named in every stem, the answer a concrete Samarkand wonder. Distractors = other real Silk Road marvels (Bukhara's Kalyan minaret, Khiva's Kalta Minor, Isfahan's square) so all four stay live. Invert the wonder — lead with the sun-faced cats, the 40 m arc, the 1941 grave — never 'What is the Registan?'. Teach 'madrasa'/'minaret' before testing. Dinner-test payoff = the Gerasimov-curse rung (flag clearly as LEGEND + coincidence) plus the Timur-dome-to-Taj lineage rung. Timur's conquests are HISTORY — keep every answer the BUILDING/place-fact, not the campaign.
topics.history_overlap: Timur's conquests and the sack that funded Bibi-Khanym are history-bank material — keep answers on the buildings, not the campaigns.

topics.name: The Kathmandu Valley — city of a thousand temples
topics.scope: A high Himalayan valley in Nepal packed with three ancient royal cities and their temple-squares. T1: at the hearts of Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur stand three Durbar ('palace') Squares — open plazas crowded with tiered wooden pagoda-temples around the old kings' palaces (answer: the Durbar squares). T2: on a hill above the valley rises the white dome of Swayambhunath, where a pair of huge painted 'Buddha eyes' gaze out from all four sides of the spire, watching every direction at once (answer: the all-seeing Buddha eyes; teach 'stupa'). T3: wild monkeys overrun Swayambhunath's long stairway, giving it the nickname the 'Monkey Temple' (answer: the Monkey Temple — the PLACE/name). T4: across the valley, Boudhanath is one of the largest stupas in the world — a vast white mound ringed by pilgrims walking clockwise round it spinning prayer wheels (answer: the giant stupa Boudhanath). T5: the valley's tiered pagoda roof-style was carried to China by the Nepali architect Arniko in the 1200s — the East-Asian 'pagoda' owes a debt to Kathmandu (answer: the pagoda exported to China — DINNER-TEST payoff). Note: a 2015 earthquake toppled several Durbar-square temples, since rebuilt.
topics.source: Wikipedia (Kathmandu Valley, Swayambhunath, Boudhanath, Araniko); UNESCO WHC #121. Verify on Grokipedia first at build time.
topics.framing_note: PLACE ladder, a Kathmandu-Valley site named in every stem. Distractors = other real stupas/temple-cities (Lhasa's Jokhang, Bagan, Borobudur, Sanchi). Teach 'stupa.' Invert — lead with 'eyes that watch all four directions' → Swayambhunath. Dinner-test payoff = the Buddha eyes and the pagoda-exported-to-China rung. LANE BORDER: the monkeys are an ANIMAL aside — keep that answer the PLACE-name ('Monkey Temple'), never monkey behaviour/biology. VISION: sacred Buddhist/Hindu sites, handled respectfully on their own terms.

topics.name: Varanasi — the eternal city on the Ganges
topics.scope: One of the oldest continuously lived-in cities on Earth, holy to Hindus, on the curving north bank of the Ganges (also called Kashi or Benares). T1: Varanasi's riverfront is a long staircase of stone 'ghats' — broad steps leading straight down into the Ganges where the whole city bathes, prays and gathers at dawn (answer: the ghats; teach 'ghat'). T2: it is among the oldest CITIES still lived in — its lanes have stayed alive for well over 3,000 years, so it is called a 'living' ancient city (answer: one of the world's oldest living cities). T3: at the Manikarnika ghat, funeral pyres burn day and night beside the river, and Hindus believe a soul cremated here escapes the cycle of rebirth (moksha) — a sacred fire kept alight for centuries (answer: the never-quenched cremation fire — DINNER-TEST payoff, treated with dignity). T4: each dusk at the Dashashwamedh ghat priests swing tiered brass lamps in the Ganga Aarti, a fire-and-chant ceremony offered to the river itself (answer: the river fire-ceremony). T5: Hindus call the city Kashi, 'the City of Light,' and hold it to be the city of the god Shiva — one of the holiest places in all Hinduism to die (answer: Shiva's city / the holiest place to die).
topics.source: Wikipedia (Varanasi, Manikarnika Ghat, Dashashwamedh Ghat); Britannica; Atlas Obscura. Verify on Grokipedia first at build time.
topics.framing_note: PLACE ladder, Varanasi or its ghat named in every stem. Distractors = other real sacred rivers/cities (Haridwar, Prayagraj's Sangam, the Nile, the Jordan). Teach 'ghat.' Invert — lead with 'a fire that has never gone out' → the eternal cremation ground. Dinner-test payoff = the cremation-fire moksha rung. VISION RAIL: this is a sacred death-ritual — describe it on Hindus' own terms with dignity, NO smug secular dismissal and NO morbid sensationalism; frame it plainly as a place of hope for liberation.

topics.name: Beijing: the imperial capital
topics.scope: Beijing's monumental north-south core. T1: at the heart of the city sits the Forbidden City, the largest palace complex on Earth -- around 8,700 rooms behind a 52-m-wide moat and a 10-m wall, where commoners were forbidden to enter for 500 years (answer: the Forbidden City). T2: legend says the palace was built with 9,999-and-a-half rooms -- one short of the 10,000 that belonged to Heaven alone -- so no emperor would out-rank the gods (answer: the 9,999-room legend). Invert: the near-10,000 count is the hook; label it LEGEND vs the real ~8,700. T3: at the round Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests (Temple of Heaven, 1420), the interlocking wooden structure is held together WITHOUT a single nail (answer: built without nails). T4: the Temple of Heaven's curved Echo Wall carries a whisper the length of its circle, and the emperor prayed there as the 'Son of Heaven' at the winter solstice (answer: the Echo Wall). T5: the whole old city is laid on one straight CENTRAL AXIS 7.8 km long -- Bell Tower to Forbidden City to front gate -- a cosmic spine UNESCO named a World Heritage site in 2024 (answer: Beijing's Central Axis). Extra rungs: the HUTONG lanes and siheyuan courtyard homes gridded since the Mongol Yuan era (the word 'hutong' is Mongolian for 'well'); the golden roof-tiles reserved for the emperor; the Summer Palace's Kunming Lake and Long Corridor; the Meridian Gate.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbidden_City (1406-1420 under the Yongle Emperor; ~8,886 rooms vs the 9,999 legend; 72 ha; 10 m wall, 52 m moat; largest preserved palace complex; residence 1420-1924); Britannica 'Forbidden City'; Association for Asian Studies on number-symbolism; UNESCO 2024 inscription of the Beijing Central Axis; standard sources on the Temple of Heaven (nail-free Hall of Prayer, Echo Wall) and hutong etymology.
topics.framing_note: Voice: scene-led (stand in the moat's shadow, walk the axis), never 'What is the largest palace?' or 'What is the capital of China?'. Every answer is a concrete architectural or urban wonder. Dinner-test payoffs = the no-nails Hall (T3) and the 9,999-room legend (T2) -- flag 9,999 as LEGEND against the documented ~8,700. Distractors = other imperial complexes (Seoul's Gyeongbokgung, Kyoto's palaces, Xi'an). Lane border: Ming/Qing dynastic events are history-bank material; keep rungs on the buildings and city form.
topics.history_overlap: Ming and Qing dynastic history (and 1949 events at Tiananmen) belong to the history bank; keep every rung on Beijing's architecture and urban form -- palace, temple, axis, hutongs.

topics.name: Gyeongju: the museum without walls
topics.scope: The old Silla capital, an open valley of tombs and temples in southeast Korea. T1: across Gyeongju's parks sit grassy HILLS the size of houses -- but they are not natural hills, they are the 1,500-year-old royal burial mounds of the Silla kings (answer: royal burial mounds, not hills). Invert: 'grassy hills in a city park' hook, 'they're royal tombs' answer. T2: one opened mound, the 'Heavenly Horse Tomb' (Cheonmachong), gave up a golden crown and a painted saddle-flap showing a white winged horse -- the burial goods of a Silla king (answer: Cheonmachong and its gold crown). T3: Gyeongju holds Cheomseongdae, a bottle-shaped stone tower built in the 630s -- the OLDEST surviving astronomical observatory in East Asia -- laid up from about 362 stones for the days of the lunar year (answer: Cheomseongdae, the oldest observatory). Teach 'observatory.' T4: in the hills above, the Seokguram Grotto shelters a serene granite Buddha positioned to catch the FIRST light of sunrise over the East Sea, carved in the 8th century with remarkable geometry (answer: Seokguram's sunrise-facing Buddha). T5: Gyeongju was the Silla capital for nearly 1,000 years (57 BCE-935 CE), and so many tombs, pagodas and temples survive across the open valley that it is nicknamed 'the museum without walls' (answer: 'the museum without walls' / a 1,000-year capital). Extra rung: Bulguksa temple's stone terraces and twin pagodas.
topics.source: World History Encyclopedia & en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheomseongdae (7th c., built under Queen Seondeok 632-647, oldest surviving observatory in East Asia, ~362 stones, 27 layers, 9.17 m); VisitKorea/AtlasObscura on Daereungwon (23 mounds) and Cheonmachong; standard UNESCO sources on Seokguram Grotto and Bulguksa.
topics.framing_note: Voice: scene-led (walk among the mounds that look like green hills), never 'What is the oldest observatory in Asia?'. Dinner-test payoffs = the tombs-that-look-like-hills (T1) and Cheomseongdae (T3); TEACH 'observatory' before testing it. The gold crowns are artifacts OF the place, fine as answers. Distractors = other tomb fields / early observatories (Xi'an mounds, the Beijing Ancient Observatory). Lane border: Silla dynastic politics are history-bank material -- keep rungs on the sites and artifacts.

topics.name: Hiroshima: the city that came back
topics.scope: The rebuilt city and the single ruin it chose to keep. T1: in the middle of Hiroshima stands a shattered, domed ruin left exactly as it was on 6 August 1945 -- the Atomic Bomb Dome, the only building near the blast's center that kept its shape (answer: the Genbaku / Atomic Bomb Dome). T2: the dome survived because the bomb detonated almost straight OVERHEAD -- about 600 m up and only ~150 m to the side -- so the downward force pressed on its walls from directly above and its steel-and-concrete skeleton stayed standing while everything around it was flattened (answer: the near-vertical overhead blast). Invert: 'why did just THIS building survive?' T3: the domed building was not a monument before the war -- it was a cheerful 1915 exhibition hall designed by a CZECH architect, Jan Letzel, which is why its European dome looked so unlike its neighbors (answer: a Czech-designed 1915 exhibition hall). T4: the ruin was nearly demolished, but Hiroshima chose to freeze it as a Peace Memorial; nearby, a monument buried under thousands of folded paper CRANES honors Sadako, a girl who folded them while dying of the bomb's radiation (answer: the Children's Peace Monument / the paper cranes). T5: trees within a kilometer of the blast -- ginkgos and a weeping willow -- put out fresh buds the very next spring and still grow today; these 'survivor trees' (hibaku jumoku) became living proof that the city, once thought barren for decades, would live (answer: the survivor trees / hibaku trees).
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshima_Peace_Memorial + Grokipedia (Hiroshima Peace Memorial, surfaced in search) -- 8:15 a.m. 6 Aug 1945; hypocenter ~150 m horizontal, ~600 m vertical; near-vertical blast preserved the shape; only structure standing near the hypocenter; built 1915, designed by Jan Letzel; preserved 1966, UNESCO 1996; standard sources on the Children's Peace Monument / Sadako and the hibaku survivor trees.
topics.framing_note: VISION: handle with gravity and plain fact -- a real catastrophe, no glib or breezy tone, and NO editorializing on the bombing decision itself (that is the history bank). Geography owns the DOME-as-structure (why it alone survived), the preserved and rebuilt city, and the survivor trees. Dinner-test payoffs = the paper cranes (T4) and the survivor trees (T5), both handled soberly; the T2 rung teaches the overhead-blast reason. Distractors = other preserved ruins / other rebuilt cities. Loading/framing tone throughout must stay respectful.
topics.history_overlap: The atomic bombing (the decision, the weapon, the war) is a history-bank episode; geography owns the dome-as-place, the rebuilt city, and the survivor trees -- keep every rung there and treat the topic soberly.

topics.name: Hong Kong: the vertical city
topics.scope: A city of towers on a drowned mountain coast. T1: Hong Kong has MORE skyscrapers than any city on Earth -- over 550 towers taller than 150 m -- crammed onto steep slopes because there is almost no flat land (answer: the most skyscrapers of any city). Invert: the 550+ count is the hook. T2: above them all rises Victoria Peak (552 m); the Peak Tram, one of the world's oldest funiculars (opened 1888), climbs a slope so steep the skyscrapers out the window appear to LEAN (answer: the Peak Tram up Victoria Peak). T3: each night the towers around Victoria Harbour fire synchronized colored lights and lasers -- the 'Symphony of Lights,' the largest permanent light-and-sound show in the world (answer: the Symphony of Lights). T4: with so many people on so little land, the demolished Kowloon Walled City once packed about 33,000 residents into a single block -- for a time the densest place humans have ever lived (answer: Kowloon Walled City, the densest place on Earth). T5: Victoria Harbour ('fragrant harbour') is a RIA -- a river valley drowned when the sea rose over a range of hills -- and its deep, sheltered water is exactly why Hong Kong became one of the world's great natural PORTS (answer: a drowned river valley / ria). Teach 'ria.' Extra rung: the Star Ferry crossing the harbour since 1888.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_with_the_most_skyscrapers + Guinness World Records (Hong Kong = most buildings 150 m+, 569 as of 2026); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Peak (552 m); standard sources on the Peak Tram (1888), the Symphony of Lights, Kowloon Walled City (~33,000 in one block), and Victoria Harbour as a ria.
topics.framing_note: Voice: scene-led (look up the leaning towers from the tram), never 'What is the densest city?'. Accuracy rail: TEACH 'ria' before the T5 answer tests it. Dinner-test payoffs = Kowloon Walled City (T4) and the ria-harbour earth-science reveal (T5). Distractors = other dense cities / natural harbours (Shanghai, Singapore, Manhattan, Sydney). Lane border: the 1997 handover and colonial history are history-bank material -- keep rungs on skyline, tram, harbour geology.

topics.name: Kyoto: the thousand-year capital of temples
topics.scope: Japan's old capital, a city of ~1,600 temples that WWII spared. T1: the Golden Pavilion (Kinkaku-ji) stands on a still pond wrapped in real GOLD LEAF, its upper floors gilded so brightly they mirror upside-down in the water (answer: Kinkaku-ji, the gold-leaf pavilion). T2: the Kinkaku-ji you see is a 1955 rebuild -- in 1950 a troubled young monk burned the original 1397 pavilion to the ground, a shock so deep the novelist Mishima wrote a famous book about it (answer: it was burned down by a monk in 1950). T3: at Fushimi Inari shrine, THOUSANDS of vermilion torii gates -- about 10,000 -- stand shoulder to shoulder up the mountainside, forming glowing orange tunnels; each was donated by a business praying for good fortune (answer: the tunnels of ~10,000 torii gates). T4: in Arashiyama a grove of giant timber BAMBOO towers overhead so densely that the creaking, hissing wind through the stalks is officially listed among Japan's '100 soundscapes to preserve' (answer: the Arashiyama bamboo grove and its protected sound). T5: Kyoto was Japan's capital for over 1,000 years (794-1868) and holds ~1,600 Buddhist temples and 400 Shinto shrines -- and it came through WWII nearly untouched because US Secretary of War Henry Stimson personally struck it from the atomic-bomb target list to spare its cultural treasures (answer: Kyoto was deliberately spared the bomb). Extra rungs: Kiyomizu-dera's nail-free wooden stage jutting over the hillside; the Gion geisha district; the Philosopher's Path; 17 UNESCO-listed sites.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinkaku-ji and /wiki/Kinkaku-ji_arson (burned 2 July 1950 by novice Hayashi Yoken, rebuilt 1955; Mishima's novel); standard sources on Fushimi Inari (~10,000 torii, Senbon Torii) and the Arashiyama bamboo soundscape; documented Stimson intervention removing Kyoto from the atomic target list.
topics.framing_note: Voice: scene-led / story-led. Dinner-test payoffs = the ~10,000-torii tunnels (T3) and the spared-the-bomb rung (T5). ACCURACY RAILS: label the torii count 'about 10,000' (a commonly cited figure); the Stimson sparing IS documented, but the popular 'he honeymooned in Kyoto' motive is DISPUTED -- frame the cultural-significance reason and flag the honeymoon story as legend. Distractors = other temple cities (Nara, Beijing) / other famous torii (Fushimi vs Itsukushima). Lane border: WWII targeting is history-bank; here it is a place-fact about why Kyoto survives intact.
topics.history_overlap: The atomic-bomb targeting decision belongs to the history bank; geography owns the place-fact that Kyoto survived intact -- keep the T5 rung on the city's preservation, not the war.

topics.name: Miyajima: the floating torii
topics.scope: Itsukushima Shrine on the sacred island in Hiroshima Bay. T1: off the shore of Miyajima island stands a giant vermilion TORII gate that at high tide appears to FLOAT on the sea, cut off from land (answer: the floating torii gate). T2: at low tide the water drains away and you can walk out across the flats to stand right beneath the ~16-m gate -- so the same gate is 'in the sea' and 'on dry land' twice a day with the TIDES (answer: the tide reveals it / it's reachable on foot at low tide). Invert with the tide. T3: the whole Itsukushima Shrine is built on stilts OVER the water because the island itself was held so SACRED that commoners were not allowed to set foot on its soil -- so the shrine floats to avoid defiling the holy ground (answer: the island is sacred, so the shrine is built over the water).
topics.source: Standard sources / UNESCO on Itsukushima Shrine, Miyajima (the ~16 m floating torii, tidal reveal, shrine built over water because the island is sacred; one of Japan's 'Three Views').
topics.framing_note: Voice: scene-led (the gate floating at high tide). RESPECT the sacred site on its own terms -- no smug secular dismissal, no advertising gloss. Dinner-test payoff = the sacred-island reason the shrine is built over water (T3). Accuracy rail: the 'floating' is a TIDAL ILLUSION -- say so plainly (T2 makes the tide the whole point). Teach 'torii.' It sits in Hiroshima Bay, adjacent to the Hiroshima ladder but a DISTINCT place -- keep them separate. Distractors = other famous torii / shrines (Fushimi Inari's gates, Ise).

topics.name: Nara: the first capital and its Great Buddha
topics.scope: Japan's first permanent capital, where sacred deer roam the streets. T1: in Nara about 1,200 wild sika DEER wander the streets and parks freely, and many have learned to BOW their heads to visitors begging for deer-crackers (answer: the bowing, free-roaming deer of Nara). T2: the deer roam untouched because for over 1,000 years they were revered as sacred MESSENGERS of the god of Kasuga Shrine, so harming one was long a serious crime (answer: they were protected as sacred messengers). T3: Nara's Todai-ji temple holds the Great Buddha (Daibutsu) -- a bronze figure about 15 m tall, cast from roughly 500 tonnes of bronze and dedicated in the year 752 (answer: the Great Buddha of Todai-ji). T4: the hall that shelters it, the Daibutsuden, was for centuries the largest WOODEN building on Earth -- and the version standing today is only two-thirds the width of the even larger original (answer: the world's largest wooden building). T5: Nara, as Heijo-kyo, was Japan's FIRST permanent capital, founded in 710 and laid out on a grid modeled on Chang'an in China -- before it, the capital moved each time an emperor died (answer: Japan's first permanent capital, modeled on Chang'an).
topics.source: Nippon.com 'Vairocana, the Great Buddha of Todaiji' and Todai-ji sources (Daibutsu ~15 m, ~500 t bronze, dedicated 752; Daibutsuden long the world's largest wooden building, now ~2/3 the original width); standard sources on Nara Park's ~1,200 sika deer, the Kasuga-messenger tradition, and Heijo-kyo (capital from 710, grid modeled on Chang'an).
topics.framing_note: Voice: scene-led (deer bowing in the temple courtyard). Dinner-test payoffs = the bowing deer (T1) and the largest-wooden-building (T4). LANE BORDER (important): the deer rungs stay on the PLACE (why the deer roam Nara + the sacred-messenger custom + the learned bow) -- never sika-deer anatomy or biology, which belong to the animal bank. Accuracy rail: the 'two-thirds of the original width' fact is real. Distractors = other Great Buddhas / early capitals (Kamakura's Daibutsu, Kyoto).

topics.name: Pingyao: the frozen Ming city
topics.scope: A complete walled Ming-Qing town in Shanxi. T1: while nearly every old Chinese city tore its walls down, Pingyao kept ITS entire Ming-dynasty wall -- a 6-km rectangle of rammed earth and brick, rebuilt in 1370, still ringing the whole town (answer: an intact Ming city wall). T2: seen from above the town is shaped like a TORTOISE -- two wells for eyes, six gates for the head, tail and four legs -- a lucky form meant to give the city the long life of the turtle (answer: the city is laid out as a tortoise). T3: inside the walls, a shop called Rishengchang opened in 1823 as China's FIRST bank -- a 'draft bank' (piaohao) that let a merchant deposit silver in one city and draw it out 1,000 km away with a paper note, instead of hauling coins past bandits (answer: Rishengchang, China's first bank). T4: because Pingyao's draft banks handled much of the Qing empire's money, this small town was once called the 'Wall Street of old China,' and its gray courtyard streets survive almost unchanged -- a whole walled Ming-Qing town, not a reconstruction (answer: the 'Wall Street of old China').
topics.source: ChinaDiscovery / ChinaGuide / Wikivoyage on Pingyao (wall ~6,163 m, rebuilt 1370 Ming, best-preserved in China; tortoise plan); standard sources on Rishengchang (est. 1823/1824 by Lei Lutai, China's first piaohao draft bank; 'Wall Street of old China').
topics.framing_note: Voice: scene-led (walk the unbroken wall, find the tortoise gates), never 'What was China's first bank?'. Dinner-test payoffs = the tortoise city-plan (T2) and the first-bank (T3). Lane border: the piaohao system is place-anchored here (the building where it began), not a general economics lecture. Distractors = other walled cities (Xi'an, Nanjing) and other 'first' claims. Accuracy rail: 'first modern-style draft bank in China,' not literally the first exchange of value.

topics.name: Seoul: palace city on the world's strangest border
topics.scope: A megacity of 10 million wedged between granite mountains and the planet's most fortified border. T1: at the city's center stands Gyeongbokgung, the 'Palace of Shining Happiness,' built in 1395; guards in bright robes still change at its gate beneath the painted eaves of the throne hall (answer: Gyeongbokgung / the Joseon royal palace). T2: behind the palace, Bukchon Hanok Village is a hillside of traditional tile-roofed HANOK houses -- curved roofs and warm ondol stone floors -- tucked between glass office towers (answer: the hanok houses / ondol-heated tiled homes). T3: only ~50 km north of this city runs the world's most heavily armed border, the Korean DMZ -- a 250-km-long, 4-km-wide strip of mines and fences that has sealed off North Korea since 1953 (answer: the DMZ / Demilitarized Zone). T4: because no one has farmed, built, or hunted inside the DMZ for 70 years, the deadliest border on Earth turned into an accidental WILDLIFE REFUGE, where endangered red-crowned cranes now winter in the no-man's-land between the armies (answer: an accidental wildlife refuge). Invert: the 'deadliest border' hook, the 'wildlife paradise' payoff. T5: Seoul sits in a bowl of granite peaks split by the Han River, and the sacred mountain Bukhansan rises right at the city edge -- making Seoul one of very few megacities with a real mountain-hiking national park inside its limits (answer: a national park mountain, Bukhansan, inside the city).
topics.source: Standard sources on Gyeongbokgung (founded 1395) and Bukchon hanok/ondol; Smithsonian Magazine and Audubon on the Korean DMZ (1953 armistice; ~250 km x 4 km; accidental wildlife refuge; 7 of 15 crane species incl. red-crowned & white-naped; ~6,168 recorded species); standard sources on Bukhansan National Park within Seoul.
topics.framing_note: Voice: scene-led. VISION: name the divided peninsula as a TIMELESS geographic fact (a fortified line across the narrow waist of the peninsula), NOT current-events commentary -- no editorializing on either government. Dinner-test payoff = the accidental-refuge rung (T4); keep ITS answer the PLACE-fact (why the abandoned strip became a refuge), never crane biology (that's the animal bank). Distractors = other palaces / other divided-place borders. Teach nothing false about the DMZ dimensions.
topics.history_overlap: The Korean War itself is a history-bank episode; geography owns the DMZ-as-place (the fortified strip and its accidental wildlife refuge), not the war's events or diplomacy.

topics.name: Shanghai: the Bund facing the future
topics.scope: Shanghai's Huangpu riverfront, past on one bank and future on the other. T1: along the west bank stands the BUND, a curving row of grand European-built stone banks and hotels from a century ago, so it looks like a slice of London dropped into China (answer: the Bund / the colonial waterfront). T2: directly across the river rises PUDONG -- farmland and warehouses as recently as 1990, now a wall of glass supertowers -- the two banks facing each other like past and future (answer: Pudong, farmland turned space-age skyline). Invert: the 'rice paddies 30 years ago' hook. T3: the tallest of those towers, the Shanghai Tower, TWISTS 120 degrees as it climbs 632 m -- China's tallest building -- its spiral skin shaped to loosen the wind's grip (answer: the Shanghai Tower, the twisting 632-m tower). T4: out to the airport runs the Shanghai MAGLEV, a train with no wheels that floats on magnets and reaches 431 km/h, long the fastest passenger train in regular service (answer: the maglev / magnetic-levitation train). T5: in the old town, the Ming-era Yu Garden folds ponds, rockeries and ZIGZAG bridges into a tiny space -- the bridges are built crooked because folklore held that evil spirits can only travel in straight lines (answer: Yu Garden's zigzag bridges). Extra rung: the Oriental Pearl Tower's stacked spheres.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Tower + Grokipedia (Shanghai Tower, surfaced in search) -- 632 m, 128 floors, tallest in China, twisting form; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_maglev_train (431 km/h, fastest in regular service 2004-2021); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bund (colonial-era banks facing Lujiazui/Pudong); standard sources on Yu Garden zigzag-bridge folklore.
topics.framing_note: Voice: scene-led (stand on the Bund looking across at Pudong at night), never 'What is China's tallest building?'. The past-vs-future contrast is the through-line. Dinner-test payoffs = the maglev (T4) and the twisting tower (T3); label the zigzag-bridge folklore AS folklore. Accuracy rail: say 'China's tallest' (Shanghai Tower is world's 2nd/3rd, not the tallest overall). Colonial-era Bund: state honestly who built it and why (treaty-port trade) without editorializing -- it's a place-fact, not a stance topic. Do NOT seed a food rung (xiaolongbao = cooking bank). Distractors = other skylines/rivers (Hong Kong, named Pudong towers).

topics.name: Tokyo: the endless city
topics.scope: The largest metropolis humans have ever built, on a three-plate collision zone. T1: at Shibuya Crossing the traffic halts on every side at once and up to 3,000 people surge across from all directions in a single light -- the busiest pedestrian crossing on Earth (answer: Shibuya Crossing / the scramble). T2: Greater Tokyo is the biggest city the world has ever built -- around 37 million people, more than the whole population of Canada, in one continuous metropolis (answer: the world's largest metro area). Invert: 'more people than all of Canada' hook. T3: right at the center, hidden behind a wide moat and stone ramparts, the Imperial Palace occupies the grounds of Edo Castle -- once the largest castle on Earth -- so a ring of forest and water fills the middle of the world's biggest city (answer: the Imperial Palace on Edo Castle's grounds). T4: Tokyo has been leveled and rebuilt twice in a century -- the 1923 Great Kanto earthquake and 1945 firebombing -- because it sits where THREE tectonic plates grind together, one of the most earthquake-prone spots on the planet (answer: a city rebuilt on a three-plate collision zone). Teach the plate-boundary reason. T5: the Tokyo Skytree rises 634 m, the tallest tower in the world, and its height was chosen as a PUN -- 6-3-4 reads 'mu-sa-shi,' the old name of the plain Tokyo stands on (answer: the Skytree, whose height spells 'Musashi'). Extra rungs: Shinjuku Station, the busiest on Earth (~3.34 million riders a day); the Yamanote loop line; Tokyo was called Edo until 1868; much of the bayfront is reclaimed landfill.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Tokyo_Area (~37 million, world's largest urban agglomeration) and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo; standard sources on Shibuya Crossing volumes, the Imperial Palace on the Edo Castle site, the Tokyo Skytree (634 m / 'Musashi' pun), and the Tokyo region's position at the junction of the Pacific, Philippine Sea and North American/Eurasian plates (1923 Great Kanto quake).
topics.framing_note: Voice: scene-led (stand in the crossing, look across the palace moat), never 'What is the largest city?'. Dinner-test payoffs = the Skytree pun (T5) and Shibuya (T1). Accuracy/lane rail: the T4 rung teaches the EARTH-SCIENCE reason Tokyo keeps rebuilding (the plate boundary) -- that's geography's lane; the 1945 firebombing itself is history-bank -- keep the answer the place/earth-process fact. Distractors = other megacities / supertall towers (Shanghai, Seoul, Skytree vs Skytree-rivals).

topics.name: Xi'an: the walled city at the end of the Silk Road
topics.scope: Xi'an, ancient Chang'an, wrapped in the most complete city wall in China. T1: Xi'an is ringed by a 14-km rectangle of wall so broad (12-15 m across the top) that people ride BICYCLES the full loop around the city on top of it (answer: you can cycle the complete circuit on the wall / the intact 14-km Ming wall, begun 1370). T2: under its old name Chang'an, Xi'an was the eastern STARTING point of the Silk Road -- the caravan route where camel trains set out across Central Asia toward Persia and Rome (answer: the Silk Road began here / eastern terminus). Invert: the 7,000-km route is the hook, 'this was its eastern end' the answer. T3: the Big Wild Goose Pagoda was built in 652 to house Buddhist scriptures the monk Xuanzang carried back on foot from INDIA (answer: it holds the sutras Xuanzang brought from India). T4: Xi'an's Great Mosque, founded by Silk Road traders, is built like a Chinese TEMPLE -- courtyards, tiled roofs, and a minaret shaped like a pagoda instead of a tower (answer: a mosque built in Chinese-temple style). T5: Xi'an served as capital for 13 dynasties over ~1,100 years (Zhou, Qin, Han, Sui, Tang); at its Tang peak Chang'an held about a MILLION people, the largest city on Earth at the time (answer: Tang Chang'an was the world's largest city). Extra rung: the Bell Tower and Drum Tower at the walled city's exact center.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortifications_of_Xi'an (14 km, begun 1370 on Tang imperial-city foundation, most complete wall in China); National Geographic 'China's other great wall'; TravelChinaGuide / ChinaHighlights on Big Wild Goose Pagoda (652, Xuanzang) and the Great Mosque; Britannica on Chang'an as Silk Road terminus and Tang-era population.
topics.framing_note: Voice: scene-led (ride the wall, watch camels leave the gate), never 'What is the capital of Shaanxi?'. Answers are place-facts or creations born there. Dinner-test payoff = the Chinese-temple-style mosque (T4). Lane border: the Silk Road as a TRADE system is history-flavored -- keep the answer the PLACE-fact (Chang'an as the eastern anchor, the wall, the pagoda), not trade economics or Tang court politics. Do NOT seed a food-origin rung (Xi'an biangbiang noodles / roujiamo belong to the cooking bank). Distractors = other walled Chinese capitals (Nanjing, Beijing, Pingyao).
topics.history_overlap: The Silk Road trade network may appear as a history-bank episode; keep rungs on Chang'an-as-place (the terminus, the wall, the pagoda, the mosque), not on the trade system's economics.

topics.name: Amsterdam — the city on piles below the sea
topics.scope: The Dutch capital, a Golden-Age trading city literally built on water and wood, much of it BELOW sea level. T1: Amsterdam is a city of CANALS — its 17th-century 'canal ring' (grachtengordel) is a set of concentric waterways dug in a half-moon around the old town (a UNESCO World Heritage site). T2: the ground is soft peat and clay, so nearly every old building stands on WOODEN PILES driven down to firm sand — the Royal Palace on Dam Square alone rests on 13,659 of them. T3: the very name says how it began — 'Amstel-dam', a DAM built across the little River Amstel around 1270 to hold back the tides. T4: the wider Netherlands lives behind DIKES and pumps land dry into POLDERS; large areas — and parts of Amsterdam — sit BELOW sea level, kept dry only by constant pumping (once by windmills). T5: because the wooden piles must stay underwater or they rot, dropping groundwater lets them decay — and centuries of soft ground leave Amsterdam's narrow gabled canal houses leaning and tilting at odd angles.
topics.source: Grokipedia (Amsterdam; Royal Palace of Amsterdam) checked first; corroborated: Wikipedia (Amsterdam; Canals of Amsterdam / grachtengordel UNESCO; Royal Palace of Amsterdam — 13,659 piles; polder; Dutch flood defences).
topics.framing_note: PLACE = Amsterdam; answers are concrete facts about the water-city (the canal ring, wooden piles, the Amstel dam, polders below sea level, the leaning houses). Invert the wonder: 'the Royal Palace stands on 13,659 of WHAT?' → wooden piles. Accuracy rail: it's the WOODEN PILES driven to firm sand that hold the city (not solid ground); 'below sea level' is true for parts of the city and much of the country, kept dry by pumping. Dinner-test payoff = a stone palace balanced on 13,659 tree-trunks sunk in the mud. Lane border: the PLACE and its land-reclamation engineering, not Dutch trade-empire history.

topics.name: Barcelona — Gaudí's growing basilica
topics.scope: The Catalan capital on the Mediterranean, shaped by one visionary architect and one radical city plan. T1: the SAGRADA FAMÍLIA is Antoni Gaudí's great basilica — begun in 1882 and, famously, a building site for over 140 years. T2: in 2026 its central TOWER OF JESUS CHRIST was topped out at 172.5 m, making the Sagrada Família the TALLEST CHURCH in the world (passing Germany's Ulm Minster). T3: Gaudí deliberately made that tower ONE METRE lower than Barcelona's Montjuïc hill — he believed his work should not rise above God's. T4: Gaudí designed with NATURE and physics — tree-like branching columns and 'catenary' arches shaped like a hanging chain flipped upside-down, so the stone stands in pure compression. T5: across the city his buildings (Casa Batlló, Casa Milà) ripple like bone and water, while the EIXAMPLE grid around them — Ildefons Cerdà's 1859 plan — gives every block CHAMFERED (cut-off) corners to open up light and sightlines. (Gaudí is buried in the Sagrada Família's crypt.)
topics.source: Grokipedia (Sagrada Família; Antoni Gaudí) checked first; corroborated: Wikipedia (Sagrada Família; Antoni Gaudí; Eixample / Cerdà Plan); 2026 completion coverage (CNN, Vatican News, designboom — Tower of Jesus Christ 172.5 m, world's tallest church; Ulm Minster 161.5 m surpassed Oct 2025).
topics.framing_note: PLACE = Barcelona; answers are concrete Gaudí/Barcelona facts (the still-growing basilica, the 172.5 m tower, the one-metre-below-Montjuïc rule, catenary/branching structure, the chamfered Eixample grid). Accuracy rail: as of 2026 the CENTRAL TOWER is complete and it IS now the world's tallest church — say the tower/height is finished while sculptural work on parts of the basilica continues (no longer flatly 'unfinished', but not fully 'finished' either). Dinner-test payoff = Gaudí capping his tower one metre BELOW the city's hill so man's work stays under God's. Settled wonder; respect for the religious intent is enough without a stance.

topics.name: Bruges — the port that froze in time
topics.scope: A medieval Flemish trading city in Belgium, laced with canals — 'the Venice of the North.' T2: its landmark is the BELFRY (Belfort), an 83 m brick tower whose top holds a CARILLON — 47 tuned bells (about 27 tonnes) played from a keyboard, ringing out over the market square. T3: Bruges was one of medieval Europe's richest ports until its lifeline, the ZWIN sea-channel, silted up in the 1400s — cutting the city off from the North Sea and shifting trade to Antwerp. T4: that collapse is exactly why Bruges is so beautiful today: too poor to rebuild, the city was 'frozen in time', preserving its medieval streets and stepped-gable houses almost whole.
topics.source: Grokipedia (Bruges; Belfry of Bruges) checked first; corroborated: Wikipedia (Belfry of Bruges — 47-bell carillon, 83 m; Bruges; the Zwin); Britannica (Brugge).
topics.framing_note: PLACE = Bruges; answers are concrete facts (the 47-bell carillon belfry, the silted Zwin, the accidental preservation). Accuracy rail: the carillon has 47 bells; the Zwin silted in the 15th century → decline → preservation (the cause-and-effect IS the wonder). Dinner-test payoff = the harbour channel silting shut, which impoverished Bruges and thereby SAVED its perfect medieval face. Lane border: keep to the PLACE, not Flemish cloth-trade economics as its own topic (history).

topics.name: Florence — Brunelleschi's impossible dome
topics.scope: The Tuscan city on the Arno where the Renaissance was born, crowned by an engineering miracle. T1: Florence's cathedral, Santa Maria del Fiore, is topped by BRUNELLESCHI'S DOME — the largest brick-and-masonry dome ever raised, finished in 1436. T2: the astonishing part is HOW it stands: it was built WITHOUT a wooden support frame ('centering') underneath — no forest could have propped a dome that wide — so it had to hold ITSELF up as it rose. T3: Brunelleschi laid the bricks in a HERRINGBONE (spina-pesce) pattern that locked each ring in place and passed the weight to the ribs, letting the masons build a self-supporting spiral. T4: it is actually a DOUBLE dome — an inner shell and an outer shell with a staircase climbing between them — which made it lighter and let visitors walk up inside the wall. T5: nobody fully knew Brunelleschi's method — he left almost no plans and reportedly won the commission by challenging rivals to stand an egg on end, then cracking its base flat. (Optional rung: the PONTE VECCHIO, the old shop-lined bridge, was the only Florence bridge the retreating Germans did NOT blow up in 1944.)
topics.source: Grokipedia (Florence Cathedral; Filippo Brunelleschi) checked first; corroborated: Wikipedia (Florence Cathedral; Ponte Vecchio); duomo.firenze.it (self-supporting dome, no centering, herringbone brick, double shell).
topics.framing_note: PLACE = Florence; answers are concrete facts about Brunelleschi's dome and the city (self-supporting, herringbone brick, double shell). Invert the wonder: 'the widest brick dome ever, and no wooden frame held it up while it was built' → it had to support itself as it rose. Accuracy rail: 'largest BRICK/masonry dome' (not largest dome of any kind — the Pantheon's is wider but concrete); the egg story is a REPORTED anecdote, flag it. Dinner-test payoff = a dome that held itself up with no scaffolding beneath it. Lane border: keep to architecture/place, not Medici politics (history) or Tuscan food (cooking).

topics.name: Granada — the Alhambra's water palace
topics.scope: On a ridge above Granada stands the ALHAMBRA, the palace-city of the Nasrid sultans — the last Muslim kingdom in Western Europe. T1: its name means 'the RED one' (al-Hamra) for the red clay walls that glow at sunset. T2: the Alhambra is a garden built around WATER — channels, pools and fountains everywhere — fed by the ACEQUIA REAL, a canal carrying SNOWMELT down from the Sierra Nevada mountains. T3: in the COURT OF THE LIONS, twelve marble lions ring a fountain and four rills run out toward the four points of the compass — an image of the four rivers of the Islamic paradise garden. T4: the ceilings drip with MUQARNAS — honeycombs of thousands of tiny plaster cells, like a stone stalactite cave, in the Hall of the Two Sisters. T5: the Alhambra was handed over in January 1492 when Granada, the last Muslim-ruled city in Iberia, fell to Ferdinand and Isabella — ending nearly 800 years of al-Andalus and, because the new rulers preserved it, leaving the palace almost intact. (The GENERALIFE summer gardens next door still run their old water staircases.)
topics.source: Grokipedia (Alhambra; Nasrid dynasty) checked first; corroborated: Wikipedia (Alhambra; Court of the Lions; Generalife; Acequia Real; Granada War / 1492); alhambradegranada.org (Court of the Lions, Nasrid palaces).
topics.framing_note: PLACE = the Alhambra/Granada; answers are concrete facts about the palace and its water (the red walls, the Sierra-Nevada snowmelt canal, the Court of the Lions, muqarnas, the 1492 handover). vision_mandated TRUE: celebrate al-Andalus / Nasrid hydraulic engineering as a FULL, sophisticated civilization (never 'exotic' or 'primitive'); respect the Islamic garden as sacred design on its own terms (no smug secular gloss); state the 1492 fall as timeless historical/geographic fact, honest and un-editorialized. Accuracy rail: the water is Sierra Nevada SNOWMELT via the Acequia Real; teach 'muqarnas' (the honeycomb vaulting) before testing it. Dinner-test payoff = a whole palace plumbed by mountain snowmelt, its lion fountain flowing to the four paradise rivers.
topics.history_overlap: The 1492 fall-of-Granada rung may overlap a history-bank Reconquista episode; keep the geography answer place-anchored (the Alhambra preserved intact), not the war narrative.

topics.name: Lisbon — the quake that shook the Enlightenment
topics.scope: Portugal's capital on the wide TAGUS estuary, a launch-point of the Age of Discovery — and site of a disaster that shook Europe's mind. T1: on All Saints' Day, 1 November 1755, a massive EARTHQUAKE struck while the churches were full; about 40 minutes later a TSUNAMI surged up the Tagus, and fires finished what the shaking and water began. T2: the quake (estimated around magnitude 8.5) killed tens of thousands and destroyed most of Lisbon in a single morning — one of Europe's deadliest natural disasters. T3: it 'shook the Enlightenment': that so many died AT CHURCH on a holy day forced thinkers like VOLTAIRE (who wove it into Candide) to argue over how a good God could allow it — a founding moment of the 'problem of evil' debate. T4: the king's minister, the MARQUIS OF POMBAL, ran perhaps the first scientific disaster survey — asking every parish how long the shaking lasted and which way it moved — an origin of modern SEISMOLOGY. T5: Pombal rebuilt downtown on a grid using the GAIOLA POMBALINA — a wooden cage hidden inside the masonry walls so a building could flex and survive the next quake — one of the world's first earthquake-resistant designs, reportedly tested by marching troops around mock-ups.
topics.source: Grokipedia (1755 Lisbon earthquake; Marquis of Pombal) checked first; corroborated: Wikipedia (1755 Lisbon earthquake; Gaiola (construction) / Pombaline architecture); Britannica (Lisbon earthquake of 1755); Hakai Magazine ('The Earthquake That Brought Enlightenment').
topics.framing_note: PLACE = Lisbon; answers are concrete facts of the 1755 event and its rebuild (the All-Saints quake+tsunami+fire, the Enlightenment reckoning, Pombal's survey, the gaiola cage). Accuracy rail: magnitude is ESTIMATED (~8.5; sources range 7.7–9) — do NOT pin an exact number as the answer; keep the answer the tsunami/fire/gaiola, not the magnitude figure. vision_mandated TRUE (lightly): handle the 'why did God allow it' shock with RESPECT (no smug secular dismissal of the faithful who died at Mass), and celebrate the Age-of-Discovery Tagus honestly. Dinner-test payoff = the hidden wooden 'cage' (gaiola) that lets Pombaline buildings flex through earthquakes.
topics.history_overlap: The Enlightenment / Voltaire response may overlap philosophy or history banks; keep the geography answer the earth-event and the rebuilt place, not the philosophy itself.

topics.name: London — the city on the tidal Thames
topics.scope: England's capital on the tidal River Thames, a city that keeps reinventing what lies under it.
