T1: at least six RAVENS are kept at the TOWER OF LONDON because legend says if the ravens ever leave, the Tower will crumble and the kingdom fall — so their wing feathers are trimmed. T2: the LONDON UNDERGROUND, opened in 1863 as the Metropolitan Railway, was the WORLD'S FIRST underground railway — steam trains running through gas-lit brick tunnels, ~38,000 riders on day one. T3: the GREAT FIRE OF 1666 began in a Pudding Lane bakery and burned for days, destroying about 13,000 houses and old St Paul's, yet the recorded death toll was tiny. T4: the fire let Christopher Wren rebuild ST PAUL'S CATHEDRAL with its great dome, whose 'Whispering Gallery' carries a whisper right around the dome's inner wall. T5: because London sits on a tidal river that funnels North Sea surges upstream, the THAMES BARRIER (built 1982) — steel gates that rotate up from the riverbed — is raised to hold back the sea. (Optional rung: the ROMAN wall of Londinium still shows in the City; London began as a Roman port around AD 47.)
topics.source: Grokipedia (Tower of London; London Underground; Great Fire of London; Thames Barrier) checked first; corroborated: Wikipedia (Tower of London ravens; History of the London Underground / Metropolitan Railway; Great Fire of London; St Paul's Cathedral; Thames Barrier); London Transport Museum ('World's first Underground').
topics.framing_note: PLACE = London; answers are concrete London wonders (the raven legend, the first Underground, the Great Fire, the whispering dome, the Thames Barrier). Invert the wonder — '38,000 rode it on day one' → the world's first subway; 'it burned 13,000 houses but killed almost no one' → the Great Fire of 1666. Accuracy rail: the raven legend is LEGEND (say so); the load-bearing fact is '1863 = world's first underground railway'. Dinner-test payoff = the six ravens whose departure supposedly topples the kingdom. Lane border: keep to the PLACE, not Stuart or Tudor politics (history bank).
topics.history_overlap: Great Fire of 1666 rung may touch a history-bank London episode; keep the geography answer the fire/place, not Restoration politics.

topics.name: Naples & the Bay of Fire
topics.scope: Naples sits on the Bay of Naples between TWO volcanoes — one famous, one far more dangerous. T1: to the east looms VESUVIUS, whose eruption in AD 79 buried the Roman towns of POMPEII and Herculaneum, freezing a whole city in ash. T2: Vesuvius is still active (it last erupted in 1944) and about 3 million people now live within reach of it — one of the most densely populated danger zones on Earth. T3: to the WEST lies the bigger threat: the CAMPI FLEGREI ('burning fields'), a SUPERVOLCANO — not a cone but a huge sunken CALDERA about 12–15 km wide, with a whole town (Pozzuoli) built inside it. T4: the ground there breathes — BRADYSEISM ('slow earthquake') lifts and drops the land by metres over years as pressure shifts below; the columns of Pozzuoli's Roman market carry sea-mollusc borings high up, proof the ground sank underwater and later rose again. T5: beneath the city runs NAPLES UNDERGROUND — tunnels the Greeks began quarrying ~2,500 years ago for tuff building stone, reused as Roman aqueducts and later as WWII air-raid shelters, all cut into the same soft volcanic rock the volcanoes laid down.
topics.source: Grokipedia (Mount Vesuvius; Campi Flegrei; Pompeii) checked first; corroborated: Wikipedia (Mount Vesuvius; Pompeii; Campi Flegrei; bradyseism; Naples underground geothermal zone); Napoli Sotterranea (Greek quarry tunnels / WWII shelters); Macellum of Pozzuoli (mollusc borings on columns).
topics.framing_note: PLACE = Naples and its bay; answers are concrete earth-science wonders of the place (Vesuvius / AD 79, the Campi Flegrei caldera, bradyseism, the tuff tunnels). Teach the terms (caldera, supervolcano, bradyseism) before testing them. Accuracy rail: the AD 79 and 1944 dates are firm; frame Campi Flegrei's danger as monitored scientific fact, not doom-mongering. Dinner-test payoff = the ground of Pozzuoli visibly rising and sinking (bradyseism), shown by sea-shell borings high on ancient columns. Lane border: the PLACE / earth-process, not Neapolitan pizza (cooking bank) — the pozzolana-ash link lives on the Rome-concrete ladder as a cross-reference.

topics.name: Paris — the city above and below
topics.scope: The French capital on the Seine, built in layers above and below ground. T1: beneath the streets lie the CATACOMBS — former limestone quarries where the neatly stacked bones of about SIX MILLION Parisians were moved in the 1780s when the old cemeteries overflowed. T2: the quarries came first — Paris was largely built from Lutetian limestone dug out from UNDER itself, leaving a honeycomb of tunnels that later swallowed the dead. T3: on the Île de la Cité, the SAINTE-CHAPELLE is a glass cage — 15 towering windows holding 1,113 scenes, built in the 1240s by King Louis IX to house the Crown of Thorns relic. T4: at street level, Hector Guimard's swirling green cast-iron MÉTRO entrances (c. 1900) are the icons of ART NOUVEAU, the 'new art' style, born in that moment. T5: the EIFFEL TOWER, 300 m of wrought iron built for the 1889 fair, is a living thermometer — iron expands in summer heat, so the tower grows about 15 cm taller and tilts slightly away from the sun. (Optional rung: PÈRE LACHAISE, opened 1804, the world's most-visited cemetery — Chopin, Wilde, Piaf, Morrison.)
topics.source: Grokipedia (Catacombs of Paris; Sainte-Chapelle; Eiffel Tower) checked first at build; corroborated: Wikipedia (Catacombs of Paris; Sainte-Chapelle; Paris Métro entrances / Hector Guimard; Eiffel Tower thermal expansion); sainte-chapelle.fr (15 windows / 1,113 scenes); history.com (Catacombs origins).
topics.framing_note: PLACE = Paris; every answer is a concrete Paris wonder (the Catacombs, the Sainte-Chapelle glass, the Métro's Art Nouveau railings, the growing iron tower). Scene-led — open on the six-million-bones tunnels or the 1,113 glowing panes, never 'What is the capital of France?'. Accuracy rail: the Catacombs hold remains MOVED from overflowing cemeteries (not people who died there), and '~6 million' is an estimate. Dinner-test payoff = the Eiffel Tower growing ~15 cm in summer heat (thermal expansion). Distractors stay live with other real Paris sites (Notre-Dame, the Louvre, the Panthéon). Lane border: keep answers to the PLACE, not French cuisine (cooking bank).

topics.name: Pisa — the tower that sank as it rose
topics.scope: In the Tuscan city of PISA, the cathedral's free-standing bell tower became the world's most famous mistake. T2: the LEANING TOWER began sinking almost as soon as building started in 1173 — because the soft ground on one side (clay, sand and shells) squashed down more than the other, tilting the whole tower. T3: builders pressed on for ~200 years, even curving the upper floors to try to correct the lean, which is why the tower is subtly BANANA-shaped. T4: by the 1990s it leaned a dangerous 5.5° and was edging toward collapse; engineers saved it by scooping soil out from under the HIGH side, easing it back to about 4° — stable, they say, for another 200 years.
topics.source: Grokipedia (Leaning Tower of Pisa) checked first; corroborated: Wikipedia (Leaning Tower of Pisa); Britannica (Leaning Tower of Pisa — construction 1173, soft subsoil, ~3.97° after stabilization); ICE (soil-extraction stabilisation).
topics.framing_note: PLACE = Pisa; answers are concrete facts about the tower's soft-soil tilt (the sinking foundation, the banana curve, the soil-extraction rescue). Invert the wonder: 'why did it start to lean before it was even finished?' → the soft clay/sand ground compressed unevenly. Accuracy rail: the lean is a FOUNDATION/soil problem (not a design choice); engineers removed soil from the HIGH side to reduce the tilt. Dinner-test payoff = fixing a leaning tower by digging dirt out from underneath the TALL side, not the low one. Lane border: keep to the PLACE and its geology, not Galileo's physics experiments (science bank — a one-line legend mention at most).

topics.name: Rome — the Eternal City's engineering
topics.scope: The Eternal City on the Tiber, built on seven hills and on 2,000-year-old engineering. T1: the PANTHEON's dome has a round hole — the OCULUS, about 9 m across — open to the sky at its top; rain falls straight through onto a slightly domed, drained floor. T2: that dome, 43.3 m across, is still the world's LARGEST UNREINFORCED CONCRETE DOME after ~1,900 years — the Romans lightened it upward, using heavy stone at the base and light pumice near the top. T3: Roman concrete outlasts modern concrete because it is SELF-HEALING — 'hot-mixed' lime leaves tiny lime clasts that dissolve and re-crystallize to fill cracks (confirmed by MIT in 2023); the key ingredient, pozzolana volcanic ash, came from Pozzuoli near Naples. T4: the APPIAN WAY (Via Appia), begun in 312 BC by Appius Claudius Caecus, was the 'queen of roads' — a stone-paved highway you can still walk today. T5: eleven AQUEDUCTS, starting with the Aqua Appia (312 BC), carried water into Rome by GRAVITY alone, dropping only a few centimetres per kilometre across miles of arches and tunnels. (Optional rungs: the COLOSSEUM's ~50,000 seats and its retractable awning; the CLOACA MAXIMA, one of the world's oldest sewers, still draining into the Tiber.)
topics.source: Grokipedia (Pantheon, Rome; Roman concrete; Appian Way; Roman aqueducts) checked first; corroborated: Wikipedia (Pantheon, Rome; Roman concrete; Appian Way; Roman aqueducts; Cloaca Maxima); MIT News 2023 (self-healing Roman concrete / lime clasts); ScienceAlert (pozzolana from Pozzuoli).
topics.framing_note: PLACE = Rome; answers are concrete Roman marvels (the open oculus, the unreinforced dome, self-healing concrete, the Appian Way, gravity aqueducts). Teach a term before testing it (oculus, aqueduct, unreinforced). Accuracy rail: the self-healing / lime-clast mechanism is the 2023 MIT finding — state it as the current best explanation, and note pozzolana ash came from near Naples (a deliberate cross-link to the Naples ladder). Dinner-test payoff = rain falling through the Pantheon's open oculus onto a drained floor. Distractors = other real Roman sites (Colosseum, Forum, Circus Maximus). Lane border: engineering/place, not emperors' biographies (history bank).

topics.name: Seville — the inland gate to the Americas
topics.scope: The Andalusian city on the GUADALQUIVIR, an inland river-port that became Spain's gateway to the New World. T2: its bell tower, the GIRALDA, began life as the MINARET of a great Almohad mosque (built 1184–1198); after the Christian conquest a Renaissance belfry was added on top, turning a minaret into a cathedral tower about 96 m tall. T3: beside it rises SEVILLE CATHEDRAL, the LARGEST GOTHIC church in the world, raised on the old mosque's footprint — its builders reportedly vowed to make one 'so beautiful that those who see it will think we were mad'. T4: inside, four crowned bearers hold the TOMB of CHRISTOPHER COLUMBUS aloft (DNA testing in 2024 confirmed his remains truly rest here). T5: for over two centuries Seville held Spain's MONOPOLY on trade with the New World — its CASA DE CONTRATACIÓN (House of Trade, from 1503) meant EVERY ship to and from the Americas had to dock in this river city 90 km from the open sea.
topics.source: Grokipedia (Casa de Contratación — seen directly in results) checked first; corroborated: Wikipedia (Giralda; Seville Cathedral; Tomb of Christopher Columbus; Casa de Contratación; History of Seville); archaeologymag.com / 2024 DNA confirmation of Columbus's Seville remains.
topics.framing_note: PLACE = Seville; answers are concrete facts (the minaret-turned-belltower Giralda, the largest Gothic cathedral, Columbus's tomb, the New-World trade monopoly on the Guadalquivir). vision_mandated TRUE: celebrate the Age of Discovery honestly AND handle the Giralda's Almohad origin with respect — a minaret RE-USED, not erased; name both civilizations plainly. Accuracy rail: the Giralda's lower shaft is the original 12th-c. Almohad minaret with a 16th-c. belfry added on top; 'largest GOTHIC church' (St Peter's is bigger but not Gothic). Dinner-test payoff = a river city 90 km inland that every treasure ship from the Americas HAD to sail to.
topics.history_overlap: The Columbus / New-World-trade-monopoly rung may overlap a history-bank Age-of-Discovery episode; keep the answer place-anchored (the inland river-port, the Giralda), not the voyages themselves.

topics.name: Venice — the city on a sunken forest
topics.scope: A city of 100+ islands built in a saltwater LAGOON, standing on a drowned forest. T1: Venice's stone palaces don't rest on rock — they stand on MILLIONS of wooden PILES driven down into the mud of the lagoon. T2: those submerged piles don't rot — starved of oxygen in the mud, the wood PETRIFIES, turning hard and stone-like over the centuries. T3: ACQUA ALTA ('high water') floods the city when high tides and south winds push the Adriatic into the lagoon; St Mark's Square, the lowest point, floods first — the great 1966 flood hit 194 cm. T4: to defend itself Venice built MOSE — 78 hollow steel gates lying flat on the seabed at the three lagoon inlets, that fill with air and swing up to seal out the sea (operational 2020). T5: on MURANO, a separate island, the Republic forced its glassmakers to move in 1291 — officially to keep their furnace fires from burning down wooden Venice, and to guard the secrets of Venetian glass. (Optional rung: Venice is slowly SINKING while the sea rises — the reason the barriers were built.)
topics.source: Grokipedia (Venice; MOSE; Murano) checked first; corroborated: Wikipedia (Venice; MOSE — 78 gates; Murano — 1291 glassmaker relocation; acqua alta records 1966=194 cm, 2019=187 cm).
topics.framing_note: PLACE = Venice; answers are concrete lagoon-city wonders (wood piles, petrified wood, acqua alta, MOSE gates, the Murano fire-move). Invert the wonder: 'stone palaces on a mudflat — what holds them up?' → millions of wooden piles. Accuracy rail: the piles PETRIFY/harden in oxygen-poor mud (mineralized, not literally turned to rock — say 'petrified'); the 1291 Murano move was partly a fire-safety measure. Dinner-test payoff = a marble city standing on a sunken forest of petrified wood. Lane border: the PLACE and its water-engineering, not Venetian trade-empire politics (history) or cuisine (cooking).

topics.name: Cartagena de Indias
topics.scope: The walled Spanish fortress-city on the Colombian Caribbean. T1: Cartagena is a walled city — about 11 km of massive stone ramparts, 'Las Murallas,' ring the old town, thick enough to walk and gather on. T2: above the city looms Castillo San Felipe de Barajas, the greatest fortress the Spanish ever built in the Americas — honeycombed with TUNNELS so defenders could move unseen and even hear attackers digging. T2: all that stone exists because Cartagena was Spain's treasure vault on the Caribbean — and pirates came for it; Francis Drake seized and ransomed the city in 1586. T3: in 1741 a British fleet of nearly 200 ships and some 25,000 men besieged Cartagena and was BEATEN by a garrison a tenth its size, led by Blas de Lezo, a commander already missing an eye, an arm, and a leg from earlier battles. T3: the Spanish blocked the main harbor mouth, Bocagrande, by sinking ships and building an underwater wall, funneling every attacker through the narrow Bocachica channel straight under the guns of the forts. T4: Cartagena was founded in 1533 and became one of the largest SLAVE markets in the Americas — enslaved Africans were bought and sold in its plazas, and the same walls that guarded silver guarded that trade.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Cartagena, Colombia (11 km walls built 1614-1796; Castillo San Felipe de Barajas 'one of the greatest fortresses built by the Spaniards,' tunnels/galleries; founded 1 June 1533 by Pedro de Heredia; Drake 1586 attack; 1741 siege, Blas de Lezo's ~2,800 defeating Vernon's ~23,600; UNESCO 1984; major slave market at Plaza de los Coches). Build stage: Grokipedia-first (blocked here); verify 'largest Spanish fort in the New World' phrasing, Blas de Lezo's specific wounds, and the Bocagrande/Bocachica harbor-blocking defense.
topics.framing_note: Stance: celebrate the Age-of-Discovery ENGINEERING (the fortress-city) honestly, and state plainly, without warping, that Cartagena was a major slave market — both are true and both belong. Every stem names Cartagena or a named fortification; every answer is a place-fact. Accuracy rail: call San Felipe 'the largest/greatest Spanish fort in the New World' (widely stated); Blas de Lezo really did repel Vernon's 1741 fleet while already missing an eye, arm, and leg. Dinner-test payoff: the half-a-man admiral who beat a fleet of 200 ships. Lane border: the sieges are battle-history (below) — keep every answer the PLACE (the walls, the fort's tunnels, the harbor defense), not a battle recap.
topics.history_overlap: Drake's 1586 raid and the 1741 siege are candidate history-bank episodes; anchor every answer to the fortifications and harbor (the place) rather than the battle narrative.

topics.name: Chicago
topics.scope: The flat city on Lake Michigan, birthplace of the skyscraper. T1: the Home Insurance Building (1885), by William Le Baron Jenney, is widely credited as the world's first SKYSCRAPER — the first tall building held up by an internal steel/iron skeleton instead of thick stone walls, so the outer walls could hang like curtains. T1: the whole downtown was physically JACKED UP out of the mud in the 1850s-60s on thousands of screw-jacks to fit sewers underneath — hotels were lifted while guests stayed inside; young George Pullman ran crews of 600 men turning 6,000 jackscrews. T2: engineers REVERSED the Chicago River in 1900 so the city's sewage would flow away from Lake Michigan (its drinking water) toward the Mississippi, by digging the Sanitary and Ship Canal. T2: the elevated railway that circles downtown, 'the L,' gives the business district its name — 'the Loop.' T3: the Great Chicago Fire of 1871 burned the wooden city, and the rebuild drew the architects who invented steel-frame design — the disaster is why the 'Chicago School' of architecture was born there. T3: the lakefront is kept 'forever open, clear and free' as public park, not private towers, thanks to Aaron Montgomery Ward's lawsuits and the 1909 Burnham Plan. T4: the Willis (Sears) Tower, 1973, at 1,451 ft was the world's tallest building for ~25 years, built as nine square 'bundled tubes' strapped together. T4: Chicago is famously FLAT because it sits on the bed of a vanished ice-age lake (glacial Lake Chicago) — the flatness is a fossil lakebed. T5: the low, swampy Chicago Portage — a natural divide where canoes crossed between the Great Lakes and Mississippi watersheds — runs right through the city and is the reason the city exists here. T5: to keep storm water out of the lake, Chicago dug the 'Deep Tunnel' (TARP) hundreds of feet down, one of the largest civil-engineering works in the world.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Home Insurance Building ('often cited as the world's first skyscraper,' Jenney, 1885, steel skeleton, 10->12 stories), Raising of Chicago (Chesbrough 1856 sewer plan, jackscrews, George Pullman, Tremont House lifted with guests inside) corroborated via Enjoy Illinois + Gizmodo, Chicago River (1900 reversal, Sanitary and Ship Canal). Build stage: Grokipedia-first (blocked here); verify Willis Tower height/bundled-tube + tallest-until-1998, glacial Lake Chicago flatness, Chicago Portage watershed divide, Burnham Plan / lakefront-public, Deep Tunnel/TARP scale.
topics.framing_note: Wonder voice: every stem names Chicago or a named Chicago place; every answer is a place/engineering fact (a named building, the reversed river, the raised streets), never a bare person or date. Invert the wonder — the hook is the impossible-sounding feat, the answer is the concrete thing. Accuracy rail: say the Home Insurance Building is 'widely credited' as the first skyscraper (the claim is genuinely debated); the reversal opened Jan 1900. Dinner-test payoff: raising the whole city on jackscrews, and reversing a river's flow. Lane border: deep-dish/Chicago hot dog = cooking bank (one-line mention only, never a food ladder).
topics.history_overlap: The Great Chicago Fire (1871) is a candidate history-bank episode; this ladder uses it only as setup and keeps the answer the architectural rebirth (a place-fact), so no full-episode duplication — flag if the history bank also ladders the fire itself.

topics.name: Havana
topics.scope: The Spanish colonial port on a narrow-necked Caribbean harbor. T1: Havana's Malecon is an 8 km sea-wall and promenade along the Atlantic; in winter cold fronts the waves explode clear over the wall and flood the road. T2: Old Havana (Habana Vieja) is the largest and best-preserved Spanish colonial old town in the Americas — a whole 16th-century city of plazas and stone, still lived in today. T2: the harbor mouth is a narrow bottleneck guarded by the great stone castle El Morro, and a heavy CHAIN was once stretched across the entrance each night to seal the port against pirates. T3: every night at nine o'clock a cannon is fired at the fortress (el canonazo de las nueve) — a 300-year-old ritual that once signaled the closing of the city gates and the raising of that harbor chain. T3: Havana was the assembly point for Spain's TREASURE FLEET — silver from across the Americas gathered in this one harbor before the guarded crossing to Europe, which is why it was fortified like a treasure chest. T4: the city owes everything to its shape — a narrow neck opening into a wide, sheltered pocket bay, the ideal natural harbor that made Havana the key to the Spanish New World.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Malecon, Havana (8 km, construction begun 1901, waves crash over during frentes frios, runs from Old Havana past Centro and Vedado to the Almendares). Build stage: Grokipedia-first (blocked here) then Wikipedia: Old Havana (UNESCO, largest colonial center), Morro Castle (Castillo de los Tres Reyes del Morro), the harbor chain/boom to La Punta, el canonazo de las nueve, Spanish treasure fleet (flota) rendezvous, Havana's pocket-bay harbor geography.
topics.framing_note: Wonder voice: every stem names Havana or a named place; every answer is a place-fact. Accuracy rail: Malecon ~8 km begun 1901; the nightly cannon and the harbor chain are documented traditions, so frame them as real customs, not folklore. Stance: treat Havana as the Age-of-Discovery hinge of the Spanish Caribbean honestly, celebrating the colonial city while keeping to place-facts. Dinner-test payoff: the chain stretched across the harbor each night and the cannon still fired at nine. Lane border: cigars/rum/classic-car culture = cooking/other banks — keep answers to the PLACE and its harbor.

topics.name: Mexico City (Tenochtitlan)
topics.scope: The vast capital in a mountain-ringed basin, built where the Aztec island-city stood. T1: Mexico City sits atop Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital founded in 1325 on an ISLAND in Lake Texcoco and reached by long causeways — an engineered water-city bigger than most European capitals of its day. T1: the Aztecs farmed on chinampas, 'floating gardens' built up from the lakebed; the canals of Xochimilco are the last living piece of that lake-city. T2: the Spanish drained the lake, and now the city is SINKING — parts drop nearly 50 cm a year as the old lakebed clay dries and compacts, up to 9 m of sinking in a century. T2: you can watch it sink — the Metropolitan Cathedral tilts on an uneven foundation and the Angel of Independence column had extra steps added at its base as the ground fell away. T3: in 1978 electric-company workers digging downtown struck a giant carved stone disk of the dismembered goddess Coyolxauhqui — they had found the Templo Mayor, the Aztec great temple, buried under the modern streets. T3: the Zocalo, one of the largest city squares on Earth, sits directly on that buried Aztec ceremonial center. T3: Chapultepec is a forested hill crowned by a castle, with a park bigger than New York's Central Park inside the city; the Nahuatl name means 'grasshopper hill.' T4: the city stands at 2,240 m (7,350 ft) in a bowl ringed by mountains — the Valley of Mexico is ENDORHEIC (no natural river out), which is why floods and drainage have plagued it for 500 years. T4: two snow-capped volcanoes, active Popocatepetl ('the smoking mountain') and Iztaccihuatl, loom over the valley. T5: the soft old lakebed clay traps and AMPLIFIES earthquake waves, so the 1985 and 2017 quakes centered far away still shook the city violently — the ground rings like jelly. T5: to drain the closed basin, engineers cut the Tajo de Nochistongo and later the giant Tunel Emisor tunnels through the mountains — a 400-year fight to move water out.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Mexico City (Tenochtitlan founded 1325 on Lake Texcoco island, altitude 2,240 m, subsidence ~50 cm/yr and up to 9 m, endorheic Valley of Mexico, 1985 quake, 17th-c drainage works), Templo Mayor (Feb 1978 CFE electrical workers, Coyolxauhqui monolith, Matos Moctezuma excavations). Build stage: Grokipedia-first (blocked here); verify Xochimilco chinampas as lake-city remnant, Metropolitan Cathedral tilt + Angel-of-Independence added steps, Zocalo size ranking, Chapultepec vs Central Park size + 'grasshopper hill,' Popocatepetl activity, lakebed seismic amplification in 1985/2017, Tunel Emisor drainage.
topics.framing_note: Stance: celebrate Tenochtitlan as a FULL engineered civilization (causeways, chinampas, aqueducts, a metropolis larger than most European capitals) — never 'primitive' or 'exotic.' Every stem names Mexico City / Tenochtitlan / a named site; every answer is a place-fact. Accuracy rail: 1325 founding, ~50 cm/yr subsidence, and the 1978 Templo Mayor discovery are documented; the Popocatepetl/Iztaccihuatl warrior-and-lover story is Aztec LEGEND — flag it as legend, and the answer is the volcanoes, not the tale. Dinner-test payoff: the sinking city, and the Aztec great temple unearthed by utility workers. Lane border: Xochimilco's axolotl biology = animal bank (keep the answer the canals/chinampas, the PLACE); Mexican cuisine = cooking bank.
topics.history_overlap: The 1521 Spanish conquest is a history-bank episode; this ladder deliberately avoids it, anchoring every answer to the place (the drained lake, the buried ruins, the sinking) — keep it that way.

topics.name: Montreal
topics.scope: The island city named for the green hill at its heart. T1: Montreal is named after Mount Royal (Mont Real), the forested hill rising out of the middle of the city — its park was designed by Frederick Law Olmsted, the same man who made Central Park. T2: Mount Royal LOOKS like an old volcano but isn't — it's the hard, eroded root of an ancient magma INTRUSION, one of the Monteregian Hills; the softer rock around it wore away and left the tough core standing. T2: the whole city sits on an ISLAND in the St. Lawrence River — the Island of Montreal. T3: because winters are brutal, Montreal built the 'Underground City' (RESO), over 30 km of climate-controlled tunnels linking malls, metro, and offices — one of the largest underground pedestrian networks in the world. T3: the city grew right at the Lachine RAPIDS — boats could not pass them, so everyone had to stop and portage here, which made Montreal the great hinge of the fur trade.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Mount Royal (eroded igneous intrusion / Monteregian Hills, NOT a volcano; Olmsted park inaugurated 1876; name from 'Mont Real'; Colline de la Croix 233 m). Build stage: Grokipedia-first (blocked here); verify Montreal on the Island of Montreal, the RESO / Underground City length, and the Lachine Rapids / head-of-navigation fur-trade role.
topics.framing_note: Wonder voice: every stem names Montreal / Mount Royal / a named place; every answer is a place-fact. Accuracy rail: correct the volcano MYTH plainly — Mount Royal is an eroded intrusion (a Monteregian Hill), not an old crater; teach the intrusion-vs-volcano distinction; Olmsted's park opened 1876. Dinner-test payoff: the 'volcano' that never erupted, and the vast underground winter city. Lane border: poutine/bagels = cooking bank — keep answers to the PLACE.

topics.name: New Orleans
topics.scope: The crescent city in the Mississippi delta, mostly below sea level. T1: most of New Orleans sits in a BOWL below sea level — the Mississippi on one side runs higher than the streets, held back by levees; without pumps the city would flood on a sunny day. T1: the oldest part, the French Quarter (Vieux Carre), was built on the natural river LEVEE — the highest ground — so it stayed mostly dry in Hurricane Katrina while newer, lower neighborhoods flooded. T2: New Orleans buries its dead ABOVE ground in stone tombs — whole 'Cities of the Dead' — the reason locals give is a water table so high that coffins once floated up out of the earth. T2: the city curves like a crescent because it hugs a great bend of the Mississippi — hence 'the Crescent City.' T3: JAZZ was born here, at Congo Square, where enslaved Africans were allowed to gather on Sundays to drum and dance, keeping African rhythms alive that later fused into a wholly new American music. T3: giant screw pumps designed by A. Baldwin Wood (1913) let the city pump itself dry and expand onto drained swamp — the pumps are why New Orleans could grow, and part of why it keeps sinking. T4: the Mississippi is trying to abandon New Orleans — it 'wants' to jump into the Atchafalaya for a shorter, steeper path to the sea, and only the Old River Control Structure upstream keeps it in its channel. T5: the delta is drowning — starved of sediment by upstream levees, coastal Louisiana loses land at a staggering rate, leaving the city ever more exposed.
topics.source: Wikipedia: New Orleans (~half the city at/below sea level, bowl topography, French Quarter on natural levee, Mississippi ~14 ft high-water above sea level, Crescent City bend). Build stage: Grokipedia-first (blocked here) then Wikipedia: St. Louis Cemetery / above-ground tombs, Congo Square + Origins of jazz (enslaved Africans, Sunday gatherings), Drainage in New Orleans / A. Baldwin Wood screw pump, Atchafalaya + Old River Control Structure, Louisiana coastal land loss.
topics.framing_note: Wonder voice: every stem names New Orleans or a named place; every answer is a place-fact. Accuracy rail: the below-sea-level bowl and the French-Quarter-on-the-natural-levee are real geography; the above-ground-tombs 'floating coffins' story is the TRADITIONAL/popular explanation (French-Spanish Catholic burial custom also plays a part) — frame it as 'the reason New Orleanians give,' with the tomb-cities themselves as the answer. Stance: celebrate Congo Square honestly — enslaved Africans' music surviving and becoming jazz, born in this PLACE. Dinner-test payoff: the above-ground tomb-cities, and the river straining to jump its course. Lane border: gumbo/beignets/Creole cooking = cooking bank (no food ladder); jazz stays as a place-born cultural creation, not a musician's biography.

topics.name: New York City
topics.scope: The world city on the island of Manhattan, at the mouth of the Hudson. T1: the Statue of Liberty is made of thin COPPER (about the thickness of two pennies) and started shiny brown — the famous green is a weathered copper patina, not paint. T1: Central Park is a rectangle of 843 acres dropped into mid-Manhattan and is entirely LANDSCAPED — the 'natural' park is the most man-made thing in the city (Olmsted & Vaux's 1858 Greensward Plan; millions of cubic feet of rock moved, topsoil trucked in). T2: the Brooklyn Bridge (opened 1883) was the world's LONGEST suspension bridge and among the first strung from steel wire; its towers were sunk on caissons where workers got 'the bends' — John Roebling died before it began, his son Washington was crippled by caisson disease, and Emily Roebling finished it. T2: Grand Central Terminal's turquoise ceiling shows the zodiac painted BACKWARDS (east where west should be), and a single dark patch was left uncleaned to show decades of tobacco grime. T3: Manhattan's numbered street GRID was drawn by the Commissioners' Plan of 1811 before the city reached there; the one great diagonal, Broadway, follows an old Native American trail and slices the grid into triangular 'squares' — Times, Herald, Madison. T3: Grand Central has 44 PLATFORMS and 67 tracks, more than any station on Earth. T4: the skyscrapers stand on hard bedrock called Manhattan SCHIST; the island's name comes from the Lenape 'Mannahatta,' island of many hills. T4: the Hudson beside Manhattan is really a tidal ESTUARY, an arm of the sea that reverses with the tides — the Lenape called it 'the river that flows both ways.' T5: the Empire State Building (1931) rose in about 410 days during the Depression, was the world's tallest for ~40 years, and its spire was designed as an airship mooring mast. T5: almost all the city's water arrives by GRAVITY alone through tunnels from Catskill reservoirs 100+ miles away, with no pumps.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Grand Central Terminal (44 platforms/67 tracks, opened 1913), Grand Central Terminal art + Untapped New York + Artnet (reversed zodiac, Cancer soot-patch left uncleaned), Central Park (843 acres, Greensward Plan, entirely landscaped, sunken transverse roads, most-visited US park), Brooklyn Bridge (1883, longest suspension span at opening, Roebling family, caisson disease). Build stage: corroborate on Grokipedia first (blocked to fetch tool here); verify Statue of Liberty copper patina, Manhattan schist, Hudson tidal-estuary Lenape name, Empire State 410-day build + mooring mast, Catskill gravity aqueduct.
topics.framing_note: Wonder voice: each rung's answer is the single most memorable specific fact, and every stem names NYC or a named NYC landmark; every answer is a place/structure fact (a named building, a landform, a design move), never a bare person or date. Invert the wonder — put the superlative in the stem ('the longest bridge in the world in 1883' -> the Brooklyn Bridge). Accuracy rail: the Statue of Liberty's green is copper patina (not bronze, not paint); the reversed ceiling is documented but the WHY (working from a flat sketch projected upward) is a leading explanation, so attribute it, don't assert it. Dinner-test payoff: the backwards zodiac ceiling and the Hudson that flows both ways. Lane border: Ellis Island immigration = history bank, Broadway shows/pizza = other banks — keep answers to the PLACE and its structures.

topics.name: Quebec City
topics.scope: The clifftop walled city on the St. Lawrence. T1: Quebec City is the ONLY city in North America north of Mexico that still has its old defensive walls all the way around — you can walk the ramparts of a genuine walled city (about 4.6 km of them). T2: it was founded in 1608 by Samuel de Champlain atop a high cliff, Cap Diamant, above the river — a natural fortress. T2: the name 'Quebec' comes from an Algonquin word meaning 'where the river NARROWS' — right here the wide St. Lawrence pinches tight, so whoever held the cliff controlled the gateway to the whole continent's interior. T3: the star-shaped Citadelle, a fortress still garrisoned today, crowns the cliff — its angled bastions were designed so no attacker could approach a wall without being caught in crossfire. T3: the Chateau Frontenac hotel towering over the old town is often called the most photographed hotel in the world — a fairy-tale castle built by a railway company.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Ramparts of Quebec City ('Old Quebec is the only intact example of a fortified walled colonial settlement in North America north of Mexico,' ramparts ~4.6 km, rebuilt 1745, saved by Lord Dufferin), Old Quebec (Champlain 1608, Cap Diamant, Chateau Frontenac, UNESCO 1985) + UNESCO WHC listing 300. Build stage: Grokipedia-first (blocked here); verify the 'Kebec = where the river narrows' etymology and the star-fort Citadelle crossfire design.
topics.framing_note: Wonder voice: every stem names Quebec City or a named place; every answer is a place-fact. Accuracy rail: 'the only walled city in North America north of Mexico with intact ramparts' is the standard sourced claim (Parks Canada / UNESCO); teach 'star fort / bastion' before leaning on it. Dinner-test payoff: the last intact walled city on the continent north of Mexico. Lane border: the 1759 battle is history (below), poutine = cooking bank — frame the cliff and the river-narrows as timeless geography.
topics.history_overlap: The 1759 Battle of the Plains of Abraham is a history-bank episode; frame the cliff and the river-narrows as timeless geography (why the site is a fortress), not the battle.

topics.name: San Francisco
topics.scope: The foggy peninsula city on hills above a great bay. T1: the Golden Gate Bridge is painted 'International Orange,' a warm red-orange chosen by architect Irving Morrow so it glows against fog and blue water — the Navy had wanted black-and-yellow stripes. T1: 'Golden Gate' is not the bridge but the narrow STRAIT it crosses, named by explorer John C. Fremont before any bridge existed. T2: San Francisco runs the last manually operated CABLE-CAR system on Earth — engineless cars that grip a moving underground cable to climb the hills (Andrew Hallidie, 1873). T2: for over 200 years Spanish ships sailed right past the Golden Gate without noticing the huge bay behind it — fog and the narrow gap hid it; it was finally found in 1769 by Portola's LAND expedition stumbling onto it from the hills. T3: the summer fog is 'advection fog' — warm inland air pulls in ocean air chilled by the cold California Current welling up offshore, and the fog pours through the Golden Gate like a river. T3: Alcatraz island sits in water so cold and currents so strong that its federal prison (1934-63) barely needed a sea wall — the bay itself was the cage. T4: the San Andreas Fault runs just offshore, and in 1906 its rupture plus three days of FIRE destroyed most of the city — the fire, not the shaking, did the worst. T4: in the 1989 Loma Prieta quake the Marina District shook hardest because it is built on landfill that turned to liquid ('LIQUEFACTION') while bedrock nearby held firm. T5: San Francisco Bay is the largest ESTUARY on the Pacific coast of the Americas — most of the Sierra Nevada's snowmelt drains to the sea through this one gap. T5: Lombard Street's eight switchback curves exist because the natural hill is too steep (27 degrees) for cars to climb straight — the crookedness is an engineering fix, not a gimmick.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Cable car (railway) ('the only known existing traditional cable car system is San Francisco... manually operated,' Hallidie 1873, Clay Street Hill Railroad). Build stage: Grokipedia-first (blocked here) then Wikipedia: Golden Gate Bridge (International Orange, Irving Morrow), Golden Gate (strait, Fremont naming), San Francisco Bay + Portola expedition (1769 land sighting, ships passing the fog-hidden strait), San Francisco fog (advection fog + California Current), Alcatraz, 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire + San Andreas Fault, 1989 Loma Prieta + Marina liquefaction, Lombard Street.
topics.framing_note: Wonder voice: every stem names San Francisco or a named SF place; every answer is a place-fact (a named landmark, a strait, an earth-process). Accuracy rail: teach 'advection fog' and 'liquefaction' before testing them; International Orange was Morrow's choice; the bay-hidden-for-200-years is documented (repeated Spanish voyages missed the fog-shrouded strait). Dinner-test payoff: the giant bay explorers missed for two centuries, and the only surviving cable-car system. Lane border: Pier 39 sea lions = animal bank; sourdough = cooking bank — keep answers to the PLACE.

topics.name: Washington, D.C.
topics.scope: The capital city designed whole on paper before it was built. T1: Washington DC was planned on purpose — Pierre L'Enfant (1791) laid grand diagonal AVENUES over a grid, with traffic circles and a long green Mall, one of the first cities in the world designed complete before construction. T2: the Washington Monument visibly CHANGES COLOR partway up — the marble is a different shade because building stopped for over 20 years (money ran out, then the Civil War) and the second batch of stone came from a different quarry. T2: that obelisk is the tallest stone structure in the world and the tallest true obelisk, 555 ft, and was the tallest building on Earth for five years until the Eiffel Tower passed it. T3: the National Mall is an AXIS — the Capitol, the Washington Monument, and the Lincoln Memorial line up in a deliberate sightline nearly 3 km long. T3: by law no ordinary building may rise far above the Capitol — the Height of Buildings Act keeps DC low and horizontal, which is why it has essentially no skyscrapers. T4: much of the monumental core — the western Mall, the Tidal Basin, the ground under the Lincoln Memorial — is RECLAIMED land, dredged and filled out of the Potomac's tidal flats and marsh.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Washington Monument (marble shade changes from 1854 funding halt + Civil War, resumed 1879 with different quarry; 555 ft; tallest structure 1884-1889 until Eiffel Tower; tallest obelisk of stacked stone; L'Enfant plan intended location moved for unstable ground). Build stage: Grokipedia-first (blocked here) then Wikipedia: L'Enfant Plan (1791 diagonal avenues over grid), National Mall axis, Height of Buildings Act of 1910, land reclamation of the tidal flats / Potomac Flats.
topics.framing_note: Wonder voice: every stem names Washington DC or a named landmark; every answer is a place/design fact, never a bare politician or date. Accuracy rail: the monument actually shows more than one break/shade — frame the answer as 'the color changes because construction stopped for decades,' which is the true and memorable core; L'Enfant designed the plan but was dismissed, so keep the answer the PLAN, not his biography. Dinner-test payoff: the monument's visible color line, a scar recording a 20-year pause. Lane border: the politics of founding the capital = history bank — stay on the designed city and its landmarks.
topics.history_overlap: The 1790 Residence Act compromise that placed the capital on the Potomac is a history-bank episode; keep answers on the designed city and its landmarks, not the political deal.

topics.name: Auckland
topics.scope: New Zealand's biggest city -- built on top of a field of VOLCANOES. T1: Auckland is dotted with about 50 small volcanoes -- roughly 53 cones, craters, and lava hills poking up among the suburbs -- the whole city sitting on a live VOLCANIC FIELD (invert: the green cones scattered across the city are -> volcanoes). T2: the biggest and YOUNGEST, Rangitoto, is a near-perfect cone that rose straight out of the SEA only about 600 years ago -- recent enough that the Maori living nearby SAW it erupt (a volcano younger than most cathedrals). T2b: because each eruption bursts up in a NEW spot (a 'monogenetic' field), geologists warn the next Auckland volcano won't reopen an old crater -- it will break out somewhere brand new (teach 'monogenetic volcanic field'). T3: Auckland is squeezed onto a narrow ISTHMUS between two harbors -- the Waitemata on the Pacific side and the Manukau on the Tasman side -- so narrow that Maori once dragged their canoes overland between the two seas. T4: with more boats per person than almost anywhere, Auckland is the 'City of Sails,' and its Sky Tower (328 m) is the tallest freestanding structure in the Southern Hemisphere. T5: the Maori name Tamaki Makaurau -- 'Tamaki desired by many' -- reflects how the fertile volcanic soil and twin harbors made it the most fought-over ground in the land.

topics.framing_note: Place-anchored: answers name the volcanic field, Rangitoto, the isthmus, the City of Sails; scene-led, never 'how many volcanoes...?'. Accuracy rail: ~53 volcanoes, Rangitoto ~600 years old and witnessed by Maori, a monogenetic field (each eruption a NEW vent). Dinner-test payoff: a whole city on a live volcanic field where the next eruption will pick a fresh spot, or Rangitoto rising from the sea within human memory. Lane border: none major.

topics.name: Brasilia
topics.scope: Brazil's capital -- a whole city conjured from empty savanna in the 1950s. T1: Brazil's capital had been Rio on the crowded coast; to pull the country inland the government built a brand-new capital, Brasília, on bare highland scrub -- and raised the entire city in just 41 MONTHS, inaugurating it in 1960 (invert: a national capital built from nothing in under four years). T2: seen from the air, the master plan -- the Plano Piloto by Lúcio Costa -- reads like a giant AIRPLANE or bird, its curved 'wings' lined with housing and its 'fuselage' holding the government (Costa himself called it a crossing of two axes). T2b: architect Oscar Niemeyer filled it with white curving concrete landmarks -- the crown-of-thorns glass Cathedral, the bowl-and-dome National Congress, the ministry towers -- making Brasília a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987 for its modernist design. T3: the city sits on the cerrado, Brazil's vast tropical SAVANNA, on a high plateau (~1,100 m) -- chosen as neutral central ground far from any existing coastal power. T4: to give the dry inland capital a shoreline, engineers dammed a river to create the artificial Lake Paranoá, wrapping the planned city in water (a made landscape).
topics.source: Grokipedia/Brasilia (attempted, HTTP 403); corroborated en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brasilia, whc.unesco.org/en/list/445 (inscribed 1987)
topics.framing_note: Place-anchored: answers name '41 months', the airplane-shaped plan, Niemeyer's cathedral, the cerrado plateau; never a bare 'capital of Brazil.' Accuracy rail: built in 41 months, inaugurated 1960; the 'airplane' is how the Plano Piloto reads from the air (Costa described it as two crossing axes). Dinner-test payoff: a national capital shaped like an airplane, built from scratch in under four years. Lane border: Kubitschek's politics belong to the history bank -- keep the anchor the CITY's plan and highland site.

topics.name: Buenos Aires
topics.scope: Argentina's riverside capital on the Río de la Plata, the 'Paris of South America.' T1: down in the old dockside barrio of La Boca, poor European immigrants and dockworkers in the late 1800s invented a smoldering partnered dance in the tenement courtyards and cantinas -- the TANGO, Buenos Aires's gift to the world (invert: a dance now performed in ballrooms worldwide was born in a rough immigrant port district -> tango, La Boca). T2: La Boca's Caminito lane is painted in wild patchwork colors because dockworkers finished their tin-shack homes with LEFTOVER PAINT scavenged from the ships. T2b: cutting through downtown is Avenida 9 de Julio -- about 110 m across with up to seven lanes each way, recorded as the WIDEST avenue in the world, the white Obelisco standing at its heart. T3: in the Recoleta district lies a CITY OF THE DEAD -- a walled cemetery of thousands of marble mausoleums laid out like streets and plazas, where Eva 'Evita' Perón rests among Argentina's elite (a necropolis you walk like a town). T4: 'Buenos Aires' means 'good airs / fair winds,' named by Spanish sailors for a patron of favorable winds; the city sits on the flat pampas beside a river so wide (~40+ km) it looks like a muddy brown sea with no far shore.

topics.framing_note: Place-anchored: answers name tango/La Boca, Caminito's ship-paint, the widest avenue, the Recoleta necropolis; never a bare 'capital of Argentina.' topics.name: Cusco
topics.scope: The Inca capital high in the Peruvian Andes (~3,400 m), whose Quechua name Qosqo means 'the navel.' T1: the Inca called their capital the NAVEL of the world -- the still point from which the empire's four quarters (Tawantinsuyu, 'the four parts together') radiated. T2: tradition holds the old core was laid out as an effigy of a sacred PUMA, with the great hilltop fortress SacsayhuamAn forming the puma's head (label as tradition/theory). T2b: SacsayhuamAn's zig-zag ramparts are built of limestone blocks, some over 100 tons, fitted so tightly without mortar that no blade slips between them. T3: the Twelve-Angled Stone on Hatun Rumiyoc street -- a single block cut with twelve corners that interlock with its neighbors -- is the emblem of Inca stonework. T3b: Inca walls survive earthquakes that topple colonial buildings on top of them, because the trapezoidal, slightly inward-leaning, mortarless blocks flex and resettle (the 1950 quake laid bare Coricancha's Inca masonry). T4: Coricancha, the Temple of the Sun, once had walls sheathed in sheets of GOLD and a garden of gold-and-silver plants. T4b: Cusco was the hub of the Qhapaq Nan, the Inca royal-road network -- roughly 40,000 km of paved highways and woven-rope suspension bridges (like Q'eswachaka) crossing the Andes, run without the wheel by relay-running chasquis. T5: the empire kept its accounts not in writing but on the QUIPU -- knotted colored cords -- administered from Cusco. Extra rung: the Inti Raymi sun festival, a June solstice celebration reborn at SacsayhuamAn.

topics.framing_note: Place-anchored: every answer names a concrete Cusco feature (the navel, the puma layout, the twelve-angled stone, the gold-walled Coricancha, the 40,000-km road hub). Scene-led, never 'what was the Inca capital?'. Accuracy rail: the PUMA-shaped layout is a scholarly TRADITION/theory -- say so, don't state it as fact; the gold is gone because the Spanish stripped it. Dinner-test payoff: the earthquake-proof mortarless walls, or Coricancha's gold. Lane border: the Inca CONQUEST and Atahualpa's ransom belong to the history bank -- reference only as why the gold is gone; keep every rung anchored to the PLACE (stones, layout, roads, altitude).
topics.history_overlap: The Inca rise/fall and Pizarro's conquest (1532-33) plus Atahualpa's gold ransom likely map to the history bank's Inca episode; keep these rungs anchored to the city fabric (masonry, layout, roads, altitude) and touch the conquest only as the reason Coricancha's gold vanished.

topics.name: La Paz & El Alto
topics.scope: Bolivia's seat of government, spilling down a canyon of the high Andes at ~3,600 m -- the highest de-facto capital city in the world (Sucre is the constitutional capital). T1: to beat the traffic of a city built on canyon walls, La Paz put its commuter transit in the SKY -- Mi Teleférico, the world's longest and highest urban CABLE-CAR network, ~33 km of gondolas on ten color-coded lines gliding over the rooftops (invert: the world's longest cable-car system isn't at a ski resort -> it's the city's bus network). T2: in most cities the wealthy live high for the view; in La Paz it is FLIPPED -- the higher and colder you climb the poorer it gets, and the rich live LOWER in the warmer, more oxygen-rich Zona Sur (an altitude inversion of the usual class map). T2b: on the canyon rim sits El Alto at ~4,000-4,150 m, one of the highest big cities on Earth, with the world's highest major international airport. T3: the glacier-capped giant looming over the skyline is Illimani, ~6,438 m, the emblem of the city. T3b: just outside town, wind and rain have carved the Valle de la Luna ('Moon Valley'), a maze of clay-and-sandstone spires -- an erosion badlands (teach 'badlands'). T4: at this altitude the air holds barely two-thirds of sea-level oxygen, so newcomers get soroche (altitude sickness) -- the thin air is the single fact that shapes everything about the city.

Accuracy rail: say 'highest DE-FACTO / administrative capital' precisely (Sucre is the constitutional capital); Mi Teleférico holds the Guinness record for largest public-transit cable-car network. Dinner-test payoff: a whole city commuting by cable car above the rooftops, or the rich-live-low inversion. topics.name: Lima
topics.scope: Peru's capital on the Pacific desert coast, founded by Pizarro in 1535 as the 'City of Kings' (Ciudad de los Reyes). T1: Lima almost never rains, sitting in one of Earth's driest coastal deserts -- yet for half the year it is wrapped in a damp gray sea-fog called the garUa, which earns it the name 'the gray city' (invert: a desert city cloaked in fog that still gets almost no rain -> the garUa). T2: rising among the apartment towers of Miraflores stands Huaca Pucllana -- a great stepped PYRAMID of millions of hand-made adobe (mud) bricks raised by the pre-Inca Lima culture around 500 AD, a thousand years before the Inca. T2b: those bricks are stood on end like books on a shelf with air-gaps between them, a flexible 'bookshelf' design that has let the pyramid ride out coastal earthquakes for ~1,500 years (teach the technique). T3: the cold Humboldt Current runs right up this coast -- it chills the air, kills the rain, and feeds one of the richest fisheries on Earth just offshore (the ocean-process that makes the desert-city what it is). T4: beneath Lima's colonial cathedral and the San Francisco monastery lie CATACOMBS packed with thousands of the colonial dead.

Scene-led, never 'what is the capital of Peru?'. Accuracy rail: the huacas are adobe pyramids of the PRE-INCA Lima culture (~200-700 AD), NOT Inca -- teach that. Dinner-test payoff: a 1,500-year-old mud pyramid standing among modern apartment blocks, or a coastal city that almost never sees rain. Lane border: Peruvian food (ceviche) is the cooking bank's; the offshore fishery is an OCEAN-process fact here, not the anchovy's biology (animal bank).

topics.name: Manaus
topics.scope: A city of nearly two million in the middle of the Amazon rainforest, reachable mostly by boat or plane. T1: just below the city two great rivers meet but REFUSE TO MIX -- the coffee-black Río Negro and the sandy-tan Río Solimões run side by side in two unblended stripes for about 6 km before finally merging into the Amazon (the 'Meeting of the Waters'). T2: the reason they don't mix: the black Negro is warm (~28 C) and slow, the pale Solimões is cold (~22 C), fast, and heavy with Andean silt -- differences of temperature, speed, and sediment keep the two waters apart (the earth-science answer). T3: in the 1890s rubber made Manaus so rich its barons built a gilded European OPERA HOUSE deep in the jungle -- the Teatro Amazonas (opened 1896) -- with roof tiles from France, marble from Italy, and a dome of 36,000 tiles in Brazil's colors. T4: Manaus exists because it stands where the rainforest's rivers converge -- before roads, the Amazon and its tributaries WERE the highways, and the city was the inland port of the rubber trade. T5: the Río Negro runs black because it drains sandy lowland forest and carries dissolved plant tannins (like strong tea) with almost no sediment -- a 'blackwater' river (teach 'blackwater vs whitewater').
topics.source: Grokipedia/Meeting_of_the_Waters (attempted, HTTP 403); corroborated en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meeting_of_Waters, /wiki/Amazon_Theatre, /wiki/Rio_Negro_(Amazon)
topics.framing_note: Place-anchored: answers name the Meeting of the Waters, the jungle opera house, the blackwater Negro; never a bare 'city in Brazil.' Accuracy rail: ~6 km side-by-side, with the temperature/speed/sediment reason stated correctly; Teatro Amazonas opened 1896. Dinner-test payoff: a gilded European opera house in the middle of the jungle, or the two-color river that will not mix. Lane border: the rubber-boom economics is history's -- keep the anchor the PLACE (the building, the rivers); Amazon WILDLIFE (pink dolphins) is the animal bank's, so keep the water/landscape the fact.

topics.name: Melbourne
topics.scope: Australia's second city, famous for hiding its best life down narrow LANEWAYS. T1: between Melbourne's grand streets runs a hidden web of skinny LANEWAYS -- once service alleys, now packed with cafes, tiny bars, and wall-to-roof STREET ART (Hosier Lane's ever-changing murals) -- the city's living rooms (invert: the city's coolest streets are its old back-alleys -> the laneways). T2: Melbourne rattles along on the LARGEST urban TRAM network in the world -- about 250 km of track, 24 routes, 500+ trams -- kept running when almost every other city tore its tramlines out. T2b: to avoid blocking those trams, drivers make a bizarre 'HOOK TURN' -- turning RIGHT from the far LEFT lane (a place-specific quirk written into the streets). T3: Melbourne was built rich and fast on the GOLD RUSH of the 1850s, when strikes at nearby Ballarat and Bendigo made Victoria one of the world's great goldfields and paid for 'Marvellous Melbourne's' grand boulevards and gardens. T4: the city sits on flat volcanic basalt plains at the head of Port Phillip Bay and is famous for 'four seasons in one day' -- cold fronts off the Southern Ocean can swing the weather wildly within hours (a place's climate quirk).

Accuracy rail: it is the LARGEST urban tram network in the world (~250 km) -- state it as such; gold rush of the 1850s. Dinner-test payoff: the hidden street-art laneways, or the world's biggest tram network. topics.history_overlap: The Victorian gold rush may be a history/economics episode; keep the rung anchored to how the gold BUILT the city (its boulevards and wealth), not the rush narrative.

topics.name: Potosi
topics.scope: A Bolivian city at ~4,000 m huddled beneath one cone-shaped mountain, Cerro Rico ('Rich Hill'). T1: in the 1600s tiny, freezing Potosí was one of the LARGEST and richest cities on Earth -- rivaling London or Paris -- because the mountain above it was riddled with SILVER (invert: a city colder and higher than almost any other was once the size of London -> the silver mountain). T2: so much silver poured out that coins minted here circulated worldwide, and the Spanish phrase 'vale un Potosí' -- 'worth a Potosí' -- came to mean 'worth a fortune.' T3: the silver was hauled out by forced laborers under the mita system, and the toll was so vast that Cerro Rico became known as 'the mountain that eats men' (death-toll estimates run into the millions but were never recorded -- label as disputed). T4: five centuries of tunneling have honeycombed Cerro Rico so completely that its summit is now SINKING and cracking -- it has lost height, a sinkhole opened near the top, and UNESCO placed the site on its 'World Heritage in Danger' list in 2014. T5: the mountain rises from the Altiplano and its silver formed in ore veins from ancient volcanic/hydrothermal fluids -- the earth-process that packed the hill (teach 'ore vein / hydrothermal').

topics.framing_note: Place-anchored: every answer is a fact about the mountain and city (the silver, 'vale un Potosí', 'eats men', the sinking summit), never a bare date. Accuracy rail: the death toll is an unrecorded ESTIMATE -- say 'estimated/disputed', never state a number as fact. Dinner-test payoff: 'the mountain that eats men,' now caving into its own tunnels. Lane border: the silver-bankrolls-an-empire ECONOMIC/colonial story brushes the history/economics banks -- keep the anchor the MOUNTAIN and its landscape; be honest both ways about the colonial human cost.
topics.history_overlap: Potosí silver funding the Spanish Empire and reshaping global bullion flows may belong to a history/economics episode; keep these rungs anchored to the mountain and city (silver, 'eats men', the sinking summit), not the imperial-finance narrative.

topics.name: Rio de Janeiro
topics.scope: Brazil's harbor city cradled between forested granite peaks and the Atlantic. T1: the name means 'River of JANUARY' -- yet there is no river; Portuguese sailors reached the great bay on 1 January 1502 and, by the traditional account, mistook its narrow mouth for a river's (label as the traditional story). T2: arms outstretched 28 m wide atop the 700 m peak of Corcovado stands Christ the Redeemer, a 30 m Art-Deco statue of soapstone completed in 1931 and later voted one of the 'New Seven Wonders of the World' (2007). T2b: the bare granite dome rising straight from the water is Sugarloaf (Pão de Açúcar), 396 m, climbed since 1912 by one of the world's first cable cars. T3: those steep bald domes are a landform -- a 'sugarloaf' or bornhardt -- ancient granite laid bare and rounded as softer rock eroded away (teach 'bornhardt/inselberg'). T3b: the deep inlet the city wraps around, Guanabara Bay, is a drowned river valley -- flooded as seas rose after the last Ice Age (a ria). T4: the green mountains INSIDE the city are the Tijuca Forest -- a hand-REPLANTED tropical rainforest; after coffee farms stripped the slopes and threatened Rio's water, workers replanted it by hand from 1861, creating one of the world's largest urban forests. T4b: samba -- the music-and-dance born in Rio's hillside neighborhoods in the early 1900s -- parades each February through a purpose-built Sambadrome at the world's biggest Carnival (a cultural creation born here). T5: the hillside favelas cling to slopes too steep to build safely, and torrential summer rain on bare granite triggers deadly landslides -- the same steep rock that makes Rio beautiful makes it dangerous.

Lane border: Brazilian food (feijoada) is the cooking bank's; samba is a cultural creation BORN here (allowed).

topics.name: Rotorua
topics.scope: A Maori town in the middle of New Zealand's geothermal heartland, where the GROUND itself steams. T1: the whole town smells of rotten eggs -- because the earth beneath Rotorua leaks SULFUR gas (hydrogen sulphide) from the hot rock below, earning it the nickname 'Sulphur City' (invert: the rotten-egg smell -> geothermal sulfur gas). T2: in the Whakarewarewa valley, Pohutu Geyser -- the LARGEST active geyser in the Southern Hemisphere -- blasts boiling water up to 30 m into the air, around twenty times a day (a named wonder). T2b: nearby, scalding pools and plopping MUD POOLS simmer, and the Champagne Pool (Wai-O-Tapu) fizzes inside a bright orange rim of arsenic and antimony minerals (a colored hot spring; earth-chemistry). T3: at the Whakarewarewa 'living village' the local Te Arawa Maori have used the geothermal ground for centuries -- bathing in the hot pools and COOKING in the natural steam and boiling springs (a place-culture that harnesses the heat). T4: all this heat exists because Rotorua sits inside the Taupo Volcanic Zone -- a stretch of the North Island being slowly pulled apart, where magma lies close beneath a thin crust and boils the groundwater (the earth-engine; teach 'geothermal / volcanic rift').

topics.framing_note: Place-anchored: answers name the sulfur smell, Pohutu Geyser, the mud/Champagne pools, the living Maori village, the Taupo Volcanic Zone; scene-led. Accuracy rail: Pohutu is the largest geyser in the SOUTHERN HEMISPHERE (not the world), ~30 m; the smell is hydrogen sulphide. Dinner-test payoff: a living village that bathes and cooks in the natural steam, or the biggest geyser south of the equator. Lane border: steam-cooking (hangi) is a place-culture MENTION of the village harnessing the ground's heat -- keep the answer the geothermal PLACE-fact, not a recipe or ingredient (cooking bank); respect the living Maori village on its own terms.

topics.name: Sydney
topics.scope: Australia's harbor city on one of the world's great natural harbors, Port Jackson. T1: Sydney's most famous building looks like a cluster of white SAILS or shells rising from the water -- the Sydney Opera House, opened in 1973 (invert: 'the sails by the water' -> the Opera House). T2: for years no one could figure out how to build those swooping shells -- until architect Jørn Utzon realized every shell could be cut from the surface of ONE imaginary SPHERE, so they'd all share the same curve and could be mass-cast from common moulds (the geometry breakthrough of 1961). T2b: the shells are clad in over a MILLION tiles (about 1,056,000) made in Sweden, in two finishes -- glossy white and matte cream -- so the roof shimmers in a subtle chevron pattern and never looks flat. T3: arching over the harbor is the steel Sydney Harbour Bridge, opened in 1932 and nicknamed 'the Coathanger' -- one of the world's widest long-span steel-ARCH bridges, which daring visitors now climb to the summit of. T3b: Sydney Harbour itself is a ria -- a river valley DROWNED by rising seas after the last Ice Age -- which is why its shoreline is so long, branching, and deep enough for great ships (teach 'ria / drowned valley'). T4: the city is built on honey-colored 'Sydney sandstone' (Hawkesbury sandstone), laid down by ancient rivers ~230 million years ago, and cut into its cliffs, harborside 'Heads', and old buildings.
topics.source: Grokipedia/Sydney_Opera_House (attempted, HTTP 403); corroborated en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Opera_House (Utzon, 1973, ~1,056,006 Hoganas tiles, sphere geometry), /wiki/Sydney_Harbour_Bridge, /wiki/Port_Jackson, /wiki/Hawkesbury_Sandstone
topics.framing_note: Place-anchored: answers name the Opera House, the one-sphere geometry, the million tiles, the Coathanger, the drowned-valley harbor; scene-led, never 'what is Sydney's famous building?'. Accuracy rail: Opera House opened 1973 and every shell is a section of ONE sphere; Harbour Bridge opened 1932. Dinner-test payoff: every sail cut from a single sphere, or the harbor as a drowned river valley. Lane border: none major.

topics.name: Ushuaia
topics.scope: The 'End of the World' city on Tierra del Fuego, facing the Beagle Channel. T1: Ushuaia is billed as the world's SOUTHERNMOST city -- the last true city before Antarctica and the main jumping-off port for Antarctic expedition ships (a smaller Chilean town, Puerto Williams, actually lies a little further south -- state the caveat). T2: the island's name Tierra del Fuego means 'Land of FIRE' because Magellan's expedition in 1520 saw the campfires and smoke of the native Yamana people burning along the shore (label as the traditional naming-story). T3: the channel in front of the city, the Beagle Channel, is named for HMS Beagle -- the survey ship that carried Charles Darwin through these waters in 1833 (the PLACE is named for the ship, not the dog).
topics.source: Grokipedia/Ushuaia (attempted, HTTP 403); corroborated en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ushuaia, /wiki/Tierra_del_Fuego, /wiki/Beagle_Channel
topics.framing_note: Place-anchored: answers name 'southernmost city / Antarctic gateway', 'Land of Fire', 'the Beagle Channel'; scene-led. Accuracy rail: state the Puerto Williams caveat honestly (Ushuaia is the southernmost CITY; a smaller Chilean town lies further south), and the Magellan-fires naming as the traditional account. Dinner-test payoff: 'Land of Fire,' named for the natives' shore-fires. Lane border: the Beagle Channel is named for the SHIP -- Darwin's voyage is a history/science episode; keep the anchor the PLACE, never the beagle-the-animal or Darwin's biology.
topics.history_overlap: Darwin's Beagle voyage is a history/history-of-science episode; here the channel is only a named PLACE anchored to the ship's passage.

topics.name: Valparaiso
topics.scope: A Chilean port tumbling down some 40 steep hills (cerros) to the Pacific. T1: because the city climbs cliffs too steep for ordinary streets, since 1883 residents have ridden little wooden ELEVATOR-CARS -- the ascensores (funiculars) -- hauled up the hillsides on cables; at their peak around 30 ran, and ~16 survive as national monuments (invert: a public 'elevator' that runs outdoors up a hillside -> Valparaíso's ascensores). T2: the hills are a maze of houses painted every color and clad in corrugated metal salvaged from ships -- an accidental rainbow that made the 'Historic Quarter of the Seaport City of Valparaíso' a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003. T3: Valparaíso was once THE great Pacific stop for sailing ships rounding Cape Horn -- until the Panama Canal opened in 1914, ships stopped taking the long way, and the boomtown fell quiet (a place undone by a distant canal). T4: the poet Pablo Neruda built one of his hillside houses here, La Sebastiana, for its sweeping view over the harbor (a cultural anchor to the place).
topics.source: Grokipedia/Valparaiso (attempted, HTTP 403); corroborated en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funiculars_of_Valparaiso, /wiki/Valparaiso, whc.unesco.org/en/list/959 (Historic Quarter, 2003)
topics.framing_note: Place-anchored: answers name the ascensores, the painted UNESCO hills, the Cape-Horn-to-Panama-Canal turn; never a bare 'port in Chile.' Accuracy rail: first ascensor 1883, ~16 of ~30 survive; UNESCO 2003. Dinner-test payoff: the outdoor hillside 'elevators' (ascensores) that are really funiculars. Lane border: none major.

topics.name: Wellington
topics.scope: New Zealand's capital, wedged between steep green hills and a harbor at the bottom of the North Island. T1: Wellington is reckoned the WINDIEST city in the world -- gales gust over 60 km/h on roughly 170+ days a year -- because the full force of the 'Roaring Forties' is funneled through the narrow Cook Strait straight onto the city (invert: 'Windy Welly' -> the Cook Strait wind funnel). T2: the city straddles a plate boundary: the active Wellington FAULT runs right through downtown, where the Australian and Pacific plates grind past each other. T2b: much of central Wellington stands on land the sea once covered -- the great 1855 Wairarapa earthquake LIFTED the harbor floor and created new dry ground the city later built on (an earth-process you can stand on). T3: Wellington is the world's SOUTHERNMOST capital of a sovereign country (~41 S) -- nearer to Antarctica than any other national capital. T4: those steep hills and clear harbor light made it 'Wellywood' -- Peter Jackson's Weta studios filmed and built The Lord of the Rings here, turning New Zealand's landscapes into Middle-earth (a cultural creation rooted in the place).
topics.source: Grokipedia/Wellington (attempted, HTTP 403); corroborated blog.metservice.com 'Windy Wellington', en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wellington, /wiki/Wellington_Fault, /wiki/1855_Wairarapa_earthquake
topics.framing_note: Place-anchored: answers name the Cook Strait wind funnel, the Wellington Fault, the lifted 1855 shoreline, the southernmost capital; scene-led. Accuracy rail: back the 'windiest city' claim with real numbers (gales ~170+ days/yr); the Wellington Fault marks the Australian/Pacific plate boundary. Dinner-test payoff: downtown built on seabed heaved out of the harbor by the 1855 quake, or the windiest capital on Earth. Lane border: The Lord of the Rings is a film (cultural creation) rooted in NZ landscape -- fine as one place-culture rung.

topics.name: Angkor / Siem Reap
topics.scope: The temple-city of the Khmer Empire on the plain north of the town of Siem Reap, Cambodia. T1: Angkor Wat is the LARGEST religious monument ever built — a single temple, moat and towers covering ~160 hectares, so vast its five-towered silhouette sits on Cambodia's national flag (invert: the flag/size is the hook, 'largest religious monument' the answer). T2: almost every Khmer temple faces the sunrise, but Angkor Wat's main gate faces WEST — the direction of the setting sun and the dead — hinting it doubled as King Suryavarman II's funerary temple. T3: at nearby Ta Prohm the jungle never left — giant silk-cotton and strangler-fig roots pour over the walls, holding the ruins together and prying them apart at once (the 'Tomb Raider temple'; teach 'strangler fig'). T4: laser scanners flown over the forest (LiDAR) stripped the canopy to reveal Angkor was the LARGEST city of the pre-industrial world — a sprawling grid of roads, canals and neighborhoods that held ~700,000–900,000 people (teach 'LiDAR'). T5: the Khmer engineered a hydraulic megacity — vast rectangular reservoirs called barays (the West Baray is ~8 km long) stored monsoon water to irrigate rice through the dry season, and when the water network failed the city was abandoned (teach 'baray'). Extra rungs: the ~200 giant serene stone faces of the Bayon; the ~50 m bas-relief gallery of the 'Churning of the Sea of Milk'; the five lotus-bud towers built as Mount Meru; the causeway of gods-and-demons at Angkor Thom's south gate; the pink sandstone miniatures of Banteay Srei.
topics.source: Grokipedia (West_Baray); Wikipedia (Angkor Wat, Ta Prohm, Angkor); Evans et al., 'Uncovering archaeological landscapes at Angkor using lidar,' PNAS 2013 (PMC3732978); NASA Earth Observatory (Angkor)
topics.framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER, scene-led, invert the superlative into the stem and make the knowable thing the answer. Key accuracy rail: Angkor Wat is the largest RELIGIOUS monument (not 'largest building'); the west-facing/funerary reading is scholarly interpretation, phrase as 'suggesting', not settled fact. Dinner-test payoff: the LiDAR rung — a hidden megacity of ~750,000 under the jungle. Frame Angkor as a PLANNED hydraulic megacity engineered by a full civilization, never a 'mysterious lost jungle temple' or 'primitive' ruin. Distractors stay live with other real Khmer/Asian temples (Borobudur, Bagan, Prambanan, Bayon vs Angkor Wat).
topics.history_overlap: The Khmer Empire's political narrative (Suryavarman II's reign, Jayavarman VII, the 15th-c. abandonment as a dynastic story) belongs to the history bank; keep every rung anchored to the PHYSICAL place — the monument, its orientation, the fig-wrapped ruins, the hydraulic city and its barays.

topics.name: Ayutthaya
topics.scope: The ruined former royal capital of Siam, an hour north of Bangkok. T1: Ayutthaya was built on an ISLAND — a moat-ringed city on land made where three rivers (the Chao Phraya, Lopburi and Pa Sak) meet (invert: the island-at-three-rivers is the hook). T2: at Wat Mahathat a stone Buddha's HEAD rests serenely at ground level, slowly cradled and swallowed by the twisting roots of a strangler fig (teach 'strangler fig'). T3: in its golden age around 1700 Ayutthaya was one of the LARGEST cities in the world — perhaps a million people — a cosmopolitan trading capital where Portuguese, Dutch, Chinese and Japanese merchants each had their own quarter. T4: the city died in a single blow — in 1767 a Burmese army sacked and burned it and stripped the gold from its Buddhas; the Siamese never rebuilt it, founding a new capital downriver that became Bangkok. Extra rungs: the three bullet-shaped prangs of Wat Phra Si Sanphet; the row of headless Buddhas along the brick galleries; the giant reclining Buddha at Wat Lokayasutharam.
topics.source: Wikipedia (Ayutthaya Kingdom, Ayutthaya Historical Park); Britannica (Ayutthaya); UNESCO World Heritage (Historic City of Ayutthaya)
topics.framing_note: Voice: scene-led; the island geography and the fig-root head are the anchors. Key accuracy rail: the tree at Wat Mahathat is commonly a strangler fig/bodhi — say 'tree roots (a strangler fig)', not a specific unverifiable species; founded 1350, sacked 1767. Dinner-test payoff: the serene Buddha head cradled in fig roots (T2). Distractors stay live with other real ruined capitals (Sukhothai, Angkor, Bagan) and Thai rivers.
topics.history_overlap: The 1767 Burmese sack as a war narrative is a history-bank episode; here it is the endpoint that explains the RUINS — keep the rung on the abandoned physical city, not the campaign.

topics.name: Bali: Uluwatu & the Subak
topics.scope: The Hindu island of Bali, its cliff-temples, rice terraces and volcanoes. T1: the sea-temple of Uluwatu clings to the edge of a sheer cliff 70 m above the crashing Indian Ocean — its name even means 'rock's end' (ulu = tip, watu = rock) (invert: the cliff-edge temple is the hook; teach the name). T2: Bali is ringed with such sea-temples, meant to be seen from the water and to guard the coast — Tanah Lot perches on its own rock, cut off by the sea twice a day at high tide. T3: Bali's emerald rice terraces are watered by the Subak — a 1,000-year-old system of shared canals, weirs and water-temples where farmers cooperatively divide every drop flowing down from the volcanoes (UNESCO 2012; teach 'Subak'). T4: all that water and rich soil come from Bali's volcanoes — sacred Mount Agung, the island's highest peak, whose ash makes the fields fertile and whose summit the Balinese hold to be the home of the gods (earth-process: volcanic soil). T5: the whole Subak landscape runs on a philosophy called Tri Hita Karana — harmony among people, nature and the divine — which is why the water-temples sit exactly at the springs and fork-points that control the flow. Extra rungs: the stepped Tegallalang rice terraces; the crater lake of Mount Batur; the kecak fire-dance performed on the Uluwatu cliff at sunset.
topics.source: Wikipedia (Uluwatu Temple, Subak (irrigation)); UNESCO World Heritage (Cultural Landscape of Bali Province: the Subak System, #1194)
topics.framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER; the cliff-edge temple and the terraced landscape are the scenes. Key accuracy rail: Subak is genuinely an engineered COOPERATIVE water system (not just 'pretty rice fields') and the fertility genuinely comes from volcanic ash — those are the earth/culture wonders; describe the temples respectfully. Dinner-test payoff: Uluwatu on the 70 m cliff, or the water-temples placed exactly on the springs. Distractors stay live with other real cliff/sea temples and terraced landscapes.

topics.name: Bangkok
topics.scope: The Thai capital on the delta of the Chao Phraya River. T1: the city Thais call Krung Thep, 'City of Angels', has a full ceremonial name so long — 168 letters in one word — that it holds the world record for the longest place name on Earth (invert: the record is the hook). T2: inside the Grand Palace glows the Emerald Buddha, Thailand's most sacred image, carved from a single block of green JADE (not emerald), whose golden seasonal robes only the King may change. T3: a few steps away at Wat Pho reclines a gilded Buddha 46 m long and 15 m high, the soles of its feet inlaid with mother-of-pearl showing 108 auspicious signs. T4: Wat Pho is also the birthplace and living school of traditional Thai massage, its healing points carved onto the temple's walls — a cultural creation born in this exact place. T5: Bangkok grew on the flat, flood-prone Chao Phraya delta, once so laced with canals (khlongs) that Westerners called it the 'Venice of the East'; floating markets still sell from boats on the water (teach 'delta'). Extra rungs: Wat Arun, the 'Temple of Dawn', its riverside spire studded with broken porcelain; Rattanakosin, the old royal island ringed by canals; the golden chedi of the Grand Palace.
topics.source: Guinness World Records (longest place name); Wikipedia (Bangkok, Wat Pho, Wat Phra Kaew / Emerald Buddha, Chao Phraya River); emerald-buddha.com (Reclining Buddha dimensions)
topics.framing_note: Voice: scene-led; put the 168-letter record and the physical measurements in the stem, keep the named thing the answer. Key accuracy rail: the Emerald Buddha is JADE, not emerald — that is itself a rung; the reclining Buddha is 46 m long / 15 m high. Dinner-test payoff: the mother-of-pearl feet with 108 signs, or the 168-letter name. Lane border (COOKING): the floating/canal market is a WATERSCAPE the geography bank owns; the dishes it sells belong to the cooking bank — a one-line mention is fine, no food-origin rung. Distractors stay live with other real Thai temples/rivers.

topics.name: Hanoi Old Quarter
topics.scope: The historic core of Vietnam's capital on the Red River delta. T1: in the heart of Hanoi lies the Old Quarter, a maze famous as the '36 Streets', where each lane was once home to a single guild — and many are STILL named for the goods sold there (Silk Street, Silver Street, Tin Street; 'Hàng' means 'merchandise') (invert: the 36 guild-streets is the hook).
