T2: at the quarter's edge sits Hoan Kiem Lake, the 'Lake of the Returned Sword', named for the legend of King Le Loi, who handed a magic sword back to a giant golden turtle that rose from the water (label LEGEND). T3: Hanoi is one of Asia's oldest capitals — founded in 1010 as Thang Long, 'City of the Ascending Dragon'. T4: the city grew on the flood-prone Red River delta and is ringed by earthen dikes that hold the river back; its very name, Hà Nội, means 'inside the river's bend' (teach 'delta / dike'). Extra rungs: the tube-house shophouses, narrow at the front and long behind; the red arched Huc Bridge to the lake's island temple; the French Quarter's tree-lined boulevards beside the old town.
topics.source: Wikipedia (Hanoi, Hoan Kiem Lake, Old Quarter of Hanoi); Facts and Details (Old Quarter of Hanoi); Ancient-Origins (Hoan Kiem legend)
topics.framing_note: Voice: scene-led; the guild-street maze and the sword lake are the anchors. Key accuracy rail: the returned-sword story is LEGEND — attribute as 'according to legend'; the founding of Thang Long (1010) and the meaning of Hà Nội are the settled facts. Dinner-test payoff: the streets still named for their trades. Lane borders: the lake's giant softshell turtle is a real animal but keep the answer the PLACE-legend, not the turtle's biology (animal bank); Hanoi's pho and street food belong to the COOKING bank — no food-origin rung.

topics.name: Hoi An
topics.scope: The perfectly preserved old trading port on the Thu Bon River in central Vietnam. T1: Hoi An is crossed by a 400-year-old Japanese Covered Bridge — a wooden footbridge with a small temple built into its middle, its two ends guarded by carved dog and monkey statues. T2: the town froze in time because its harbor SILTED UP — the Thu Bon River filled the old port with mud, so the sea trade moved to nearby Da Nang and left the merchant town almost untouched for centuries (earth-process: siltation). T3: on every full moon the town switches off its electric lights and floats hundreds of glowing silk lanterns down the river. Optional extra: the yellow-washed merchant shophouses of the old town, a UNESCO-listed trading port that mixed Vietnamese, Chinese and Japanese quarters.
topics.source: Wikipedia (Hội An, Japanese Covered Bridge / Chùa Cầu); UNESCO World Heritage (Hoi An Ancient Town, 1999)
topics.framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER; three gem rungs, each a different concrete wonder. Key accuracy rail: the town is preserved BECAUSE the harbor silted and trade left — that siltation is the real geographic cause (the T2 dinner-test payoff), not just 'it's old'. Lane border (COOKING): Hoi An's famous cao lau noodles belong to the cooking bank — a passing mention is fine, no food-origin rung. Distractors stay live with other real preserved ports/bridges.

topics.name: Hue Imperial Citadel
topics.scope: The last imperial capital of Vietnam, on the Perfume River. T1: on the river's north bank stands the Imperial Citadel of Hue — a vast square fortress of moats, gates and brick ramparts that was the home of Vietnam's last emperors (the Nguyen dynasty, 1802–1945). T2: deep inside lies the Forbidden Purple City, an inner palace so private that only the emperor, his family and eunuch servants could enter — modeled on Beijing's Forbidden City. T3: the river winding past is the Perfume River (Sông Hương), named for the scent of flowers that drift into it from orchards upstream in autumn. T4: scattered in the pine hills around Hue are the grand garden-TOMBS the Nguyen emperors built for themselves — walled palaces of pavilions, lotus ponds and stelae, some designed and used as retreats while the emperor still lived. Extra rungs: the seven-tiered Thien Mu Pagoda on a bluff over the river; the Meridian Gate (Ngo Mon) entrance; the layered nesting of Capital City, Imperial City and Forbidden Purple City.
topics.source: Wikipedia (Imperial City of Huế); UNESCO World Heritage (Complex of Huế Monuments, #678); vietnamdiscovery.com (Forbidden Purple City)
topics.framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER; the nested citadel and the Perfume River are the scenes. Key accuracy rail: the 'Forbidden Purple City' name deliberately echoes Beijing's — that parallel is the T2 wonder; the Perfume River's name comes from upstream flowers (fact, tell it as such). Dinner-test payoff: the emperors' garden-tombs designed to be lived in before death. Distractors stay live with other real Asian palace-cities (Beijing's Forbidden City, Seoul's Gyeongbokgung).
topics.history_overlap: The Nguyen dynasty's political history is a history-bank topic; keep rungs anchored to the physical citadel, the river and the tombs.

topics.name: Luang Prabang
topics.scope: The old royal town on a river peninsula in northern Laos. T1: Luang Prabang sits on a finger of land where the Mekong meets the Nam Khan — a peninsula between two rivers whose waters flow side by side in visibly different colors (invert: the two-color confluence is the hook). T2: every dawn hundreds of barefoot, saffron-robed monks walk in a long silent line through the streets while kneeling townspeople place sticky rice into their bowls — the alms-giving called Tak Bat. T3: climb the 300-plus steps of Mount Phousi in the town's center to watch the two rivers curve around gilded temple roofs at sunset. T4: south of town, Kuang Si Falls tumbles over pale LIMESTONE terraces into pools of impossible turquoise — the color comes from calcium carbonate dissolved out of the rock and re-deposited as travertine (teach 'limestone / travertine'). Extra rungs: the golden royal temple of Wat Xieng Thong with its sweeping low roofs; the town's status as a whole UNESCO-listed living townscape (1995); the confluence sandbars that appear in the dry season.
topics.source: Wikipedia (Luang Prabang, Kuang Si Falls); UNESCO World Heritage (Town of Luang Prabang, 1995); Rainforest Cruises (Tak Bat guide)
topics.framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER; the two-river peninsula and the dawn procession are the scenes. Key accuracy rail: Kuang Si's turquoise is a real earth-process (dissolved limestone / travertine), not dye — that IS the T4 wonder; the alms ritual is a living practice, describe it respectfully and plainly (no advertising gush). Dinner-test payoff: the turquoise travertine pools, or the silent dawn line of monks. Distractors stay live with other confluences and limestone falls (Plitvice, Pamukkale).

topics.name: Manila: Intramuros
topics.scope: The old Spanish walled city inside modern Manila, in the Philippines. T1: in the middle of the sprawling modern capital stands Intramuros — Latin for 'within the walls' — a whole Spanish colonial town sealed behind massive stone ramparts and a moat, begun in 1571 (teach the name 'Intramuros'). T2: its oldest survivor is San Agustin Church, finished in 1607 — the oldest stone church in the Philippines. T3: in 1945 the Battle of Manila leveled almost everything inside the walls; of the seven great churches of Intramuros, San Agustin was the ONLY one left standing. T4: Manila grew where the Pasig River empties into Manila Bay, a huge sheltered natural harbor famous for its sunsets — the very prize the Spanish, and later others, fought so hard to hold. Extra rungs: Fort Santiago guarding the river mouth; the walls built partly from adobe and coral stone; the grid of the walled quarter with the cathedral at its heart.
topics.source: Wikipedia (Intramuros, San Agustin Church (Manila)); UNESCO World Heritage (Baroque Churches of the Philippines, 1993); National Museum of the Philippines (San Agustin Church)
topics.framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER; the walled city and the lone surviving church are the anchors. Key accuracy rail: Intramuros founded 1571, San Agustin completed 1607 and the only Intramuros church to survive the 1945 battle — keep these exact. Dinner-test payoff: seven churches, one survivor (T3). Colonialism honest BOTH ways: the walls were Spain's fortress that literally kept Filipinos 'outside the walls' (extra muros), AND the Spanish left the enduring architecture and faith that define the city today — state both plainly, no cheerleading and no sneering. History overlap noted below.
topics.history_overlap: The Spanish conquest and the 1945 Battle of Manila are history-bank episodes; here they explain the WALLS and why only one church survived — keep the rungs on the physical walled city and San Agustin, not the campaigns.

topics.name: Shwedagon Pagoda / Yangon
topics.scope: Myanmar's holiest shrine, crowning Singuttara Hill in Yangon. T1: rising nearly 100 m over the city, the Shwedagon Pagoda is a mountain of GOLD — its great bell-shaped stupa sheathed head to foot in real gold plates and gold leaf renewed by the faithful (invert: 'a mountain of gold' is the hook). T2: at its very tip sits a diamond-studded orb crowned by a single ~72-carat diamond that flashes red, then green, then white as you walk around the base. T3: the shrine is said to enshrine relics of four Buddhas, including eight hairs of the Buddha Gautama — which is why pilgrims circle it clockwise, barefoot. T4: around the base sit eight 'planetary posts', one for each day of the Burmese week (which splits Wednesday into two) — worshippers pour water over the corner for the day they were born. Extra rungs: the stupa's terraced octagonal base; the ring of smaller golden shrines and bells; the covered stairways guarded by giant chinthe (lion-dogs) at the four gates.
topics.source: Wikipedia (Shwedagon Pagoda); official shwedagonpagoda.org.mm; renown-travel.com (99.36 m height)
topics.framing_note: Voice: scene-led; the gold and the crowning diamond are the hooks. Key accuracy rail: the relics (eight Buddha hairs) are religious tradition — attribute as 'is said to enshrine', do not assert as physical fact; sources vary on the top diamond (72 vs 76 carat), so phrase 'about 72 carats'. Dinner-test payoff: the color-flashing diamond at the very tip. Respect the sacred site plainly — no smug secular dismissal and no advertising-brochure gush. Distractors stay live with other gold/relic stupas (Shwezigon, Kyaiktiyo Golden Rock).

topics.name: Singapore
topics.scope: The equatorial island city-state at the tip of the Malay Peninsula. T1: Singapore is a tiny island that keeps getting BIGGER — it has grown roughly a quarter larger (from ~582 to ~723 km²) by piling sand into the sea, making it the fastest-growing country on Earth by land reclamation (invert: 'a country that keeps growing' is the hook; teach 'land reclamation'). T2: on the waterfront stand the Supertrees of Gardens by the Bay — 18 towering steel 'trees' up to 50 m tall, wrapped in living plants, that harvest rainwater and glow at night. T3: with almost no land to spare, Singapore dammed the sea — the Marina Barrage turned a saltwater bay in the heart of downtown into a giant FRESHWATER reservoir for drinking water. T4: having no big rivers and no room, Singapore imports so much sand to build new land that some neighboring countries banned selling it to them. T5: Singapore sits almost exactly on the equator, guarding the Strait of Malacca — the narrow sea-gate through which a huge share of the world's ships and oil must squeeze — which is why the city became one of Earth's greatest ports (teach 'strait / chokepoint'). Extra rungs: Jewel Changi's Rain Vortex, the world's tallest indoor waterfall; the 'garden city' of vertical greenery and rooftop parks; reclaimed Jurong Island, built by merging small islands into a petrochemical hub.
topics.source: Wikipedia (Land reclamation in Singapore, Gardens by the Bay); Guinness World Records (fastest-growing country through land reclamation); Mothership.SG (25% land-area growth); BiblioAsia NLB ('Land From Sand')
topics.framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER; the paradox of a country GROWING is the hook. Key accuracy rail: quote the reclamation growth as ~24–25% (from ~582 km² in the 1960s to ~723 km²) — do not round to '50%'; the Supertrees number 18, 25–50 m tall. Dinner-test payoff: the land-that-grows-by-importing-sand pairing (T1/T4). Distractors stay live with other real reclaimed/port cities and Asian gardens. This is settled engineering wonder — no stance needed.

topics.name: Yogyakarta: Borobudur & Prambanan
topics.scope: Two rival 9th-century masterpieces on the volcanic plain near Yogyakarta, central Java. T1: rising from the jungle is the LARGEST Buddhist temple on Earth — not a tower but a stone mountain of nine stacked terraces you climb like a pilgrim, crowned by one great dome (Borobudur). T2: seen from above Borobudur is a giant MANDALA, a Buddhist diagram of the cosmos; pilgrims walk clockwise up past ~2,672 carved relief panels that tell the path from earthly desire to enlightenment (teach 'mandala'). T3: on the top three round terraces sit 72 bell-shaped stone stupas, each a stone lattice cage hiding a seated Buddha inside; the crowning central stupa is deliberately EMPTY — the void of enlightenment. T4: for centuries Borobudur lay buried under volcanic ash and jungle from nearby Mount Merapi, one of the world's most active volcanoes, until it was dug out in the 1800s. T5: a short drive away soar the spires of Prambanan, the largest Hindu temple in Indonesia — its central Shiva tower rises ~47 m, so Java holds two giant rival temples, Buddhist and Hindu, built within a century of each other. Extra rungs: Borobudur assembled from ~2 million interlocking volcanic blocks WITHOUT mortar; the hidden 'buried foot' reliefs at its base; Prambanan's carved Ramayana galleries; both temples fed by the fertile ash of the same volcanic Kewu plain.
topics.source: Wikipedia (Borobudur, Prambanan); Guinness World Records (largest Buddhist temple, 2012); National Geographic (Borobudur Temple Compounds); UNESCO World Heritage (Borobudur, Prambanan)
topics.framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER; invert 'largest Buddhist temple' into the scene. Key accuracy rail: Borobudur is the largest BUDDHIST temple / monument (Guinness); Prambanan the largest HINDU temple in Indonesia — keep the two claims distinct. Handle the burial honestly: it was buried by volcanic ash/jungle and cleared in the 1800s — do NOT say a colonial figure 'discovered' a temple local villagers had always known; phrase as 'cleared / excavated'. Dinner-test payoff: the 72 stone bells each hiding a Buddha, over one empty central dome. Distractors stay live with Angkor Wat, Bagan, and Prambanan-vs-Borobudur cross-pairs.
topics.history_overlap: The Sailendra / Medang (Mataram) dynastic history belongs to the history/ancient bank; keep rungs on the monuments' form, the mandala structure, the volcanic burial, and Merapi.

strands.strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe

topics.name: Athens
topics.strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
topics.scope: The birthplace of Western civic life, crowned by its sacred rock. T1: the Acropolis (Greek for 'high city') is a flat-topped rock rising about 150 m over Athens, a natural citadel you can see from almost anywhere in the city, its summit crowned with ancient temples (answer = the Acropolis, the high citadel-rock; teach 'acropolis'). T2: on top stands the Parthenon (447-432 BC), the temple of Athena, built of gleaming Pentelic marble that weathers to a warm honey-gold in the sun (answer = the Parthenon / marble that turns golden). T3: the Parthenon has almost NO straight lines -- its columns swell slightly in the middle (entasis) and lean inward, and the floor curves gently up in the center -- deliberate optical tricks so the temple LOOKS perfectly straight to the eye (answer = the built-in curves / optical refinements; teach entasis). T3: the Agora, the open marketplace at the foot of the rock, was the civic heart of Athens -- where citizens gathered to trade, vote and argue, and where Socrates buttonholed passersby with questions (answer = the Agora, the civic marketplace). T4: on the Erechtheion's 'Porch of the Maidens', six carved stone women (the Caryatids) stand in place of columns, holding the roof on their heads (answer = the Caryatids). T4: all that marble came from Mount Pentelicus, northeast of the city -- roughly 13,000 blocks of Pentelic marble quarried and hauled up onto the rock (answer = quarried from Mt Pentelicus). T5: the Parthenon stood nearly whole for over 2,000 years until 1687, when a Venetian cannon-shell struck Ottoman gunpowder stored inside and blew the roof and center apart in an instant (answer = a 1687 gunpowder explosion wrecked it).
topics.source: WebSearch (2026-07): Wikipedia 'Acropolis of Athens', 'Parthenon'; Britannica 'Parthenon', 'Acropolis of Athens'; UNESCO WHC list #404 (Acropolis); archeyes.com / thearchaeologist.org (optical refinements, entasis, stylobate curvature).
topics.framing_note: Voice: PLACE -> WONDER, the rock and its marble are the stars; invert nothing that turns it into a definition-shell -- lead with the scene ('on top of the rock stands...'). Accuracy rail: keep the optical-refinement numbers loose in the seed (the stylobate rises a few cm at center; columns lean inward) and let the build research nail exacts; the 1687 explosion is a well-documented event, state it as fact. Dinner-test payoff: the temple with no straight lines that only LOOKS straight (T3). LANE BORDER: Socrates' trial, execution and ideas belong to the history/philosophy banks -- this Agora rung's answer is the PLACE (the marketplace that was the city's civic heart), Socrates a one-line mention.
topics.history_overlap: Socrates (trial/philosophy) and Pericles' Golden Age are history/philosophy episodes; the 1687 Morosini bombardment is a history event -- keep every rung's answer a PLACE fact (the rock, the marble, the Agora, the ruin's cause) rather than a person or a war.

topics.name: Bergen
topics.strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
topics.scope: Norway's western port, the 'gateway to the fjords'. T1: Bergen sits in a natural bowl ringed by SEVEN mountains, its old harbor front lined with a row of tall, narrow, pointed wooden gable-houses -- the Bryggen wharf (answer = the seven mountains / the Bryggen waterfront). T2: Bryggen was the Hanseatic wharf -- a walled German merchant trading post (a Kontor) that ran Norway's dried-cod trade for about 400 years, and it's the last of only four such Hanseatic Kontors in Europe still standing (UNESCO-listed) (answer = the Hanseatic wharf/Kontor). T2: Bryggen has burned to the ground again and again over the centuries -- and each time the townspeople rebuilt it on the exact same medieval street plan, with the same leaning colorful gables (answer = rebuilt on the same medieval plan after every fire). T3: invert the wonder -- Bergen is the RAINIEST city in Europe, with rain falling on roughly 230 days a year; locals joke you can spot a Bergener because they never carry an umbrella, just wait it out (the extreme rain-count is the hook; 'the rainiest city' the answer -- dinner-test). T3: the rain has a cause you can see: wet Atlantic air blowing in off the sea slams into the seven mountains, is forced upward, cools, and wrings its water out right over the city (answer = the mountains force the wet air up and it rains; teach orographic rainfall). T4: the Floibanen funicular railway climbs steeply up Mount Floyen for a view over the whole city, and from Bergen's harbor boats set out into Norway's great fjords -- earning it the title 'gateway to the fjords' (answer = the funicular / fjord gateway; teach fjord).
topics.source: WebSearch (2026-07): Wikipedia 'Bryggen'; visitnorway.com / hurtigruten.com (Bergen, seven mountains, gateway to fjords); planetware.com (City of Seven Mountains); Floibanen (opened 1918).
topics.framing_note: Voice: PLACE -> WONDER, Bergen/Bryggen named in each stem; invert on the rain (230 days -> rainiest city). Accuracy rail: teach 'orographic rainfall' (moist air forced up mountains, cools, rains) as the real mechanism, not just the wet-city trivia; Bryggen is 'the only Hanseatic Kontor still preserved' -- keep that precise. Dinner-test payoff: Europe's rainiest city, ~230 rainy days a year (T3). LANE BORDER: the dried COD (stockfish) is a food/animal -- name it only as the goods the Kontor traded; the answer stays the PLACE (the wharf, the trading post), never the fish's biology or the dish.

topics.name: Budapest
topics.strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
topics.scope: Hungary's capital astride the Danube, the 'City of Spas'. T1: Budapest is really TWO old towns joined into one -- hilly, castle-topped Buda on the west bank and flat, bustling Pest on the east, first linked by the Chain Bridge in 1849 (answer = Buda + Pest, split by the Danube; teach the two halves). T2: invert the wonder -- more than 100 natural hot springs bubble up beneath the city, more than any other capital, which is why it's called the 'City of Spas' (the 100+ springs are the hook; 'the thermal springs' the answer). T2: the Szechenyi Baths, a lemon-yellow palace of a bathhouse, is the LARGEST medicinal bath in Europe, fed by a spring drilled 1,256 m down that comes up at 77 degrees C -- in winter people play chess in the steaming outdoor pools while snow falls (answer = Szechenyi, Europe's largest medicinal bath). T3: all that hot water rises through a huge maze of THERMAL CAVES hollowed in the limestone under the Buda hills -- one of the largest thermal-water cave systems in the world (answer = the thermal cave system; teach that warm water dissolves limestone into caves). T3: the springs exist because Budapest sits right on a geological FAULT line, where the Buda hills meet the Pest plain and deep-warmed water can rise to the surface (answer = a fault line lets the hot water up). T4: beneath Buda Castle hill runs a labyrinth of caves and cellars cut into the soft limestone, used over the centuries as shelters, storerooms and even a wartime hospital (answer = the castle-hill cave labyrinth). T4: the Hungarian Parliament on the Pest riverbank is one of the largest parliament buildings in the world, its neo-Gothic spires doubled in the Danube at night (answer = the Parliament building).
topics.source: WebSearch (2026-07): Wikipedia 'Szechenyi thermal bath', 'Spas in Budapest'; Lonely Planet (Budapest thermal baths guide); National Geographic (Hungary thermal spas); bathsbudapest.com.
topics.framing_note: Voice: the earth-process (geothermal water rising through karst) IS the wonder and the place is named in every stem. Accuracy rail: keep the spring count as 'over 100' (sources vary 80-123) and the Szechenyi spring figures exact (1,256 m, 77 C); teach that hot mineral water dissolving limestone makes the cave network (karst) before leaning on it. Dinner-test payoff: chess players in a steaming outdoor pool in the snow (T2). LANE BORDER: this is the PLACE's geothermal geology -- no spa 'health cure' claims stated as medical fact.

topics.name: Dubrovnik
topics.strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
topics.scope: The walled 'Pearl of the Adriatic' on Croatia's Dalmatian coast. T1: Dubrovnik's whole old town is wrapped in a complete unbroken ring of stone SEA-WALLS -- you can walk the full circuit, roughly 1,940 m, all the way around the city above the rooftops and the sea (answer = the complete walkable city walls). T2: invert the wonder -- those walls rise up to 25 m high and up to 6 m thick on the land side, and in all their centuries no hostile army ever BREACHED them (the massive fortifications are the hook; 'never breached' the answer -- a dinner-test payoff). T2: inside the walls the main street, the Stradun, is paved end to end in white limestone polished to a glassy shine by centuries of footsteps (answer = the polished limestone Stradun). T3: the walls guarded the Republic of Ragusa, a tiny sea-trading city-state that kept its independence for centuries less by armies than by shrewd diplomacy and tribute-paying (answer = the Republic of Ragusa). T4: the whole Dalmatian coast is bright white KARST limestone -- rock dissolved and sculpted by water -- and it's that gleaming limestone against a clear blue sea that makes Dubrovnik the 'Pearl of the Adriatic' (answer = the white karst limestone coast; teach karst).
topics.source: WebSearch (2026-07): Grokipedia 'Walls of Dubrovnik'; Wikipedia 'Walls of Dubrovnik'; wallsofdubrovnik.com (dimensions, never breached); historyhit.com (Dubrovnik City Walls).
topics.framing_note: Voice: the PLACE (the walls, the coast) is the wonder, Dubrovnik named in the stem. Accuracy rail: keep the wall figures exact (~1,940 m circuit, up to 25 m high, up to 6 m thick landward) and 'never breached by a hostile army' as the verified claim; teach 'karst' before the limestone-coast rung. Dinner-test payoff: walls that no army ever broke through (T2). A one-line modern-fame aside (Dubrovnik played King's Landing in Game of Thrones) is fine but NOT its own rung. Distractors = other real walled cities / other coastal superlatives.
topics.history_overlap: The Republic of Ragusa's diplomacy and trade history sit adjacent to the history bank; keep this rung's answer the PLACE/polity name anchored to the walls, not a narrative of its statecraft.

topics.name: Krakow
topics.strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
topics.scope: Poland's old royal capital on the Vistula, a medieval city that survived the war. T1: beneath Wawel Hill yawns a real cave, the 'Dragon's Den' (Smocza Jama), where legend says the fire-breathing Wawel Dragon once lived -- and a bronze dragon at the cave mouth still puffs real fire for visitors (answer = the Dragon's Den cave; label the dragon as legend). T2: that cave is a natural KARST cavern -- limestone slowly dissolved by groundwater into a chain of corridors and chambers about 80 m long under the castle hill (answer = a karst limestone cave; teach karst). T2: Krakow's Old Town came through WWII almost untouched while Warsaw and most Polish cities were flattened -- leaving one of Europe's best-preserved medieval centers (answer = it survived the war nearly intact). T3: invert the wonder -- the Main Market Square (Rynek Glowny), laid out in 1257 with each side over 200 m long, is the LARGEST medieval town square in Europe (the huge open square is the hook; 'largest medieval square' the answer). T3: right in the middle of that square stands the Cloth Hall (Sukiennice), a long Renaissance market hall where merchants have traded cloth and goods for some 700 years (answer = the Cloth Hall). T4: every hour a live trumpeter plays the 'hejnal' from the tower of St Mary's Basilica -- and the tune BREAKS OFF abruptly mid-note, said to honor a medieval watchman shot in the throat as he sounded the alarm (answer = the trumpet call cut off mid-note; label the arrow as legend). T4: Wawel Castle crowns the hill as the old coronation seat of Polish kings, and in the cathedral doorway hang giant 'dragon bones' -- really a whale bone and a mammoth bone -- long believed to protect the city (answer = the 'dragon bones' / really whale and mammoth bones; legend).
topics.source: WebSearch (2026-07): Wikipedia 'Wawel Dragon', 'Main Square, Krakow', 'St. Mary's Trumpet Call'; krakow.travel (hejnal, market square); inyourpocket.com (Wawel dragon, dragon bones).
topics.framing_note: Voice: place-anchored wonder, Krakow/Wawel named in the stem. Accuracy rail: the dragon, the arrow-in-the-throat and the protective bones are LEGEND -- word them as legend/oral tradition, with the sober fact (the cave is real karst; the 'dragon bones' are actually whale and mammoth bones) as the answer where possible. Dinner-test payoff: the hourly trumpet that stops mid-note for a slain medieval watchman (T4). Distractors = other real Polish/European squares, caves, towers.

topics.name: Moscow
topics.strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
topics.scope: Russia's capital on the Moskva, gathered around the Kremlin. T1: Red Square gets its name from an old Russian word 'krasnaya', which once meant 'beautiful' -- not the color red and nothing to do with communism; it is really the 'Beautiful Square' (answer = 'red' once meant 'beautiful'; teach the word before testing). T2: on the square stands St Basil's Cathedral, built for Ivan the Terrible in 1555-61 to mark the conquest of Kazan -- nine separate chapels fused into one, topped with candy-swirl onion domes each painted differently (answer = St Basil's, nine churches in one; the tale that Ivan blinded the architects is apocryphal -- label as legend). T2: the Kremlin itself is a great triangular fortress of red-brick walls and 20 towers, still the seat of Russian power and one of the largest active medieval fortresses in Europe (answer = the Kremlin fortress). T3: the Moscow Metro was built as 'palaces for the people' -- stations like Komsomolskaya hung with chandeliers, faced in marble, and roofed with mosaics of Russian war heroes (answer = the palace-stations). T4: invert the wonder -- Park Pobedy station lies about 84 m underground, Moscow's DEEPEST, reached by one of Europe's longest escalators at roughly 126 m (the extreme depth is the hook; 'the deepest station' the answer). T4: GUM, the grand glass-roofed shopping arcade, runs the whole east side of Red Square like an indoor street of iron and glass (answer = the GUM arcade). T5: many metro stations were dug so deep on purpose -- they doubled as bomb shelters, and during WWII thousands sheltered underground, with a command post built into one station (answer = the metro as bomb shelter).
topics.source: WebSearch (2026-07): Grokipedia 'Park Pobedy (Moscow Metro)'; Wikipedia 'Saint Basil's Cathedral', 'Red Square', 'Moscow Metro', 'Komsomolskaya (Koltsevaya line)'; rbth.com / rusmania.com (metro stations); worldatlas.com (deepest stations).
topics.framing_note: Voice: scene-led, Moscow landmark always named. Accuracy rail: label the 'Ivan blinded the architects' story as popular legend (almost certainly untrue); the 'Red Square = Beautiful Square' etymology must be TAUGHT in the stem's setup enough to be fair but the answer still requires knowing which meaning is original. Be factually honest about the metro: a genuine engineering marvel AND a Soviet showpiece built under Stalin. Dinner-test payoff: Park Pobedy 84 m down with a 126 m escalator (T4). Distractors = other real deep metros / other onion-domed churches.
topics.history_overlap: The Kremlin as the seat of Tsarist/Soviet/modern political power invites history-bank episodes; keep these rungs on the PLACE (the fortress walls, the domes, the deep stations), not on regimes or leaders' deeds.

topics.name: Prague
topics.strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
topics.scope: The Czech capital on the Vltava, a spired 'City of a Hundred Towers' that came through WWII almost intact. T1: on the Old Town Square, every hour a crowd gathers as the Orloj (Astronomical Clock) puts on its show -- two little doors open and the Twelve Apostles parade past while a carved skeleton (Death) rings a bell and flips his hourglass (answer = the parading Apostle figures / the moving skeleton). T2: invert the wonder -- that clock, first recorded in 1410, is over 600 years old, the world's OLDEST astronomical clock still running (the huge age is the hook; 'oldest still-working astronomical clock' is the answer). T2: Golden Lane inside Prague Castle is a row of tiny candy-colored cottages built INTO the castle wall for Rudolf II's guards, later home to the goldsmiths that gave it its name (answer = Golden Lane / the goldsmiths). T3: Charles Bridge, begun in 1357 under Charles IV, is lined with 30 blackened baroque statues of saints -- the most-rubbed is St John of Nepomuk (answer = the 30 saint statues). T3: legend says the bridge's masons mixed egg yolks (even eggs shipped in from whole villages) into the mortar to harden it -- and modern lab tests really did find organic binders in it (answer = eggs in the mortar; label as legend that testing partly confirmed). T4: St Vitus Cathedral, rising inside the castle, was begun in 1344 and not finished until 1929 -- nearly 600 years under construction (answer = ~600 years to build). T4: Prague Castle is often called the largest coherent ancient castle complex in the world, spreading over roughly 70,000 square metres above the river (answer = largest ancient castle complex). T5: in the 1618 Defenestration of Prague, angry Protestants threw two royal officials (and a secretary) out a high Prague Castle window -- and all three SURVIVED the ~20 m fall, landing in the moat below (legend says a dung heap broke their fall); the event helped ignite the Thirty Years' War (answer = they survived the fall).
topics.source: WebSearch (2026-07): Wikipedia 'Prague astronomical clock', 'Charles Bridge', 'List of statues on Charles Bridge', 'Golden Lane'; prague.eu (Prague City Tourism, Old Town Hall/Orloj, Charles Bridge); Britannica 'Prague Castle'; charlesbridgehostel.com (egg-mortar lab tests). Grokipedia checked for Prague sights.
topics.framing_note: Voice: scene-led, place is always visible in the stem ('on the Old Town Square...', 'inside Prague Castle...'). Accuracy rail: the egg-mortar and the dung-heap survival are LEGEND that some evidence supports -- word them as legend/tradition, not flat fact; the clock is the world's THIRD-oldest astronomical clock overall but the OLDEST still operating (state it precisely so a distractor 'the very first astronomical clock ever built' stays wrong-but-adjacent). Distractors = other real European clocks/bridges/castles. Dinner-test payoff: the Defenestration survivors landing in a dung heap (T5). Keep answers PLACE-anchored: the clock rung's answer is the parading figures, not 'what time it shows'.
topics.history_overlap: The 1618 Defenestration as the CAUSE of the Thirty Years' War is a history-bank episode; keep this geography rung's answer on the vivid place-fact (three men survived a fall from a Prague Castle window), not on the war's diplomacy or outcome.

topics.name: Reykjavik
topics.strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
topics.scope: Iceland's capital, the city the earth heats. T1: invert the wonder -- Reykjavik sits at about 64 degrees N, near the Arctic Circle, making it the world's NORTHERNMOST capital of a sovereign country (the extreme latitude is the hook; 'northernmost capital' the answer). T2: almost the whole city is warmed straight from the ground -- nearly every home is heated by naturally hot GEOTHERMAL water piped up from volcanic rock, so Reykjavik burns almost no oil or coal for heat and its air stays clean (answer = geothermal district heating). T2: the city's very name says it -- 'Reykjavik' means 'Smoky Bay', for the plumes of steam the first Norse settlers saw drifting up from the hot springs (answer = the name means 'Smoky Bay'; teach before testing). T3: Hallgrimskirkja, the great pale church towering on the hill, was designed to look like Iceland's BASALT COLUMNS -- the natural hexagonal rock pillars that form when thick lava cools slowly (answer = shaped like basalt columns; teach basalt). T4: Reykjavik lies so far north that midsummer brings a near-endless 'midnight sun' that barely sets, while midwinter gives only a few hours of dim daylight (answer = the midnight sun and dark winters).
topics.source: WebSearch (2026-07): Wikipedia 'Hellisheidi Power Station' (Reykjavik ~90% geothermal district heating); guidetoiceland.is (Hallgrimskirkja basalt-column design); lifeinnorway.net ('14 Facts About Reykjavik', northernmost capital, Smoky Bay).
topics.framing_note: Voice: the earth-process (a city heated by volcanic ground) IS the wonder; Reykjavik named every stem. Accuracy rail: precise wording -- 'northernmost capital of a SOVEREIGN state' (so Nuuk, Greenland, a non-sovereign capital, is a live wrong-but-adjacent distractor); ~90% of Reykjavik buildings use geothermal district heat, so say 'nearly all', not 'all'. Teach 'basalt' before the Hallgrimskirkja rung. Dinner-test payoff: a whole capital heated by hot water straight from the ground (T2). Distractors = other far-north capitals / other volcanic-island facts.

topics.name: St Petersburg
topics.strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
topics.scope: Russia's imperial 'Venice of the North', raised on the Neva delta. T1: for weeks around midsummer the city glows through the 'White Nights' -- the sun barely sets and the sky never goes fully dark, so people fill the streets and bridges past midnight (answer = the White Nights). T2: Peter the Great founded the city in 1703 by sheer decree on a cold, mist-shrouded MARSH at the mouth of the Neva -- tens of thousands of laborers drained swamp and drove wooden piles, and so many died it's called 'the city built on bones' (answer = built on a drained marsh, by decree). T2: over 60 rivers and canals thread across more than 40 islands, crossed by hundreds of bridges -- earning it the name 'Venice of the North' (answer = the canal-and-island city / Venice of the North). T3: invert the wonder -- the Hermitage, spread through the green-and-white Winter Palace, holds around three million objects, making it the world's SECOND-largest art museum (the vast collection is the hook; 'second-largest art museum' the answer); it grew from Catherine the Great's 1764 purchase. T3: every night in shipping season the Neva's drawbridges rise to let ocean ships pass -- and if you're caught on the wrong bank, you're stranded until dawn (answer = the drawbridges open at night). T4: at Peterhof, Peter's seaside palace, more than 100 fountains including the Grand Cascade run with NO pumps at all -- gravity alone drives the water down from springs and reservoirs about 20 km away (answer = the gravity-fed fountains, no pumps). T4: the Bronze Horseman statue of Peter rears on the 'Thunder Stone' -- a single granite boulder of roughly 1,500 tonnes, among the largest stones ever moved by people, hauled to the city over a track of bronze balls (answer = the Thunder Stone / a giant moved boulder). T5: the city sits so far north (about 60 degrees N) that the Neva freezes solid every winter and the summer sun scarcely dips -- its polar-edge latitude shapes the whole rhythm of the year (answer = its far-north latitude).
topics.source: WebSearch (2026-07): Wikipedia 'Saint Petersburg', 'Hermitage Museum', 'Peterhof Palace', 'List of bridges in Saint Petersburg'; introducingsaintpetersburg.com (Hermitage, history); russiable.com (drawbridge schedules); go.peterhofmuseum.ru (gravity fountains). Grokipedia checked.
topics.framing_note: Voice: the PLACE and its earth/engineering are the wonder; invert on the Hermitage (millions of objects -> second-largest). Accuracy rail: the human cost of building on the marsh is real -- state it plainly and honestly (thousands of forced laborers died) without turning it into a lecture; the Hermitage is second-largest by GALLERY SPACE/collection, so keep a 'largest art museum in the world' (the Louvre) as a live wrong-but-adjacent distractor. Dinner-test payoff: Peterhof's fountains running for 300 years on gravity alone (T4). Keep answers place-anchored, not a bare 'Peter the Great' name.
topics.history_overlap: Peter the Great's westernizing reforms and the Great Northern War are history-bank material; keep the founding rung's answer on the SITE fact (a capital willed into being on a drained Neva marsh), not on Peter's policies.

topics.name: Stockholm
topics.strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
topics.scope: Sweden's capital, a city floating on water. T1: Stockholm is built across 14 islands, right where the freshwater Lake Malaren pours into the salty Baltic Sea, all stitched together by around 50 bridges (answer = a city spread over 14 islands). T2: invert the wonder -- those 14 are only the start: beyond the city the Stockholm Archipelago scatters outward into roughly 30,000 islands, islets and bare rock skerries (the staggering island count is the hook; 'the 30,000-island archipelago' the answer). T2: Gamla Stan, the old town crowded onto one small island, is one of Europe's best-preserved medieval city cores -- a knot of narrow lanes and ochre houses around the Royal Palace (answer = Gamla Stan, the medieval island core). T3: the Vasa, a towering royal warship, capsized and SANK right in Stockholm harbor in 1628 -- barely 1,300 m into her maiden voyage -- because she was built far too tall and heavy with cannon and rolled over in a light gust (answer = she sank on her maiden voyage). T4: the cold, low-salt Baltic water kept out the wood-eating shipworms, so when the Vasa was raised in 1961 after 333 years on the bottom, about 98% of her was still original oak -- now standing whole in her own museum (answer = raised 98% intact after 333 years). T4: the Stockholm Metro is called the 'world's longest art gallery' -- more than 90 stations painted, sculpted or blasted straight into the bare bedrock, like T-Centralen's cave-like blue vines (answer = the metro art gallery).
topics.source: WebSearch (2026-07): Wikipedia 'Vasa (ship)', 'Vasa Museum', 'Geography of Stockholm'; visitstockholm.com ('world's longest art gallery' metro); dailyscandinavian.com (14 islands).
topics.framing_note: Voice: PLACE and its water-geography lead; invert on the archipelago (14 islands -> 30,000). Accuracy rail: the Baltic-preservation science is the real reason the Vasa survived (brackish, low-oxygen water blocks shipworm) -- state it as the mechanism, ~98% original wood; keep '1628 sank / 1961 raised / 333 years' exact so a swapped-number distractor stays wrong. Dinner-test payoff: a 17th-century warship pulled up almost whole after 333 years (T4). LANE BORDER: the shipworm is an animal -- name it only as the agent the Baltic water excludes; the answer stays the PLACE/preservation fact.

topics.name: Tallinn
topics.strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
topics.scope: Estonia's capital, a medieval walled town that still works. T1: Tallinn's Old Town is a fairy-tale medieval city that people still live and work in -- cobbled lanes, red-tiled roofs, and a ring of stone walls topped with pointed watchtowers (answer = the intact walled medieval town). T2: invert the wonder -- of the town wall's original 46 towers, about half still stand, making it one of the best-preserved medieval city walls in northern Europe (the surviving array of towers is the hook; 'the medieval town wall' the answer). T2: the town has an upstairs and a downstairs: Toompea, the upper town perched on a limestone hill for nobles, clergy and rulers (Estonia's parliament sits there today), and the merchants' lower town below (answer = Toompea, the upper town on the hill; teach the two-level plan). T3: Tallinn grew wealthy as a HANSEATIC League trading city, and its merchants' guildhalls and spired churches survive nearly intact -- UNESCO-listed since 1997 (answer = a Hanseatic trading city). T4: Toompea's hill is a natural limestone cliff -- part of the Baltic Klint, a great pale escarpment that runs for hundreds of km along the coast, giving the upper town its natural rampart (answer = the limestone klint/escarpment; teach escarpment).
topics.source: WebSearch (2026-07): UNESCO WHC list #822 (Historic Centre of Tallinn); Wikipedia 'Tallinn Old Town'; historyhit.com (Tallinn Old Town, 46 towers).
topics.framing_note: Voice: place-anchored, Tallinn/Toompea named in the stem; the wonder is the near-complete survival of a whole medieval town. Accuracy rail: '46 original towers, about half surviving' -- keep the fraction honest (roughly 20-26 stand today per sources); the Baltic Klint escarpment is real geology worth teaching. Dinner-test payoff: a living medieval town whose stone wall still bristles with watchtowers (T1-T2). LANE BORDER: the Hanseatic League's TRADE/economics stays a place-identity fact here, not an economics lesson.

topics.name: Vienna
topics.strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
topics.scope: The Habsburg imperial capital on the Danube, the 'City of Music'. T1: at the Prater fairground the giant red Ferris wheel (the Riesenrad), built in 1897, turns slowly over the city -- one of the world's oldest, and for decades the tallest Ferris wheel on Earth (answer = the Riesenrad / long the world's tallest). T2: the WALTZ -- the whirling close-hold three-step dance -- was born in Vienna's ballrooms and was once banned as scandalously improper until the Congress of Vienna (1814-15) made it respectable; Johann Strauss II, the 'Waltz King', turned it into the city's signature (answer = the waltz, born in Vienna's ballrooms). T2: Viennese coffee-house culture is so distinctive that UNESCO listed it as 'intangible cultural heritage' in 2011 -- one small coffee buys a marble table for hours, with newspapers clipped on wooden frames (answer = the coffee house, a UNESCO cultural treasure). T3: the Ringstrasse -- Emperor Franz Joseph in 1857 ordered the old medieval city walls torn DOWN and replaced with a grand tree-lined boulevard ringed by monumental buildings (answer = the boulevard built where the city walls once stood). T3: at the Central Cemetery (Zentralfriedhof), a cluster of honorary graves holds Beethoven, Schubert, Brahms and Strauss side by side -- yet Mozart isn't really there: he has only a monument, his true grave lost in an unmarked pauper's plot across town (answer = the composers' graves / Mozart's grave is lost). T4: the Spanish Riding School in the Hofburg, founded in 1572, is the world's OLDEST classical dressage academy still running, where white Lipizzaner stallions perform leaps called 'airs above the ground' (answer = the school / oldest riding academy). T4: the Hofburg palace was the winter seat of the Habsburg dynasty for over 600 years, the heart of an empire (answer = the Habsburg palace). T5: Vienna is the 'City of Music' because Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven all lived and worked within its walls -- the birthplace of what's called the First Viennese School (answer = Vienna, home of the great classical composers).
topics.source: WebSearch (2026-07): Wikipedia 'Wiener Riesenrad', 'Spanish Riding School'; wien.info / austria.info (official Vienna tourism: Viennese waltz, coffeehouse culture UNESCO 2011, Ringstrasse); visitingvienna.com (Riesenrad, Zentralfriedhof composers).
topics.framing_note: Voice: the CREATION born in the place is the wonder (the waltz, the coffee house) -- Vienna is always the anchor in the stem. Accuracy rail: state the waltz was 'popularized/made respectable' at the Congress of Vienna, not literally invented in one night; the coffee-house UNESCO listing is 2011, the waltz listing 2017 -- keep them distinct so a swapped-date distractor stays wrong. Dinner-test payoff: Mozart's grave being LOST while lesser names lie in honor (T3). LANE BORDER: the Lipizzaner is a horse -- its biology (foals born dark, coats turning white by age 6-10) belongs to the ANIMAL bank; keep this rung's answer the PLACE/institution (the 450-year-old riding school in the Hofburg), a one-line horse mention at most.

topics.name: Wieliczka Salt Mine
topics.strand: Cities of central, northern & eastern Europe
topics.scope: A satellite gem just outside Krakow: a 700-year-old salt mine turned underground cathedral. T1: below the town of Wieliczka near Krakow, miners dug salt for some 700 years (from the 13th century until 1996) -- and deep in the tunnels they carved an entire CHAPEL, St Kinga's Chapel, out of the rock itself: altar, statues, staircases and even the floor tiles (answer = the underground salt chapel). T2: everything that glitters in that chapel is SALT -- the 'crystal' chandeliers, the carved reliefs of Bible scenes, the altar -- all cut by miners from grey, faintly see-through rock salt; lick a wall and it tastes of salt (answer = it is all carved from rock salt). T3: the mine chases a thick bed of rock salt left behind when an ancient sea slowly dried up and evaporated long ago -- following it, miners hollowed out passages reaching 327 m deep and stretching over 287 km underground (answer = salt from a dried-up ancient sea / an evaporite bed).
topics.source: WebFetch (2026-07): Wikipedia 'Wieliczka Salt Mine' -- confirmed: operated ~700 years (13th c. to 1996), depth 327 m, over 287 km of passages, chapels and statues carved by miners from rock salt.
topics.framing_note: Voice: the wonder is that a mine became a cathedral of salt -- Wieliczka named in the stem. Accuracy rail: depth (327 m) and passage length (287 km) are Wikipedia-confirmed; the geological detail 'an ancient sea dried up' is the general (true) mechanism for a rock-salt/evaporite bed -- the build's research should confirm the exact Miocene age (~13-14 million years) before stating a number, so seed it as 'an ancient sea that evaporated' not a hard date. Dinner-test payoff: a full cathedral -- chandeliers and all -- carved from salt (T1). Note: this is a distinct site near Krakow, not part of the city proper; kept as a mini because it is a canonical UNESCO geography wonder.

strands.strand: Cities of the Middle East & North Africa

topics.name: Alexandria
topics.strand: Cities of the Middle East & North Africa
topics.scope: Alexander's Mediterranean city, home to two vanished wonders. T2: founded by Alexander the Great in 331 BC, Alexandria guarded its harbor with a ~110 m tower of fire -- one of the Seven Wonders -- the PHAROS lighthouse. T3: the Pharos toppled in a chain of medieval EARTHQUAKES, and its stones were reused to build a fort still standing on the very spot -- Fort Qaitbay. T3: Alexandria held the ancient world's greatest LIBRARY, which set out to collect every book on Earth. T4 (dinner-test): ships entering the harbor were searched for scrolls, which were COPIED for the Library -- and often the original kept and the copy handed back. T4: under the modern city lie Roman burial halls that blend Egyptian, Greek, and Roman art in one carved tomb -- the CATACOMBS of Kom el Shoqafa. T4: a lone 25 m granite column the crusaders misnamed still stands -- 'POMPEY'S PILLAR,' actually raised for the emperor Diocletian. T5: it was in Alexandria that Eratosthenes measured the whole EARTH'S size from the angle of a shadow, around 240 BC.
topics.source: Grokipedia (Lighthouse of Alexandria) checked first; corroborated by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lighthouse_of_Alexandria, Britannica 'Lighthouse of Alexandria'. Verified: ~100-130 m Pharos, Seven Wonders, damaged by quakes AD 956-1303 (destructive 1303), Fort Qaitbay built ~1477 from its stones; founded 331 BC.
topics.framing_note: Place = Alexandria; the ships-searched-for-scrolls rung is the dinner-test. Accuracy rail: the Library's loss was GRADUAL (fires, funding decline, neglect over centuries) -- do NOT assert one dramatic burning by Caesar destroyed it; the Pharos fell to earthquakes. 'Pompey's Pillar' is a genuine MISNAME -- flag it. Distractors live as the other Seven Wonders and other ancient libraries (Pergamon, Ashurbanipal's at Nineveh, Celsus at Ephesus).
topics.history_overlap: Cleopatra / Caesar episodes belong to history -- keep these rungs anchored to the PLACE and its structures to avoid overlap; integrator should check.

topics.name: Baghdad
topics.strand: Cities of the Middle East & North Africa
topics.scope: The Abbasid capital where a golden age of learning was born on the Tigris. T2 (named shape): Caliph al-Mansur built Baghdad in 762 as a perfectly ROUND city -- circular walls with the palace at the exact center. T3: Baghdad's HOUSE OF WISDOM gathered scholars who translated Greek, Persian, and Indian books into Arabic and pushed math and astronomy forward. T3 (dinner-test, born here): a Baghdad scholar, al-Khwarizmi, wrote the book that gave us the word 'ALGEBRA' -- and his own name became the word 'algorithm.' T4 (vivid): in 1258 the Mongols sacked Baghdad and hurled so many books into the Tigris that the river was said to run BLACK WITH INK. T4 (earth/place): Baghdad sits between the Tigris and Euphrates in MESOPOTAMIA -- 'the land between the rivers,' the ancient cradle of cities. T5 (surviving place): one Abbasid college still stands -- the 13th-century MUSTANSIRIYA MADRASA on the Tigris, among the oldest universities on Earth still in use.
topics.source: Grokipedia (House of Wisdom / Baghdad) checked first; corroborated by Britannica 'Bayt al-Hikmah', en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Wisdom. Verified: al-Mansur's Round City founded 762; House of Wisdom flourished under Harun al-Rashid & al-Ma'mun, largest book repository by mid-9th c, al-Khwarizmi a patron; Mongol sack 1258, Tigris 'ran black with ink.'
topics.framing_note: Place = Baghdad; the Tigris-ran-black-with-ink rung is the dinner-test. Accuracy rail: the House of Wisdom and Round City are GONE -- anchor rungs to the enduring Tigris/Mesopotamia setting, to the surviving Mustansiriya, and to creations genuinely BORN here (algebra), and label vanished wonders AS vanished so no rung implies you can visit them. Distractors live as other centers of learning (Cordoba, Al-Azhar, Timbuktu) and other Mesopotamian cities (Babylon, Ur, Nineveh).
topics.history_overlap: The Abbasid golden age and the 1258 Mongol sack may be history-bank episodes -- keep the PLACE (round city, river, madrasa) the anchor; integrator should check.

topics.name: Cairo & the Giza Pyramids
topics.strand: Cities of the Middle East & North Africa
topics.scope: A ~20-million-person megacity whose western desert edge meets the last of the Seven Wonders. T1: on the desert rim of Cairo stand the last survivor of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world -- the three PYRAMIDS OF GIZA. T2 (invert the number): the Great Pyramid of Khufu rose 146 m and stayed the TALLEST building on Earth for ~3,800 years. T3: guarding the plateau is a limestone lion with a human face carved from a single rock ridge -- the GREAT SPHINX. T3: built from ~2.3 million blocks, the Great Pyramid is the ONLY one of the Seven Wonders still standing. T3: the pyramids sit on the Nile's WEST bank -- the side of the setting sun, where Egyptians placed their dead. T4: inside medieval 'Islamic Cairo' rise the Citadel of Saladin and AL-AZHAR, a university running since 972 AD. T4 (dinner-test): a living neighborhood spreads through Cairo's huge cemeteries, where families dwell among the tombs -- the CITY OF THE DEAD (al-Qarafa). T4: a medieval bazaar has traded here since the 14th century -- KHAN EL-KHALILI. T5 (earth/history): the pyramids' smooth white limestone CASING was stripped away to build medieval Cairo, exposing the stepped core we see now. T5: Cairo's Arabic name, al-Qahira, means 'the Victorious,' named for the planet Mars rising as the city was founded in 969. T5 (earth-process): the Nile's yearly flood laid black silt that made Egypt farmable -- Egyptians called their land KEMET, 'the Black Land.'
topics.source: Grokipedia (Great Pyramid / Cairo) checked first; corroborated by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza, Britannica 'Great Pyramid of Giza' and 'Pyramids of Giza'. Verified: original height 146.6 m, tallest structure ~3,800 yrs, only intact ancient Wonder, ~2.3 M blocks, Khufu's tomb; Sphinx ~73 m long / ~20 m high limestone; casing later removed.
topics.framing_note: Place = Cairo/Giza; the City of the Dead (families living among the tombs) is the dinner-test. Accuracy rail: Great Pyramid = 146 m original, only surviving ancient Wonder, ~2.3 M blocks, Khufu -- keep exact; don't repeat the debunked 'slaves built it' line (skilled paid laborers). Distractors live as other pyramids (Djoser's Step Pyramid, the Bent Pyramid, Nubian/Meroe pyramids, Chichen Itza). Ful/koshari are COOKING -- no food rung.
topics.history_overlap: The Al-Azhar founding (972) and the Kemet/Nile-flood civilization framing may touch a history-bank Egypt episode -- keep rungs anchored to the PLACE (plateau, west bank, Nile silt); integrator should check.

topics.name: Damascus
topics.strand: Cities of the Middle East & North Africa
topics.scope: A leading claimant for the oldest continuously inhabited city on Earth. T2 (invert): people have lived in Damascus without a break for thousands of years -- habitation reaches back before 2000 BC -- making it a top claimant for the world's OLDEST continuously inhabited city. T3: at its heart stands one of the oldest and grandest mosques on Earth, built 705-715 AD on an old temple-then-church site -- the UMAYYAD (Great) MOSQUE. T3 (dinner-test): inside that mosque is a shrine that Christians AND Muslims alike hold to contain the head of JOHN THE BAPTIST. T4: a Roman-era avenue still crosses the old city -- the 'STREET CALLED STRAIGHT' (Via Recta), named in the Bible's story of Paul. T4 (earth-process): Damascus is a desert OASIS fed by the Barada river spilling from the Anti-Lebanon mountains -- the green Ghouta that let a city survive on the desert's edge. T5 (craft/trade born here): patterned 'DAMASCUS STEEL' blades, prized for watery ripples in the metal, were forged and traded through the city -- and the original recipe is now LOST.
topics.source: Grokipedia (Damascus / Umayyad Mosque) checked first; corroborated by UNESCO 'Ancient City of Damascus', en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_Mosque, Britannica 'Great Mosque of Damascus'. Verified: origins 3rd millennium BC (Tell Ramad far older); Umayyad Mosque 705-715 AD by al-Walid I, earliest surviving stone mosque, John-the-Baptist head shrine; Via Recta the Roman decumanus, ~1,500 m.
topics.framing_note: Place = Damascus; the John-the-Baptist-head shrine is the dinner-test. Accuracy rail: attribute the relic AS tradition ('Christians and Muslims believe...'); Damascus-steel's exact crucible technique is genuinely LOST/debated -- say so, don't assert a method. Keep it TIMELESS place geography -- no rung touching the modern war. Distractors live as other 'oldest city' claimants (Jericho, Aleppo, Byblos, Uruk) and other great early mosques.
topics.history_overlap: Paul's conversion on the Straight Street may be a history/theology episode -- one rung; keep it anchored to the PLACE (the surviving Roman avenue); integrator should check.

topics.name: Dubai
topics.strand: Cities of the Middle East & North Africa
topics.scope: A former pearl-diving port turned instant desert megacity of record-breaking engineering. T2 (invert): rising straight from the desert coast of the UAE is the TALLEST building in the world, 828 m of steel and glass -- the BURJ KHALIFA. T3 (dinner-test): off Dubai's shore engineers built a human-made island shaped like a PALM TREE, so large you can pick it out from space -- Palm Jumeirah. T3 (place-history): within living memory Dubai was a small port whose divers made their living hunting the Gulf's oyster beds -- PEARL DIVING -- until oil and then trade transformed it. T4 (earth/place): Dubai sits on the hot, shallow PERSIAN GULF, whose warm salty water and pearl-oyster beds made the coast rich long before any skyscraper.
topics.source: Grokipedia (Burj Khalifa / Dubai) checked; standing knowledge corroborated by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burj_Khalifa and /Palm_Jumeirah (web-search budget exhausted before a live re-verify). Facts used: Burj Khalifa 828 m, world's tallest since 2010; Palm Jumeirah artificial archipelago; Dubai a pre-oil pearling/trading port on the Persian Gulf.
topics.framing_note: Place = Dubai; the palm-shaped human-made island you can see from space is the dinner-test. This is the strand's deliberate MODERN contrast (engineering marvel vs. ancient marvels). Accuracy rail: Burj Khalifa 828 m, tallest since 2010 -- keep exact. Lane/tone: keep answers to concrete place/engineering and the pearling past, NOT luxury-brand or mall advertising. Distractors live as other tall towers (Shanghai Tower, Petronas, Empire State) and other Gulf cities / artificial islands (Abu Dhabi, Doha, The World islands).

topics.name: Fes
topics.strand: Cities of the Middle East & North Africa
topics.scope: Morocco's medieval spiritual capital and its labyrinth medina. T2 (invert & dinner-test): in Fes stands what Guinness records as the world's OLDEST still-running university -- founded in 859 AD by a WOMAN, Fatima al-Fihri -- AL-QARAWIYYIN. T3: Fes el-Bali is one of the world's largest CAR-FREE urban areas -- a medieval medina of thousands of tangled lanes where deliveries still move by DONKEY. T3: the city's leather is still cured in medieval stone vats of colored dye you smell before you see -- the CHOUARA TANNERY, worked by hand for a thousand years. T4: al-Qarawiyyin's LIBRARY holds manuscripts over a thousand years old -- one of the oldest working libraries on Earth. T4: Fes was founded around 789 by the IDRISID dynasty and became Morocco's scholarly and spiritual heart. T5 (engineering): the medina's fountains, mills, and tanneries all run on the Oued Fes river, deliberately SPLIT into channels threaded through the old city.
topics.source: Grokipedia (University of al-Qarawiyyin) checked first; corroborated by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_al-Qarawiyyin, World History Encyclopedia 'Fatima Al-Fihri and Al-Qarawiyyin University', en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chouara_Tannery. Verified: founded 859 by Fatima al-Fihri, Guinness 'oldest continually operating higher-learning institution'; Chouara Tannery in Fes el-Bali, hand methods unchanged since medieval times.
topics.framing_note: Place = Fes; the oldest-university-founded-by-a-woman-in-859 rung is the dinner-test. Accuracy rail: al-Qarawiyyin founded 859 by Fatima al-Fihri, Guinness-recognized oldest continually operating -- keep exact. Lane: leatherwork is a craft BORN here (place-anchored, fine), but keep it about the tannery/place, not a how-to-tan product ladder. Distractors live as other ancient universities (Bologna, Oxford, Al-Azhar, Nalanda) and other Moroccan medinas.

topics.name: Isfahan
topics.strand: Cities of the Middle East & North Africa
topics.scope: A Safavid Persian capital so grand a proverb calls it 'half the world.' T2 (invert): Isfahan is so beautiful a Persian proverb says seeing it is like seeing HALF the world -- 'Isfahan nesf-e jahan.' T2: its heart is one of the largest public squares on Earth, ~89,600 m2, laid out around 1600 by Shah Abbas -- NAQSH-E JAHAN Square. T3: on the square's south side rises a mosque whose great dome is skinned in tens of thousands of blue tiles -- the SHAH (Imam) Mosque. T3 (dinner-test): the square doubled as a royal POLO ground, and stone goalposts from 400 years ago still stand at each end. T4: the jewel-like SHEIKH LOTFOLLAH Mosque has no minaret and no courtyard -- because it was the shah's PRIVATE family mosque. T4: the Zayanderud river is crossed by Safavid bridges that double as dams and gathering places -- the 33-arch SI-O-SE-POL. T5 (craft born here): those glowing domes get their color from lustrous glazed TILEWORK in turquoise and cobalt, a Persian craft perfected here.
topics.source: Grokipedia (Shah Abbas Square) checked first; corroborated by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naqsh-e_Jahan_Square, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Si-o-se-pol, UNESCO 'Meidan Emam, Esfahan'. Verified: square 160x560 m = 89,600 m2, built 1598-1629 under Shah Abbas I; four monuments (Shah Mosque S, Ali Qapu W, Sheikh Lotfollah E, Qeysarie Gate/Bazaar N); Si-o-se-pol 33 arches, 1599-1602.
topics.framing_note: Place = Isfahan; the square-was-a-polo-field (goalposts still standing) rung is the dinner-test. Accuracy rail: Naqsh-e Jahan ~89,600 m2, Shah Abbas I, ~1600 -- keep exact; invert the 'half the world' proverb rather than asking 'what is Isfahan's nickname?'. Distractors live as other Isfahan monuments (Ali Qapu, Khaju Bridge, Chehel Sotoun) and other great squares (Tiananmen, Red Square) and Persian sites (Persepolis, Shiraz).

topics.name: Istanbul
topics.strand: Cities of the Middle East & North Africa
topics.scope: The only great city on two continents, split by the Bosphorus strait. T1: Istanbul is the only big city that sits on TWO continents at once, Europe and Asia, split by a narrow saltwater strait -- the BOSPHORUS. T2: for nearly 1,000 years the world's largest cathedral stood here, raised in just ~6 years in 537 AD by Emperor Justinian, its vast dome seeming to float -- HAGIA SOPHIA. T3: one building lived four lives -- Hagia Sophia went church, then MOSQUE (1453), then museum, then mosque again (2020). T3: beneath the streets hides a 'sunken palace' of water -- a Byzantine reservoir of 336 marble columns, two resting on carved MEDUSA HEADS -- the Basilica Cistern. T3: before Istanbul the city was CONSTANTINOPLE, and before that the Greek town of Byzantium. T4: the city held off attackers for a thousand years behind the triple THEODOSIAN WALLS -- until 1453, when Mehmed II's giant cannon finally breached them. T4: one of the world's oldest and largest covered markets is a roofed labyrinth of ~4,000 shops -- the GRAND BAZAAR. T4 (earth/geo): the Bosphorus is not a river but a STRAIT linking the Black Sea to the Mediterranean -- the only sea-gate out of the Black Sea. T5: Ottoman sultans ruled for ~400 years from TOPKAPI PALACE above the water. T5: the six-minaret SULTAN AHMED (Blue) Mosque faces Hagia Sophia across a square.
topics.source: Grokipedia (Istanbul / Hagia Sophia) checked first; corroborated by Britannica 'Hagia Sophia', en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia and /Basilica_Cistern. Verified: built 532-537 under Justinian, architects Anthemius & Isidorus, largest cathedral ~1,000 yrs, reconverted to mosque 2020; Basilica Cistern built post-Nika-Revolt 532 (336 columns / 2 Medusa bases widely documented).
topics.framing_note: Place = Istanbul; the Medusa-head Basilica Cistern is the dinner-test payoff. Accuracy rail: Hagia Sophia = 537 AD, Justinian, largest cathedral for ~1,000 yrs -- keep those exact. Scene-led ('beneath the streets hides...'), never 'What is the capital of Turkey?'. Distractors live as other Istanbul sites (Galata Tower, Dolmabahce) and other straits (Dardanelles, Gibraltar, Hormuz). Turkish delight / kebabs are COOKING -- no food rung here.
topics.history_overlap: The 1453 fall of Constantinople to Mehmed II may be a history-bank episode -- keep that rung anchored to the WALLS/cannon as a place fact; integrator should check for a duplicate siege ladder.

topics.name: Marrakech
topics.strand: Cities of the Middle East & North Africa
topics.scope: A Moroccan 'Red City' of ochre walls at the foot of the Atlas. T2 (invert & earth-material): Marrakech is the 'Red City' because its walls and houses are built from local red-OCHRE earth (rammed pise). T2: its great square fills each night with storytellers, snake charmers, musicians, and food stalls -- a living theatre UNESCO named a Masterpiece of Oral Heritage -- JEMAA EL-FNA. T3: above the medina rises the 77 m minaret of the 12th-century KOUTOUBIA Mosque, the model for sister towers in Spain and Morocco. T3: the medina is a walled maze of covered SOUKS organized by craft -- a dyers' alley, a metalworkers' alley, a slipper alley. T4: Marrakech was founded around 1070 by the ALMORAVIDS, desert Berbers, as a caravan capital between the Sahara and the Atlas. T4 (dinner-test, teach the term): the city drinks Atlas snowmelt carried for miles underground through gently sloping tunnels -- a KHETTARA (qanat) water system.
topics.source: Grokipedia (Marrakesh) checked first; corroborated by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kutubiyya_Mosque, UNESCO 'Medina of Marrakesh', en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marrakesh. Verified: Koutoubia minaret 77 m; Jemaa el-Fna UNESCO Oral & Intangible Heritage (2001); red walls built by Ali ibn Yusuf 1122-23; founded 1070-72 by the Almoravids.
topics.framing_note: Place = Marrakech; Jemaa el-Fna as a living oral-heritage theatre is the memorable payoff (and the khettara is the teach-a-term T4). Accuracy rail: Koutoubia = 77 m; Jemaa el-Fna's UNESCO honor is for its LIVING oral tradition. Lane border: the square's food stalls exist, but a tagine/couscous rung is COOKING -- keep answers on the PLACE (the square, the ochre walls, the underground water). Distractors live as other Moroccan sites (Fes, Chefchaouen, Ait Benhaddou) and other famous squares.

topics.name: Old Sanaa
topics.strand: Cities of the Middle East & North Africa
topics.scope: A Yemeni highland capital of decorated mud-brick towers, lived in for 2,500 years. T2 (named place-form): Old Sanaa is packed with thousands of TOWER HOUSES five to nine stories tall, built of earth and brick and iced with white gypsum patterns like gingerbread. T3 (teach the term): their upper rooms glow through fan-shaped stained-glass windows set in gypsum -- QAMARIYA windows. T3 (label legend): people have lived in Sanaa without a break for more than 2,500 years -- legend even credits its founding to Shem, a son of Noah. T4: you enter the walled old city through a great fortified gate -- BAB AL-YEMEN. T4 (engineering): the lower floors are heavy STONE and the upper floors lighter rammed earth and fired brick -- a design that let mud towers rise nine stories and stand for centuries. T5 (dinner-test): the Great Mosque of Sanaa, one of Islam's oldest, hid in its roof a PALIMPSEST -- an early Quran written over an even older erased text (the 'Sanaa manuscript').
topics.source: Grokipedia (Old City of Sana'a) checked first; corroborated by UNESCO WHS 'Old City of Sana'a', en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sana'a, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sana'a_manuscript. Verified: 6,000+ multi-story tower houses (stone base, rammed-earth/fired-brick upper), white gypsum decoration, qamariya windows, inhabited 2,500+ yrs, UNESCO 1986 (in danger); Sanaa palimpsest = early Quranic manuscript.
topics.framing_note: Place = Sanaa; the qamariya windows and the roof-hidden Sanaa palimpsest are the memorable payoffs. Accuracy rail: 2,500+ yrs inhabited is solid; the Shem/son-of-Noah founding is LEGEND -- label it. Keep it timeless place geography -- no rung touching the current war. Distractors live as other mud/earth-brick cities (Shibam, Djenne, Timbuktu, Bam).

topics.name: Shibam
topics.strand: Cities of the Middle East & North Africa
topics.scope: A 16th-century walled town of mud-brick high-rises, the 'Manhattan of the Desert.' T3 (dinner-test, named place): in a Yemeni desert valley stands a cluster of ~500 mud-brick TOWER BLOCKS five to eleven stories high, packed tight inside a wall -- explorer Freya Stark called it the 'MANHATTAN OF THE DESERT' (Shibam). T4 (invert): Shibam is the OLDEST city on Earth built vertically -- the first true skyscraper city, raised entirely from sun-dried MUD BRICK about 500 years ago. T5 (engineering): the towers are wider at the base and thinner as they climb -- the walls TAPER because the upper bricks are made smaller, spreading the weight so mud can stand ~30 m tall.
topics.source: Grokipedia (Shibam) checked; corroborated by National Geographic 'This Ancient Mud Skyscraper City is the Manhattan of the Desert', en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shibam, ArchDaily. Verified: ~500 mud-brick tower houses 5-11 stories, 16th c, oldest metropolis built vertically, walls taper upward, Freya Stark coined 'Manhattan of the desert' in the 1930s.
topics.framing_note: Place = Shibam; the 'Manhattan of the Desert' mud-brick skyscrapers ARE the dinner-test. Accuracy rail: ~500 towers, 5-11 stories, sun-dried mud brick, 16th c, tapering walls; attribute the nickname to Freya Stark. Distinct from Sanaa (decorated tower-house capital) -- this ladder is the SKYSCRAPER-cluster gem. Distractors live as other earthen architecture (Sanaa, Djenne's Great Mosque, Taos Pueblo, Bam citadel).

topics.name: Death Valley
topics.scope: A below-sea-level furnace in California's Mojave. T1: Furnace Creek recorded 56.7 C (134 F) on July 10, 1913 — the hottest reliable AIR temperature ever measured on Earth (some experts dispute the exact reading; note it). T2: Badwater Basin is the lowest point in North America, 86 m BELOW sea level — a bright salt flat cracked into hexagons. T3: on Racetrack Playa, heavy 'sailing stones' glide across the flat mud leaving long trails behind them; the mystery was SOLVED in 2014 — thin sheets of winter ice, floated by meltwater and nudged by light wind, drag the rocks. T4: Death Valley is a rain-shadow desert — five mountain ranges strip Pacific storms of their moisture before they ever reach the valley floor. T5: after a rare wet winter the dead-looking floor erupts in a 'superbloom' of wildflowers from seeds that waited years. Extra rung: the valley is still sinking as the crust pulls apart (Basin and Range extension).
topics.source: Grokipedia (checked first) + Wikipedia 'Death Valley' and 'Highest temperature recorded on Earth'; NPS Death Valley weather pages; PNAS/Scripps 2014 sailing-stones study (Norris & Lorenz). Verified: 56.7 C air record July 10 1913 (disputed by some); Badwater -86 m; sailing stones solved 2014 (ice + wind).
topics.framing_note: Scene-led; invert the superlative (the 134 F record is the hook). Accuracy rail: 1913 is the hottest reliably-recorded AIR temperature — keep it DISTINCT from the Lut Desert's satellite SURFACE-temperature record (a perfect adjacent distractor). The sailing-stones answer is the SOLVED mechanism (ice + wind), a settled 2014 finding — NOT 'still a mystery'. Dinner-test payoff: the self-moving sailing stones (T3).

topics.name: The 'Door to Hell' (Darvaza gas crater)
topics.scope: A crater of fire in Turkmenistan's Karakum Desert. T1: in the middle of the Karakum sand sits the 'Door to Hell' (Darvaza) — a ~70-m-wide crater that has been ON FIRE continuously for over 50 years. T2: it wasn't natural — a Soviet gas-drilling rig collapsed into an underground cavern (commonly dated ~1971, though the date is disputed) and engineers set the escaping methane alight, expecting it to burn out in days; it never stopped. T3: Turkmenistan now wants to put it out or tap the gas, because the crater has leaked and burned methane for half a century.
topics.source: Grokipedia 'Darvaza gas crater' (checked first) + Wikipedia 'Darvaza gas crater'; Popular Science and Discover Wildlife on recent extinguishing efforts. Verified: ~60-70 m wide, ~30 m deep; burning since ~1971 (date disputed, possibly 1980s); Soviet drilling collapse and deliberate ignition is the standard but not fully documented account; Turkmenistan seeking to reduce/extinguish it.
topics.framing_note: A short 'strange place' gem, scene first. Accuracy rail: the exact ignition DATE is disputed (commonly 1971, possibly 1980s) and the 'lit deliberately to burn off gas' account is the standard but not fully documented story — hedge as such, no false precision. Dinner-test payoff: it's been burning nonstop for 50+ years (T1). Human-made, but a genuine famous desert landmark — geography's 'strange place' lane, no lane conflict.

topics.name: The Atacama
topics.scope: A hyperarid desert down Chile's northern coast. T1: the Atacama is the driest nonpolar place on Earth — some weather stations have NEVER recorded a drop of rain, and parts may go decades between showers. T2: its skies are the clearest and driest anywhere, so the world's great telescopes live here — ALMA on the Chajnantor plateau and the Very Large Telescope on Cerro Paranal (invert: the no-rain/clear-sky superlative is the hook, 'the world's observatories' the answer). T3: NASA tests Mars rovers here because the sterile, bone-dry soil is Earth's closest match to the surface of Mars (a 'Mars analog'). T4: once every few years a freak rain wakes long-dormant seeds and the sand erupts into the 'desierto florido' — the flowering desert — a carpet of millions of blooms. T5: the Chinchorro people mummified their dead on this coast ~7,000 years ago — the world's OLDEST artificial mummies, made ~2,000 years before Egypt's. Extra rungs (deep): the 86-m Atacama Giant geoglyph on Cerro Unita (purpose debated); the salt pillars of Valle de la Luna; the nitrate 'white gold' ghost town of Humberstone (UNESCO); the lithium-rich brine of the Salar de Atacama.
topics.source: Grokipedia (checked first) + Wikipedia 'Atacama Desert' and 'Chinchorro mummies'; ESO / NASA on Atacama observatories and Mars-analog research; National Geographic and Ancient Origins on Chinchorro. Verified: driest nonpolar desert with stations lacking recorded rain; ALMA/VLT sites; Chinchorro artificial mummification from ~5050 BC, ~2,000 yr before Egypt.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led wonder tour. Accuracy rail: state 'driest' carefully — some STATIONS have no recorded rain, but coastal fog (camanchaca) still brings moisture, so frame as 'driest nonpolar desert', not 'no water ever'. The Atacama Giant's meaning is DISPUTED (astronomical calendar?) — label it. Dinner-test payoff: the Chinchorro mummies (T5), oldest on Earth, a cultural creation genuinely born in this desert (geography's lane: the place + its people's marvel, not a history-bank episode). Distractors: other real driest/clearest-sky places and other ancient mummy cultures keep all four live.

topics.name: The Gobi
topics.scope: A cold rain-shadow desert across Mongolia and northern China. T1: the Gobi is a COLD desert — a place where summer can hit +45 C yet winter plunges to -40 C, colder than most of Canada. T2: it exists because it sits in the RAIN SHADOW of the Himalayas and Tibetan Plateau — the mountains wring the monsoon dry before it can reach the basin (teach 'rain shadow'). T3: at the red-sandstone Flaming Cliffs (Bayanzag), Roy Chapman Andrews's 1923 expedition found the world's first recognized dinosaur EGGS — the discovery that proved dinosaurs laid eggs. T4: the Khongoryn Els or 'Singing Dunes' boom a deep drone as sand avalanches down slopes ~300 m tall. T5: the Gobi is the last wild refuge of the two-humped Bactrian camel — fewer than ~1,000 truly wild ones remain (place-fact: the desert is its last stronghold). Extra rung: the Gobi is slowly GROWING toward Beijing, driving China's tree-planting 'Great Green Wall'.
topics.source: Grokipedia 'Flaming Cliffs' (checked first) + Wikipedia 'Gobi Desert' and 'Flaming Cliffs'; AMNH on Roy Chapman Andrews and the 1923 dinosaur-egg discovery. Verified: cold-desert temperature swing; rain-shadow origin; 1923 first recognized dinosaur eggs at Bayanzag; wild Bactrian camel last refuge.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led. Accuracy rail: teach 'rain shadow' before testing it; the dinosaur-egg find is 1923 at the Flaming Cliffs (Roy Chapman Andrews, a real paleontologist — not a movie hero). Dinner-test payoff: the first dinosaur eggs ever found (T3). Lane border: the Bactrian-camel rung's ANSWER stays a PLACE-fact (the Gobi is its last wild home), NOT the camel's hump biology (that's the animal bank). Distractors: other cold deserts and other famous fossil sites keep choices live.

topics.name: The Kalahari
topics.scope: A red 'thirstland' across Botswana and Namibia. T1: the Kalahari's sand glows rusty RED from iron oxide — but it's a semi-desert 'thirstland,' not a true desert, catching just enough rain for grass and scattered trees. T2: the Okavango River pours INTO the Kalahari and dies there, fanning out into the Okavango Delta — a vast green wetland that never reaches any sea (teach 'endorheic' / inland delta). T3: the blinding Makgadikgadi salt pans are the ghost of a giant ancient lake — Lake Makgadikgadi — once bigger than Switzerland, which dried up thousands of years ago. T4: marooned on that white salt sea sits Kubu Island, a rocky ridge of ancient baobab trees that once stood on the vanished lake's shore. T5: the central Kalahari is the ancestral land of the San (Bushmen), among Earth's oldest continuous cultures, who find water in the driest sand through buried tsama melons and 'sip-wells' (knowledge born of this place).
topics.source: Grokipedia (checked first) + Wikipedia 'Kalahari Desert', 'Okavango Delta', 'Lake Makgadikgadi', 'Makgadikgadi Pan'; UNESCO Okavango Delta listing.
