LANE: the caves DEPICT animals, but the wonder is the ART and the PLACE -- keep answers about the paintings/caves, never a painted creature's biology (that would be the animal bank).

topics.name: The Pantheon (Rome's unbeaten concrete dome)
topics.scope: The Pantheon in Rome, a temple rebuilt under Hadrian (~AD 118-128). T1: nearly 1,900 years on, the Pantheon still wears the largest UNREINFORCED concrete dome on Earth -- no modern concrete dome built without steel has ever surpassed it. T2: the dome is a perfect half-sphere -- its height equals its interior width (43.3 m) -- so a full 43-meter ball would fit exactly inside. T3: at the very top gapes the oculus, a ~9-meter hole open to the open sky; rain really does fall through it and drains away through slanted holes in the sloped marble floor (teach: oculus means 'eye'). T4: the Romans made the concrete LIGHTER toward the top -- heavy travertine chips near the base, light volcanic pumice near the oculus -- so the dome would not crush itself under its own weight. T5: almost every other ancient Roman temple was quarried away for its stone -- the Pantheon survived nearly intact because in AD 609 it was converted into a Christian church.
topics.source: Grokipedia (checked first, automated fetch blocked); corroborated on Wikipedia: Pantheon, Rome -- verified 'still the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome'; 43.3 m equal height/diameter with a fitting sphere; oculus with sloped drained floor; lightweight-aggregate gradient (travertine to tufa/pumice); Hadrian rebuild with the Agrippa inscription; survival via conversion to a church in 609.
topics.framing_note: Voice: INVERT THE WONDER -- put the record (biggest unreinforced concrete dome, still) in the stem as the hook. Accuracy rail: keep it precise to 'unreinforced concrete dome' (not all domes), and teach 'oculus' before testing it. Dinner-test payoff: rain actually falling through the open oculus, and the still-champion concrete dome. LANE: the Hadrian/Agrippa attribution is a mild history point -- geography keeps the PLACE and its engineering. Note a light cross-link: the Rome city-ladder samples the Pantheon's oculus among several Rome wonders; this ladder deep-dives the single monument.
topics.history_overlap: The Hadrian-rebuilt / Agrippa-inscription attribution is a minor history point; keep the ladder on the building's engineering (the concrete dome, oculus, weight gradient, its survival).

topics.name: Troy (the mound of Hisarlik)
topics.scope: A grassy mound called Hisarlik in northwest Turkey, the site of legendary Troy. T1: Hisarlik is not ONE Troy but at least nine cities stacked on top of each other over ~3,000 years, piling ~15 m of ruins into a single hill (each city built on the rubble of the last). T2: Homer's Iliad set the Trojan War at this place; the walls and towers are real, but the wooden-horse trick survives only as legend -- no horse was ever dug up. T3: in the 1870s Heinrich Schliemann used Homer as a treasure-map and drove a huge trench into the mound -- and his crude digging cut straight THROUGH the layer thought to be Homer's Troy, wrecking part of it. T4: the gold hoard he trumpeted as 'Priam's Treasure' came from the Troy II layer -- a city roughly 1,000 years too OLD to be King Priam's (the war-era city is Troy VI/VIIa, ~1250 BC). T5: at the Troy VIIa level archaeologists found a burn layer, scattered sling-stones and arrowheads, and bodies left unburied -- physical hints that a real city here was stormed and destroyed around the time of Homer's tale.
topics.source: Grokipedia (grokipedia.com) checked first for Troy/Schliemann (blocked to automated fetch, 403); corroborated with well-established encyclopedic accounts (Wikipedia: Troy; Hisarlik; Heinrich Schliemann; Priam's Treasure). Layer dating (Troy I-IX, Troy VI/VIIa as candidate war city) and the Troy II misdating of 'Priam's Treasure' are standard archaeological consensus.
topics.framing_note: Voice: PLACE->WONDER, lead with the scene (the layered hill), never 'Who found Troy?'. The accuracy rail is the LEGEND flag -- the wooden horse is myth (say so) and 'Priam's Treasure' is famously misdated (the treasure is real, the Priam label is wrong). Dinner-test payoff: the 'nine cities in one hill' rung and the 'treasure is 1,000 years too old' rung. Distractors stay live with other real Bronze-Age/archaeology facts, never the deduced answer. LANE: the Trojan War narrative and Schliemann's biography are the HISTORY bank's -- geography keeps the PLACE (the stratified mound, the destruction stratum, the walls).
topics.history_overlap: The Trojan War as a Homeric/history episode and Heinrich Schliemann's biography likely appear in a history-bank ladder; keep geography anchored to the physical mound and its stacked cities, not the war narrative or Schliemann's life story.

topics.name: Ajanta Caves
topics.scope: A horseshoe of caves cut into a river-gorge cliff in India, hiding the finest ancient paintings in Asia. T2: some 30 Buddhist halls and monasteries were carved into the curving cliff above a bend of the Waghora river (answer = 30 rock-cut caves). T3: on their walls survive the largest body of ancient Indian PAINTING -- glowing frescoes of the Buddha's past lives (answer = the Ajanta frescoes / Jataka tales). T3: the most famous single figure is a gentle, downcast-eyed prince holding a blue lotus (answer = the Bodhisattva Padmapani). T4: after the site fell silent, jungle hid it for over a thousand years -- until 1819, when a British officer chasing a TIGER stumbled onto a cave mouth (answer = rediscovered on a tiger hunt, 1819). T4/T5: the caves come in two kinds -- living-quarters for monks, and pillared worship-halls built around a stupa (answer = viharas and chaitya halls). T5: they were cut in two bursts centuries apart, the finest work under the 5th-century Vakataka emperor Harishena before being abruptly abandoned (answer = two phases / the 460-480 CE Vakataka phase).
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajanta_Caves (30 rock-cut Buddhist caves above the Waghora, phases ~2nd c BCE and 460-480 CE under Vakataka emperor Harishena, Jataka-tale wall paintings, Bodhisattva Padmapani, rediscovered 1819 by British officer John Smith on a tiger hunt, viharas + chaitya-grihas).
topics.framing_note: Place ladder; the tiger-hunt rediscovery (T4) is the dinner-test payoff, the Padmapani fresco the signature image. Scene-led. Distractors = Ellora, other painted caves (Sigiriya, Dunhuang), other bodhisattvas, all real. Keep answers to the caves and their art, not the general history of Buddhism.
topics.history_overlap: Harishena and Vakataka dynastic history belong to history; the 1819 rediscovery is a place-fact (surface it here), but keep it about the SITE, not colonial administration.

topics.name: Angkor Thom & the Bayon
topics.scope: The last great walled capital of the Khmer Empire, raised by Jayavarman VII, with the Bayon temple at its exact center. T2: from the Bayon's towers, more than 200 giant serene stone FACES gaze out in every direction, each wearing the same faint smile (answer = the smiling stone faces of the Bayon). T3: those faces are read two ways at once -- as a Buddhist bodhisattva of compassion AND as the god-king himself (answer = Avalokiteshvara). T3: you enter the 9-square-km city through monumental gate-towers each crowned with four more of those outward-gazing faces (answer = the face-towers / gopura gates). T4: the Bayon's lower galleries carve not gods but ORDINARY LIFE -- a market, a cockfight, a woman giving birth, a naval battle on the Tonle Sap (answer = everyday life of the Khmer). T4/T5: Jayavarman VII switched the empire's state religion, which is why his capital's temple is Buddhist where Angkor Wat began Hindu (answer = Mahayana Buddhism). T5: a causeway into the city is lined with rows of stone giants gripping a serpent -- the Churning of the Ocean of Milk rebuilt as a bridge (answer = the gods-and-demons causeway).
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayon (~200 large faces, ~54 towers originally / 37 standing, Jayavarman VII late 12th-early 13th c, Avalokiteshvara-and/or-king dual reading, everyday-life bas-reliefs, Mahayana Buddhist state temple); Angkor Thom layout (9 sq km walled city, face-gates, causeway) from established domain knowledge.
topics.framing_note: Place ladder anchored on the Bayon/Angkor Thom; the serene many-faced towers are the T2 hook and dinner-test image. Scene-led, no 'what is the Bayon?' definition shell. Label the faces' identity as scholarly READING (bodhisattva AND king) rather than settled fact -- accuracy rail. Distractors = other Angkor temples and other Buddhist/Hindu iconography, all real. Keep answers to the site's carvings and layout.
topics.history_overlap: Jayavarman VII's reign and the empire's political peak belong to history; keep answers to the faces, gates, everyday-life reliefs, and the causeway.

topics.name: Angkor Wat
topics.scope: The largest religious monument on Earth, a 12th-century temple-city in the Cambodian jungle covering ~400 acres (162 ha). T1: its five stone towers are built to model a sacred mountain from Hindu myth, the home of the gods (invert the wonder: 'the world's biggest temple is a map of the cosmos' is the hook; answer = Mount Meru). T1 bonus: it is the only building pictured on any national flag (answer = Cambodia's flag). T2: the wide moat ringing the temple isn't just defense -- on the cosmic map it stands for the primordial ocean at the world's rim (answer = the cosmic ocean). T2/T3: nearly every Khmer temple faces the sunrise, but Angkor Wat faces the OPPOSITE way, which scholars tie to the god Vishnu and to death (answer = it faces west). T3: a 49-metre carved gallery shows gods and demons hauling a giant serpent to churn the sea for the elixir of immortality (answer = the Churning of the Ocean of Milk). T3: unlike its jungle-swallowed neighbours, Angkor Wat was never truly abandoned -- one community kept worshipping here, which is why it survived intact (answer = Buddhist monks). T4: it began as a shrine to the Hindu god Vishnu, then Cambodia's changing faith reconsecrated it to the religion it still serves (answer = Buddhism). T4: its 5-10 million sandstone blocks were floated ~50 km from one quarry-mountain by canal (answer = Phnom Kulen / Mount Kulen). T5: airborne laser scanning finally mapped 'greater Angkor' beneath the forest as one of the largest pre-industrial cities on Earth, ~1,000 sq km (answer = LIDAR). T5: the whole city ran on giant reservoirs called barays, a water grid whose failure in drought helped doom Angkor (answer = the barays / West Baray).
topics.source: Grokipedia (checked first per source priority; returned 403 at fetch time); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angkor_Wat (Guinness 'largest religious structure' 162.6 ha, Suryavarman II 1122-1150, Vishnu->Buddhist, five towers=Mount Meru / moat=cosmic ocean, west-facing, 49 m Churning-of-the-Ocean-of-Milk relief, Phnom Kulen sandstone ~40-50 km, LIDAR-revealed greater Angkor + barays, on Cambodia's flag).
topics.framing_note: Scene-led place ladder: every stem names Angkor Wat and the scene; the player must KNOW the wonder (Mount Meru, the west orientation, the Churning relief), never deduce it from a stem clause. Invert the wonder on T1 -- lead with 'the world's largest temple' as HOOK, make Mount Meru the answer. Distractors = other real Angkor/Khmer features and other world temples so all four stay live. Respect the Hindu-Buddhist cosmology as genuine sacred meaning, no smug secular gloss. Dinner-test payoff = the LIDAR-revealed hidden mega-city (T5) and the only-building-on-a-flag gem.
topics.history_overlap: Suryavarman II's reign, the Khmer Empire's rise, and the 15th-century abandonment/relocation to Phnom Penh are history-bank episodes -- keep every answer a place-wonder (towers, moat, orientation, relief, sandstone source, LIDAR extent, barays), not a dynasty timeline.

topics.name: Bagan
topics.scope: A plain in Myanmar where, at dawn, hot-air balloons drift over thousands of brick spires poking out of the mist along the Irrawaddy. T1: this ~40-square-mile plain is studded with temples and pagodas -- not dozens but THOUSANDS (invert the wonder: the balloon-at-dawn scene is the hook; answer = over 2,000 surviving temples). T2: at its 11th-13th-century height as the Pagan Kingdom's capital, the count was even more staggering before time and quakes thinned it (answer = more than 10,000 originally). T3: the whitewashed, gilded Ananda is the plain's most beloved temple, its dim corridors lit to reveal towering standing Buddhas (answer = the Ananda Temple). T3: the massive, brooding Dhammayangyi is the LARGEST temple on the plain, its inner sanctums mysteriously bricked up (answer = Dhammayangyi). T4: the plain sits in an active seismic zone -- a 2016 earthquake damaged nearly 400 monuments in a single day (answer = the 2016 earthquake). T5: nearly every structure here is BRICK, not carved stone like Angkor or Borobudur -- which is why Bagan reads as a forest of red-brown spires (answer = it is built of brick).
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bagan (Pagan Kingdom capital 9th-13th c, >10,000 temples originally / >2,200 surviving, Ananda ~1105, Dhammayangyi largest 1167-70, 2016 earthquake damaged ~400 monuments, 104 sq km on the Irrawaddy).
topics.framing_note: Place ladder; the sea-of-thousands-of-spires-at-dawn is the T1 hook and dinner-test image. Invert the wonder -- lead with the balloon-at-dawn scene, make the count and the named temples the answers, never 'what is the largest temple city?'. Distractors = Angkor, Borobudur, other temple-cities, other named Bagan temples. The 2016 quake is the earth-process anchor; keep answers place-facts.
topics.history_overlap: Pagan Kingdom political history and its fall to the Mongols belong to history; keep answers to the plain, the named temples, the brick, and the quake.

topics.name: Borobudur
topics.scope: The largest Buddhist monument on Earth, a 9th-century stone mountain on Java you climb like a pilgrim. T1: seen from above, the whole monument forms one giant geometric diagram of the Buddhist universe -- a shape you walk (answer = a mandala). T1/T2: you don't go INSIDE Borobudur; you spiral UP its terraces from base to summit, and the climb itself is the journey through the cosmos (answer = you climb it / it's a walked pilgrimage). T2: ringing the top terraces sit 72 bell-shaped stone cages, each hiding a Buddha you can just glimpse through the stone lattice (answer = the 72 perforated stupas). T3: along the galleries runs the world's most complete set of Buddhist story-carvings -- 2,672 relief panels tracing the Buddha's path (answer = the 2,672 relief panels / largest Buddhist relief series). T3: the three stacked levels have names -- the world of desire at the base, of form above, of formlessness at the crown (answer = Kamadhatu / Rupadhatu / Arupadhatu). T4: built by the Sailendra dynasty ~825 CE, then lost for centuries under jungle and volcanic ash (answer = buried under ash and jungle). T4: it stands in one of the most volcano-dense regions on Earth, in view of one of the world's most active volcanoes (answer = Mount Merapi). T5: a 1970s-80s UNESCO rescue took the monument APART -- over a million blocks numbered, cleaned, and rebuilt on a new hidden foundation (answer = dismantled and reassembled stone by stone).
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borobudur (world's largest Buddhist temple, 2,672 relief panels, 504 Buddha statues, 72 perforated stupas, Sailendra ~9th c / ~825 CE, giant mandala, three cosmological levels Kamadhatu/Rupadhatu/Arupadhatu, abandoned under volcanic ash + jungle, Raffles 1814, 1975-82 dismantle-and-rebuild with >1 million stones).
topics.framing_note: Place ladder; the mandala-you-climb is the controlling image, the 72 latticed stupas the dinner-test payoff. Scene-led -- never 'what is the largest Buddhist temple?'. Teach 'mandala' before testing it (§16 teach-before-test). Distractors = Prambanan, Bagan, other stupas, other cosmology terms, all real. Respect the pilgrimage meaning on its own terms. LANE: Merapi is the geographic/volcano anchor (the earth-process the place sits in) -- keep the answer the volcano's name/place-fact, light touch, not volcanology mechanics.
topics.history_overlap: The Sailendra dynasty's politics belong to history; keep answers to the structure, cosmology, burial, and restoration. Raffles' 1814 rediscovery can surface here as a place-fact, but the colonial-administration story leans history.

topics.name: Ellora Kailasa Temple
topics.scope: The most astonishing rock-cut monument on Earth, at Ellora in India. T2: this full-size, multi-storey Hindu temple was not built up from blocks -- it was CARVED DOWNWARD out of one solid cliff, from the top first (answer = carved top-down from a single rock). T2/T3: to free the temple, workers chiselled away and hauled out an estimated 200,000 tonnes of rock -- and there is no way to add a piece back or fix a slip (answer = ~200,000 tonnes removed / it is a single monolith). T3: it is designed as a stone model of the Himalayan peak that Hindus believe is the god Shiva's home (answer = Mount Kailash). T3: it is Cave 16, the masterpiece, in a line of 34 rock-cut caves, raised by an 8th-century Rashtrakuta king (answer = Cave 16 / King Krishna I). T4: the same Ellora cliff holds Buddhist, Hindu AND Jain cave temples side by side, cut as those faiths shared the region (answer = three religions in one cliff). T4: the temple's outer wall carves the demon-king Ravana trapped SHAKING Mount Kailash while Shiva pins the mountain with one toe (answer = Ravana shaking Kailash). T5: full-size stone elephants, courtyards, galleries and a gateway were all left standing from the living rock as the quarry was cut away around them -- nothing was assembled (answer = it is all one continuous stone).
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kailasa_Temple,_Ellora (carved top-down from a single monolith, ~200,000 tonnes of rock removed, Rashtrakuta king Krishna I 8th c, Cave 16, dedicated to Shiva / modeled on Mount Kailash, 32.6 m tall); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellora_Caves (34 rock-cut caves; Buddhist, Hindu and Jain).
topics.framing_note: Place ladder; the carved-downward-from-one-rock, no-undo fact is the controlling wonder and dinner-test payoff -- lead with it. Accuracy rail: it is a SUBTRACTIVE monolith (200,000 tonnes removed), NOT stacked blocks -- keep that precise. Teach 'rock-cut' before leaning on it. Distractors = Ajanta, Petra, other monoliths, other Shiva sites, all real. Respect it as a living Hindu temple, not a mere feat.
topics.history_overlap: Krishna I and Rashtrakuta dynastic history belong to history; keep answers to the carving method, scale, iconography, and the three-faith cliff.

topics.name: Konark Sun Temple
topics.scope: A 13th-century temple on India's Odisha coast, built as a colossal stone chariot for the sun god. T2: the entire temple is shaped as the war-chariot of Surya the sun god -- a giant vehicle carved in stone (answer = a chariot of the sun god / Surya). T3: that chariot rides on 24 huge, richly carved stone WHEELS and is pulled by seven straining stone horses (answer = 24 wheels and 7 horses). T3: the wheels aren't just decoration -- their spokes and hub work as SUNDIALS, casting shadows that tell the time of day (answer = the wheels are working sundials). T4: European sailors used it as a navigation landmark and called it the 'Black Pagoda,' opposite the 'White Pagoda' up the coast (answer = the Black Pagoda). T4/T5: its towering main spire has COLLAPSED -- only the great audience hall still stands, and legend blames a lodestone at the top that once wrecked ships' compasses (answer = the main tower collapsed / lodestone legend).
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konark_Sun_Temple (~1250 CE, King Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty, giant stone chariot of Surya with 24 carved wheels + 7 horses, wheels function as sundials, main shikhara collapsed / ~39 m jagamohana survives, 'Black Pagoda' sailors' landmark on the Odisha / Bay of Bengal coast).
topics.framing_note: Place ladder; the wheels-that-tell-time (T3) is the dinner-test payoff, the whole-temple-is-a-chariot the controlling image. Scene-led. Accuracy rail: the sundial function is real; the ship-wrecking 'lodestone at the summit' is legend -- flag it as such. Distractors = other Surya/sun temples, other chariot iconography, other coastal landmarks, all real. Keep answers to the temple's form and setting.
topics.history_overlap: Narasimhadeva I and Eastern Ganga dynastic history belong to history; keep answers to the chariot form, the wheels/sundials, the collapse, and the Black-Pagoda landmark.

topics.name: Leshan Giant Buddha
topics.scope: The largest pre-modern stone Buddha on Earth, carved into a cliff where three rivers meet in China. T2: a monk began carving this Buddha in 713 CE hoping the huge holy figure would CALM the deadly rapids that were wrecking boats at the river junction (answer = to calm the turbulent waters). T3: it is colossal -- 71 m tall, so big that a grown person is dwarfed by its EAR alone and can stand on a single toenail (answer = 71 metres / the world's largest stone Buddha). T3: it sits at the meeting of three rivers, gazing across the water at a sacred mountain (answer = the confluence of the Min, Dadu and Qingyi). T4: hidden inside the statue is an ingenious DRAINAGE system -- channels cut through its hair, collar and body carry rainwater away so it doesn't erode (answer = a hidden drainage system). T4/T5: whether or not it calmed the river spiritually, cutting it dumped so much rock into the water that the currents really were tamed (answer = the discarded rock actually calmed the currents). T5: it took ~90 years and three generations to finish, stalling when the monk's funds ran out and resuming under later patrons (answer = ~90 years, 713-803).
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leshan_Giant_Buddha (71 m, largest/tallest pre-modern stone Buddha, monk Hai Tong began 713 CE to calm turbulent waters, confluence of Min/Dadu/Qingyi facing Mount Emei, hidden internal drainage channels, ~90 years to completion ~803 CE).
topics.framing_note: Place ladder; the calm-the-rapids origin plus the hidden-drainage engineering are the dinner-test payoffs, the toenail/ear scale the T3 hook. Scene-led. Accuracy rail: keep 'it really did tame the river' as the PHYSICAL side-effect of dumped rock (fact), distinct from the spiritual intent. Distractors = other giant Buddhas (Bamiyan), other river/mountain sites, all real. Respect it as a sacred image.
topics.history_overlap: None major -- Tang-dynasty context is light; keep answers to the statue, the river confluence, and the engineering.

topics.name: Mohenjo-daro & the Indus Cities
topics.scope: One of the world's first great cities, built ~2500 BCE on the Indus -- and one of its deepest mysteries. T1: 4,500 years ago its streets were laid in a neat GRID of right angles, like a planned modern city, long before Greece or Rome (answer = a planned grid of streets). T2: nearly every house connected to covered brick DRAINS running under the streets -- the world's oldest citywide sewage system (answer = covered street drains / sewers). T3: at its heart sits a great watertight brick POOL, sealed with tar, that may be the world's oldest ritual bath (answer = the Great Bath). T3: we can read Egyptian and Sumerian writing, but the Indus people's SCRIPT has never been cracked -- thousands of tiny inscribed seals stay silent (answer = the undeciphered Indus script). T4: we don't even know what the city called itself -- its modern name just means 'Mound of the Dead' in the local tongue (answer = its true name is unknown). T4: unlike Egypt it left no giant royal tombs, no obvious king's palace or temple -- hinting at a strangely equal society (answer = no kings' palaces or tombs found). T4: two objects star from the ruins -- a poised soapstone 'Priest-King' and a tiny, confident bronze 'Dancing Girl' (answer = the Dancing Girl / Priest-King). T5: at the sister-city of Lothal, archaeologists found what may be the world's oldest DOCK, a brick basin linked to the sea (answer = the Lothal dockyard). T5: after centuries the Indus cities were quietly abandoned -- leading theories blame a shifting, drying river and a failing monsoon, not conquest (answer = river shift / monsoon failure -- flag as leading theory).
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohenjo-daro (~2500 BCE, grid plan, ~700 wells + citywide covered drainage 'one well per three houses', Great Bath 12x7 m sealed with bitumen, undeciphered Indus script, name = 'Mound of the Dead Men' in Sindhi, Priest-King soapstone + Dancing Girl bronze ~10.5 cm, abandonment); Lothal / Harappan sites (brick dockyard basin) from established domain knowledge.
topics.framing_note: Place ladder; the undeciphered-script + unknown-name pair (T3/T4) is the dinner-test mystery payoff, the covered drains the 'they had sewers before Rome' hook. Accuracy rail: label the abandonment as leading THEORY (river shift / monsoon), not settled fact, and the 'egalitarian, no kings' reading as an interpretation. Distractors = Egypt, Sumer/Ur, other early cities, other Indus sites (Harappa, Dholavira, Lothal), all real. LANE: the Dancing Girl / Priest-King are ARTIFACTS of the place (fine as place-facts); the monsoon-failure rung ties to the climate theme but keeps the answer the site's fate.
topics.history_overlap: The Indus Civilization's broad rise-and-fall as a chapter of world history overlaps history; geography keeps the URBAN wonders (grid, drains, Great Bath, script, artifacts, dockyard). A pure 'what caused the collapse' debate with no site anchor belongs to history.

topics.name: Prambanan
topics.scope: The soaring Hindu answer to Borobudur, a few miles away on the same Javanese plain. T2: where Borobudur is a low broad mandala, Prambanan spikes UPWARD -- its central tower stabs 47 m into the sky, the tallest Hindu temple in Indonesia (answer = the 47-metre central Shiva tower). T3: its three main towers honor the Hindu trinity, and the biggest belongs to the destroyer-god (answer = Shiva / the Trimurti). T4: carved along the inner balustrades, panel after panel, runs one great Indian epic of a prince, a stolen wife, and a monkey army (answer = the Ramayana). Bonus: local legend says a jilted spirit-summoner built '1,000 temples' here overnight and turned a princess to stone (answer = the Roro Jonggrang legend -- flag as folklore).
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prambanan (9th c ~850 CE, Mataram Kingdom, dedicated to the Trimurti, 47 m central Shiva temple, largest Hindu temple site in Indonesia / 2nd-largest in SE Asia, Ramayana bas-reliefs, originally 240 temples, Roro Jonggrang / 1,000-temple legend).
topics.framing_note: Short ladder that plays off Borobudur (up-spiking Hindu vs broad Buddhist) -- a deliberate contrast pair; a nearby-sister distractor keeps it live. Scene-led. Accuracy rail: label the Roro Jonggrang tale explicitly as legend. Distractors = Borobudur, Angkor, Indian temples, the other Trimurti gods. Keep answers to place/architecture facts.
topics.history_overlap: None significant.

topics.name: Sigiriya
topics.scope: A sheer rock tower jutting 180 m straight out of the Sri Lankan jungle, with a palace on top. T1: a 5th-century king built his royal palace not on a hill but on the FLAT SUMMIT of this 180-metre rock column (answer = on top of the rock). T2: the only way up once passed THROUGH a giant brick lion -- you climbed the staircase between its paws and into its open mouth, which named the rock 'Lion Rock' (answer = the Lion Gate / Sinhagiri). T3: sheltered in a rock pocket halfway up survive vivid painted 'cloud maidens,' among the oldest surviving frescoes in Sri Lanka (answer = the Sigiriya frescoes / damsels). T3: below them runs a wall once polished so glassy the king could see his own reflection walking past (answer = the Mirror Wall). T4: that Mirror Wall is now covered in over a thousand poems scratched by visitors 1,200+ years ago -- ancient graffiti admiring the maidens (answer = ancient graffiti / poems). T4/T5: King Kashyapa built this fortress-capital partly out of fear, having seized the throne from his father -- then lost his last battle at its foot (answer = King Kashyapa). T5: at the rock's base spread symmetrical water gardens whose fountains STILL spurt in the rainy season, among the oldest landscaped gardens on Earth (answer = the water gardens / working fountains).
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigiriya (~180 m granite inselberg, King Kashyapa 477-495 CE, Lion Gate / Sinhagiri, cloud-maiden frescoes, Mirror Wall with 1,500+ poems from the 8th-10th c, ancient water gardens with fountains that still work in the wet season).
topics.framing_note: Place ladder; the climb-through-a-lion's-mouth to a palace in the sky is the controlling image and dinner-test payoff. Scene-led. Kashyapa (T4/T5) is anchored to the PLACE (built it, died at its foot) so his name is a place-fact, not a bare-name answer. Distractors = other rock forts, other fresco sites, other ancient gardens, all real. Keep answers to the rock, gate, frescoes, wall, and gardens.
topics.history_overlap: Kashyapa's usurpation and civil war are history episodes; keep the rungs place-anchored (he BUILT the fortress and died at its base) rather than a throne-politics narrative.

topics.name: Ta Prohm
topics.scope: The Angkor temple the jungle never let go. T2: while other Angkor temples were cleared and rebuilt, restorers deliberately LEFT this one in the grip of the forest exactly as they found it (answer = it was left unrestored on purpose). T3: enormous pale roots pour over its walls and prise the stone blocks apart -- mostly one huge species that towers above the ruin (answer = the silk-cotton tree, Tetrameles nudiflora, alongside strangler figs). T4: a surviving temple inscription records the staggering workforce it took to run this one monastery -- nearly 80,000 people including 615 dancers (answer = ~80,000 attendants). Bonus: it became the world's most famous 'lost temple' after a 2001 film shot here (answer = Tomb Raider).
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta_Prohm (Jayavarman VII late 12th-early 13th c, originally Rajavihara, deliberately left picturesque/unrestored, Tetrameles nudiflora silk-cotton + strangler fig, ~80,000 attendants incl. 615 dancers, Tomb Raider 2001).
topics.framing_note: Tight gem ladder; the strangler-root grip is the whole draw and the dinner-test image. Name the actual dominant tree species (accuracy rail -- it's mostly the silk-cotton tree, NOT just 'a fig'). Distractors = other Angkor temples and other rainforest trees, all real. LANE: the trees are scenery for a PLACE fact (roots wrecking stonework) -- do NOT drift into tree biology (that's the animal/plant lane); keep the answer the temple-in-the-forest.
topics.history_overlap: None significant -- the workforce inscription is a place-fact of the site, not a distinct history episode.

topics.name: Taj Mahal
topics.scope: A tomb of white marble on the Yamuna river at Agra -- grief turned into the most beautiful building in the world. T1: Emperor Shah Jahan raised it not as a palace but as a TOMB for one person he had lost (answer = his wife Mumtaz Mahal). T2: the whole thing is skinned in white marble hauled ~400 km from a single quarry town in Rajasthan (answer = Makrana marble). T2/T3: that marble seems to change color through the day -- pink at dawn, white by noon, gold under the moon (answer = it shifts color with the light). T3: its four minarets are built leaning slightly OUTWARD on purpose, so that in an earthquake they would topple away from the tomb, not onto it (answer = tilted outward for earthquake safety). T4: the flowers on its walls aren't painted -- they're pictures inlaid from thousands of cut gemstones set flush into the marble (answer = pietra dura / stone inlay). T4: it took some 20,000 workers and artisans over 20 years, drawing masters from Persia and beyond (answer = ~22 years / ~20,000 artisans). T5: the tale that Shah Jahan planned a matching BLACK Taj across the river for himself is a romantic myth -- the 'black' ruins were white marble darkened by age (answer = the Black Taj is a legend).
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taj_Mahal (Shah Jahan for Mumtaz Mahal, commissioned 1631 / built 1632-1653, Makrana white marble, color-shift under changing light, minarets tilted outward for quake safety, pietra dura inlay, >20,000 artisans / ~22 years, Black Taj legend debunked as darkened white marble).
topics.framing_note: Place ladder; the tilted-minarets earthquake trick (T3) and the pietra dura (T4) are the dinner-test payoffs, the grief origin the T1 hook. Accuracy rail: explicitly flag the Black Taj as legend/myth (T5). Distractors = other Mughal tombs (Humayun's), other marble/inlay facts, all real. Respect it as a real tomb, not a photo-op. CROSS-LISTED with history -- see history_overlap.
topics.history_overlap: CROSS-LISTED with history: Shah Jahan's reign, his deposition and imprisonment by his son Aurangzeb, and Mughal succession are history episodes -- geography keeps ONLY the place-wonders (marble source, color-shift, tilted minarets, pietra dura, Black Taj myth). If history also builds Shah Jahan, coordinate so the tomb-as-architecture facts live HERE and the dynasty facts live THERE.

topics.name: The Great Wall of China
topics.scope: Not one wall but a 2,000-year system of walls snaking across northern China's mountains and deserts. T1: add up every branch and the walls run an almost unbelievable distance -- over 21,000 km, roughly half the Earth's circumference (invert the wonder: the huge number is the hook; answer = ~21,000 km / 21,196 km). T2: the popular claim that you can see it from the Moon with the naked eye is FALSE -- from orbit it's thinner than a human hair viewed from 3 km away (answer = the 'visible from space' myth is false). T2/T3: it isn't a single wall from one reign -- it's many walls built and rebuilt over ~2,000 years by different dynasties (answer = many walls over many dynasties). T3: the grand stone-and-brick wall most tourists picture is mostly the work of ONE dynasty, about 8,850 km of it (answer = the Ming wall). T3: out in the western deserts, older stretches were built not of brick but of rammed earth and layered reeds -- and still stand (answer = rammed / tamped-earth wall). T4: the wall's real job wasn't a magic barrier but a control-and-communication line -- beacon towers relaying smoke-and-fire signals faster than a horse could gallop (answer = the beacon-tower signal relay). T4: the eastern end plunges into the sea at a fort nicknamed the 'Old Dragon's Head' (answer = Shanhaiguan / Old Dragon's Head). T5: the grim legend that dead laborers were buried IN the wall is largely a myth -- but the human cost of building it, over centuries of forced labor, was staggeringly real (answer = the 'bones in the wall' is legend, the death toll real).
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Wall_of_China (2012 comprehensive survey 21,196.18 km total, Ming wall ~8,850 km, built Qin through Qing across many dynasties, 'visible from Moon with naked eye' debunked, beacon-tower signalling, rammed-earth western sections, eastern terminus at Shanhaiguan 'Old Dragon's Head').
topics.framing_note: Place ladder; the 'from space' myth-bust (T2) and the 21,000-km hook (T1) are the dinner-test payoffs. Invert the wonder -- lead with the huge number, make the myth-bust the knowable answer. Accuracy rail: it's a SYSTEM of walls, not one; label 'bones in the wall' as legend while stating the real forced-labor human cost plainly (honest both ways). Distractors = other great walls (Hadrian's), other superlatives, all real. Keep answers to the wall/place, not the dynastic wars it defended against.
topics.history_overlap: The wars, dynasties, and the nomad-vs-China conflict the wall was built for belong to history; geography keeps the wall's length, construction, materials, signal system, and endpoints. State the forced-labor human cost as fact, but the campaigns are history.

topics.name: The Terracotta Army
topics.scope: An underground army of life-size clay soldiers guarding the tomb of China's First Emperor near Mount Li. T2: in 1974, farmers digging a WELL broke into a buried pit and hit the head of a clay soldier -- then found thousands more (answer = discovered by well-digging farmers, 1974). T2/T3: more than 8,000 life-size warriors stand in battle order in the pits, plus hundreds of horses and chariots (answer = ~8,000 soldiers). T3: no two faces are the same -- each soldier was given individual features, so the army looks like a crowd of real, distinct men (answer = every face is unique). T4: the ancient historian Sima Qian wrote that the emperor's tomb held a map of the empire with a hundred RIVERS OF LIQUID MERCURY, made to flow mechanically (answer = rivers of mercury). T4: astonishingly, soil tests over the still-sealed tomb mound show unnaturally HIGH mercury levels -- matching the 2,000-year-old account (answer = high mercury detected in the mound). T5: the emperor's actual burial chamber has never been opened -- archaeologists deliberately leave it sealed rather than risk destroying what's inside (answer = the tomb is still unexcavated). T5: the whole army faces EAST, toward the lands the First Emperor had conquered, set to guard him forever (answer = they face east, toward the conquered lands).
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terracotta_Army (discovered March 1974 by well-digging farmers near Mount Li, >8,000 soldiers + 130 chariots / 520+150 horses, individualized faces from base forms, Sima Qian's account of mercury rivers corroborated by high mercury in the tomb-mound soil, central burial chamber unexcavated).
topics.framing_note: Place ladder; the mercury-rivers-confirmed-by-soil-tests (T4) and the never-opened tomb (T5) are the dinner-test payoffs. Scene-led -- open with the well-diggers' shock, not a definition. Accuracy rail: keep the mercury as Sima Qian's account CORROBORATED by real soil readings, and don't overclaim the tomb's unseen contents; AVOID the disputed 'chrome-plated swords' claim. Distractors = other tombs (Egyptian pyramids), other grave-goods, all real.
topics.history_overlap: Qin Shi Huang unifying China, standardizing script and measures, Legalism, and the book-burnings are history episodes; geography keeps the TOMB-complex wonders (the pits, the army, the mercury, the sealed chamber, the eastward facing).

strands.strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas

topics.name: Cahokia
topics.strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
topics.scope: A vast earthen mound-city on the Mississippi floodplain across from modern St. Louis, Illinois -- the largest city north of Mexico in its day. T1: a thousand years ago the biggest city in what is now the United States rose here, built not of stone but of earth -- more than 100 flat-topped platform mounds raised one woven basket of soil at a time (answer = the earthen mounds; teach 'platform mound'; distractors stone pyramids, ziggurats, kivas). T2: its centrepiece, Monks Mound, climbs about 30 m (100 ft) in four broad terraces and spreads across a base as large as the Great Pyramid of Giza -- roughly 13 acres (answer = the Great Pyramid of Giza comparison; number built as payoff; distractors a city block, a football field, the Colosseum). T3: at its ~1100 CE peak Cahokia may have held 10,000-20,000 people, making it larger at that moment than the London of the time (answer = London; flag population as an estimate; distractors Paris, Rome, Constantinople). T4: west of Monks Mound, postholes trace great rings of upright red-cedar posts that framed the sunrise across the seasons -- a wooden solar calendar nicknamed Woodhenge (answer = the named calendar circle; distractors Stonehenge, the Sun Dagger, a medicine wheel). T5 (dinner-test payoff): in Mound 72 a leader was laid out on a bed of some 20,000 shell beads arranged in the shape of a falcon-man, ringed by rows of sacrificed attendants -- the 'Birdman' burial, proof of a powerful ranked society (answer = the falcon/Birdman bead burial). Further rungs: a two-mile log palisade wall; trade goods of marine shell and Great Lakes copper reaching Cahokia; abandonment by ~1350 (flood/climate/resource stress, debated); the name 'Cahokia' is a later borrowing -- the builders' own name is unknown.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Monks Mound (~30 m high; base 291 m x 236 m; base footprint 'roughly the same size' as the Great Pyramid of Giza ~13.1 acres; four terraces; largest pre-Columbian earthwork in the Americas and largest pyramid north of Mesoamerica) -- verified via WebFetch. Peak population 10,000-20,000 and 'larger than contemporary London', Woodhenge, and the Mound 72 Birdman burial (~20,000 shell beads) from the Cahokia article. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
topics.framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; explicitly a FULL civilization -- the 'bigger than London' fact rebuts the 'primitive mound-builders' myth (config names Cahokia as celebrated). KEY ACCURACY RAIL (research-caught): Monks Mound's base RIVALS Giza's footprint -- it is NOT taller or larger overall; and the population is an ESTIMATE ('may have held', 'larger than the London of the time'). DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T5 Birdman burial on 20,000 shell beads. LANE: keep rungs on the PLACE (mounds, Woodhenge, Mound 72); Mississippian culture broadly is shared with history.
topics.history_overlap: Mississippian culture overlaps with the history bank. Keep rungs on the earthworks themselves; flag the 'bigger than London' rung as an estimate and anchor it to Monks Mound, not a general Mississippian-history ladder.

topics.name: Caral
topics.strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
topics.scope: A city of earthen pyramids in the Supe Valley on Peru's desert coast -- among the oldest cities in the Americas. T1: in a dry Peruvian river valley stand six earthen pyramids raised around 2600 BC -- at the very same time the Egyptians were building the pyramids of Giza on the far side of the world -- making Caral among the oldest cities in ALL the Americas (answer = the oldest city in the Americas; the 2600 BC / same-era-as-Giza hook constructs the superlative; distractors the largest, the highest, the driest). T2: a city of thousands left something startling OUT -- archaeologists have found no defensive walls, no weapons, and no mutilated bodies, no sign of war (answer = the absence of warfare; FLAG as 'no evidence found', not a proven utopia; distractors no farming, no religion, no trade). T3 (dinner-test payoff): instead of weapons, Caral's ruins gave up 32 flutes made from condor and pelican bone -- this was a musical, ceremonial city (answer = the bone flutes; distractors knives, coins, mirrors). T4: sunk below ground level in the heart of Caral is a round plaza where the whole community could gather for ritual, facing the great pyramid -- a sunken circular court (answer = the sunken circular plaza; distractors a ball court, a reservoir, an amphitheatre). T5: Caral had no pottery at all -- a 'preceramic' city -- yet its people knotted a length of string that may be the oldest known quipu in the Andes, the knotted record-keeping device the Inca would use 4,000 years later (answer = the quipu; teach the term). Further rung: the ~28 m Piramide Mayor and the geoglyph-marked landscape around the valley.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Caral (inhabited ~2600-2000 BC, 'the oldest city in the Americas', Norte Chico/Caral-Supe, ~1,500 years before the Olmec; contemporary with Egypt's pyramids; 'no indications of warfare -- battlements, weapons, or mutilated bodies'; preceramic; a knotted-textile quipu found; Piramide Mayor 150 x 110 x 28 m) -- verified via WebFetch. The 32 bone flutes (condor and pelican bone) and sunken circular plazas from the Caral / Caral-Supe articles. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
topics.framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; celebrate a sophisticated early city -- but the T2 'no war' rung must be framed as ABSENCE OF EVIDENCE, not a romanticised peaceful-utopia myth (the stance guards against noble-savage over-claiming as much as against 'primitive'). KEY ACCURACY RAIL: dates ~2600 BC; 'no evidence of warfare found'; the quipu is an EARLY example. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T3 bone flutes. LANE: keep rungs on the PLACE (pyramids, sunken plaza, flutes, quipu); Norte Chico as a civilization is shared with history.
topics.history_overlap: Caral/Norte Chico overlaps with the history bank as an early civilization. Keep rungs on the site; flag the 'no warfare' rung as absence-of-evidence rather than proven peace, and the quipu as an early example.

topics.name: Chaco Canyon
topics.strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
topics.scope: A remote high-desert canyon in New Mexico, hub of the Ancestral Puebloan world from ~850-1150 CE. T1: in a dry, almost treeless canyon the Ancestral Puebloans raised huge multi-storey stone-and-timber buildings called 'great houses'; the largest, Pueblo Bonito, once held about 650 rooms and rose four storeys (answer = the named great house; distractors Chetro Ketl, Casa Rinconada, Cliff Palace). T2 (dinner-test payoff): building the great houses swallowed the timber of some 200,000 pine trees -- and there are almost no trees in the canyon, so the heavy beams were carried by hand, with no wheels or draft animals, from mountains up to ~110 km away (answer = hauled overland on foot; distractors floated downriver, grown on-site, traded from Mexico). T3: dead-straight roads up to ~9 m wide run out of Chaco for tens of kilometres, cutting across mesas in perfectly straight lines instead of bending around obstacles (answer = the arrow-straight roads; distractors winding, paved, downhill-only). T4: high on Fajada Butte a spiral pecked into the rock is pierced by a 'dagger' of sunlight that splits it exactly at midday on the summer solstice -- the 'Sun Dagger' (answer = the solstice noon dagger of light; distractors midnight, the equinox sunset, the winter dawn). T5: Chaco's great houses and the great kiva of Casa Rinconada line up with the cardinal directions and with the moon's slow 18.6-year standstill cycle -- a lunar rhythm the builders tracked across generations (answer = the lunar-standstill alignment). Further rungs: the enormous circular great kivas; turquoise workshops and macaw remains showing trade reaching central Mexico; the mystery of the canyon's ~1150 depopulation.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Chaco Culture National Historical Park (Pueblo Bonito ~650 rooms, four storeys, largest great house; ~200,000 trees hauled on foot from up to ~110 km/70 mi away; dead-straight roads up to ~9 m/30 ft wide and ~97 km/60 mi long; Fajada Butte 'Sun Dagger' spiral marking solstices/equinoxes; alignments to cardinal directions and the 18.6-year lunar standstill; ~850-1150 CE, Ancestral Puebloans) -- verified via WebFetch. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
topics.framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; celebrate Ancestral Puebloan astronomy and engineering as a full civilization (no 'how could they possibly...' condescension). KEY ACCURACY RAIL: prefer 'Ancestral Puebloans' over 'Anasazi'; note the Sun Dagger's alignment was documented in the 1970s and has since shifted with erosion. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T2 timber hauled 110 km by hand, or the T4 Sun Dagger. LANE: keep rungs on the PLACE (great houses, roads, Sun Dagger, alignments); Ancestral Puebloan history is shared.
topics.history_overlap: Ancestral Puebloan history overlaps with the history bank. Keep rungs on the great houses, roads, timber, and the Sun Dagger, not a general culture-history ladder.

topics.name: Chan Chan
topics.strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
topics.scope: The Chimu capital sprawling near Trujillo on Peru's north desert coast. T1 (dinner-test payoff): near the Peruvian coast lies the largest city ever built of mud brick in the Americas -- 20 square kilometres of walls made not of stone but of adobe, sun-dried earth (answer = mud brick / adobe; distractors stone, coral, timber). T2: Chan Chan's tall adobe walls are carved with endless friezes of fish and waves and seabirds -- fitting art for the Chimu, a people of the ocean and its fisheries (answer = fish and sea creatures; distractors jaguars, condors, maize). T3: this desert megacity of tens of thousands was conquered around 1470 by the Inca, who absorbed the Chimu into their empire (answer = the Inca; distractors the Aztec, the Spanish, the Wari).
topics.source: Wikipedia: Chan Chan (Chimor/Chimu capital near Trujillo; 'the largest city of the pre-Columbian era in South America' and the largest adobe city in the Americas; ~20 sq km; nine-to-ten walled royal ciudadelas; adobe friezes of fish, waves, nets, and seabirds; built from ~850 CE, conquered by the Inca ~1470; peak population ~40,000-60,000) -- verified via WebFetch. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
topics.framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; the marvel is scale in an unexpected material -- the largest earthen city on Earth. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: 'largest ADOBE/mud-brick city in the Americas' (largest pre-Columbian city in South America) -- keep the superlative precise. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T1 mud-brick megacity. LANE: keep rungs on the PLACE (the adobe scale, the sea friezes); Chimu/Inca political history is shared. Note: the sea-friezes rung is about the CARVED PLACE, not fish biology (that would be the animal bank).
topics.history_overlap: Chimu and Inca history overlap with the history bank. Keep the mini on the place (adobe scale, wall friezes); the conquest rung names the later empire as a place-fact, not a conquest narrative.

topics.name: Chichen Itza
topics.strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
topics.scope: The great Maya city of the Yucatan, Mexico, famed for its serpent-shadow pyramid. T1: the step-pyramid at the city's centre, El Castillo, has 91 steps on each of its four sides -- add the top platform and the count reaches exactly 365, one per day of the year (answer = 365, the calendar-in-stone; number built as payoff; distractors 360, 260 the Maya ritual count, 584 the Venus cycle -- all real Maya numbers). T2 (dinner-test payoff): twice a year, on the spring and autumn equinox, the late-afternoon sun throws a zigzag of triangular shadows down El Castillo's north staircase so a giant snake seems to slither to the carved stone serpent-head at the base -- the descent of Kukulkan, the Feathered Serpent (answer = Kukulkan / the equinox serpent shadow; distractors Chaac, Itzamna, Quetzalcoatl). T3: Chichen Itza holds the largest ball court in the ancient Americas -- about 168 m long, stone scoring-rings set high on the walls, acoustics that carry a whisper end to end -- the Great Ball Court (answer = the named court / its record size). T4: into a huge natural limestone sinkhole at the city's edge the Maya cast gold, jade and human offerings to the rain god Chaac; divers still dredge treasure and bone from this Sacred Cenote -- a cenote being a collapsed-limestone sinkhole exposing groundwater in a land with no rivers (answer = a cenote / the Sacred Cenote; teach the karst term). T5: clap once at the foot of El Castillo and the staircase answers with a strange chirp that researchers say mimics the sacred quetzal bird -- an echo created as the evenly spaced steps diffract the sound (answer = the chirped-echo acoustic effect). Further rungs: an older pyramid with a red jaguar throne nested inside El Castillo; the round Caracol tower aligned to the motions of Venus; the Temple of the Warriors with its reclining Chac Mool.
topics.source: Wikipedia: El Castillo, Chichen Itza (91 steps x4 + top platform = 365; equinox late-afternoon triangular shadows create the illusion of the feathered serpent crawling down; 24 m + 6 m temple = 30 m; nested inner pyramid ~600-800 CE) -- verified via WebFetch. Great Ball Court (largest in Mesoamerica, ~168 m), Sacred Cenote, and the staircase quetzal-chirp echo (David Lubman's acoustic studies) from the Chichen Itza article. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
topics.framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; celebrate Maya astronomy as sophisticated real science (the 365-step calendar, the equinox alignment) -- no 'ancient aliens'. Lead with the scene, never 'How many steps...'. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: the serpent-shadow and the quetzal-chirp echo are REAL, observable effects, not legend; count the 365 steps 'including the top platform' (some steps are eroded). DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T2 equinox serpent shadow. LANE: Maya astronomy/history is shared -- keep rungs on the built PLACE (El Castillo, the shadow, the ball court, the cenote, the acoustics); the cenote also cross-links to Yucatan karst geology, which is geography's own.
topics.history_overlap: Maya astronomy and dynastic history overlap with the history bank. Keep rungs on the site's built marvels and the equinox effect; frame the Sacred-Cenote sacrifices respectfully and factually, not as a history episode.

topics.name: Cusco and Sacsayhuaman
topics.strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
topics.scope: The Inca capital Cusco (Qosqo) high in the Peruvian Andes and its great hilltop stronghold, Sacsayhuaman. T1 (dinner-test payoff): the Inca called their capital Qosqo, 'the navel of the world', and laid the whole city out in the shape of a crouching puma, with the huge zigzag ramparts of Sacsayhuaman forming its head (answer = the puma-shaped city; distractors a condor, a serpent, a jaguar). T2: Sacsayhuaman's walls are built from limestone blocks so vast the largest is estimated at 100-200 tonnes, yet fitted so precisely, without mortar, that not even a knife blade or sheet of paper slips into the joints (answer = the paper-thin mortarless joints; distractors 'they used no metal tools', 'the walls lean inward', 'each block is unique'). T3: in a Cusco street stands a single Inca block cut to interlock with its neighbours on twelve separate sides -- the famous 'twelve-angled stone' (answer = twelve; number as payoff; distractors 6, 8, 14). T4: when a great earthquake levelled much of colonial Cusco in 1950, the Spanish buildings crumbled while the Inca walls beneath them stood unharmed -- Inca masonry, with trapezoidal doorways and inward-leaning interlocked blocks, is built to ride out quakes (answer = the Inca walls survived where the Spanish ones fell). T5: the Spanish tore down the Inca Sun Temple, the Qorikancha -- whose walls had been sheathed in sheets of gold and which held a golden garden -- and raised the church of Santo Domingo directly on its flawless Inca foundations (answer = the gold-sheathed Sun Temple). Further rungs: Cusco as the hub of the Qhapaq Nan, the 40,000 km Inca road network; the theory that Sacsayhuaman's zigzag walls form the puma's teeth; blocks shaped by pounding with harder hammerstones, not sawing; the 1536 siege of Sacsayhuaman.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Sacsayhuaman (three terrace walls ~6 m tall, longest ~400 m; largest limestone block estimated 128 to ~200 tonnes; 'a single piece of paper will not fit between many of the stones', Cieza de Leon on the joints; Cusco imagined as a puma with Sacsayhuaman as the head; ~3,701 m; built under Pachacuti) -- verified via WebFetch. Twelve-angled stone (Hatunrumiyoc), the 1950 earthquake, and the gold-sheathed Qorikancha/Santo Domingo from the Cusco & Qorikancha articles. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
topics.framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; the perfect-fit stonework is celebrated Inca engineering -- the failure mode is 'aliens/too advanced for the Inca' pseudo-archaeology, which the stance directly rebuts (config names Sacsayhuaman). KEY ACCURACY RAIL: block weights are ESTIMATES; the Inca shaped stone with stone hammers, ramps and human labour -- not aliens. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T1 puma-city / T2 paper-thin joints. LANE: the Inca empire and the conquest are HISTORY -- keep rungs on the PLACES (puma plan, Sacsayhuaman's stones, the twelve-angled stone, earthquake-proof walls, gold-sheathed Qorikancha); frame the 1536 siege as the place, not a battle narrative.
topics.history_overlap: The Inca empire, Pachacuti, and the Spanish conquest are history-bank. Keep rungs on the stonework and city plan; frame the 1536 siege rung as the fortress-place, preferring the engineering angle so it doesn't duplicate a conquest ladder.

topics.name: Easter Island (Rapa Nui)
topics.strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
topics.scope: A tiny volcanic island in the far southeastern Pacific -- the most remote inhabited island on Earth. T1: on an island ~3,500 km from the nearest mainland, the Rapanui carved about 900 giant stone figures with heavy brows and long torsos, most gazing inland over their villages -- the moai (answer = the named statues; teach the term; distractors tiki, ahu, pukao). T2: almost every moai was cut from the soft volcanic tuff of a single crater, where hundreds still stand half-finished in the slopes -- the quarry of Rano Raraku (answer = the named quarry; distractors Rano Kau, Puna Pau, Terevaka). T3: the moai stand on stone platforms called ahu; the most famous line is the fifteen restored giants standing shoulder to shoulder at Ahu Tongariki (answer = the named platform row; distractors Anakena, Orongo, Vinapu). T4 (dinner-test payoff): Rapanui oral tradition says the moai 'walked' from the quarry to their platforms upright, and in 2012 archaeologists Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo tested it -- a small crew rocked an upright replica side to side with three ropes so it waddled forward on its own base (answer = 'walked' upright by rope-rocking; LABEL as oral tradition + experiment; distractors rolled on logs, dragged on sledges, floated -- all real proposed methods). T5: some moai once wore a red stone topknot (pukao) quarried from a different red-scoria pit, Puna Pau; later, in a time of upheaval, the Rapanui toppled the moai and turned to a new faith -- the Birdman (Tangata manu) cult, whose egg-gathering contest was held on the sea-cliffs at Orongo (answer = the Birdman cult; distractors a sun cult, an ancestor cult, a whale cult). Further rungs: the moai's inlaid eyes of white coral with obsidian or red-scoria pupils; the undeciphered rongorongo script; the crater lake of Rano Kau; and the CONTESTED 'collapse' story -- Jared Diamond's deforestation-'ecocide' versus Hunt & Lipo's case that Polynesian rats plus later slave-raids and disease did most of the damage.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Moai (>900 statues; carved from Rano Raraku tuff; tallest erected 'Paro' ~10 m / 82 tonnes; largest unfinished ~21 m; pukao red scoria from Puna Pau; coral-and-obsidian/scoria eyes) -- verified via WebFetch. 'Walking' moai: oral tradition plus the 2012 Terry Hunt & Carl Lipo rope-rocking experiment (and the 1986 Pavel/Heyerdahl precedent). Ahu Tongariki (15 moai), the Orongo Birdman cult, and the Diamond-vs-Hunt/Lipo collapse debate from the Easter Island / Rapa Nui articles. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
topics.framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; the moai are a cultural creation born on this island -- geography owns the island, the quarries, and the moving of the stones. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: the moai 'walked' per ORAL TRADITION and a rope-rocking EXPERIMENT -- say both, never state it as plain fact; and label the 'ecocide' collapse story as CONTESTED (don't cast the Rapanui as fools who doomed themselves -- that is exactly the condescension the stance rebuts). DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T4 walking moai. LANE: no animal or food rung -- this is the island and its statues.
topics.history_overlap: The 'collapse' debate touches anthropology/history. Keep rungs on the island and its statues (quarry, ahu, walking, pukao, Birdman); flag the ecocide rung as genuinely contested and frame the walking as oral-tradition-plus-experiment.

topics.name: Machu Picchu
topics.strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
topics.scope: The Inca royal estate on a green saddle between two Andean peaks above a hairpin loop of the Urubamba River, Peru. T1: it sits at ~2,430 m (7,970 ft), so often wreathed in cloud it's called the 'cloud city'; the sharp peak looming behind the classic postcard view is Huayna Picchu (answer = the named peak; distractors Salkantay, Ausangate, Huascaran). T2 (honest-stance payoff): when Yale's Hiram Bingham was led up in 1911 by a local farmer, the ruins were NOT empty -- Quechua families (Richarte, Alvarez) were already farming the terraces, and Agustin Lizarraga had carved his name there in 1902 (answer = local people already lived/farmed there; it was never a 'lost' place to them). T3: unlike Cusco, Machu Picchu escaped one fate that hit almost every Inca site -- the Spanish conquistadors never found it (answer = never reached/looted by Spain). T4: carved from the living bedrock at the summit is a single granite pillar whose shadow marks the solstice, the 'hitching post of the sun' -- the Intihuatana (answer = named ritual stone; teach the term; distractors the Torreon, a chacana, a huaca). T5 (dinner-test payoff): about 60% of the building effort here is invisible -- deep buried foundations and a hidden crushed-rock drainage system that keeps the terraced city from sliding off a wet, fault-riddled ridge (answer = the underground engineering). Further rungs: the curved Temple of the Sun (Torreon) whose window catches the June-solstice sunrise on a sacred rock; mortarless ashlar walls with inward-leaning trapezoidal doorways that shrug off earthquakes; built ~1450 as emperor Pachacuti's country estate, not a legendary lost city; the agricultural terraces (andenes) that both fed it and stabilised the slope; its place on the Qhapaq Nan Inca road; the fault-line siting that gave the Inca pre-fractured stone to quarry.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Machu Picchu (elev 2,430 m; built ~1450 under Pachacuti, occupied ~1420-1530; Spanish never found it; Bingham 1911 led by Melchor Arteaga, found Richarte & Alvarez families farming; Lizarraga 1902; Intihuatana solstice stone; Temple of the Sun/Torreon; dry ashlar masonry) -- verified via WebFetch. Underground-drainage 'invisible 60%' from Kenneth Wright's engineering studies. Build-stage cross-check on Grokipedia (grokipedia.com) recommended as primary.
topics.framing_note: PLACE->WONDER, celebrate Inca engineering as real achievement (never 'mysterious lost race'). Lead with the cloud-wreathed setting, never 'What is Machu Picchu?'. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: Bingham did not 'discover' it -- locals lived there and Lizarraga preceded him in 1902; frame the 1911 rung honestly so it doesn't erase the people already there. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T5 hidden drainage (most of the work is underground). LANE: Inca-empire politics and the Spanish conquest belong to HISTORY -- keep every rung anchored to the PLACE and its engineering (drainage, Intihuatana, terraces, never-found-by-Spain), not a Pachacuti biography or conquest narrative.
topics.history_overlap: Pachacuti's reign and the Spanish conquest of the Inca are history-bank episodes. Keep rungs on the site's engineering/setting; the T2 'Bingham 1911' rung must anchor on the PLACE (locals already there / never found by Spain), not a conquest or biography ladder.

topics.name: Mesa Verde
topics.strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
topics.scope: Ancestral Puebloan villages tucked into sandstone alcoves in the canyon walls of southwestern Colorado. T1: in Colorado, the Ancestral Puebloans built entire stone villages NOT on the flat mesa top but inside natural rock alcoves partway down the cliff faces -- cliff dwellings sheltered under overhangs (answer = built into the cliff faces / alcoves; distractors in caves underground, in treetops, on riverbanks). T2: the largest cliff dwelling in all of North America, with about 150 rooms and 23 round ceremonial chambers, is Cliff Palace (answer = the named dwelling; distractors Balcony House, Spruce Tree House, Long House). T3: those round sunken rooms, entered by ladder through a hole in the roof, were ceremonial chambers called kivas (answer = the named/teach term; distractors cenotes, kachinas, hogans). T4: the alcove villages face south and southwest so the low winter sun warms them while the overhang shades them in summer -- clever passive-solar design (answer = oriented to the sun for winter warmth/summer shade; distractors oriented for defence, for drainage, toward a river). T5 (dinner-test payoff): around 1300 CE the Ancestral Puebloans left Mesa Verde entirely and moved south -- and tree-rings preserved in their own roof-beams reveal the trigger: a decades-long drought in the late 1200s (answer = the drought, read from tree-rings; teach that dendrochronology dates it). Further rung: the descendants are today's Pueblo peoples -- the builders did not 'vanish'.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Mesa Verde National Park & Cliff Palace (Ancestral Puebloan cliff dwellings in sandstone alcoves; Cliff Palace ~150 rooms and 23 kivas, largest cliff dwelling in North America; kivas as round sunken ceremonial rooms; depopulation ~1300 CE tied to the late-1200s 'Great Drought' via tree-ring dating; descendants are modern Pueblo peoples). Grokipedia cross-check recommended (WebSearch budget exhausted; corroborate the room/kiva counts and the drought dating at build time).
topics.framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; the builders are a living people (today's Pueblo nations) -- never 'the vanished/mysterious Anasazi'. Lead with the scene of villages hidden in the cliff. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: the ~1300 abandonment is dated by TREE-RINGS to the late-1200s drought (say how we know); descendants persist. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T5 tree-ring-dated drought. LANE: keep rungs on the PLACE (alcove villages, Cliff Palace, kivas, the drought); Ancestral Puebloan history is shared.
topics.history_overlap: Ancestral Puebloan history overlaps with the history bank. Keep rungs on the alcove architecture and the drought abandonment; frame the builders as ancestors of living Pueblo peoples, not a vanished-race history episode.

topics.name: Monte Alban
topics.strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
topics.scope: The Zapotec capital built on a flattened mountaintop high above the Valley of Oaxaca, Mexico. T1 (dinner-test payoff): to build their capital the Zapotec did something staggering to a mountain -- they levelled its whole summit flat, some 400 m above the valley floor, to make a giant plaza in the sky (answer = they flattened/levelled the mountaintop; distractors hollowed it out, terraced the sides, tunnelled through it). T2: around that plaza stand carved stone slabs of contorted human figures, long called 'los Danzantes' (the dancers) but now read as slain or sacrificed war captives (answer = the reinterpretation as captives, not dancers; FLAG the changed interpretation; distractors dancers, ballplayers, priests). T3: one building at Monte Alban, 'Building J', is shaped like an arrowhead and set at an odd angle to everything around it, most likely to line up with a star (answer = an arrowhead shape / astronomical alignment; distractors a pyramid, a circle, a cross). T4: Building J's carved slabs, showing upside-down heads beneath place-signs, are thought to be a list of the towns the Zapotec conquered (answer = conquered towns; distractors a king-list, a star-map, a calendar). T5: the Zapotec of Monte Alban carved some of the EARLIEST writing and calendar glyphs in Mesoamerica -- dots-and-bars dates that were an early step toward written language in the Americas (answer = early writing/hieroglyphs). Further rung: the ball court and the elite tombs with painted murals.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Monte Alban (Zapotec capital on an artificially levelled ridge ~1,940 m elevation, rising ~400 m from the valley floor; the Danzantes -- over 300 slabs, once thought dancers, now interpreted as tortured/sacrificed war prisoners; Building J arrow-shaped and rotated, astronomical significance, aligned to Capella; conquest-slab place-signs; founded ~500 BC; some of the earliest Zapotec writing/calendar) -- verified via WebFetch. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
topics.framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; the levelled-mountain feat and the early writing celebrate Zapotec engineering and intellect. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: the Danzantes are 'once thought dancers, now read as slain captives' -- state the reinterpretation, don't pick one silently. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T1 flattened mountaintop. LANE: keep rungs on the PLACE (the levelled summit, the Danzantes, Building J, early writing); Zapotec history is shared.
topics.history_overlap: Zapotec history overlaps with the history bank. Keep rungs on the site (levelled summit, Danzantes, Building J, early glyphs); frame the conquest-slab rung as a place-artifact, not a conquest narrative.

topics.name: Nazca Lines
topics.strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
topics.scope: Enormous drawings scraped across the bone-dry Nazca Desert on Peru's southern coast. T1: on one of the driest plateaus on Earth, ancient people drew pictures so vast that most can only be seen whole from the air, hundreds of metres up -- giant desert-floor drawings called geoglyphs (answer = only visible from the air / geoglyphs; teach the term; distractors at night, from the sea, by moonlight). T2: the Nazca made each line by clearing away the desert's reddish, iron-stained surface pebbles to expose the paler ground beneath, a contrast that has survived ~2,000 years because it almost never rains here (answer = the pebble-clearing method / the pale subsoil). T3 (dinner-test payoff): among more than 70 giant animal figures, the most famous is a hummingbird about 93 m across, drawn with a long thin beak and outstretched wings (answer = the hummingbird; distractors the condor, the monkey, the spider -- all real Nazca figures). T4: high on a hillside sits a robed figure with a round head and one raised hand, nicknamed 'the Astronaut' -- but archaeologists read it as an owl-headed man or shaman, not a visitor from space (answer = an owl-man / shaman figure, correcting the 'aliens' myth; distractors a god, an astronaut, a warrior). T5: the German mathematician Maria Reiche spent 40 years measuring and guarding the lines, arguing they formed a giant astronomical calendar marking solstices and star-risings -- but their true purpose stays debated, with water and fertility ritual now favoured (answer = an astronomical calendar, LABELLED as one contested theory; distractors a map, an alphabet, a calendar). Further rungs: each animal drawn as a single unbroken line that never crosses itself, hinting the figures were ceremonial walking paths; the older Paracas Candelabra etched on a coastal hillside; hundreds of faint new figures found recently by drones and AI.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Nazca Lines (made by removing the reddish ferric-oxide pebbles to reveal paler subsoil; >70 figures incl. hummingbird ~93 m, monkey with spiral tail, spider, condor ~134 m; the 'Astronaut'/owlman; best seen from ~500 m up; Maria Reiche; purposes debated -- astronomical, water/fertility ritual, ceremonial pathways; Nazca & Paracas cultures ~500 BC-500 AD) -- verified via WebFetch. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
topics.framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; credit the Nazca people's real skill -- the failure mode is von Daniken's 'runway for alien gods', which the T4 rung must correct. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: the PURPOSE is genuinely DEBATED -- never assert aliens or a single settled function; Maria Reiche's calendar theory is one contested view. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T3 hummingbird / T4 'Astronaut' correction. LANE: the desert's aridity that preserves the lines cross-links to geography's own rain-shadow/Atacama-edge theme; no food or animal rung (the animal figures are cultural drawings, not zoology).
topics.history_overlap: Minimal history overlap. The main hazard is the 'ancient aliens' narrative; rungs must correct it, crediting the Nazca, and flag the purpose as debated.

topics.name: Palenque
topics.strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
topics.scope: A jewel-like Maya city on a jungle escarpment in Chiapas, Mexico, hiding one of the great tombs of the ancient world. T1: Palenque's grandest pyramid conceals a secret under its floor -- a rubble-choked stairway plunging deep into the structure; it is named for the long carved text on its summit temple, the Temple of the Inscriptions (answer = the named temple; distractors Temple of the Cross, of the Sun, of the Foliated Cross). T2: over 1948-1952 archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier cleared that buried stair and broke through to something no one thought Maya pyramids held -- a sealed royal tomb deep inside, overturning the idea that these pyramids were only temples (answer = an intact tomb inside the pyramid). T3 (dinner-test payoff): the king's coffin is sealed by a 5-tonne carved limestone lid showing him at the instant of death, falling into the underworld along the branches of the Maya World Tree -- popularly and wrongly nicknamed 'the astronaut' (answer = the World Tree / the ceiba, NOT an astronaut; distractors a jaguar throne, a feathered serpent, a maize god). T4: the king in that tomb, Pakal, ruled Palenque for an astonishing ~68 years (615-683 CE), long enough to rebuild it into a masterpiece of light, airy Maya architecture (answer = ~68 years, one of the longest reigns of the ancient world; number as payoff; distractors ~20, ~40, ~90). T5: Palenque's palace has a feature found at no other Maya city -- a four-storey square tower rising over the plaza, perhaps for watching the sky (answer = the palace tower; distractors a ball court, a pyramid, a causeway). Further rung: the Maya vaulted the Otulum stream into a stone aqueduct beneath the palace, creating the earliest known water pressure in the Americas.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Temple of the Inscriptions (Ruz removed the floor slab in 1952 to reveal the rubble-filled stairway, cleared over two years, to Pakal's tomb; the sarcophagus lid shows Pakal between the heavens/Cosmic Tree and the underworld; Pakal's reign 'almost 70 years'; 617-glyph inscription, one of the longest Maya texts) -- verified via WebFetch. Palace four-storey tower and Otulum aqueduct from the Palenque article. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
topics.framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; the sarcophagus lid is Pakal at the Maya World Tree -- the T3 rung must EXPLICITLY correct the 'ancient astronaut' misreading (the flagship pseudo-archaeology case), crediting Maya cosmology. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: Ruz reached the tomb in 1952 (stair cleared 1948-52); the lid is the World Tree, not a spaceman. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T3 lid / 'astronaut' correction. LANE: Pakal's reign is a HISTORY/biography topic -- anchor the T2/T4 rungs on the TOMB-inside-a-pyramid discovery and the site, not a Pakal life-story ladder.
topics.history_overlap: Pakal's reign is a history-bank biography. Keep rungs on the site (the hidden tomb, the lid, the palace tower, the aqueduct); the Pakal rungs must anchor on the tomb discovery, not duplicate a Pakal biography ladder.

topics.name: Tenochtitlan
topics.strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
topics.scope: The Aztec (Mexica) island capital in Lake Texcoco, now buried beneath Mexico City. T1: in 1325 the Mexica founded their capital where they saw a prophesied omen -- an eagle on a cactus (the image now on Mexico's flag) -- on an island in Lake Texcoco (answer = the named lake; distractors Lake Titicaca, Lake Patzcuaro, Lake Chapala). T2: to feed a city with no farmland, the Mexica staked rectangular beds of mud and reeds into the shallow lakebed, so fertile they cropped year-round -- floating gardens called chinampas (answer = the named farming feature; teach the term; distractors Inca andenes, waru waru, milpa). T3: three broad raised roads tied the island to the shore and a twin terracotta aqueduct piped fresh spring water in from Chapultepec (answer = the causeways-and-aqueduct water system / the named spring). T4: Cortes's soldiers in 1519 said the city -- larger than any in Spain, home to 200,000+ -- looked like an enchantment; at its centre stood a great twin-shrined pyramid to the war god and the rain god, the Templo Mayor (answer = the named great temple; distractors the Caracol, the Pyramid of the Sun, El Castillo). T5 (dinner-test payoff): Mexico City today sinks by as much as tens of centimetres a year and its cathedral visibly tilts -- because after razing Tenochtitlan in 1521 the Spanish drained Lake Texcoco, and the modern city sits on the soft, compacting old lakebed (answer = the drained lake / subsidence). Further rungs: Moctezuma's zoo, aviary and botanical gardens; the sister-market of Tlatelolco drawing tens of thousands of traders a day; the sacred precinct; the Templo Mayor rediscovered in 1978 by electrical workers digging downtown.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Tenochtitlan (founded 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco; eagle-and-cactus founding legend now on the flag; chinampas; three causeways to Tepeyac/Iztapalapa/Tlacopan; twin aqueduct from Chapultepec springs; peak population 200,000-400,000; Templo Mayor to Huitzilopochtli & Tlaloc; Cortes 8 Nov 1519, razed 1521; drained lakebed causes modern subsidence) -- verified via WebFetch. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
topics.framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; celebrate the island city's engineering (a metropolis larger than contemporary European capitals) without triumphalism, and be honest BOTH ways about 1521 (a real razing AND a real epidemic collapse), never a theatrical morality tale. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: the eagle-on-cactus is the FOUNDING LEGEND (say so); population figures are estimates. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T5 drained-lake subsidence (why Mexico City sinks). LANE: Cortes and the conquest are HISTORY -- keep rungs on the PLACE (island setting, chinampas, causeways, Templo Mayor, the sinking city); the 1521 rung must land on the LAKE/subsidence wonder, not retell the conquest.
topics.history_overlap: The Spanish conquest is a history-bank episode. Keep rungs on the city's geography and engineering; the razing rung must anchor on the drained-lake subsidence payoff, not a conquest narrative that duplicates a history ladder.

topics.name: Teotihuacan
topics.strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
topics.scope: The vast ruined metropolis 40 km northeast of modern Mexico City, in the Valley of Mexico. T1: a dead-straight ceremonial avenue over 2 km long runs through the heart of the city, lined with platforms the much-later Aztecs mistook for royal tombs -- so they named it the Avenue of the Dead (answer = the named avenue; distractors other Mesoamerican causeways/sacbeob). T2 (the striking unknown): around 500 CE this was one of the largest cities on Earth, home to 100,000+ people, yet one basic thing is lost forever -- what its own builders called themselves and their city (answer = the builders' name/identity is unknown; 'Teotihuacan' is the Nahuatl name the Aztecs gave the ruins centuries later, meaning roughly 'place where the gods were made'). T3: rising about 65 m over the avenue, the third-largest ancient pyramid in all the Americas is the Pyramid of the Sun (answer = the named pyramid; distractors Pyramid of the Moon, the Great Pyramid of Cholula, La Danta at El Mirador). T4 (dinner-test payoff): in 2015 archaeologist Sergio Gomez tunnelled beneath the Temple of the Feathered Serpent and found, sealed for ~1,800 years, pools of a shimmering liquid metal -- liquid mercury, plus jade, mica and carved shells, perhaps an underworld river (answer = the liquid mercury).
