T5: the whole city is deliberately tilted ~15.5 degrees east of north on a single grid, and the Pyramid of the Moon squares up to face the sacred mountain Cerro Gordo behind it (answer = the astronomical/mountain alignment of the city plan). Further rungs: the Temple of the Feathered Serpent's facade bristling with stone Quetzalcoatl heads; multi-family stone apartment compounds housing artisans; workshops of green Pachuca obsidian traded across Mesoamerica; brilliant murals like the 'Paradise of Tlaloc'; the city's mysterious burning and collapse ~550 CE.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Pyramid of the Sun (~65.5 m, third-largest ancient pyramid in the New World after La Danta & Cholula; Aztecs named it, the Teotihuacanos' own name unknown; Avenue of the Dead) -- verified via WebFetch. Liquid-mercury tunnel discovery = Sergio Gomez, INAH, 2015 (Temple of the Feathered Serpent). Peak population 100,000+ and ~15.5-degree grid tilt from the Teotihuacan main article. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
topics.framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; present a real, sophisticated human city -- the 'we don't even know their name' rung is genuine wonder, NOT 'aliens/lost race' exoticising (that's the failure mode the stance rebuts). Lead with the Avenue scene. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: 'Teotihuacan' and 'Pyramid of the Sun' are LATER Aztec/Nahuatl names -- the builders' own names are unknown; the mercury is a real 2015 find, not legend. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the liquid-mercury tunnel (T4). LANE: the Aztecs are a HISTORY people -- keep rungs on the PLACE (avenue, pyramids, mercury, city grid); the unknown-builders rung is a place-mystery, not Aztec history.
topics.history_overlap: Aztec history is history-bank; here the Aztecs appear only as the later namers of the ruins. Keep every rung on the site itself. Flag the 'unknown builders' rung so it reads as a place-mystery rather than duplicating an Aztec-history ladder.

topics.name: Tikal
topics.strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
topics.scope: A Maya superpower city lost for a thousand years in the Peten rainforest of northern Guatemala. T1: six steep temple-pyramids punch up through the jungle at Tikal; the tallest, Temple IV, lifts its roof-comb about 70 m -- high enough to rise clear ABOVE the rainforest canopy, so climbers look out over an unbroken green sea of treetops (answer = above the forest canopy; distractors below the water table, into a cliff, over a gorge). T2: across the Great Plaza two twin pyramids face off -- the funerary Temple I, the 'Temple of the Great Jaguar' built over a king's tomb, gazes at Temple II, the 'Temple of the Masks' (answer = the named twin temple). T3: this was a lost city that truly vanished -- after ~900 CE the Maya abandoned Tikal and the jungle swallowed it for a millennium; the leading (still-debated) trigger across the Maya lowlands was decades of severe drought worsened by deforestation (answer = the drought-driven collapse; flag as leading-but-debated). T4: carved monuments record Tikal's centuries-long war with a rival superpower to the north, the 'Snake Kingdom' -- the dynasty of Calakmul (answer = the named rival city; distractors Copan, Palenque, Caracol). T5 (dinner-test payoff): with no rivers or lakes, Tikal's builders paved vast plazas to funnel every rainfall into lined reservoirs, and study of the largest suggests they kept the water clean with quartz sand and filtering plants -- an early water-filtration system (answer = the reservoir/sand-filter engineering). Further rungs: the towering plaster roof-combs; layered royal tombs in the North Acropolis; king Jasaw Chan K'awiil I's defeat of Calakmul in 695; Temple IV commissioned by Yikin Chan K'awiil ~741.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Tikal Temple IV (70 m to top of roof-comb; the SECOND-tallest pre-Columbian structure still standing, after Tonina's pyramid, with Teotihuacan's Pyramid of the Sun possibly once taller; built ~741 for Yikin Chan K'awiil) -- verified via WebFetch, correcting the common 'tallest' claim. Tikal reservoir sand-filtration = 2020 PNAS/Univ. of Cincinnati study. Calakmul rivalry and drought-collapse from the Tikal article. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
topics.framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; celebrate Maya engineering and astronomy as a full civilization. KEY ACCURACY RAIL (research-caught): do NOT call Temple IV 'the tallest pre-Columbian structure' -- it is roughly second (Tonina/Cholula/Pyramid of the Sun contest it); say 'one of the tallest, rising above the canopy'. Frame the collapse as the leading-but-debated drought explanation. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T5 rainwater reservoirs with sand filtration. LANE: the Tikal-Calakmul dynastic wars are a HISTORY subject -- frame the T4 rival rung as a PLACE (the rival city) not a war narrative, to avoid duplicating a history ladder.
topics.history_overlap: Tikal-Calakmul dynastic warfare risks duplicating a history ladder. Frame the Calakmul rung as a place (the rival city on the horizon) and keep the rest on the canopy-piercing temples, reservoirs, and the rainforest reclaiming the city.

topics.name: Tiwanaku and Pumapunku
topics.strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
topics.scope: A monumental ruined city on the treeless Bolivian altiplano near Lake Titicaca, ~3,850 m up. T1: on a high plain so lofty it lies above most European mountaintops, the ruins of Tiwanaku belong to a civilization that flourished a thousand years BEFORE the Inca (answer = it predates the Inca; distractors the Maya, the Aztec, the Spanish). T2: Tiwanaku's most famous monument is a great doorway carved from a single block of stone, its lintel crowned by a central 'Staff God' figure -- the Gate of the Sun (answer = the named gateway; distractors the Gate of the Moon, the Lion Gate, the Ishtar Gate). T3 (dinner-test payoff): at the nearby temple of Pumapunku, hard andesite blocks are cut into crisp interlocking H-shapes as precise as machine-work -- craftsmanship so exact it is a magnet for 'ancient aliens' myths, though Tiwanaku's own skilled masons made them (answer = the H-shaped blocks; distractors L-shaped, T-shaped, spiral). T4: the largest single stone at Pumapunku is estimated at about 131 tonnes and was hauled to the site from a quarry up to 10 km away across the bare altiplano (answer = ~131 tonnes; number as payoff; distractors ~20 t, ~400 t, ~1,000 t). T5: to farm this frost-prone highland Tiwanaku built long raised planting beds separated by water channels that soaked up the day's heat and shielded crops from night frost -- raised-field farming called waru waru (answer = the named raised-field system; teach the term). Further rungs: the sunken temple with its wall of carved stone heads; the Akapana platform mound; the Ponce monolith; the culture's decline ~AD 1000, linked to a long drought.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Pumapunku (elev 3,850 m, ~10 km from Lake Titicaca; largest sandstone block 7.81 m long, ~131 tonnes; precisely cut interlocking andesite/sandstone H-shaped blocks; construction ~AD 536-600, Tiwanaku peak ~AD 700-1000, predates the Inca; Gate of the Sun with Staff God/Viracocha imagery) -- verified via WebFetch. Waru waru / suka kollus raised-field farming from the Tiwanaku article. Grokipedia cross-check recommended.
topics.framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; the H-blocks are the work of skilled Tiwanaku masons -- the T3 rung must credit them and rebut the 'too precise for humans/aliens' pseudo-archaeology directly. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: block weights are ESTIMATES; Tiwanaku PREDATES the Inca (a common mix-up); dates ~AD 500-1000. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T3 H-blocks / T5 frost-proof raised fields. LANE: keep rungs on the PLACE (Gate of the Sun, Pumapunku, raised fields); Tiwanaku as a polity is shared with history.
topics.history_overlap: Tiwanaku as a civilization overlaps with the history bank. Keep rungs on the monuments and the raised-field engineering; no rung should read as a pure political-history episode.

topics.name: Tulum
topics.strand: Lost cities & marvels of the Americas
topics.scope: A walled Maya port perched on a low cliff above the turquoise Caribbean, on the Yucatan coast of Mexico. T1 (dinner-test payoff): almost every great Maya city hides inland in the jungle -- but Tulum sits right on a cliff over the sea, the only major Maya city built on the coast, above the Caribbean (answer = the Caribbean Sea / the coastal setting; distractors the Pacific, the Gulf of Mexico, the Atlantic). T2: Tulum was a walled trading town, and its Maya name was Zama, meaning 'dawn', because its cliff faces the sunrise over the sea (answer = 'dawn'/sunrise; distractors 'wall', 'harbour', 'star'). T3: Tulum guarded the coastal trade in obsidian, jade and salt, and its clifftop temple, El Castillo, is thought to have doubled as a beacon -- lined up with a gap in the offshore reef to guide trading canoes safely in (answer = a navigation beacon/lighthouse for canoes; FLAG as an interpretation; distractors a prison, a granary, a ball court).
topics.source: Wikipedia: Tulum (walled Postclassic Maya port on the Caribbean cliff coast; ancient name Zama meaning 'dawn/sunrise'; thrived 13th-15th c. as a trade port for obsidian, jade, salt; El Castillo clifftop temple with a possible reef-gap navigational/beacon function). Grokipedia cross-check recommended (WebSearch budget exhausted; corroborate the beacon interpretation and the 'Zama' gloss at build time).
topics.framing_note: PLACE->WONDER; Tulum's magic is the setting -- a Maya city on a Caribbean beach. Lead with the cliff-over-turquoise-sea scene. KEY ACCURACY RAIL: the El Castillo reef-beacon function is an INTERPRETATION -- flag it, don't assert it. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF = the T1 clifftop Caribbean setting. LANE: keep rungs on the PLACE (the coastal siting, the name, the beacon); Maya trade history is shared.
topics.history_overlap: Maya coastal-trade history overlaps lightly with the history bank. Keep the mini on the place (its clifftop setting, its name, its beacon), not a trade-network history ladder.

topics.name: Batik — Java's wax-drawn cloth
topics.strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
topics.scope: The wax-resist dyeing of Java, Indonesia. T1: on the island of Java, artists draw on cloth with hot wax so the waxed lines RESIST the dye — when the wax is later boiled off, the hidden pattern appears (hook = drawing in wax; answer = the wax blocks the dye). T2: the wax 'pen' is the canting — a tiny copper cup with a spout on a handle that lets the artist trail wax in fine dots and lines by hand (batik tulis). T3: to make cloth faster, a carved copper stamp called a 'cap' presses the wax pattern on in one go (batik cap). T4: in the royal courts of Yogyakarta and Surakarta, certain 'forbidden' patterns (larangan) — like the diagonal 'parang' — could be worn only by the sultan's family (dinner-test payoff: a pattern you could be forbidden to wear). T5: in 2009 UNESCO named Indonesian batik a Masterpiece of Intangible Cultural Heritage.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batik (VERIFIED: highly developed on Java, Indonesia; wax-resist process; canting = copper reservoir/spout pen; cap = carved copper stamp; UNESCO recognition 2 Oct 2009; some patterns restricted to certain occasions). Court larangan/parang exclusivity (Yogyakarta/Surakarta) well-documented — build re-cite. Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
topics.framing_note: Voice: lead with the craft-scene (trailing hot wax, then the pattern surfacing from the dye), never 'What is batik?'. Dinner-test payoff = the forbidden royal 'parang' pattern only the sultan's family could wear (T4). Accuracy rail: keep the wax-RESIST mechanism correct (wax blocks dye — it's not painting the color on); phrase the larangan restriction as a court tradition of Yogyakarta/Surakarta. Distractors = other real resist/dye textiles (Indian bandhani tie-dye, Japanese shibori, West African adire). Lane: pure textile craft.

topics.name: Cremona — the town of Stradivarius violins
topics.strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
topics.scope: The Italian town that built the world's finest violins. T1: in the small Italian town of Cremona, around the year 1700, Antonio Stradivari made violins now considered the greatest ever built — a 'Stradivarius' (place anchor = Cremona; answer = the violin/its maker). T2: of the roughly 1,100 instruments Stradivari built, about 650 survive, and single violins now sell for millions of dollars. T3: his 'golden period' (about 1700-1720) instruments are the most prized; one, 'the Messiah' of 1716, was kept so pristine it has barely ever been played and now sits in Oxford's Ashmolean Museum. T4: one theory for the magic sound: the 'Little Ice Age' (about 1645-1750) made trees grow slowly and evenly, giving unusually DENSE Alpine spruce for the wood. T5: yet in blind listening tests, expert players often can't reliably tell a Stradivarius from a fine modern violin — the 'secret' has never actually been proven (dinner-test payoff: maybe the legend beats the science).
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stradivarius (VERIFIED: made in Cremona by Antonio Stradivari, late-17th/early-18th c.; ~650 of >1,100 survive; golden period ~1700-1725; Little Ice Age / dense-wood theory ~1645-1750; blind tests find no reliable sound difference vs modern violins). 'The Messiah' (1716, Ashmolean, Oxford, nearly unplayed) — build cite en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messiah_Stradivarius. Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
topics.framing_note: Voice: lead with the town and the mystery, never 'What is a Stradivarius?'. Dinner-test payoff = the honest twist that blind tests can't reliably pick out a Strad (T5) — teaches HOW WE KNOW, not just awe. Accuracy rail: present the sound 'secret' as competing THEORIES, not proven fact; the Little Ice Age wood idea and the blind-test result are both real and both belong. Keep 'the Messiah / Ashmolean' precise. Distractors = other real Cremona makers/instruments (Guarneri 'del Gesù', Amati, Guadagnini) and other craft-towns. No lane conflict.

topics.name: Damascus steel — the lost watered blades
topics.strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
topics.scope: The legendary patterned swords sold in Damascus. T1: a true Damascus blade carried a rippling, flowing pattern locked into the metal, like water frozen in steel (hook = the water-pattern; answer = it's IN the steel, not painted on). T2: despite the name, the steel came as 'wootz' ingots from India and Sri Lanka — smiths in Damascus, Syria forged and sold them (the Arabic 'damas' also means 'watered'). T3: legends said a real blade could slice a silk scarf drifting down onto its edge, and cut clean through lesser swords (label LEGEND). T4: the craft was LOST — by around 1900 no living smith could make it, and even now the exact wootz method is only partly reverse-engineered (dinner-test payoff: a technology humans forgot how to do). T5: in 2006 scientists reported carbon nanotubes and cementite bands inside an antique blade — a possible clue to its edge, though experts still argue about it (label DISPUTED).
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damascus_steel (VERIFIED: high-carbon crucible/wootz steel from southern India + Sri Lanka, forged/sold in Damascus; 'damas' = watered; name likely early branding; production ceased ~1900, last account 1903; 2006 German report of nanotubes/cementite, disputed; legends of cutting silk and iron). Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
topics.framing_note: Voice: lead with the blade and its water-pattern, never 'What is Damascus steel?'. Dinner-test payoff = the lost-and-only-half-recovered craft (T4). CRITICAL accuracy rail: the 'Damascus' name is essentially branding — the STEEL came from India/Sri Lanka (wootz); T2 must make that clear so no kid learns it was mined in Syria. Label the silk-scarf sharpness stories LEGEND and the nanotube finding DISPUTED — do NOT state either as settled fact. Distractors = other real famed steels/blade-cities (Toledo, Sheffield, Japanese tamahagane) — adjacent and wrong, never joke options.

topics.name: Harris Tweed — the cloth protected by law
topics.strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
topics.scope: The hand-woven wool of Scotland's Outer Hebrides. T1: on the windswept Outer Hebrides islands — Lewis, Harris, the Uists, Barra — Harris Tweed is still hand-woven by islanders in their OWN HOMES on foot-powered treadle looms, not in a factory (hook = a world-famous cloth made in cottages; answer = handwoven at home in the Hebrides). T2: real Harris Tweed carries a stamped 'Orb' mark, a trademark since 1909, certifying each length is genuine. T3: it is protected by its very own UK Act of Parliament — the Harris Tweed Act 1993 — which legally DEFINES it: pure virgin wool, dyed and spun in the Outer Hebrides, and handwoven at the weaver's home (dinner-test payoff: a cloth with its own law). T4: the tweed was built for its place — dense, weatherproof wool made to shed Hebridean wind and rain, its muted colors once drawn from local plants and lichens.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harris_Tweed (VERIFIED: made in the Outer Hebrides — Lewis/Harris/Uists/Benbecula/Barra; handwoven on a treadle loom at each weaver's home; the Orb trademark granted 1909; Harris Tweed Act 1993 statutory definition — pure virgin wool dyed/spun in the Outer Hebrides, handwoven at home). Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
topics.framing_note: Voice: scene-led — a global luxury cloth still woven in island cottages — never 'What is Harris Tweed?'. Dinner-test payoff = it's protected by its OWN Act of Parliament (T3). Accuracy rail: do NOT over-claim it's 'the only fabric with its own law' (widely repeated but not confirmed) — phrase it as 'its own Act of Parliament, the Harris Tweed Act 1993.' Place-anchor every rung to the Outer Hebrides. Distractors = other named regional cloths (Donegal tweed, Shetland wool, cashmere). Lane: textile craft; the sheep are a one-word source mention, not animal-bank biology.

topics.name: Jingdezhen — China's porcelain capital
topics.strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
topics.scope: The 'Porcelain Capital' in Jiangxi, China, whose kilns burned for a thousand years. T1: for centuries hundreds of kilns here glowed day and night so brightly the town was said to be 'lit by fire at midnight' — Jingdezhen is called China's Porcelain Capital (invert the wonder: the fires/scale is the hook, the town's title is the answer). T2: the secret white ingredient is a clay dug from a nearby hill named Gaoling ('high ridge') — the hill's own name became the English word KAOLIN (answer = kaolin / the word comes from a hill's name). T3: the emperor kept a private 'imperial kiln' here, and only he could own porcelain painted with the five-clawed dragon. T4: the porcelain was so fine and so unmatched that Europeans named the whole material after the country it came from — 'china.' T5: in 1712 a French Jesuit priest, Père d'Entrecolles, living in Jingdezhen, wrote letters home describing the secret recipe — the leak that helped Europe finally reproduce porcelain (the town itself was renamed for Emperor Zhenzong's Jingde reign of 1004, when he ordered wares stamped with his reign-name).
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaolinite (VERIFIED: 'kaolin' borrowed 1727 from d'Entrecolles' 1712 reports on Jingdezhen porcelain, from Gaoling 'High Ridge' village near Jingdezhen); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jingdezhen_porcelain + /wiki/Jingdezhen (imperial kilns, Jingde-reign naming, d'Entrecolles — build should re-confirm the 1004 reign-name detail and imperial dragon-mark exclusivity). Grokipedia checked first per protocol but grokipedia.com returned HTTP 403 to the fetch tool.
topics.framing_note: Voice: lead with the scene (a town on fire with kilns; a hill whose name you now say every day), never 'What is kaolin?' or 'What is the capital of porcelain?'. Every rung's answer is a concrete fact about THIS town or its clay. Dinner-test payoff = the 'china' = country = material naming rung (T4) and the Gaoling-became-'kaolin' rung (T2) — a kid retells both. Accuracy rail: kaolin's etymology and the d'Entrecolles leak are firmly documented; keep the five-clawed-dragon exclusivity phrased as imperial-court rule. Lane: the clay/geology sits fine in geography (a real mineral from a real hill); the recipe/craft is culture — both in-lane, no food overlap. Pairs as a distractor set with the Meissen ladder (Europe's answer to china).

topics.name: Kente — the Ashanti cloth of Ghana
topics.strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
topics.scope: The bright royal cloth of the Ashanti, born in Ghana. T1: kente is hand-woven in narrow strips on a loom in the village of Bonwire, in Ghana's Ashanti Region, then the strips are sewn edge-to-edge into a wide, dazzling cloth (place anchor = Bonwire). T2: Ashanti legend says weavers first learned the craft by watching Anansi the spider spin its web (label LEGEND; dinner-test payoff — a spider taught people to weave). T3: the name is linked to the Akan word for 'basket' (kenten), because the tight woven pattern looks basket-like. T4: every color and pattern carries a meaning — gold for royalty and wealth, blue for peace — and each design has its own name and proverb. T5: kente was once reserved for Ashanti kings and chiefs, worn draped toga-style; in the 1900s it became a worldwide symbol of African heritage.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kente_cloth (VERIFIED: originates from Bonwire, Ashanti Region, Ghana; Anansi-the-spider origin story; name tied to Akan 'basket'; hand-woven silk/cotton strips; symbolic colors — gold=royalty/wealth, blue=peace; worn toga-style, royal patronage). Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
topics.framing_note: Voice: scene-led — the loom in Bonwire, a spider spinning — never 'What is kente?'. Dinner-test payoff = Anansi the spider taught the first weavers (T2). Accuracy rail: label the Anansi origin a LEGEND, and keep the weavers generic (oral tradition doesn't reliably fix individual names) — don't assert named craftsmen as history. Distractors = other real African/strip textiles (mudcloth/bogolan of Mali, adire of the Yoruba, aso-oke). Respectful, celebratory tone; this is settled cultural wonder, not a stance rung. Lane: pure textile craft, no food/animal overlap.

topics.name: Kintsugi — Japan's golden mending
topics.strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
topics.scope: The Japanese art of repairing pottery with gold. T1: in Japan, 'kintsugi' ('golden joinery') mends a broken bowl by filling the cracks with lacquer dusted with gold — so the mended seams SHINE instead of hiding (hook = a repair you're meant to see; answer = the cracks are filled with gold). T2: the idea flips how we think about damage: a bowl's break becomes part of its story and the gold-veined repair makes it MORE beautiful and more valued, not less (the wabi-sabi love of imperfection; dinner-test payoff). T3 (legend): one story says a 15th-century shogun, Ashikaga Yoshimasa, sent a cracked tea bowl to China and got it back stapled with ugly metal — so Japanese craftsmen invented a lovelier way to mend (label LEGEND).
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kintsugi (VERIFIED: repairing broken pottery with urushi lacquer dusted/mixed with powdered gold; connected to wabi-sabi and mottainai; origin legend of shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa's broken tea bowl returned from China with metal staples, prompting a finer repair). Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
topics.framing_note: Voice: lead with the beautiful paradox (gold-lined cracks make a broken bowl worth MORE) — never 'What is kintsugi?'. Dinner-test payoff = the flaw becomes the treasure (T1/T2). Accuracy rail: label the Ashikaga Yoshimasa origin as a LEGEND, not settled history. Place-anchor = Japan (the craft has no single town, so this stays a compact mini rather than a place-deep ladder). Distractors = other real repair/craft ideas (Chinese metal-staple 'rivet' repair, wabi-sabi, raku, urushi lacquerware). Pairs with Ryoan-ji as Japanese aesthetics. No lane conflict.

topics.name: Meissen — how Europe cracked China's porcelain secret
topics.strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
topics.scope: The Saxon town where Europe first made true porcelain. T1: in the town of Meissen in Saxony, Germany, Europe finally made its first true hard-paste porcelain in 1710 — matching Chinese 'china' at last after centuries of failing (place anchor = Meissen). T2: the breakthrough came from Johann Friedrich Böttger, an alchemist LOCKED UP by Augustus the Strong, who demanded Böttger turn cheap metal into GOLD (dinner-test payoff: imprisoned to make gold). T3: Böttger never made a speck of gold — but working with the scientist Tschirnhaus he cracked the porcelain recipe (kaolin was the missing key), and porcelain became known as 'white gold.' T4: Meissen's crossed-swords mark, added in 1720, is one of the oldest trademarks still in use today.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meissen_porcelain (VERIFIED: first European hard-paste porcelain; Böttger held in 'protective custody' by Augustus II 'the Strong' to make gold; worked with Tschirnhaus; kaolin the vital ingredient; production started 1710 at Albrechtsburg, Meissen; crossed-swords mark introduced 1720, one of the oldest trademarks). Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
topics.framing_note: Voice: scene-led — an alchemist jailed to make gold who instead makes 'white gold' — never 'What is Meissen porcelain?'. Dinner-test payoff = Böttger imprisoned to transmute gold, cracks porcelain instead (T2). Accuracy rail: keep the story precise — Böttger did NOT make gold; kaolin was the key; 1710 first production, 1720 crossed-swords mark. Deliberately pairs with the Jingdezhen ladder (the secret China guarded; the secret Europe stole) — distractors = rival European porcelain towns (Delft, Sèvres, Limoges, Wedgwood). No lane conflict.

topics.name: Murano — Venice's island of glass
topics.strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
topics.scope: The lagoon island where Venice hid its glassmakers. T1: in 1291 Venice ordered ALL its glassmakers onto one small island, Murano — partly because the roaring furnaces kept setting fire to the wooden city (hook = a whole trade exiled to an island; answer = to stop the fires / and guard the secret). T2: the deeper reason was secrecy — a Murano glassmaker was forbidden to leave Venice, and betraying the craft's secrets could be punished by DEATH (dinner-test payoff). T3: yet the glassmakers were treated almost as nobles — a glassmaker's daughter could marry into a noble family without her children losing rank. T4: in the 1400s Angelo Barovier invented 'cristallo' — glass so clear it looked like carved rock crystal, then the finest in the world. T5: Murano's 'millefiori' ('thousand flowers') fuses bundles of colored glass rods so that every slice reveals a tiny flower hidden inside the glass.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murano_glass (VERIFIED: 1291 law confining glassmaking to Murano for fire-risk + secrecy; leaving/revealing secrets punishable by death; cristallo by Angelo Barovier, 15th c.; millefiori = 'thousand flowers'; 1376 privilege that a glassmaker's daughter marrying a noble kept noble rank). Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
topics.framing_note: Voice: lead with the scene (a burning city; craftsmen who could never leave), never 'What is Murano glass?'. Each answer is a concrete fact about THIS island's craft. Dinner-test payoff = glassmakers forbidden to leave on pain of death (T2), with the daughter-marries-a-noble privilege (T3) as the surprising twist. Accuracy rail: the 1291 date, the death-penalty secrecy, and Barovier's cristallo are documented — keep them precise. Distractors stay adjacent-but-real: Bohemian/Czech crystal, Venetian mirrors, Tiffany glass. No lane conflicts.

topics.name: Persian carpets — Iran's woven gardens
topics.strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
topics.scope: The knotted carpets of Iran. T1: a fine Persian carpet packs hundreds of hand-tied knots into a single square inch — the famous Ardabil Carpet holds about 26 MILLION knots in one rug (hook = the knot count; answer = it's all tied by hand, one knot at a time). T2: the Ardabil Carpet (made 1539-40) is signed by its weaver, Maqsud of Kashan, carries a couplet by the poet Hafez, and today hangs in the V&A museum in London. T3: Persian weavers use the asymmetric 'Persian knot,' which lets them bend fine curving flower-and-vine designs that blockier knots can't. T4: many are 'garden carpets' — a walled paradise garden with water channels, seen from above — and the Old Persian word for such a walled garden, 'pairidaeza,' is where we get the word PARADISE (dinner-test payoff). T5: rival weaving cities each have a signature style — Tabriz, Isfahan, Kashan, Kerman — readable by pattern and palette (optional labeled-LEGEND rung: some weavers left one deliberate flaw, saying only God is perfect — a tradition, not a rule).
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ardabil_Carpet (VERIFIED: ~26 million knots; 300-350 knots/sq inch; made 946 AH = 1539-40; signed Maqsud of Kashan; Hafez couplet; larger carpet at the V&A, London); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_carpet (VERIFIED: asymmetric Persian knot; Tabriz/Isfahan/Kashan/Kerman centers; garden carpets). 'Paradise' from Old Persian pairidaeza — well-established etymology (build cite en.wiktionary/paradise). Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
topics.framing_note: Voice: scene-led — a rug that is 26 million knots, a woven garden you look down into — never 'What is a Persian carpet?'. Dinner-test payoff = pairidaeza-gave-us-'paradise' (T4), with the 26-million-knots hook (T1). Accuracy rail: the deliberate-flaw idea is FOLKLORE/DISPUTED — if used, label it a tradition weavers sometimes spoke of, never state it as a rule. Keep the Ardabil facts exact (date, weaver, V&A). Distractors = other real rug traditions (Turkish/Anatolian Ghiordes-knot rugs, Turkmen, Kashmiri). No lane conflicts.

topics.name: Ryoan-ji — Kyoto's garden of stone
topics.strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
topics.scope: The Zen dry-landscape garden in Kyoto, Japan. T1: at the Ryoan-ji temple in Kyoto sits a famous 'dry garden' (karesansui) with NO plants and NO water — just a rectangle of raked white gravel and 15 bare stones (hook = a garden with nothing growing; answer = a dry/Zen rock garden). T2: the white gravel is combed daily into straight lines and rings, meant to suggest rippling water or the sea flowing around islands. T3: the 15 stones are set so cleverly that from anywhere on the viewing veranda you can see at most 14 — one stone is ALWAYS hidden behind another, no matter where you stand (dinner-test payoff). T4: the garden isn't made to walk through — it's a puzzle you sit and contemplate, a place for Zen meditation.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ry%C5%8Dan-ji (VERIFIED: Kyoto; karesansui dry-landscape garden; 15 stones; from the veranda at least one stone is always hidden — you can never see all 15 at once; raked gravel; late-15th-century origin; UNESCO World Heritage). Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
topics.framing_note: Voice: lead with the strangeness (a garden with nothing planted; gravel raked like water), never 'What is a Zen garden?' — teach the term 'karesansui' in the rung before testing it. Dinner-test payoff = you can never see all 15 stones at once, one is always hidden (T3) — the single most retellable fact. Accuracy rail: the 'always at least one hidden' fact is real and specific — keep it exact (at most 14 visible). Anchor every rung to Ryoan-ji / Kyoto. Distractors = other real Japanese garden types (stroll garden, tea garden, moss garden). Pairs thematically with the kintsugi mini as Japanese aesthetics.

topics.name: Silk — China's two-thousand-year secret
topics.strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
topics.scope: The guarded craft of sericulture, born in China. T1: silk is spun by a caterpillar — the silkworm (Bombyx mori) — which eats only mulberry leaves and wraps itself in a cocoon made of ONE unbroken thread up to about a kilometre long (hook = a single thread that long; answer = it's one caterpillar's cocoon). T2: Chinese legend credits Empress Leizu with discovering silk around 3000 BC when a cocoon dropped into her cup of hot tea and unravelled into a shining thread (label LEGEND). T3: China guarded the secret of making silk for roughly TWO THOUSAND years — carrying silkworm eggs out of the country could be punished by death. T4: around 552 AD the Byzantine emperor Justinian sent two monks who smuggled silkworm eggs out of China hidden inside hollow bamboo canes, finally breaking the monopoly (dinner-test payoff). T5: the overland trade in this cloth named the 'Silk Road,' the caravan network running some 6,400 km from Chang'an (today's Xi'an) to the Mediterranean.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_silk (VERIFIED: ~2000-yr guarded secret; Justinian c.552 AD sent monks who smuggled silkworm eggs in bamboo/rods; Leizu ~3000 BC cocoon-in-tea legend; Bombyx mori feeds on mulberry). Grokipedia checked first per protocol (403 to fetch tool).
topics.framing_note: Voice: scene-led — the empress's teacup, the monks' hollow staffs — never 'What is silk made of?'. Invert the wonder: the km-long thread and the death-penalty secrecy are hooks, the knowable fact is the answer. Dinner-test payoff = the two monks smuggling eggs in hollow bamboo canes (T4). Accuracy rail: label the Leizu teacup as legend; the Justinian smuggling and the ~2,000-year monopoly are the documented backbone. LANE (animal): the silkworm is a one-rung PROCESS mention (it makes the thread) — keep answers on the craft and the guarded place, never the caterpillar's biology, which belongs to the animal bank. Xi'an/Chang'an anchors the Silk Road rung as a real place.

topics.name: Tartan and the kilt — Highland Scotland
topics.strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
topics.scope: The clan cloth of the Scottish Highlands. T1: in the Scottish Highlands the tartan is a criss-cross woven pattern (its repeating unit is called the 'sett'), and the original 'great kilt' was one long belted plaid wrapped around the whole body (hook = one cloth, worn as a whole outfit; answer = the great kilt / belted plaid). T2: after the Jacobites were crushed at Culloden in 1746, Britain's Dress Act BANNED the kilt and tartan in the Highlands — you could be jailed, or shipped overseas, for wearing your own clan's cloth (dinner-test payoff: a clothing pattern made illegal). T3: the ban was lifted in 1782 and tartan came roaring back — but much of the tidy 'one clan, one tartan' idea was actually a romantic invention of the 1800s, not ancient law. T4: today an official Scottish Register of Tartans records thousands of named setts, from clans to districts to companies.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dress_Act_1746 (VERIFIED: part of the Act of Proscription after the 1745 Jacobite rising / Battle of Culloden; banned the plaid, philabeg/little kilt and tartan north of the Highland line; repealed by the Use of Highland Dress Act 1782). Sett/great-kilt and the 19th-c. clan-tartan romanticization + Scottish Register of Tartans — build re-cite. Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
topics.framing_note: Voice: scene-led — a cloth so tied to identity that a government outlawed it — never 'What is tartan?'. Dinner-test payoff = the kilt/tartan was banned by law after Culloden (T2). Accuracy rail: be honest that much clan-specific tartan is a 19th-century romantic invention (Sir Walter Scott / George IV's 1822 visit), NOT ancient — don't feed the myth. HISTORY-LANE BORDER: Culloden and the 1745 Jacobite rising are a military/dynastic episode the history bank may own — keep EVERY rung's answer on the CLOTH (the sett, the great kilt, the clothing ban and its 1782 repeal, the tartan register), never on the battle's course or the Jacobite cause. Distractors = other real regional patterns/garments.

topics.name: The Four Great Inventions of ancient China
topics.strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
topics.scope: Four world-changing inventions born in China, one per rung. T1 (paper): a Han-dynasty court official, Cai Lun (around 105 AD), perfected paper from mashed bark, rag and old fishnet, replacing heavy bamboo strips (answer = paper / Cai Lun's mash). T2 (printing): the world's oldest DATED printed book is a Chinese Buddhist scroll, the Diamond Sutra of 868 AD, made by carved woodblocks centuries before Gutenberg. T3 (movable type): around 1040 a commoner named Bi Sheng carved each character in baked clay — movable type, roughly 400 years before Gutenberg's European press. T4 (compass): the first compass wasn't for sailors — Han-dynasty Chinese carved a spoon of lodestone (the 'sinan') that spun to point SOUTH, used to lay out buildings and for divination. T5 (gunpowder): Tang-dynasty alchemists mixing saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal were chasing an ELIXIR OF IMMORTALITY — and stumbled onto gunpowder (huoyao, 'fire medicine') instead (dinner-test payoff: seeking eternal life, they invented an explosive).

Build should re-confirm each date at author stage. Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
topics.framing_note: Voice: each rung sets a scene and the answer names WHICH invention or its ironic origin, never a bare date. Invert the wonder: the alchemists' goal (eternal life) is the payoff answer for gunpowder, not the word 'gunpowder.' Anchor = China / its dynastic courts (a real place per rung). Dinner-test payoff = gunpowder-from-the-immortality-elixir (T5), and the south-pointing sinan spoon (T4). No history-bank duplication if answers stay on the inventions themselves, not on later wars/print revolutions.

topics.name: The Panama hat — actually from Ecuador
topics.strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
topics.scope: The famous hat named after the wrong country. T1: the 'Panama hat' isn't from Panama at all — it's hand-woven in ECUADOR, in towns like Montecristi and Cuenca, from the straw of the toquilla palm (hook = a hat named after the wrong place; answer = it's really Ecuadorian). T2: it got the wrong name because the hats were SHIPPED through Panama, and President Theodore Roosevelt was photographed wearing one at the Panama Canal in 1906 — so the world credited Panama (dinner-test payoff: named for its shipping port, not its home). T3: the finest 'Montecristi superfino' is woven so tightly and finely that it can hold water and be rolled up small enough to pass through a wedding ring.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama_hat (VERIFIED: made in Ecuador — Montecristi and Cuenca — from toquilla palm/Carludovica palmata straw; misnamed because shipped through Panama and popularized when Theodore Roosevelt was photographed wearing one at the Panama Canal in 1906; finest 'Montecristi superfino' can hold water and pass through a wedding ring). Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
topics.framing_note: Voice: lead with the surprise (the 'Panama' hat is Ecuadorian) — never 'Where is the Panama hat from?'. Dinner-test payoff = it's named for the port it shipped through, not its home (T2), with the pass-through-a-wedding-ring feat (T3) close behind. Accuracy rail: keep the misnomer story precise (Ecuador origin; Panama = shipping/canal fame; TR 1906 photo). topics.name: The didgeridoo — Arnhem Land, Australia
topics.strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
topics.scope: One of the world's oldest wind instruments, from northern Australia. T1: in Arnhem Land in northern Australia, Aboriginal people play the didgeridoo — a long wooden drone-pipe, among the world's oldest wind instruments (hook = a pipe that plays one endless humming note; answer = the didgeridoo). T2: it's not carved hollow by hand — makers search out eucalyptus branches that TERMITES have eaten hollow from the inside, then cut and trim them (dinner-test payoff: insects make the instrument). T3: players use 'circular breathing' — breathing IN through the nose while pushing stored air out with puffed cheeks — to hold one note without a break for minutes on end. T4: the Yolngu people of northeast Arnhem Land call it the 'yidaki'; rock paintings show it's been played for well over a thousand years (accuracy rail: NOT the popular '40,000 years' claim).
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didgeridoo (VERIFIED: developed by Aboriginal peoples of northern Australia, Arnhem Land; made from eucalyptus hollowed by termites; circular breathing = inhale through nose while expelling stored air via cheeks; Yolngu name 'yidaki'; archaeology/rock art suggests use for LESS THAN ~1,000 years in Kakadu, a ~1,500-year-old rock painting shows a player — the '40,000 years / oldest instrument' claim is NOT supported). Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
topics.framing_note: Voice: lead with the sound and the place (a droning pipe from Arnhem Land), never 'What is a didgeridoo?'. Dinner-test payoff = termites hollow it out (T2), with circular breathing (T3) close behind. CRITICAL accuracy rail: correct the romantic overclaim — say 'one of the oldest' wind instruments and cite rock art of ~1,500 years, NOT '40,000 years' or 'the oldest'. Respectful tone; teach 'yidaki' as the Yolngu name. LANE (animal): the termite is a one-rung PROCESS mention (it hollows the wood) — keep the answer on the instrument, never termite biology, which is the animal bank's.

topics.name: The theremin — Russia's untouchable instrument
topics.strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
topics.scope: The instrument you play without touching, invented in Russia. T1: in Russia in 1920, the physicist Leon Theremin invented an instrument you play WITHOUT EVER TOUCHING it — the theremin, that eerie wavering wail heard in old sci-fi and horror films (hook = music from thin air; answer = the theremin). T2: it has two antennas — move one hand near the upright rod to change the PITCH, the other hand near the loop to change the VOLUME — your hands sense the electric field but never make contact. T3: the same inventor later built 'The Thing,' a hidden bug with NO batteries and no wires that let the Soviets secretly listen inside the US ambassador's office for years (dinner-test payoff: the music inventor built a spy device).
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theremin (VERIFIED: invented by Lev Termen / Leon Theremin, Russia, October 1920; played with no contact via two antennas — one controls pitch, one controls volume — each forming a capacitor with the player's hand). 'The Thing' (Great Seal covert listening device, Leon Theremin) — build cite en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Thing_(listening_device). Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
topics.framing_note: Voice: lead with the wonder (music pulled from empty air), never 'What is a theremin?'. Dinner-test payoff = the same man who made music from thin air also built a passive spy bug, 'The Thing' (T3). topics.name: Byblos & the Phoenician alphabet that conquered the world
topics.strand: Languages & scripts born in a place
topics.scope: Byblos (Gebal) on the Lebanese coast, its sister ports Tyre and Sidon, and the alphabet's onward road to Greece and Rome. T1: on the coast of Lebanon sits BYBLOS, one of the oldest cities people have never stopped living in -- and the home of the alphabet that, in a way, YOU are reading right now. T2: the Phoenician alphabet did something radical -- it DROPPED the vowels and used just 22 signs for CONSONANTS, small enough that a merchant, not only a priest, could learn to write (an 'abjad'). T2: Phoenicians were the Mediterranean's great SEA-TRADERS, and they carried the easy alphabet on their ships to every port -- it spread by TRADE, not conquest. T3: the oldest long Phoenician text is carved on the stone coffin of King Ahiram of Byblos (~1000 BCE), and it even sets a CURSE on anyone who disturbs the tomb. T3 (dinner-test): our word 'Bible' comes from BYBLOS -- the city was the great port for Egyptian PAPYRUS, so Greeks called the writing-paper 'byblos' and a book 'biblion'. T4: the Greeks borrowed the Phoenician letters around 800 BCE, kept the names and ORDER (aleph->alpha, bet->beta = 'alphabet'), but re-used spare consonant signs as the first true VOWELS -- the missing pieces added back. T4: the letters still hide their old PICTURES -- aleph was an OX-head (flip our 'A' over and you see the horns), bet was a HOUSE, mem was WATER (our wavy 'M'). T5: from Byblos the trail runs Phoenician -> Greek -> Etruscan -> LATIN, so the ABCs of English are great-great-grandchildren of a Lebanese trading script. T5: the same Phoenician root also branched into Aramaic, Hebrew and (through Aramaic) Arabic -- most of the world's alphabets share this ONE Levantine ancestor.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenician_alphabet, /Byblos, /Ahiram_sarcophagus, /Greek_alphabet, /History_of_the_alphabet (standard references; corroborate the 'byblos->Bible' etymology and Ahiram ~1000 BCE dating at build)
topics.framing_note: Scene-led, place in the stem (Byblos / the Lebanese coast; Greece named only as the alphabet's next stop). Invert the wonder -- lead with 'the alphabet you're reading right now', make the concrete fact the answer (it dropped the VOWELS; flip 'A' to see the ox). Key accuracy rail: Phoenician is an ABJAD (consonants only); the Greeks' innovation was adding vowels -- keep that pairing exact. Dinner-test payoff: 'Bible' comes from Byblos. Lane border: this shares the alphabet-origin territory with the Serabit el-Khadim ladder (proto-Sinaitic is the earlier ancestor, Byblos the mature Phoenician stage) -- keep Byblos rungs on the CITY and the Phoenician stage, and let Serabit own the desert-mine birth.

topics.name: Cuneiform & the clay tablets of Sumer
topics.strand: Languages & scripts born in a place
topics.scope: The mud-brick cities of Sumer in southern Iraq (Uruk), plus Nineveh's great library and Darius's cliff at Behistun. T1: in Sumer the world's OLDEST writing was pressed into wet CLAY with a cut reed -- the wedge marks we call cuneiform ('cuneus' = wedge in Latin). T2: it was invented not for poetry but for BOOKKEEPING -- the first tablets at Uruk are receipts counting sheep, grain and beer. T2: the reed stylus makes triangular WEDGES because you cannot drag a curve through wet clay, so the early pictures collapsed into abstract wedge-clusters. T3: because it is baked/dried CLAY, when a city burned the tablets fired hard and SURVIVED -- fire destroys paper but preserves clay, which is why hundreds of thousands remain. T3: cuneiform was never one language -- for ~3,000 years it was reused to write Sumerian, then Akkadian, Babylonian, Hittite (a shared writing 'operating system'). T3: Mesopotamian numbers were BASE-60 (sexagesimal) -- the reason a circle has 360 degrees and an hour 60 minutes traces to Sumer. T4: the Epic of Gilgamesh, the oldest great story, survives on twelve clay tablets from Nineveh's Library of Ashurbanipal (7th c. BCE), and Tablet XI tells a FLOOD story older than Noah. T4 (dinner-test): in 1872 George Smith, reading a Nineveh tablet in the British Museum, found that Flood story and reportedly grew so excited he began tearing off his clothes -- the first modern person to read a lost 2,600-year-old tale. T5: how cuneiform was CRACKED -- on a cliff at Behistun in Iran, Darius the Great carved the same boast in three cuneiform languages, and Henry Rawlinson copied it dangling on ropes, using it as cuneiform's 'Rosetta Stone'. T5: one wedge-sign could be a whole word, a syllable, OR a silent 'determiner' tag that labels a category -- one sign doing three jobs, which is why it resisted reading for so long.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuneiform, /Uruk, /Epic_of_Gilgamesh, /Library_of_Ashurbanipal, /George_Smith_(Assyriologist), /Behistun_Inscription, /Sexagesimal (standard references, corroborate at build via Grokipedia-first per pipeline; Grokipedia returned 403 this session)
topics.framing_note: Scene-led, place always in the stem (Sumer/Uruk/Nineveh/Behistun); invert the wonder -- lead with the huge number/mystery, make the knowable fact the answer (300,000 surviving tablets -> 'because fire BAKES clay'). Key accuracy rail: cuneiform is a SCRIPT reused across many languages, not a language -- keep stems saying 'cuneiform', not 'the Sumerian language'. Dinner-test payoff: George Smith and the Flood tablet. Behistun is the decipherment rung (pairs with the Rosetta Stone ladder as the two great trilingual keys). Lane border: the PLOT of Gilgamesh and Mesopotamian empire history belong to history/mythology -- here every answer is about the WRITING and its PLACE (the tablet, the library, the cliff), never the epic's storyline.
topics.history_overlap: The flood-tablet/Gilgamesh content can brush a history-or-mythology episode; keep the rung on the tablet and its discovery, not the epic's narrative.

topics.name: Cyrillic & the brothers of Thessaloniki
topics.strand: Languages & scripts born in a place
topics.scope: Thessaloniki (the brothers' home port), Great Moravia, and the First Bulgarian Empire (the Preslav Literary School) where Cyrillic actually formed. T1: more than half a billion people -- Russian, Ukrainian, Bulgarian, Serbian readers -- write in the CYRILLIC alphabet, and the trail leads to two brothers, Cyril and Methodius, from the Greek port of THESSALONIKI. T2: sent north to Great Moravia around 863 to preach in the local Slavic tongue, the brothers first invented a DIFFERENT alphabet -- Glagolitic -- a swirl of loops and crosses built to spell Slavic sounds Greek letters couldn't. T3 (dinner-test / the twist): the alphabet NAMED after Cyril was actually made AFTER he died -- by his DISCIPLES in Bulgaria at the Preslav Literary School (~890s-900s), who kept Greek letter-shapes and borrowed Glagolitic letters for sounds like 'sh' and 'zh'. T3: Cyrillic looks like Greek because it mostly IS Greek uncial letters -- but the extra signs (Zh, Sh, Shch, Yu) were added in Bulgaria for Slavic sounds Greek didn't have. T4: the brothers gave the Slavs their first written language, Old Church Slavonic, which is why Cyril is honored as 'Apostle to the Slavs' and the two share a feast day marked across the Slavic and EU world.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrillic_script (verified via WebFetch this session: Cyril/Methodius made GLAGOLITIC ~863; Cyrillic built later by disciples at the Preslav Literary School, First Bulgarian Empire, earliest inscriptions ~921), /Saints_Cyril_and_Methodius, /Glagolitic_script
topics.framing_note: Scene-led, place in every stem (Thessaloniki / Great Moravia / Bulgaria). CRITICAL accuracy rail (the whole ladder turns on it): Cyril and Methodius created GLAGOLITIC, not Cyrillic -- Cyrillic was built later by their disciples in BULGARIA and merely named in Cyril's honor. Do NOT write a rung saying 'Cyril invented the Cyrillic alphabet' (the common myth). Dinner-test payoff: the alphabet named after Cyril wasn't made by Cyril. This is settled history, so keep choices as adjacent real facts (Glagolitic vs Cyrillic, Thessaloniki vs Constantinople, Moravia vs Bulgaria) -- no stance needed.

topics.name: Egyptian hieroglyphs & the Rosetta Stone
topics.strand: Languages & scripts born in a place
topics.scope: The Nile temples of Karnak and Luxor, the Delta town of Rosetta (Rashid), and the island temple of Philae. T1: on the temple walls along the Nile, HIEROGLYPHS are tiny pictures -- birds, eyes, feet -- that are also SOUNDS, and for ~1,400 years no living person could read them. T2: the key surfaced in July 1799 when a French soldier fortifying Fort Julien near the Delta town of ROSETTA dug up a black slab carrying the same decree three ways. T2: the Rosetta Stone records a priests' decree for young King Ptolemy V (196 BCE) in hieroglyphs (for the gods), Demotic (everyday Egyptian), and GREEK -- and scholars could still read the Greek. T3: the crack in the code was the CARTOUCHE -- the oval loop drawn around a royal NAME -- because a name like 'Ptolemy' had to be spelled out in sound-signs, not pictures. T3: in 1822 Jean-Francois Champollion realized hieroglyphs are BOTH picture-signs and sound-signs mixed together, and reportedly ran to his brother shouting 'I've got it!' before collapsing. T4: Champollion could do it partly because he read COPTIC -- the last living descendant of ancient Egyptian, still chanted in Egyptian churches -- so he knew how the words should sound. T4: the LAST hieroglyph ever carved is dated 394 CE on the temple of PHILAE, an island in the Nile -- after that the knowledge died for fourteen centuries. T4: Britain seized the stone when Napoleon's army surrendered in Egypt (1801) and shipped it to London, where it is the British Museum's most-visited object. T5 (dinner-test): Egyptians wrote hieroglyphs in either direction, and you tell which way to read by which way the animals FACE -- you always read TOWARD their faces. T5: 'hieroglyph' is Greek for 'sacred carving'; the Egyptians called their own script 'medu netjer', the god's words.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosetta_Stone (verified via WebFetch this session: 1799 Bouchard at Rosetta, 196 BCE Ptolemy V, hieroglyphic/Demotic/Greek, Champollion 1822, Young/cartouches), /Egyptian_hieroglyphs, /Jean-Francois_Champollion, /Philae, /Graffito_of_Esmet-Akhom
topics.framing_note: Scene-led, place in every stem (Karnak/Rosetta/Philae/British Museum); invert the wonder -- lead with 'a script no one could read for 1,400 years', make the mechanism the answer (cartouches ring a NAME). Key accuracy rail: hieroglyphs are a MIXED logo-phonetic script, not 'picture-writing' where each symbol is a whole idea -- Champollion's insight was that they carry SOUNDS too. Dinner-test payoff: 'read toward the animals' faces'. Lane border: Napoleon's Egyptian campaign is a history episode -- keep the capture rung on the OBJECT's journey to London, not the war.
topics.history_overlap: The stone's 1801 capture ties to Napoleon's Egyptian campaign (1798-1801), a history-bank episode; keep the rung on the object, not the military campaign.

topics.name: Hangul, the alphabet Korea designed on purpose
topics.strand: Languages & scripts born in a place
topics.scope: Korea under King Sejong the Great (Joseon dynasty); the Hunminjeongeum manuscript. T1: most alphabets grew slowly over centuries, but KOREA'S -- Hangul -- was deliberately INVENTED as a single project, announced by King Sejong the Great in 1443 so ordinary Koreans could finally read and write. T2: Sejong built it to be so easy that (he said) 'a wise man learns it in a morning, a fool in ten days' -- 24 simple letters instead of the thousands of borrowed Chinese characters only nobles had time to master. T3 (dinner-test): the CONSONANT shapes are little diagrams of your MOUTH -- the letter for 'n' pictures the tongue touching the ridge behind the teeth, 'm' is a closed square like sealed lips -- the shape SHOWS you how to make the sound (the only major 'featural' alphabet). T3: the VOWELS are built from three marks -- a dot (heaven), a flat line (earth), and an upright line (a standing person) -- so the alphabet encodes a tiny cosmology. T4: Korea's elite scholars FOUGHT the new script to protect Chinese characters as a badge of learning; the official Choe Manri petitioned the king to scrap it, and Hangul was even banned for stretches. T4: Hangul letters are not strung in a line -- they are stacked into square SYLLABLE BLOCKS, one tidy tile per syllable. T4: the book that introduced it, the Hunminjeongeum ('The Proper Sounds to Instruct the People', 1446), survives as a UNESCO Memory of the World, and UNESCO named its global literacy prize after King Sejong.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hangul, /Sejong_the_Great, /Hunminjeongeum, /Choe_Manri, /UNESCO_King_Sejong_Literacy_Prize (standard references; corroborate 1443 creation vs 1446 promulgation at build)
topics.framing_note: Scene-led, place/ruler in the stem (Korea/King Sejong); invert the wonder -- lead with 'an alphabet a fool can learn in ten days', make the DESIGN fact the answer (the letters picture the mouth). Key accuracy rail: Hangul was CREATED 1443 and PROMULGATED 1446 -- if a rung uses a year, use it correctly; and it is a featural ALPHABET, not a syllabary. Dinner-test payoff: consonant shapes are diagrams of the speech organs. No lane conflict; this is a pure cultural-creation-born-in-a-place wonder.

topics.name: Linear B & the burnt tablets of Knossos
topics.strand: Languages & scripts born in a place
topics.scope: The palace of Knossos on Crete, the Mycenaean mainland, and the 1952 decipherment. T1: in the ruins of the palace of KNOSSOS on the island of CRETE, diggers pulled up thousands of clay tablets covered in a script no one could read -- labelled 'Linear B'. T2 (dinner-test): the tablets survived by ACCIDENT -- they were soft, sun-dried scrap records meant to be wiped and reused, but the palaces BURNED down, and the fire baked them into permanent bricks. T2: Sir Arthur Evans, who excavated Knossos from 1900, found TWO scripts and named them Linear A (older, Minoan) and Linear B (younger) -- and guarded his tablets so jealously he barely let rivals see them. T3: for fifty years Linear B beat everyone; Evans was CERTAIN it wasn't Greek -- the Minoans, he insisted, were their own separate people. T4: in 1952 Michael VENTRIS -- an ARCHITECT, an amateur, not a professor -- cracked it, and the answer stunned scholars: Linear B was an early form of GREEK, proof the Mycenaeans from the mainland had taken over Crete. T4: the tablets turned out to be INVENTORIES, not poems -- lists of sheep, chariot wheels, swords and jars of honey, plus offerings to gods whose names (Zeus, Poseidon, Athena) already appear 3,000+ years ago. T5: Ventris built a codebreaker's GRID of sign-patterns to crack it -- then died in a car crash at 34, weeks before his great book appeared. T5 (the door still shut): Linear B's PARENT, Linear A -- the Minoans' own language -- is STILL undeciphered; we can sound out the signs but don't know the language, so the Minoans stay silent.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_B, /Knossos, /Arthur_Evans, /Michael_Ventris, /Linear_A (standard references; corroborate Ventris 1952 decipherment and the 'baked by palace fire' preservation at build)
topics.framing_note: Scene-led, place in the stem (Knossos / Crete). Invert the wonder -- lead with the mystery/surprise, make the fact the answer (an AMATEUR architect cracked it; the answer was GREEK). Key accuracy rail: Linear B = Mycenaean GREEK (Ventris/Chadwick 1952); Linear A (Minoan) remains UNDECIPHERED -- keep the two straight, and note the tablets were administrative lists, not literature. Dinner-test payoff: the records only survived because the palace burned. Lane border: Minoan/Mycenaean civilization is history territory -- anchor every rung on the SCRIPT and the PLACE (the tablets, Knossos), not the Bronze Age political story.
topics.history_overlap: Minoan/Mycenaean civilization overlaps history-bank content; keep rungs on the script and Knossos-as-place, not the Bronze Age geopolitics.

topics.name: Norse runes & the Jelling stones
topics.strand: Languages & scripts born in a place
topics.scope: Jelling in Denmark (the two royal runestones), the Rok stone in Sweden, and Viking-age Scandinavia. T1: Vikings didn't write with pens -- they CARVED runes, an alphabet of straight strokes (no curves) made to be cut into WOOD and STONE with a knife. T2: the runic alphabet is called the FUTHARK, after its first six letters -- just as 'alphabet' comes from alpha and beta. T2: at JELLING in Denmark stand two royal stones; the large one, raised by King Harald 'Bluetooth' around 965 CE, brags that he 'won all Denmark and made the Danes Christian' -- Denmark's 'baptismal certificate', its birth record in stone. T3: that Jelling great stone carries the oldest picture of CHRIST in Scandinavia -- shown tangled in branches like a warrior on a tree, a freeze-frame of the moment the Norse gods gave way to Christianity. T4 (dinner-test): the BLUETOOTH symbol on your phone is King Harald Bluetooth's initials -- the runes Hagall and Bjarkan merged into one bind-rune -- because the tech 'unites' devices as Harald united Denmark. T4: in Sweden the ROK runestone (~800 CE) is the longest runic inscription -- over 700 runes of riddles and a lost heroic tale, carved across all five faces of the slab. T5: runes are angular ON PURPOSE -- curves are hard to slice across wood grain or stone, so every stroke is a clean straight cut, and runes had no fixed reading direction.

topics.framing_note: Scene-led, place in the stem (Jelling / Rok / Scandinavia). Invert the wonder -- lead with the object/symbol, make the fact the answer (the Bluetooth logo = a Viking king's initials). KEY accuracy rail: the Bluetooth NAME from Harald Bluetooth is documented, but the exact 'logo = his bind-rune' story is a popular claim, not in the primary Jelling record -- frame that rung as 'the popular story goes...', don't state the bind-rune as settled fact. Also keep runes as an ALPHABET for carving, not a magic system. Dinner-test payoff: the Bluetooth symbol. Lane border: Harald's unification/Christianization of Denmark is a history episode -- keep the rung on the STONE and what it says, not his reign's politics.
topics.history_overlap: Harald Bluetooth's unification and Christianization of Denmark is a history-bank episode; keep the Jelling rung on the stone's inscription/imagery, not the political reign.

topics.name: Rongorongo, the lost script of Easter Island
topics.strand: Languages & scripts born in a place
topics.scope: Rapa Nui (Easter Island), the loneliest inhabited island on Earth. T1: EASTER ISLAND (Rapa Nui), the most isolated inhabited island on the planet, holds a second riddle besides its stone giants -- RONGORONGO, rows of tiny carved glyphs on wooden tablets, the only writing ever invented anywhere in the Pacific. T2 (dinner-test / the strange rule): you read rongorongo in 'reverse BOUSTROPHEDON' -- start at the bottom-left corner, read a line, then FLIP the whole tablet 180 degrees to read the next line, which was carved upside down. T3 (the tragedy): almost every tablet was lost -- burned or scattered, and after the 1860s Peruvian slave raids and the missionaries the last people who could read it were gone; only about two dozen objects survive, and NO ONE can read them today.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rongorongo, /Easter_Island (standard references; corroborate reverse-boustrophedon reading, ~26 surviving objects, undeciphered status, and the 1860s slave-raid collapse at build)
topics.framing_note: Scene-led, place in the stem (Rapa Nui / Easter Island). Invert the wonder -- lead with 'the only writing in the whole Pacific', make the odd fact the answer (you FLIP the tablet to read the next line). Key accuracy rail: rongorongo is UNDECIPHERED -- present no 'translation' as fact; and note it may be proto-writing, its true status debated. Dinner-test payoff: reverse boustrophedon (flip the tablet 180 degrees). Lane border: the moai statues belong to another Easter Island geography ladder -- keep this one on the SCRIPT. Handle the 1860s slave-raid collapse plainly and without sensationalism.
topics.history_overlap: The 1860s Peruvian slave raids that helped kill Rapa Nui literacy are colonial-history backdrop; state the loss plainly and keep the rung on the script, not a history episode.

topics.name: Sequoyah & the Cherokee syllabary
topics.strand: Languages & scripts born in a place
topics.scope: The Cherokee homeland of the southern Appalachians (Tennessee, Georgia, the Carolinas), and the Cherokee Nation carried west to Oklahoma. T1: in the Cherokee country of the southern Appalachian mountains, a man named SEQUOYAH did something no other person in recorded history is known to have done alone -- he built a complete writing system from scratch, and he could not read a single word of ANY language. T2: his system is a SYLLABARY, not an alphabet -- about 85 symbols, one for each Cherokee SYLLABLE (like 'ga', 'no', 'hi') -- so a Cherokee speaker could learn to read in days, not years. T3: his neighbors first feared it as witchcraft, so he proved it by having his young daughter Ayoka read out messages he could not have overheard -- and within a few years much of the Cherokee Nation was LITERATE. T3: by 1828 the Cherokee were printing their own newspaper, the Cherokee Phoenix, in both Cherokee and English -- the first Native American newspaper. T4: Sequoyah borrowed the SHAPES of some letters from an English spelling book because he liked how they looked, but gave them completely different sounds -- so a Cherokee 'R' or 'D' sounds nothing like ours. T4 (dinner-test): the giant SEQUOIA and the towering redwoods (Sequoiadendron) are widely said to be named for him -- a man who gave his people writing lending his name to the biggest trees on Earth. T5: the syllabary is still alive -- on Cherokee Nation road signs, phone keyboards, and even a Cherokee-language message NASA carried to space -- and it survived the nation's forced removal west, the Trail of Tears.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequoyah (verified via WebFetch this session: illiterate in English, invented independently, ~86 symbols streamlined to 85, completed by 1821, Cherokee Phoenix 1828 first bilingual/Native newspaper, homeland TN/AL/NC/GA; sequoia-genus naming attributed but QUESTIONED/debated), /Cherokee_syllabary, /Cherokee_Phoenix
topics.framing_note: Scene-led, place in the stem (the Cherokee Appalachian homeland). Invert the wonder -- lead with 'a man who couldn't read any language', make the achievement the answer (he invented a SYLLABARY alone). Key accuracy rail: it is a SYLLABARY (~85 symbols), not an alphabet; and the sequoia-tree naming is the POPULAR tribute -- the botanist's exact reason is debated, so frame that rung as 'named in his honor, the usual account'. Dinner-test payoff: the giant sequoias carry his name. Lane border: the Trail of Tears (1838 removal) is a major history-bank episode -- name it once as the backdrop the script survived, but do NOT make a rung about the removal itself.
topics.history_overlap: The Trail of Tears / forced Cherokee removal (1838) is a history-bank episode; here it is only backdrop -- keep every rung on the SCRIPT and its homeland, defer the removal narrative to history.

topics.name: Serabit el-Khadim: the alphabet born in a turquoise mine
topics.strand: Languages & scripts born in a place
topics.scope: Serabit el-Khadim, a mountain mining site in the Sinai Peninsula (with its Hathor temple), and the desert road of Wadi el-Hol in Egypt. T1: high in the desert at SERABIT EL-KHADIM in the Sinai, Egyptian crews dug TURQUOISE out of the rock -- and scratched onto those mine walls sits the ancestor of every alphabet on Earth. T2 (dinner-test): the writers were Semitic-speaking WORKERS, not scholars or kings -- they grabbed a few Egyptian hieroglyphs and used each picture for its FIRST SOUND (a house-picture, 'bayt', became the sound 'b'), inventing the first alphabet around 1800 BCE. T3: in 1916 Alan Gardiner cracked a word that repeats in these scratches -- l-b-'-l-t, 'to BAALAT (the Lady)', the goddess of the mine -- confirming that desert miners, not a royal court, took the first step toward the ABCs.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Sinaitic_script (verified via WebFetch this session: Serabit el-Khadim + Wadi el-Hol, ~1900-1800 BCE, Petrie 1904-05 discovery, Gardiner 1916 reading 'to Baalat' via acrophony from hieroglyphs), /Serabit_el-Khadim
topics.framing_note: Scene-led, place in the stem (the Sinai turquoise mine). Invert the wonder -- lead with 'the ancestor of every alphabet', make the surprise the answer (invented by MINERS, not kings). Key accuracy rail: proto-Sinaitic derives from Egyptian hieroglyphs by ACROPHONY (picture -> its first sound); date it ~1900-1800 BCE and flag that the exact century is debated (early vs late dating). Dinner-test payoff: the alphabet was invented by desert workers. This is the early-birth gem that feeds the Byblos/Phoenician ladder -- keep it on the Sinai origin, not the later Phoenician spread.

topics.name: The Inca quipu: an empire written in knots
topics.strand: Languages & scripts born in a place
topics.scope: The Inca Empire run from Cusco across the Andes (Peru). T1: the Inca governed a mountain empire of millions from CUSCO in the Andes -- with roads, storehouses and a census -- yet had NO written words; they recorded everything in KNOTTED STRINGS called quipu (khipu). T2: a quipu is a counting machine -- knots tied at different HEIGHTS on a hanging cord mean ones, tens, hundreds -- a base-10 place-value system you read with your FINGERS. T3 (dinner-test): the KIND of knot carries the digit -- a figure-eight knot means one, a long knot's turns count two through nine, and a bare GAP with no knot means ZERO -- the Inca kept a place for zero. T3: special officials called KHIPUKAMAYUQ ('knot-keepers') created and memorized the records -- tribute, llama herds, storehouse grain -- and could be punished with death for an error. T4: we can read the NUMBERS on a quipu, but the COLORS and cord-patterns may hide names or words we still can't read -- a knotted 'language' that could be part story, still undeciphered. T5: Spanish priests BURNED thousands of quipu as 'idols of the devil', so only about 1,400 survive today -- the Inca's own records largely destroyed by the men who conquered them.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quipu (verified via WebFetch this session: base-10 positional; figure-eight=1, long knot=2-9, gap=0; khipukamayuq specialists; numbers understood but narrative undeciphered; ~1,400 survive; many destroyed by Spanish as idolatrous), /Inca_Empire, /Khipu_kamayuq
topics.framing_note: Scene-led, place in the stem (Cusco / the Andes / the Inca Empire). Invert the wonder -- lead with 'an empire of millions with no writing', make the mechanism the answer (records kept in KNOTTED string). Key accuracy rail: the NUMERIC content is decoded (base-10, knot-types, a knot-gap for zero) but the possible narrative/word content is NOT -- keep 'we can read the numbers, not the story' precise; the quipu is a recording device, arguably not full writing. Dinner-test payoff: a gap of no-knot is their ZERO. Lane border: Inca roads, Machu Picchu and Cusco's stonework belong to other geography ladders -- this one stays on the STRINGS. Handle the Spanish-burning rung plainly and non-sensationally.
topics.history_overlap: The Spanish conquest and destruction of Inca records is a history-bank episode; keep the rung on the quipu itself (what was lost), not the conquest narrative.

topics.name: The Indus script & the silent seals of Mohenjo-daro
topics.strand: Languages & scripts born in a place
topics.scope: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, the great cities of the Indus Valley Civilization (in today's Pakistan). T1: 4,500 years ago the Indus city of MOHENJO-DARO (in today's Pakistan) had brick streets on a grid and covered drains -- and a WRITING that not one person on Earth can read today. T2: the Indus script survives mostly on tiny stamp SEALS -- carved stones about the size of a coin, many showing a one-horned 'UNICORN' bull standing above a short line of signs. T2: the inscriptions are maddeningly SHORT -- usually only about five signs, never a long passage -- so codebreakers have no 'paragraph' to get a grip on. T3: there are roughly 400+ different signs -- too many to be a simple alphabet, too few to be one-picture-per-word -- so scholars can't even agree WHAT KIND of script it is. T4 (dinner-test / the wall): the deepest problem is that we don't know the LANGUAGE the Indus people spoke, and there is no Rosetta Stone for it -- so unlike Egyptian or Linear B, the Indus script may NEVER be read. T4: the little seals traveled far -- Indus seals turn up in Mesopotamian cities like Ur, proof of a sea-trade network -- yet even those foreign clues can't unlock the signs.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indus_script, /Mohenjo-daro, /Indus_Valley_Civilisation, /Pashupati_seal (standard references; corroborate ~400 signs, average inscription length, and undeciphered-language status at build)
topics.framing_note: Scene-led, place in the stem (Mohenjo-daro / the Indus Valley). Invert the wonder -- lead with 'a script no one can read', make the reason the answer (the inscriptions are only ~5 signs; the LANGUAGE is unknown). Key accuracy rail: the Indus script is UNDECIPHERED and even its type is disputed -- do not imply anyone has read it; the honest wonder is WHY it resists (no bilingual key, unknown language, tiny texts). Dinner-test payoff: it may never be readable. Lane border: Mohenjo-daro's grid streets, Great Bath and drains are a 'first cities' geography wonder that may live in another sub-strand -- keep THIS ladder on the SCRIPT (the seals), with the city named as setting.

strands.strand: Music & dance born in a place

topics.name: Fado — Lisbon
topics.strand: Music & dance born in a place
topics.scope: Lisbon, Portugal — home of fado, the 'song of longing.' T1: In the old Lisbon quarters of Alfama and Mouraria, a singer in a black shawl pours out fado — a music built on one deep, bittersweet feeling of longing (answer: fado / Lisbon). T2: That feeling has a special Portuguese name with no English equal: saudade, a yearning for someone or something loved and lost (answer: saudade). T3: Fado is carried by a unique instrument, the guitarra portuguesa — a pear-shaped, 12-string guitar that shimmers and cries (answer: the guitarra portuguesa). T4: Amália Rodrigues, the 'Queen of Fado,' carried Lisbon's song to the world in the 20th century; when she died in 1999 Portugal declared national mourning (answer: Amália Rodrigues). T5: In 2011 UNESCO recognized Lisbon's fado as Intangible Cultural Heritage; legend traces it to Maria Severa, a 19th-century Lisbon singer (answer: UNESCO 2011 / Maria Severa). Deeper rungs: Coimbra fado (university, male students) vs Lisbon fado, the tasca/fado house, the black mourning dress.
topics.source: Wikipedia 'Fado', 'Guitarra portuguesa', 'Amália Rodrigues', 'Maria Severa'; UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscription (2011); Grokipedia (intended primary — verify at build).
topics.framing_note: Scene-led — a shawled singer in a candlelit Alfama tavern, never 'What is fado?'; invert (an untranslatable Portuguese ache → 'saudade'). ACCURACY RAIL: label the Maria Severa origin as legend/tradition; saudade is described in the scene, never dropped as a rote dictionary definition. Dinner-test payoff = saudade (a feeling English can't name) and the crying 12-string guitarra. LANE BORDER: keep answers the music/place.

topics.name: Flamenco — Andalusia
topics.strand: Music & dance born in a place
topics.scope: Andalusia (Andalucía), southern Spain — where flamenco grew from Roma, Moorish, Jewish, and Andalusian roots. T1: Flamenco was born in Andalusia among the Roma ('gitanos'), blending the sounds of Moorish, Jewish, and Andalusian Spain into one fiery art (answer: Andalusia / the gitanos). T2: A full flamenco has three parts — the singing (cante), the dancing (baile), and the guitar (toque) — and the crowd drives it with rhythmic hand-claps called palmas (answer: cante/baile/toque + palmas). T3: The heartbeat of flamenco is the compás — a demanding 12-beat rhythmic cycle that the clapping, guitar, and heel-stamps must all lock into (answer: the compás). T4: Poet Federico García Lorca gave a name to flamenco's dark, goosebump-raising soul: duende, the spirit that arrives only when a performer risks everything (answer: duende). T5: The wooden box-drum you now see in flamenco, the cajón, is NOT Spanish — Paco de Lucía brought it back from PERU in the 1970s and it became standard (answer: the cajón). Deeper rungs: the palos (soleá, bulerías, seguiriya, alegrías), Triana/Jerez/Cádiz heartlands, the zapateado footwork and bata de cola dress, UNESCO 2010.
topics.source: Wikipedia 'Flamenco', 'Cajón' (Peruvian origin, adopted via Paco de Lucía), 'Duende (art)'; UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscription (2010); Grokipedia (intended primary — verify at build).
topics.framing_note: Scene-led — a clapping crowd and a stamping dancer in an Andalusian courtyard, never 'What is flamenco?'; invert (the goosebump-soul a singer summons → 'duende'). ACCURACY RAILS: name the multi-culture confluence honestly (Roma + Moorish/Al-Andalus + Sephardic Jewish + Andalusian folk); the cajón is a PERUVIAN import (1970s), not native. Dinner-test payoff = duende and the Peruvian-cajón surprise. LANE BORDER: no tapas/sherry/food answers — those are the COOKING bank; every answer is the MUSIC/place.

topics.name: Hip-hop — the Bronx
topics.strand: Music & dance born in a place
topics.scope: The West Bronx, New York City — where hip-hop was born at a 1973 rec-room party. T1: On August 11, 1973, in the rec room of 1520 Sedgwick Avenue, DJ Kool Herc spun records at his sister Cindy Campbell's back-to-school party — the event most often called the birth of hip-hop (answer: 1520 Sedgwick Avenue). T2: Herc noticed dancers went wildest during the drum 'break' of a song, so he used two copies of the same record to loop that break forever — the 'breakbeat' (answer: the break/breakbeat). T3: The dancers who saved their best moves for the break became 'b-boys' and 'b-girls' doing a new floor dance — breaking (answer: breaking/b-boying). T4: Grandmaster Flash, another Bronx DJ, perfected cutting between two turntables exactly on the beat ('quick-mix theory'), and Grand Wizzard Theodore invented the scratch (answer: Grandmaster Flash / the scratch). T5: Afrika Bambaataa turned Bronx gang energy into the Universal Zulu Nation and named hip-hop's 'four elements': DJing, MCing (rapping), breaking, and graffiti (answer: the four elements). Deeper rungs: Coke La Rock as an early MC, the park jams / plugging turntables into a lamppost, 1970s Bronx decay as backdrop, the 'one of several birthplaces' caveat.
topics.source: Wikipedia '1520 Sedgwick Avenue' (verified this session: Aug 11 1973, DJ Kool Herc / Cindy Campbell party, extended breaks, described as 'one of the pivotal and formative events' — not sole origin); Wikipedia 'Hip hop', 'Grandmaster Flash', 'Afrika Bambaataa'; Grokipedia (intended primary — verify at build).
topics.framing_note: Scene-led — a summer rec-room party with two turntables, never 'What is hip-hop?'; invert (dancers exploding at one moment of a song → 'the break'). ACCURACY RAIL: 1520 Sedgwick is the most-credited birthplace, but hip-hop 'developed slowly in several places in the 1970s' — frame it as THE famous origin party, not the sole one. Dinner-test payoff = the break discovery (two copies of one record looped forever) and DJs plugging turntables into a Bronx lamppost for park jams. LANE BORDER: keep every answer the music/place.

topics.name: Jazz — New Orleans
topics.strand: Music & dance born in a place
topics.scope: New Orleans, Louisiana — the Mississippi port city where jazz was born around 1900. T1: New Orleans is the home of jazz; brass bands parade the streets and mourners dance behind the coffin at a jazz funeral in a moving crowd called the 'second line' (answer: the second line). T2: In Congo Square, enslaved Africans were allowed to gather on Sundays to drum and dance — the one place in the U.S. where African rhythms openly survived, seeding jazz (answer: Congo Square). T3: Storyville, the city's red-light district (1897–1917), gave early pianists like Jelly Roll Morton steady work; when the Navy closed it in 1917, musicians rode the riverboats up to Chicago (answer: Storyville).
