T5: that beat matches wobbles in Earth's orbit — a ~100,000-yr change in orbital shape, a ~41,000-yr nod of the tilt, a ~23,000-yr axis wobble — the 'Milankovitch cycles' worked out by Serbian scientist Milutin Milanković.
topics.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milankovitch_cycles (~100k eccentricity / ~41k obliquity / ~23-26k precession, Milanković, 65°N insolation, the 100,000-year problem — verified). Great Lakes ~fifth of world surface fresh water, Central Park striations (Umpire/Rat Rock), Doggerland -120 m, Greenland ~3 km, Antarctica ~70% fresh water/~4.8 km, EPICA Dome C ~800 kyr: standard textbook, corroborate exact figures at build. Grokipedia 403 — re-check via browser.
topics.framing_note: Every rung names a place you can point to (Great Lakes, Central Park, the North Sea, Greenland, Antarctica, Dome C) — even the Milankovitch capstone must stay anchored in Antarctica's ice / the deep-sea record, not floated as pure theory. Dinner-test payoff = Doggerland (a drowned country under the North Sea) and the Central Park scratches a kid can go touch. ACCURACY RAIL: verify the 'fifth of world's surface fresh water' (Great Lakes) and '~70%' (Antarctica) wording at build; the ~100,000-yr dominance is the eccentricity MATCH — mark the mechanism ('100,000-year problem') as still debated, not settled. LANE BORDER: Ice-Age megafauna (mammoths) are the ANIMAL bank — keep answers the LANDSCAPE/ice, not the beasts.

topics.name: The horn, the arete, the cirque, and the tarn
topics.scope: Where glaciers gnaw a mountain from several sides at once, they leave sharp peaks, knife ridges, and armchair hollows. T2: the Matterhorn (4,478 m) on the Swiss-Italian border above Zermatt is the textbook HORN — a near-perfect pyramid with four faces to the four compass points. T3: the horn forms because FOUR separate glaciers, each carving a bowl (a 'cirque') into a different side, ate inward until only a sharp spire was left (invert: the pyramid shape is the hook, 'four cirque glaciers' the answer). T3: a CIRQUE is the armchair-shaped hollow a glacier scoops at its head; Snowdonia's Cwm Idwal in Wales and the 'corries' of the Scottish Highlands are classic bowls. T4: a TARN is the little lake that fills a cirque after the ice melts — like the tarns cupped high in England's Lake District. T4: an ARETE is the knife-edge ridge left where two cirques bite toward each other from opposite sides — Crib Goch on Snowdon is a famous one climbers straddle. T5: read together, a horn + aretes + cirques + tarns are a 'fingerprint' set that tells you a peak was sculpted by ice, not folded by tectonics — the whole alpine skyline is glacier-carved.
topics.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matterhorn (4,478 m, Swiss-Italian border above Zermatt/Breuil-Cervinia, four faces to the cardinal points, 'four cirques led to the shape' — verified). Cwm Idwal / Scottish corries / Lake District tarns / Crib Goch arete: standard textbook, corroborate at build. Grokipedia 403 — re-check via browser.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led on the Matterhorn's shape, never 'What is a horn?'; teach cirque/arete/tarn before testing each. Dinner-test payoff = the horn = a mountain carved to a point by glaciers eating it from four sides. ACCURACY RAIL: the Matterhorn's four faces do face roughly the cardinal directions and four cirques shaped it — state 'four,' matching the source; don't invent a count of glaciers still present today. Distractors = the other real glacial landforms (arete vs cirque vs tarn vs horn) so all four choices are live and adjacent. Pure landform geography — no lane conflict.

topics.name: U-shaped valleys and hanging-valley waterfalls
topics.scope: A river cuts a V; a glacier grinds it into a broad, flat-floored, cliff-walled U — and strands its side-streams high above. T1: Yosemite Valley, California — sheer granite walls (El Capitan, the largest exposed granite monolith) frame a flat green floor a mile wide; ice widened and polished a river gorge into the classic U. T2: Bridalveil Fall drops from a HANGING VALLEY — a smaller side-glacier couldn't cut as deep as the main ice, so its valley was left hanging and its stream now free-falls into Yosemite. T2: the Lauterbrunnen Valley, Switzerland — a 'true cleft' with ~1,000 m limestone walls said to hold 72 waterfalls; Staubbach Falls free-falls 297 m (Switzerland's highest), and the valley gave Tolkien his picture of Rivendell. T3: glacial POLISH — grit-armored ice buffed the bedrock to a shine you can still see and slip on at Yosemite's Pothole and Lembert Domes. T3: Glacier National Park, Montana — U-troughs, hanging-valley falls, turquoise meltwater lakes; the namesake glaciers are nearly gone. T4: a fjord is simply a U-valley the sea drowned — the same shape, flooded. T5: the trough shape reveals HOW ice erodes — it plucks and grinds along its whole width and base, unlike a river cutting a narrow channel; the U vs V is the fingerprint that tells geologists ice, not water, shaped a valley.
topics.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lauterbrunnen (U-shaped 'true cleft,' ~1,000 m walls, 72-waterfall count, Staubbach 297 m 'highest free-falling in Switzerland,' Tolkien/Rivendell 1911 — verified). Yosemite U-shape/El Capitan/Bridalveil hanging valley/glacial polish + Glacier NP: standard textbook, corroborate at build. Grokipedia 403 — re-check via browser.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led on the walls/waterfall, never 'What is a U-shaped valley?'; teach 'hanging valley' and 'glacial polish' before testing them. Dinner-test payoff = the hanging-valley waterfall (Bridalveil) — a stream left dangling in mid-cliff. ACCURACY RAIL: do NOT repeat the myth that a glacier sliced Half Dome in half — Half Dome's face is jointing/rockfall + exfoliation, and Yosemite Valley is a river gorge glaciers WIDENED/deepened/polished, not a pure ice creation; frame Yosemite via the U-shape, polish, and hanging valleys, which ARE unambiguously glacial. Verify Lauterbrunnen's '72 waterfalls' as a tourism count and Staubbach 297 m at build. No lane conflict.

topics.name: Cold currents & the coastal deserts they make
topics.scope: How a chilly sea can bake a shore bone-dry. T1: the Atacama in northern Chile is the driest place on Earth outside the poles — some weather stations have NEVER recorded rain — and the cold Humboldt Current just offshore is a main reason why (the hook: a desert sitting on an ocean beach; the answer: the cold current dries it, because cold water chills the air so it cannot rise and rain, only fog). T2: that fog has a name and a use — the camanchaca rolls in off the cold sea, and Atacama villages string giant mesh 'fog catchers' (atrapanieblas) to harvest drinking water from the mist in a land with no rain. T3: across the ocean the same trick repeats — the cold Benguela Current chills Namibia's coast into the Namib Desert, where towering dunes pour straight into the surf and morning fog is the only reliable water. T4: that fog-bound Namibian shore, where ships vanished in the murk and their hulks still rust in the dunes, earned the name the Skeleton Coast. T5: the Namib's Deadvlei — a blinding white clay pan studded with ~900-year-old blackened camel-thorn trees too DRY to rot, ringed by some of Earth's tallest dunes (300 m+) at Sossusvlei.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humboldt_Current (fetched: current is 'largely responsible for the aridity of the Atacama'); Grokipedia.com pages for Atacama Desert, Benguela Current, Namib Desert, Skeleton Coast, Deadvlei/Sossusvlei are primary and checked first at build (403 here). Build-verify: zero-rain Atacama stations, camanchaca + atrapanieblas fog catchers, Namib dune heights, Deadvlei tree age.
topics.framing_note: Voice: place -> wonder; the recurring answer is the cold-current-makes-a-coastal-desert mechanism and the named places it built. LANE BORDER: desert life that drinks fog (Namib beetles, welwitschia) belongs to the animal/plant bank — keep every answer the PLACE (Skeleton Coast, Deadvlei, the fog catchers). ACCURACY RAIL: the current is A major cause of the aridity (with the subtropical high and the Andes rain-shadow), not the sole cause — phrase as 'a main reason.' Distractors are other real deserts/currents (Sahara/trade winds, Gobi/rain-shadow, Kalahari). Dinner-test payoff: Deadvlei's 900-year-old trees too dry to rot.

topics.name: Coral reefs & the heat that bleaches them
topics.scope: The world's biggest living structure and why it turns white. T1: off Australia's northeast coast the Great Barrier Reef runs about 2,300 km — the largest living structure on Earth, built by tiny coral over millions of years and so vast it can be seen from space. T2: a reef's color comes from microscopic algae (zooxanthellae) living INSIDE the coral; when the sea gets too hot the coral expels them and turns bone-white — coral bleaching (the hook: why a whole reef suddenly goes white; the answer: bleaching). T3: back-to-back marine heatwaves in 2016 and 2017 bleached and killed a large share of the northern Great Barrier Reef — the worst in its recorded history. T4: not every reef is a postcard — off Belize the Great Blue Hole is a ~300 m-wide, ~125 m-deep sapphire pit in the reef, a drowned Ice-Age cave that collapsed and flooded when the seas rose. T5: reefs even build LAND — a coral atoll is a ring of reef around a vanished, sunken volcano; Darwin worked out that as the volcano subsides the coral grows UP to keep pace, leaving a lagoon ring (the Maldives, Bikini). Teach 'atoll.'
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coral_bleaching (fetched: bleaching = expulsion of symbiotic zooxanthellae under heat stress, Great Barrier Reef mass bleaching 2016 and 2017 killing 29-50%+ of coral); Grokipedia.com pages for Great Barrier Reef, Great Blue Hole, Atoll are primary and checked first at build (403 here). Build-verify: GBR ~2,300 km and 'seen from space,' Great Blue Hole dimensions, Darwin's subsidence theory of atolls.
topics.framing_note: Voice: place -> wonder; teach 'bleaching' and 'atoll' before testing them. LANE BORDER: the coral POLYP as an animal belongs to the animal bank — geography owns the REEF as a place/structure, bleaching as an earth-process, and atoll/blue-hole geology; keep every answer a place, structure, or process. ACCURACY RAILS: 'seen from space' is fine, but AVOID the disputed 'only living thing visible from space' claim; state the 2016-2017 bleaching plainly as observed fact without catastrophizing beyond the evidence and without dismissal (honest both ways). Distractors are other real reefs/features (Belize Barrier Reef, Ningaloo, Chagos, the Maldives). Dinner-test payoff: the Great Blue Hole, a drowned Ice-Age cave, and Darwin's sinking-volcano insight.

topics.name: Giant waves & where the sea floor builds them
topics.scope: Why the biggest waves stand up over hidden seabed. T1/T2: at Nazare in Portugal surfers ride waves as tall as an 8-storey building — the biggest ever surfed (Sebastian Steudtner's ~26 m in 2020) — because a deep undersea gorge, the Nazare Canyon, points straight at the beach and funnels and stacks the swell into a giant at Praia do Norte (invert the wonder: the record height is the hook, the underwater canyon is the reason). T3: in the open sea a 'rogue wave' can rear from nowhere — the Draupner wave, recorded off Norway on New Year's Day 1995 at 25.6 m, was the first rogue ever caught by instruments, proving sailors' old tales true (the hook: a wall of water twice the height of its neighbours; the answer: a rogue wave / the Draupner wave). T4: Hawaii's Jaws (Pe'ahi) on Maui and California's Mavericks break huge because shallow reefs and rock shelves trip the swell and stand it up — the SEA FLOOR, not the wind, decides where giants form. T5: contrast the gentlest giant — a tsunami crosses the deep barely a metre high, so the biggest wave you can SURF and the deadliest wave are opposite kinds of water.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazare,_Portugal (fetched: Nazare Canyon converges and enlarges the swell, Steudtner 26.2 m record 2020, McNamara 23.8 m 2011, Praia do Norte / Guinness); Grokipedia.com pages for Draupner wave and Jaws/Mavericks are primary and checked first at build (403 here). Build-verify: Draupner 25.6 m on 1 Jan 1995 as first instrumentally recorded rogue wave; the reef/shelf mechanism at Jaws and Mavericks.
topics.framing_note: Voice: reveal the hidden cause — the shape of the sea FLOOR — behind each named giant wave. ACCURACY RAIL: keep record heights and dates exact; the Draupner wave is significant as the first INSTRUMENTALLY recorded rogue, not the largest ever. Distractors are other real big-wave places (Teahupo'o, Mavericks, Jaws, Mullaghmore). Dinner-test payoff: the Nazare Canyon aiming an 8-storey wave at one beach, and the Draupner wave proving sailors' rogue-wave tales real. Ties to the tsunami ladder for the T5 contrast — do not re-test tsunami science here.

topics.name: Maelstroms — the sea's great whirlpools
topics.scope: Where a hard tide squeezes through a narrow strait it spins into a whirlpool. T2: off Norway's Lofoten Islands the Moskstraumen is the original 'maelstrom' — the whirlpool Edgar Allan Poe and Jules Verne turned into legend (the whirlpool is REAL; the ship-swallowing is literary exaggeration). T3: nearby, Norway's Saltstraumen is often called the world's strongest tidal current — about 400 million tonnes of seawater force through a ~150 m strait every six hours, spinning whirlpools up to 10 m across. T4: Scotland's Gulf of Corryvreckan, between Jura and Scarba, roars so loud it is heard miles off — George Orwell nearly drowned in it while writing Nineteen Eighty-Four — and Japan's Naruto Strait whirlpools (up to ~20 m across) are a national spectacle crossed by a viewing bridge (the hook: a whirlpool that nearly drowned a famous writer, or one that spins 20 m wide; the answer: the named strait).
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saltstraumen (fetched: 'one of the strongest tidal currents in the world,' ~400 million cubic metres every six hours, whirlpools up to 10 m across and 5 m deep; the 'strongest' superlative is noted as debated); Grokipedia.com pages for Moskstraumen, Corryvreckan, Naruto whirlpools are primary and checked first at build (403 here). Build-verify: Moskstraumen/Poe/Verne, Corryvreckan/Orwell, Naruto ~20 m whirlpools.
topics.framing_note: Voice: place -> wonder; each rung names a concrete strait and its whirlpool. ACCURACY RAILS: label the maelstrom's ship-swallowing power as LEGEND/literature (Poe, Verne) versus the real but bounded whirlpool; say Saltstraumen is 'often called' or 'among' the strongest — the superlative is disputed. Distractors are the other real whirlpools in the ladder (Moskstraumen, Saltstraumen, Corryvreckan, Naruto, Old Sow). Dinner-test payoff: George Orwell nearly drowning in Corryvreckan, or the 20 m Naruto whirlpools crossed by a bridge.

topics.name: Ocean gyres, the garbage patch & the shoreless Sargasso Sea
topics.scope: The ocean's five great whirlpools and what they trap. T1: wind and Earth's spin bend the surface currents into five vast, slow whirlpools called gyres, each turning across a whole ocean basin. T2: in the calm heart of the North Pacific Gyre, halfway between California and Hawaii, the currents gather floating plastic into the Great Pacific Garbage Patch — a drifting soup about TWICE the size of Texas (accuracy rail: NOT a solid island — mostly fingernail-size microplastics, and roughly HALF its mass is lost fishing nets). T3: the North Atlantic Gyre encloses a sea with NO coastline at all — the Sargasso Sea, walled only by four currents (Gulf Stream, North Atlantic, Canary, North Equatorial): the one sea on Earth with no land shore. T4: its surface drifts with golden Sargassum weed and its windless middle, the 'horse latitudes,' once becalmed sailing ships for weeks (invert the wonder: the seaweed and dead calm are the hook, 'the Sargasso Sea' is the answer). T5: every European and American eel is born in that one shoreless patch of open ocean, then swims thousands of miles to distant rivers and returns only to spawn — a nursery with no shore.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pacific_garbage_patch (fetched: North Pacific Subtropical Gyre, ~1.6M km2 ~2x Texas, mostly microplastics, ~half the mass is fishing nets, between California and Hawaii) and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sargasso_Sea (fetched: only sea with no land boundaries, four bounding currents, sargassum, horse-latitudes calm, eel spawning); Grokipedia.com primary at build (403 here).
topics.framing_note: Voice: reveal the hidden machinery (gyres) and the strange things it concentrates. ACCURACY RAIL: kill the 'island of trash you can walk on' myth — the patch is a diffuse soup of microplastics twice the size of Texas, about half its mass discarded fishing gear. LANE BORDER: eel migration BIOLOGY belongs to the animal bank; here the answer is the place-fact — all these eels are born in the one sea with no shore. Distractors are other real seas/gyres (Mediterranean, Caribbean, the Indian Ocean gyre). Dinner-test payoff: a whole sea with no coastline, walled only by four currents.

topics.name: The Gulf Stream & the mild edge of Europe
topics.scope: The Atlantic's warm 'river in the sea' and the temperate Europe it makes. T1: a warm current is born in the Gulf of Mexico, funnels through the Straits of Florida, and races northeast up the US East Coast past Cape Hatteras carrying tropical warmth (invert the wonder: it shifts more water than every river on Earth combined — the answer is the Gulf Stream). T2: London and Dublin lie FARTHER NORTH than icy Labrador yet rarely hard-freeze, because the Gulf Stream's far arm — the North Atlantic Drift — ferries that warmth to Britain and Ireland (the latitude paradox is the hook, the Drift is the answer). T3: the warm current climbs the whole coast of Norway, keeping ports like Tromso and Hammerfest ICE-FREE all winter above the Arctic Circle. T4: palm trees and subtropical gardens grow on Scotland's west coast (Inverewe Garden) and southwest Ireland (Garinish Island) near 57-58 degrees N, warmed by the same drift. T5: in 1768 Benjamin Franklin, puzzled that mail packets crossed the Atlantic slower than merchant ships, had Nantucket whaler Timothy Folger sketch the warm current the packets were fighting — the first CHART of the Gulf Stream. Deep extras: the warm-core eddies that spin off the meander; and why every ocean has a fast, warm 'western boundary current' on its west side — Japan's Kuroshio being the Gulf Stream's Pacific twin.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Stream (fetched: Gulf of Mexico origin, Straits of Florida, ice-free Norwegian coast/Tromso, Franklin+Folger 1768 chart — Franklin CHARTED it, did not 'discover' it); Grokipedia.com/page/Gulf_Stream is the primary reference and MUST be checked first at build (blocked by HTTP 403 in this harness). Build-verify: Inverewe/Garinish palm gardens, London-vs-Labrador latitudes, Kuroshio analogue.
topics.framing_note: Voice: place -> wonder; every rung's answer is a concrete fact about the current or the coast it warms, never a bare human name. ACCURACY RAIL: the T5 answer is the Gulf Stream CHART / the warm current the packets fought — Franklin and Folger are context; do NOT let the answer become 'Benjamin Franklin,' and do NOT claim he 'discovered' or solely 'named' it (he charted it). Distractors are other real currents (Kuroshio, Canary, Labrador, California), keeping all four live. Dinner-test payoff: palm trees thriving in Scotland at Arctic-of-Labrador latitudes. Scene-led, never 'What is the Gulf Stream?'.
topics.history_overlap: T5 touches Benjamin Franklin in 1768; if the history bank runs a Franklin ladder, keep this rung's answer the Gulf Stream chart (a place/ocean fact), not Franklin's biography or the postal service.

topics.name: The Humboldt Current, upwelling & the world's richest fishery
topics.scope: The cold current off Peru that feeds the planet. T1: off Peru the tropical sea runs strangely COLD (as low as ~16 degrees C) because the Humboldt Current sweeps chilly water north up South America's coast. T2: coastal winds shove the surface water offshore and cold, nutrient-rich deep water RISES to replace it (upwelling), fueling a plankton bloom that makes this Earth's single richest fishery — the Peruvian anchoveta, once about 20% of the ENTIRE world's fish catch (over 12 million tonnes in 1970). T3: millions of seabirds gorging on those anchovies buried Peru's Chincha Islands under guano metres deep — mined in the 1800s as the world's most prized fertilizer (the guano boom, valuable enough to be fought over). T4: every few years warm water returns near Christmas and switches the upwelling OFF — the anchovies vanish and the fishery crashes; Peruvian fishermen named this warming El Nino, 'the Christ child' (the great 1972 crash). T5: El Nino's warm pool does not stop at Peru — it reorders weather across the whole Pacific, drying out Australia and Indonesia while flooding the South American coast (a teleconnection). Deep extras: the Benguela (Namibia) and California upwellings as cousins; and why the world's biggest fisheries all sit on cold, west-coast, upwelling currents.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humboldt_Current (fetched: cold northward flow ~16C, upwelling productivity, anchoveta ~20% of world catch / >12Mt 1970 collapsing in the 1972 El Nino, Atacama aridity, El Nino disruption); Grokipedia.com/page/Humboldt_Current is primary at build (403 here). Build-verify: Chincha Islands guano boom and Chincha Islands War; El Nino teleconnection to Australian drought.
topics.framing_note: Voice: reveal the hidden mechanism (cold current -> upwelling -> bloom) and the wonders it built. LANE BORDER: the anchoveta is a FISH — its biology belongs to the animal bank; geography owns the current, the upwelling process, the guano ISLANDS, and El Nino. Keep every answer a place/process, never fish anatomy. ACCURACY RAIL: El Nino is named for the Christ child (Christmas warming off Peru) — attribute the naming to Peruvian fishermen; the 1972 crash is the datable anchor. Distractors are other real currents/fisheries (Benguela, California, the cod banks). Dinner-test payoff: the guano boom — bird droppings mined as the world's most prized fertilizer, worth a war.
topics.history_overlap: T3 guano boom / Chincha Islands War (1864-66) and T4 the 1972 fishery collapse may touch history- or economics-bank episodes; keep answers the guano ISLANDS/deposits and the El Nino process (place/earth-science), not the war's diplomacy or market economics.

topics.name: The global conveyor belt (thermohaline circulation)
topics.scope: Earth's oceans as one connected, slow-turning loop. T1: warm water rides the surface one way and cold water creeps along the deep floor the other — a single linked 'global conveyor belt' threading every ocean. T2: the engine sits in the far North Atlantic near Greenland and Iceland, where cold, salty, HEAVY water sinks and pulls the whole belt along (the hook: what drives a planet-sized loop with no motor; the answer: dense water sinking — deep-water formation). T3: the coldest, densest water on Earth is manufactured around Antarctica — as winter sea ice freezes it squeezes out its salt (brine rejection), and Antarctic Bottom Water plunges down the Weddell Sea to the deepest abyss. T4: a single parcel of water may take about 1,000 YEARS to ride the whole loop and resurface in the North Pacific — the ocean's slowest clock. T5: if Greenland's melting ice freshens the North Atlantic, the sinking could weaken and the belt could slow (the AMOC-slowdown scenario) — the real, modeled science behind the movie 'sudden ice age' fear. Deep extras: the heat released as water sinks is what warms Europe (ties to the Gulf Stream ladder); the Labrador Sea as a second sinking site; and the two knobs behind the name — 'thermo' (temperature) and 'haline' (salt).
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermohaline_circulation (fetched: N Atlantic/Norwegian Sea sinking, Antarctic Bottom Water via brine rejection, ~1000-year transit surfacing in N Pacific, freshening-from-melt slowdown); Grokipedia.com is primary and checked first at build (403 here). Build-verify: Labrador Sea deep-water site; honest framing of the AMOC-collapse scenario.
topics.framing_note: Voice: reveal HOW the whole ocean moves as one system; teach 'thermohaline' before testing it. ACCURACY RAIL for T5: state observed warming and freshening plainly as fact, but present an ABRUPT belt collapse as a MODELED scenario, not a certainty — no catastrophizing beyond the evidence and no smug dismissal (the bank's honest-science voice, honest both ways). Distractors are other real ocean features (surface gyres, the Gulf Stream, upwelling) so the sinking-engine answer stays earned. Dinner-test payoff: a drop of water taking a thousand years to go around. Lane border with the Gulf Stream ladder: this ladder owns the sinking/deep-water/timescale story, the Gulf Stream ladder owns the warmth-to-Europe story.

topics.name: The tides & the record-breaking Bay of Fundy
topics.scope: The daily heartbeat of the sea, biggest in the Bay of Fundy. T1: twice a day the whole ocean rises and falls, pulled mostly by the Moon's gravity (with the Sun helping) — the tide; the Moon actually raises a bulge on BOTH sides of Earth, which is why most coasts get TWO high tides a day. T2: in Canada's Bay of Fundy the tide climbs about 16 m — a five-storey wall of water — twice daily, the biggest tides on Earth; the bay's funnel shape and natural resonance amplify it, and about 100 BILLION tonnes flow in and out each tide, twice all the world's rivers combined (the hook: five storeys, more than every river; the answer: the Bay of Fundy). T3: the record — a 21.6 m monster at Burntcoat Head in the Minas Basin in October 1869, when the Saxby Gale storm stacked on top of a spring tide. T4: twice a month, at new and full Moon, the Sun and Moon pull in a straight line and tides swell highest — 'spring tides' (from 'springing up,' not the season); at the quarter Moon they pull crossways and tides go slack — 'neap tides.' T5: Fundy's tide runs so hard it makes the Reversing Falls at Saint John, where a river rapid literally flows UPHILL when the tide floods in. Deep extras: France's Mont-Saint-Michel, where the tide sweeps the flats fast enough to strand walkers (famed in lore as 'swift as a galloping horse'); the Rance estuary in Brittany, the world's first tidal power station (1966); why the open-ocean tide is barely a metre but funnels into giants only in the right-shaped bays; and the ~12h25m cycle that walks the tide later each day with the Moon.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Fundy (fetched: ~16 m average world-record range, 21.6 m maximum in Oct 1869 during the Saxby Gale, ~100 billion tonnes per half-cycle = twice all the world's rivers); Grokipedia.com primary at build (403 here). Build-verify: Reversing Falls at Saint John, Mont-Saint-Michel tide speed, Rance 1966, spring/neap etymology, the 12h25m period.
topics.framing_note: Voice: reveal HOW the Moon runs the sea, anchored to the world-record place. TEACH THE TERMS: 'spring' and 'neap' before testing them, and note 'spring' is not the season. ACCURACY RAIL: ~16 m is the average maximum range; 21.6 m in 1869 was a storm-amplified record, not the routine tide — keep them distinct. Label the Mont-Saint-Michel 'galloping horse' as a saying, not a measured speed. Distractors are other big-tide/famous coasts (Ungava Bay, the Severn estuary, Mont-Saint-Michel, Puerto Gallegos). Dinner-test payoff: the Reversing Falls where a river runs uphill on the tide.

topics.name: Tidal bores — rivers that run backwards
topics.scope: The wave that climbs a river against the current. T1: when a big incoming tide funnels into a narrowing river mouth it can pile into a single wave that travels UPSTREAM against the flow — a tidal bore. T2: on the Amazon the bore is the pororoca — Tupi for 'great roar,' heard before it is seen — a wall of water up to about 4 m high rushing as far as 800 km inland. T3: surfers ride it for miles — in 2003 Brazil's Picuruta Salazar surfed the pororoca 12.5 km in 37 minutes, among the longest rides in surfing history (the hook: 12.5 km and 37 minutes; the answer: the pororoca). T4: China's Qiantang River near Hangzhou has the world's BIGGEST bore, the 'Silver Dragon,' up to about 9 m — crowds have gathered to watch it each autumn for over 1,000 years. T5: England's Severn Bore (up to ~2 m, surfable) and France's Seine 'mascaret' show the bore is a worldwide river trick, born wherever a huge tide meets a shelving, funneling estuary — not a one-river freak.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pororoca (fetched: waves up to 4 m, travels up to 800 km inland, Tupi 'great roar,' Picuruta Salazar's 2003 record ride of 12.5 km in 37 minutes); Grokipedia.com pages for Pororoca, Qiantang (Silver Dragon), Severn bore are primary and checked first at build (403 here). Build-verify: Qiantang ~9 m and 1,000-year viewing tradition, Severn/Seine bores.
topics.framing_note: Voice: place -> wonder; teach 'tidal bore' before testing it. Every rung names a concrete river and keys a place fact. ACCURACY RAIL: pororoca is Tupi for 'great roar' (the name is itself the wonder); Salazar's ride is the datable anchor. Distractors are other real bore rivers (Severn, Qiantang, Seine, Petitcodiac). Dinner-test payoff: surfing one wave 12.5 km up the Amazon for 37 minutes. Lane border/link: the bore is a tide effect — cross-reference but do NOT re-test the tide mechanism owned by the Bay-of-Fundy ladder.

topics.name: Tsunamis — the wave that empties the sea first
topics.scope: The wall of water an earthquake throws across an ocean. T1: a tsunami is not a wind wave — it is the whole water column shoved by an undersea earthquake, crossing the deep ocean as fast as a jet (~800 km/h) yet only rearing up at the shore (teach: 'tsunami' means 'harbour wave,' not 'tidal wave'). T2: the deadliest struck on 26 Dec 2004 — a magnitude ~9.2 quake off Sumatra sent waves across the whole Indian Ocean and killed about 228,000 people in 14 countries, the deadliest tsunami in recorded history. T3: the warning sign — the sea often SUCKS OUT first, baring the seabed and stranding fish, because the wave's trough reaches shore before its crest (drawback). T4: at Maikhao Beach in Thailand a 10-year-old British girl, Tilly Smith, recognized that receding sea and frothing from a geography lesson two weeks earlier and got her whole beach evacuated in time — geography literally saving lives. T5: on 11 Mar 2011 a magnitude ~9.0 quake off Japan drove a tsunami that ran up ~40 m at Aneyoshi in Miyako and overwhelmed the Fukushima plant — yet centuries-old stone markers on the hills ('do not build below this point') had marked older tsunami lines, and the villages that heeded them survived. Deep extras: Lisbon 1755 (quake, then the harbour draining, then the wave, then fire); why the deep-ocean wave is only ~1 m high but piles up at the coast; the Pacific 'Ring of Fire' as the tsunami zone; and the DART buoy warning network born after 2004.
topics.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Indian_Ocean_earthquake_and_tsunami (fetched: Mw ~9.2, 26 Dec 2004, ~227,898 dead across 14 nations, drawback from the leading trough, Tilly Smith at Maikhao Beach) and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Tohoku_earthquake_and_tsunami (fetched: Mw ~9.0, 11 Mar 2011, runup ~38.9-40.5 m at Aneyoshi/Miyako, ~19,759 deaths); Grokipedia.com primary at build (403 here). Build-verify: Aneyoshi tsunami stones, Lisbon 1755, DART buoys, ~800 km/h deep-water speed.
topics.framing_note: Voice: reveal how we KNOW a tsunami is coming (drawback) and how knowledge saves lives. TEACH the term ('harbour wave,' not 'tidal wave'). ACCURACY RAIL: the sea withdraws only when the TROUGH leads — say 'often,' not always; keep magnitudes and dates exact. Distractors are other real quakes/waves (Lisbon 1755, Krakatoa 1883, the 1958 Lituya Bay megatsunami). Dinner-test payoffs: Tilly Smith's geography lesson evacuating a beach, and the ancestral Aneyoshi tsunami stones. STANCE: honor the local/ancestral knowledge in the stone markers on its own terms, no smug modern framing.
topics.history_overlap: 2004, 2011, and 1755 Lisbon are also history-bank-eligible disasters; the geography frame keeps every answer the WAVE-SCIENCE and the PLACE (the drawback, the Aneyoshi stones), not casualty counts, blame, or reconstruction politics.

topics.name: Continents in collision: the great mountain belts
topics.scope: One process -- two landmasses ramming together with nowhere left to subduct, so the crust crumples upward -- across the world's collision ranges. T1: India is still ploughing north into Asia, and the Himalayas are STILL rising -- up to ~10 mm a year at Nanga Parbat, the fastest uplift on Earth. T2: the very summit rock of Mount Everest (8,849 m) is marine limestone -- seafloor stone hoisted 8.8 km into the sky, so the highest point on Earth was once an ocean bottom. T3: the whole Tibetan Plateau -- an area the size of Western Europe raised ~4.5 km high -- was thickened and lifted by the same India-Asia collision that began ~50 million years ago. T4: the Alps rose as Africa pushed into Europe, and the summit of the Matterhorn is a fragment of the AFRICAN plate stranded on top of European rock. T5: the Appalachians of eastern North America were once as tall as the Himalayas -- raised when Pangaea assembled ~300 million years ago -- and have been worn down to green stubs ever since; their torn-off other half now stands in Scotland and Scandinavia.
topics.source: Grokipedia (Geology of the Himalaya; Matterhorn; Appalachian Mountains -- checked first, fetch blocked 403) corroborated via Wikipedia (Geology of the Himalaya; Mount Everest geology; Tibetan Plateau; Alps; Matterhorn; Appalachian Mountains) + USGS.
topics.framing_note: Theme = continent-continent collision toured by named range; the Himalayas are the flagship. Dinner-test payoff: seafloor stone at the top of Everest (T2) and the African summit of the Matterhorn (T4). Accuracy rail: Everest's summit is Ordovician marine LIMESTONE bearing marine fossils (crinoid/shell fragments) -- keep the rung on 'marine limestone at the summit'; the famous Himalayan ammonite 'shaligrams' come from LOWER rock (the Kali Gandaki), so do not pin ammonites AT the summit. Lane border: the Ganges/Indus born of the range are geography, but keep answers on the mountains and their rock, not river culture. Distractors = other real ranges/collisions, all live.

topics.name: From rift to ocean: the Red Sea and the Afar Triangle
topics.scope: The next chapter of rifting -- where the land-tear has already let the sea in and a real ocean is being born. T2: the Red Sea is a baby ocean -- Arabia is splitting away from Africa along a spreading ridge, and the sea is genuinely widening (a single 2005 rifting spasm in Afar opened the crust by several metres in weeks). T3: at the Afar Triangle in Ethiopia three rifts meet at a triple junction, one of the only places on Earth where mid-ocean-ridge spreading happens on dry land you can walk across. T4: Afar's Danakil Depression lies over 100 m BELOW sea level and holds Erta Ale, a volcano with a near-permanent boiling lava lake. T5: nearby Dallol paints the desert with acid-yellow, green and white hydrothermal terraces over a buried salt dome -- one of the hottest, most alien-looking landscapes anywhere on Earth.
topics.source: Grokipedia (Red Sea; Afar Triangle; Erta Ale; Dallol -- checked first, fetch blocked 403) corroborated via Wikipedia (Red Sea; Afar Triangle; 2005 Dabbahu rifting episode; Erta Ale; Dallol).
topics.framing_note: Direct sequel to the East African Rift ladder, so open at T2 (no baby-tier); theme = a rift that has already become a sea. Dinner-test payoff: Erta Ale's permanent lava lake below sea level (T4) and Dallol's alien colours (T5). Accuracy rail: the 2005 Dabbahu episode really opened an ~8 m-wide, ~60 km-long crack in weeks; keep 'a new ocean' as the Wilson-cycle projection it is. Keep answers on the LANDFORM/process, not the region's modern politics. Distractors = other real rift/spreading features, all live.

topics.name: Hotspots: the island chains a drifting plate builds
topics.scope: One process -- a fixed plume of deep heat while the plate slides overhead, printing a line of volcanoes like a conveyor belt -- across the world's hotspot trails. T1: on Hawaii's Big Island, Kilauea still erupts, while the older islands to the northwest (Kauai is ~5 million years old) are long extinct and eroding -- the chain gets steadily older the farther you go from the hot spot. T2: read backwards, the Hawaiian-Emperor chain is a ~6,000 km trail of dead volcanoes recording exactly where the Pacific plate has drifted -- complete with a sharp ~47-million-year-old BEND where the plate changed course. T3: the next Hawaiian island, Kamaehuakanaloa (formerly Loihi), is already erupting -- but still a seamount hidden underwater off the Big Island's coast. T4: the same kind of plume sits under a CONTINENT at Yellowstone; as North America crept southwest, the hotspot left a trail of dead calderas across Idaho's Snake River Plain before parking under Wyoming. T5: India once drifted over the Reunion hotspot ~66 million years ago and it flooded the land with the Deccan Traps -- a lava field the size of a country -- while that same plume today still builds the island of Reunion far to the south.
topics.source: Grokipedia (Hotspot (geology); Hawaiian-Emperor seamount chain; Yellowstone hotspot; Reunion hotspot -- checked first, fetch blocked 403) corroborated via Wikipedia (Hawaiian-Emperor seamount chain; Yellowstone hotspot; Reunion hotspot; Deccan Traps) + USGS/Hawaiian Volcano Observatory.
topics.framing_note: Theme = a stationary plume + a moving plate = an age-ordered island chain, the classic 'proof' of plate motion. Dinner-test payoff: the Hawaiian chain as a recording of the plate's whole path with its 47-Myr bend (T2) and the next island already growing underwater (T3). Lane border: Hawaii's/Galapagos's unique ANIMALS are the animal bank -- keep answers on the ISLANDS and their ages/geology, never the wildlife. Yellowstone here = the hotspot TRACK across the Snake River Plain (one rung); its geysers/caldera live in the dedicated Yellowstone ladder -- no same-fact overlap. Accuracy rail: the ~47-50 Myr bend's cause is debated (plate-motion change and/or plume drift) -- flag it as debated. Distractors = other real hotspot chains, all live.

topics.name: Megathrust: the deepest trenches and the strongest quakes
topics.scope: The other face of subduction -- where the diving slab locks then lurches, it carves the deepest trenches and unleashes the biggest earthquakes and tsunamis on Earth. T1: where the old, cold Pacific plate bends down into the Mariana Trench it makes the deepest point in any ocean -- the Challenger Deep, ~10,935 m down; drop Mount Everest in and its summit would still be ~2 km underwater. T2: the largest earthquake ever recorded struck off Chile in 1960 -- magnitude ~9.5 on the Nazca-South America subduction zone, its tsunami crossing the entire Pacific to strike Japan. T3: Alaska's 1964 'Good Friday' quake (~M9.2) rode the Aleutian megathrust -- the second-largest ever measured. T4: Japan's 2011 Tohoku quake (~M9.0) shoved the main island of Honshu about 2.4 m eastward and nudged Earth's axis. T5: the Cascadia zone off Washington and Oregon last ruptured on the night of 26 January 1700 -- a date pinned down by an 'orphan tsunami' that flooded Japan's coast with no local earthquake to explain it -- and is now considered overdue.
topics.source: Grokipedia (Challenger Deep; Cascadia subduction zone -- checked first, fetch blocked 403) corroborated via Wikipedia (Challenger Deep; 1960 Valdivia earthquake; 1964 Alaska earthquake; 2011 Tohoku earthquake; Cascadia subduction zone; 1700 Cascadia earthquake) + USGS.
topics.framing_note: Theme = the megathrust's superlatives (deepest trench, biggest quakes) toured by named place. Dinner-test payoff: the Challenger Deep swallowing Everest (T1) and the 1700 orphan-tsunami detective story (T5). Accuracy rail: the Pacific plate subducts beneath the small Mariana plate; the 1700 date really was fixed from Japanese tsunami records + Washington's drowned 'ghost forests'. Numbers here are EARNED payoffs (the stem builds the expectation the depth/magnitude then shatters), never cold trivia. Distractors = other real trenches / megathrust quakes, all live.
topics.history_overlap: The 1960 Chile / 1964 Alaska / 2011 Tohoku / 2004 Sumatra quakes may appear as history episodes -- geography's answer must be the EARTH fact (the trench, the fault type, the plate, the orphan-tsunami dating trick), never the relief-effort or death-toll story.

topics.name: Pangaea's ghost: how we know the map moves
topics.scope: The evidence and the engine -- the deep 'why' behind the whole strand, still anchored to named places. T2: the Atlantic is still opening about as fast as your fingernails grow (~2.5 cm a year), so Europe and North America drift a little farther apart every single year. T3: the coastlines of West Africa and eastern South America fit together like puzzle pieces -- and matching fossils and rock belts run straight across the join -- the clue that convinced Alfred Wegener the continents once formed one land, Pangaea. T4: the Mediterranean is the shrinking leftover of an old ocean (the Tethys) being squeezed shut as Africa pushes into Europe -- and it once dried out almost completely into salt flats ~5.5 million years ago. T5: oceans open and close in a slow cycle -- new crust shoved out at spreading ridges, old crust dragged down by cold slabs sinking at trenches -- so today's scattered continents will gather into a new supercontinent hundreds of millions of years from now.
topics.source: Grokipedia (Continental drift; Pangaea; Wilson cycle; Messinian salinity crisis -- checked first, fetch blocked 403) corroborated via Wikipedia (Continental drift; Alfred Wegener; Pangaea; Messinian salinity crisis; Wilson cycle) + USGS 'This Dynamic Earth'.
topics.framing_note: The capstone 'how do we KNOW' ladder -- keep it place-anchored (the African/South American coastline fit, the drying Mediterranean) so it never floats into abstraction. Dinner-test payoff: continents that fit like puzzle pieces (T3) and the Mediterranean once a dry salt basin (T4). Accuracy rail: attribute continental drift to Wegener (1912) and frame the matching FOSSILS as place-evidence (the same fossils appear on BOTH shores) without sliding into the organism's biology -- the wonder is the two continents once joined. Slightly harder ladder (few T1 rungs) -- the strand's easy openers live in the earlier ladders. Distractors = other real earth-history facts, all live.

topics.name: The East African Rift: a continent tearing itself apart
topics.scope: One process -- a continent splitting along a divergent boundary ON LAND -- toured down the East African Rift. T1: a vast crack ~6,000 km long runs from the Red Sea down through Ethiopia, Kenya and Tanzania, slowly prising Africa into two plates. T2: in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Nyiragongo cradles one of the world's largest lava lakes; its lava is so runny and fast it raced downhill into the city of Goma in 2002. T3: Tanzania's Ol Doinyo Lengai is the only volcano on Earth that erupts carbonatite lava -- unearthly cool (~510 C) black lava that turns snow-white within days as it weathers. T4: the rift floor cracked and dropped so deep it cradles Lake Tanganyika -- the world's second-deepest and among its oldest lakes, a sliver of water ~1.4 km deep. T5: geologists expect the Somali side to eventually split off entirely, and in roughly 10 million years the ocean to flood in and turn the Horn of Africa into a separate landmass.
topics.source: Grokipedia (East African Rift; Ol Doinyo Lengai; Mount Nyiragongo -- checked first, fetch blocked 403) corroborated via Wikipedia (East African Rift; Ol Doinyo Lengai; Mount Nyiragongo; Lake Tanganyika) + Smithsonian GVP.
topics.framing_note: Theme = a divergent boundary caught in the act on dry land. Dinner-test payoff: Ol Doinyo Lengai's cool black-then-white lava (T3) and Africa's coming ocean (T5). Lane border: rift-lake CICHLID fish swarms are the ANIMAL bank -- keep the answer the LAKE and its rift-made depth, never the fish's biology; the rift's early-human 'Cradle of Mankind' fossils lean HISTORY/anthropology, so keep answers on the landform/process. Accuracy rail: 'only active carbonatite volcano' and its ~510 C lava are established; frame the future ocean as the ~10-Myr geological prediction it is. Distractors = other real rift volcanoes/lakes, all live.

topics.name: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge: where the seafloor is born (and Iceland stands on it)
topics.scope: One process -- two plates pulling apart and erupting fresh ocean floor into the gap -- shown where that ridge actually breaks the surface. T1: the Mid-Atlantic Ridge is part of the longest mountain range on Earth: a ~65,000 km volcanic seam that runs along the seafloor around the whole globe, almost all of it hidden underwater. T2: Iceland is the rare place the ridge rises into daylight; at Thingvellir the rift opens as walkable cliffs and fissures between the North American and Eurasian plates. T3: at Iceland's Silfra fissure divers glide through crystal-clear glacial meltwater in the gap between two continental plates. T4: in November 1963 a brand-new island, Surtsey, erupted straight out of the sea off Iceland's south coast, and has been a sealed natural laboratory watched ever since. T5: Iceland only exists because it sits on the spreading ridge AND over a deep mantle hotspot at the same time -- double the magma, which is why the ridge here piles into a plateau above the waves instead of lying 2.5 km down.
topics.source: Grokipedia (Mid-Atlantic Ridge; Thingvellir; Surtsey; Iceland hotspot -- checked first, fetch blocked 403) corroborated via Wikipedia (Mid-Atlantic Ridge; Thingvellir; Silfra; Surtsey; Iceland plume) + USGS.
topics.framing_note: Theme = spreading centres manufacture new crust; Iceland is the window onto it. Dinner-test payoff: Surtsey the island born in living memory (T4) and Silfra's swim between continents (T3). Accuracy rail: the Iceland plate boundary is a broad rift ZONE of many fissures, not one tidy crack -- Thingvellir/Silfra dramatize it, so frame 'walk/dive between the plates' as the beloved-but-simplified truth it is; the 'longest mountain range' means the whole mid-ocean-ridge system. Distractors = other real ridges/rift features + 'a hotspot island', all live.

topics.name: The Ring of Fire: a rim of subduction volcanoes
topics.scope: One process -- an ocean plate diving under a continent MELTS into a chain of volcanoes -- toured around the Pacific rim. T1: a horseshoe of volcanoes ~40,000 km long rings the Pacific and holds about three-quarters of the world's active volcanoes (over 450 of them) -- the 'Ring of Fire'. T2: in the Andes the Nazca plate dives under South America and lifts Ojos del Salado on the Chile-Argentina border -- at 6,893 m the highest volcano on Earth, with the world's highest lake in its summit crater. T3: in the U.S. Pacific Northwest the Cascade arc rises behind the Cascadia subduction zone -- Mount St. Helens tore its own north face off in the 1980 blast. T4: on Indonesia's Sunda arc, Tambora's 1815 eruption was the largest in recorded history and chilled the whole planet into 1816's 'year without a summer'. T5: subduction volcanoes are the EXPLOSIVE kind -- seawater dragged down with the slab lowers the rock's melting point and makes sticky, gas-rich magma, unlike the runny lava of a hotspot shield like Hawaii (contrast a named Ring-of-Fire cone with a named hotspot volcano).
topics.source: Grokipedia (Ring of Fire; Ojos del Salado -- checked first, fetch blocked 403) corroborated via Wikipedia (Ring of Fire; Ojos del Salado; 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora; Mount St. Helens) + Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program.
topics.framing_note: Theme = subduction builds a RING of volcanoes; every rung a different named cone/arc. Dinner-test payoff: Ojos del Salado the highest volcano with a lake in its crater (T2) and Tambora dimming the whole planet's sky (T4). Accuracy rail: '~75% of active volcanoes / 90% of quakes' is the standard USGS figure -- state it as '~three-quarters of the world's active volcanoes'. Lane border: an eruption's effect on CROPS/famine leans history -- keep answers on the volcano and its plate, never the human toll. Distractors = other real Ring-of-Fire volcanoes/arcs, all live.
topics.history_overlap: Tambora/Krakatoa/St. Helens may also surface as history disasters -- keep the geography answer the earth-process/place fact (the arc, the plate, the eruption's scale on the land), not a casualty narrative.

topics.name: The three ways plates meet (a plate-boundary field guide)
topics.scope: The recognition base for the whole earthsystem strand: the three kinds of plate boundary, each anchored to its signature place. T1: at Iceland's Thingvellir you can stand in a rift valley where the North American and Eurasian plates PULL APART -- a divergent boundary, the ground literally opening in fissures. T2: along South America's Pacific coast one plate DIVES beneath another and the Andes rise -- a convergent (subduction) boundary. T3: in California the Pacific and North American plates SLIDE PAST each other along the San Andreas Fault, neither made nor destroyed -- a transform boundary (invert the wonder: 'plates that only scrape sideways, making no new land' -> transform). T4: the crust is broken into a few giant slabs (the Pacific plate is the largest, flooring most of the ocean) that drift only a few centimetres a year -- about as fast as your fingernails grow. T5: in Ethiopia's Afar region THREE rift arms meet at one spot -- a triple junction where the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden and East African rifts all pull in different directions.
topics.source: Grokipedia (Plate tectonics; checked first, direct fetch blocked 403) corroborated via Wikipedia (Plate tectonics; Thingvellir; Afar Triangle) + USGS 'This Dynamic Earth'.
topics.framing_note: The vocabulary spine every other earthsystem ladder leans on -- keep it SCENE-LED and easy (open with Thingvellir's walkable crack, never 'define divergent'). Teach each term by its PLACE before testing it; the answer is the boundary TYPE recalled as knowledge, not deduced from a stem that already says 'pull apart' -- describe the place's drama, then ask the name. Distractors = the other real boundary types + 'a hotspot', all live. Dinner-test payoff: the fingernail-speed drift (T4) and the three-way Afar tear (T5). No same-fact overlap with the dedicated ladders -- this one hands out the map, they go deep.

topics.name: Transform faults: the plates that grind past each other
topics.scope: One process -- plates sliding sideways, making no new crust and destroying none, just loading stress until it snaps -- across the world's great strike-slip faults. T1: California's San Andreas Fault is where the Pacific plate scrapes northwest past North America; it does not collide, it SLIDES. T2: on the Carrizo Plain the fault is so bare you can see streambeds bent sideways where the ground has crept past -- and in 1906 it lurched up to ~6 m at once, wrecking San Francisco. T3: because the land west of the fault is drifting northwest, Los Angeles is slowly sliding toward San Francisco -- they will be neighbours in ~20 million years. T4: Turkey's North Anatolian Fault behaves like a zipper: since 1939 its big quakes have marched steadily westward toward Istanbul, each rupture loading the next segment. T5: the Dead Sea sits in a pull-apart gap along the Dead Sea Transform -- which is why the lowest dry land on Earth (~430 m below sea level) lies right on a sliding plate boundary.
topics.source: Grokipedia (San Andreas Fault; North Anatolian Fault; Dead Sea Transform -- checked first, fetch blocked 403) corroborated via Wikipedia (San Andreas Fault; 1906 San Francisco earthquake; North Anatolian Fault; Dead Sea Transform) + USGS.
topics.framing_note: Theme = transform boundaries, San Andreas the flagship. Dinner-test payoff: LA drifting toward SF (T3) and the offset streambeds you can walk on the Carrizo Plain (T2). Accuracy rail: San Andreas ~1,200 km, right-lateral, ~33-37 mm/yr; frame the LA-SF meet-up as the far-future projection it is. Teach 'transform / strike-slip' via the sliding scene before naming it. Not a current-events border topic -- keep it timeless earth science. Distractors = other real transform faults + subduction/rift red-herrings that stay live.
topics.history_overlap: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake may also be a history episode -- keep the geography answer the FAULT/plate fact (transform boundary, the offset ground, the Carrizo Plain), never the fire-and-relief narrative.

topics.name: Cenotes — sinkholes to a flooded underworld
topics.scope: The Yucatan's windows into the water hidden under the limestone. T1: the Yucatan Peninsula has almost NO rivers on its surface — rain sinks straight through the porous limestone — so the Maya drank from cenotes: natural wells where the cave roof collapsed and exposed the cool groundwater below. T2: the Maya believed a cenote was a doorway to Xibalba, the watery underworld; at the Sacred Cenote of Chichen Itza, divers and dredges later recovered jade, gold, and human remains — offerings cast in to petition Chaac, the rain god. T3: seen from the air, the peninsula's densest RING of cenotes traces a huge buried arc — the rim of the Chicxulub crater, the ~66-million-year-old scar of the asteroid impact tied to the dinosaurs' extinction; the cenotes line up over its fractured edge (invert: the mysterious ring -> the buried crater). T4: the flooded caves behind the cenotes join into the LONGEST underwater cave system on Earth — Sistema Sac Actun near Tulum, over 370 km of submerged passage mapped by cave divers. T5: nearby El Zacaton is the world's deepest known water-filled sinkhole, a flooded pit over 300 m deep, so hard to reach that NASA tested an autonomous diving robot in it. Extra rungs: a 'how a cenote forms' rung; the Dos Ojos / Ik Kil cenotes as named examples. Distractors: other water features (a spring, a lava tube, a blue hole — Belize's Great Blue Hole is an apt adjacent distractor).
topics.source: Wikipedia: Cenote (fetched: limestone-collapse formation, Ring of Cenotes over the Chicxulub crater rim, Sacred Cenote offerings to Chaac, Xibalba portal belief, Sistema Sac Actun >376 km). Build-research (Grokipedia-first, corroborate Wikipedia): Chicxulub crater, El Zacaton, Sistema Sac Actun.
topics.framing_note: Teach 'cenote' and 'sinkhole/collapse.' Every answer is a place-fact (the well, the underworld belief, the crater ring, the longest underwater cave, the deepest sinkhole). VISION-MANDATED: treat the Maya's sacred cenote and Xibalba with respect on their own terms — state the offerings plainly, no smug 'they merely thought,' no gore-tourism. Dinner-test payoff: the Ring of Cenotes tracing the dinosaur-killer crater. Lane border: the Maya CIVILIZATION as a human story belongs to the history bank — keep answers here place- and water-anchored. Distractors are adjacent real water features.
topics.history_overlap: The Maya civilization and Chichen Itza as a human-history episode may live in the history bank; keep every answer here anchored to the cenote/water/crater (the well, the crater ring, the underwater cave), not to Maya political history.

topics.name: Classic karst — the land that named itself
topics.scope: The bare Slovenian plateau that gave geography one of its words, and the plumbing hidden beneath it. T1: on the stony Kras (Karst) plateau above the Adriatic, rain sinks into the limestone instead of running off in streams — a landscape so distinctive that scientists borrowed its very name, 'karst,' for every place on Earth that behaves this way (teach the term through its birthplace). T2: the Reka River flows across the surface and then simply VANISHES underground into the Skocjan Caves, thundering through one of the largest underground river canyons in the world before it disappears into the dark. T3: that lost river isn't gone — it runs unseen through the rock for tens of kilometers and RESURGES as the Timavo springs near the coast by Trieste, bursting back into daylight close to the sea. T4: a polje is a flat-floored karst plain that turns into a lake and back into a meadow with the seasons — Lake Cerknica in Slovenia fills in the wet season and drains away through swallow-holes in summer, an 'intermittent lake.' T5: teach the karst toolkit — a doline (sinkhole) is a closed pit that drains underground; a ponor (swallow-hole) gulps a whole stream; a resurgence spits it back out — a whole land plumbed by dissolved rock instead of surface rivers. Distractors: other landforms/processes (glacial valleys, volcanic craters, coastal features).
topics.source: Wikipedia: Karst (fetched: etymology from the Kras/Karst plateau, polje, doline/sinkhole, sinking rivers, karst springs/resurgence). Build-research (Grokipedia-first, corroborate Wikipedia): Skocjan Caves, Reka River / Timavo, Lake Cerknica, Postojna Cave.
topics.framing_note: This is the vocabulary ladder — teach 'karst,' 'polje,' 'doline/sinkhole,' 'ponor/resurgence,' the terms the tower-karst and cenote ladders lean on. Every stem names a real place (Kras, Skocjan, Timavo, Cerknica). Invert on T2 (a river that disappears -> the Skocjan swallow). Dinner-test payoff: the Reka/Timavo river that vanishes and reappears, and the lake that comes and goes. Lane border: Postojna's blind cave 'baby dragon' (the olm) is the animal bank — if Postojna appears, key the CAVE, not the amphibian. Distractors keep all four live.

topics.name: Drainage basins & the continental divide
topics.scope: The invisible ridge-lines that decide which ocean a raindrop reaches. T1: along the Continental Divide of the Americas — the crest of the Rocky Mountains — rain landing on the west side runs to the Pacific and rain on the east side runs (via the Gulf of Mexico) to the Atlantic; the ridge sorts every drop. T2: at Triple Divide Peak in Montana's Glacier National Park, meltwater from ONE summit can set off for three different seas — the Pacific, the Atlantic (Gulf of Mexico), and Hudson Bay toward the Arctic — a rare 'hydrological apex.' T3: the Amazon basin drains about 7 million km2 — roughly 40% of the entire South American continent — the largest drainage basin on Earth (invert the wonder: the giant basin is the hook, 'the Amazon' the answer). T4: the Casiquiare in Venezuela is a natural 'bifurcation' — a river that branches off the upper Orinoco and flows into the Rio Negro, secretly linking the Orinoco and Amazon basins that are supposed to be separate. T5: divides can move — 'river capture' (stream piracy), where a fast-cutting stream beheads a neighbor and steals its headwaters; geologists think the Casiquiare is slowly capturing more of the upper Orinoco this way. Distractors: other real divides/basins (the Congo basin, the Mississippi basin, Australia's Great Dividing Range).
topics.source: Wikipedia: Casiquiare canal (fetched, corroborated bifurcation Orinoco<->Rio Negro/Amazon & slow stream-capture); Amazon River (fetched: ~7M km2 basin, largest); plus canonical pages to research at build (Grokipedia-first per PIPELINE, corroborate Wikipedia): Continental Divide of the Americas, Triple Divide Peak, Drainage divide.
topics.framing_note: PLACE in every stem (a named ridge, peak, or basin); the answer is which ocean the water reaches, or the named divide/bifurcation — never a bare number. Teach 'drainage basin/watershed' and 'continental divide' before testing. Invert on T3 (basin size -> 'the Amazon'). Dinner-test payoff: Triple Divide Peak (one snowflake, three seas) and the Casiquiare (a river that cheats by belonging to two basins). Distractors are other real divides/basins so all four choices stay live. Pure earth-process — no food/animal content.

topics.name: Endorheic basins — water with no way out to the sea
topics.scope: Places where water flows IN and only evaporation takes it out, so the salt piles up. T1: the Dead Sea lies about 430 m BELOW sea level — the lowest dry land on Earth — and is so salty (roughly ten times the ocean) that a swimmer bobs like a cork; the Jordan River feeds it but nothing drains out. T2: the Caspian Sea is the world's LARGEST lake — bigger than all five North American Great Lakes combined — yet it reaches no ocean, losing water only to the sky (invert: the giant size is the hook, 'a closed sea with no outlet' the answer). T3: Utah's Great Salt Lake is the shrunken remnant of Ice-Age Lake Bonneville; where it dried it left the dead-flat, blinding-white Bonneville Salt Flats, hard enough to set world land-speed records on. T4: the Aral Sea was the world's fourth-largest lake until, from the 1960s, Soviet planners diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya to irrigate cotton; the sea collapsed into the toxic 'Aralkum' desert, stranding rusting fishing ships tens of kilometers from any water. T5: the Okavango River in Botswana never reaches the sea at all — it spreads into the Kalahari as a huge inland delta that pulses green in the dry season and then vanishes into sand. Extra rungs: Salar de Uyuni (Bolivia), the ~10,000 km2 salt-flat 'mirror' left by dried paleolakes; the Great Basin of the U.S. (no drop reaches an ocean); the shrinking of Lake Chad. Distractors: other salt/closed lakes and salt flats.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Aral Sea (fetched: Soviet Amu Darya/Syr Darya diversion for cotton from the 1960s, once 4th-largest lake, Aralkum desert, stranded boats at Moynaq). Build-research (Grokipedia-first, corroborate Wikipedia): Dead Sea, Caspian Sea, Great Salt Lake / Lake Bonneville, Okavango Delta, Salar de Uyuni, Endorheic basin.
topics.framing_note: Teach 'endorheic (no outlet to the sea)' before testing. Every answer is a place-fact (why it's salty / lowest / dried), never a bare number. VISION-MANDATED on the Aral rung: name the Soviet cotton diversion plainly as the cause — honest environmental record written on the land, active voice (planners diverted the rivers), no euphemism. Dinner-test payoff: the Aral's ships stranded in the desert, and floating on the Dead Sea. Lane border: the WILDLIFE of these basins (Caspian sturgeon, Okavango game) is the animal bank — keep the answer the landform/hydrology (inland delta, no outlet, salt flat), never a creature. Distractors are other real closed lakes.

topics.name: Estuaries & tidal bores — where river meets the tide
topics.scope: The mixing zones where a river's fresh water wrestles the sea's tide. T1: an estuary is where a river's fresh water meets and blends with the salty tide — like Chesapeake Bay, which is really the DROWNED valley of the Susquehanna River, flooded when the ice-age sea rose (a 'ria'). T2: in the funnel of Canada's Bay of Fundy the tide climbs about 16 m (52 ft) twice a day — the highest tides on Earth — enough that boats tied up at low tide sit on bare mud far below the docks (invert: the 16 m twice-a-day hook -> Bay of Fundy). T3: when a big incoming tide is squeezed into a narrowing river it can rear up into a single wave that races UPSTREAM — a tidal bore; the Qiantang River's 'Silver Dragon' in China is the world's largest, a wall of water up to ~9 m that crowds gather to watch each autumn. T4: on the Amazon a tidal bore called the pororoca rolls tens of kilometers up the river mouth — surfers ride a single wave for minutes (one rode it about 12 km for 37 minutes). T5: teach why bores happen — you need a huge tidal range AND a shallow, funnel-shaped, narrowing channel (the recipe behind the Severn bore in England as well as the Fundy and Qiantang giants); without the funnel the tide just rises quietly. Distractors: other coastal/river features (fjord, delta, lagoon, rip current).
topics.source: Wikipedia: Bay of Fundy (fetched: highest tidal range, ~16 m, funnel resonance); Tidal bore (fetched: Qiantang 'Silver Dragon' up to ~9 m and largest, Amazon pororoca ~4 m and 37-min surf ride, Severn bore, funnel + >6 m tidal-range recipe). Build-research (Grokipedia-first, corroborate Wikipedia): Chesapeake Bay, Ria, Estuary.
topics.framing_note: Teach 'estuary,' 'ria (drowned river valley),' and 'tidal bore' before testing; every stem names a real place. Invert on T2 (16 m twice a day -> Bay of Fundy). Dinner-test payoff: surfing the Amazon's pororoca and the Qiantang 'Silver Dragon.' ACCURACY NUANCE: Fundy's 'highest tides' claim is shared with Ungava Bay's Leaf Basin — say Fundy has the famous highest-average tidal range, don't over-claim a single global record. Pure hydrology — no animal/food. Distractors keep all four live.

topics.name: Groundwater — the hidden rivers under our feet
topics.scope: The vast unseen water in the rock — springs, aquifers, and rivers that run underground. T1: in the Palawan rainforest of the Philippines, the Puerto Princesa underground river flows for kilometers THROUGH a limestone mountain and out to the sea — you can take a boat into the dark along it (a navigable underground river). T2: most of the world's fresh LIQUID water isn't in rivers at all — it's groundwater, soaked into rock and sand below the surface; where that saturated rock (an 'aquifer') meets the ground it bursts out as a spring, like Florida's Silver Springs and Wakulla Springs, gushing crystal-clear from the limestone. T3: the Great Artesian Basin under eastern Australia is one of the largest groundwater basins on Earth — water that fell on distant highlands seeps for thousands of years and rises on its own at desert 'mound springs,' the only water for hundreds of dry kilometers (invert: what lets people survive the outback -> the artesian basin). T4: the Ogallala (High Plains) Aquifer waters much of the U.S. Great Plains, but it holds 'fossil' water banked since the Ice Age that barely refills — and in places pumping is drawing it down faster than a lifetime can replace it. T5: teach 'aquifer' and 'water table' — beneath the Sahara lies the Nubian Sandstone Aquifer, fossil water from a wetter age, which Libya pumped through the 'Great Man-Made River' pipelines to the coast: mining water that will not return. Distractors: other water sources (glacier, reservoir, desalination, a surface river).
topics.source: Wikipedia: Puerto Princesa Subterranean River National Park (fetched: navigable underground river ~8.2 km flowing directly to the sea, limestone karst, UNESCO / New7Wonders). Build-research (Grokipedia-first, corroborate Wikipedia): Aquifer, Great Artesian Basin, Silver Springs (Florida) / Wakulla Springs, Ogallala Aquifer, Nubian Sandstone Aquifer / Great Man-Made River.
topics.framing_note: This ladder covers the sub-strand's 'groundwater' explicitly — teach 'aquifer,' 'water table,' 'spring/artesian,' and 'fossil water.' Every stem names a real place (Puerto Princesa, Silver/Wakulla Springs, the Great Artesian Basin, the Ogallala, the Nubian aquifer). Invert on T3 (surviving the outback -> the artesian basin). Dinner-test payoff: a river you ride a boat INTO a mountain (Puerto Princesa), and 'fossil water' older than farming. The depletion rungs state facts plainly with no policy verdict. Pure hydrology/place. Distractors keep all four live.

topics.name: River deltas — where a river drops its load
topics.scope: The fans of new land a river builds where it finally meets still water. T1: where the Nile hits the Mediterranean it splays into a green triangle so like the Greek letter Delta that the ancient Greeks named the whole landform after it — the Nile Delta, ancient Egypt's breadbasket. T2: the Mississippi doesn't fan — it pokes long skinny fingers into the Gulf of Mexico, a 'bird's-foot' delta, built where the river dumps mud faster than the sea can sweep it away. T3: the Ganges and Brahmaputra together build the LARGEST delta on Earth, the Bengal delta, whose seaward fringe is the Sundarbans, the world's biggest tidal mangrove forest (the answer is the delta/Sundarbans landform, not the tiger). T4: the Danube Delta on the Black Sea is Europe's largest and best-preserved wetland — a maze of reed channels where the river is still adding new land each year. T5: a delta is a tug-of-war between a river building land and the sea plus the delta's own sinking weight tearing it down — starved of mud by upstream dams and levees, the Mississippi delta is now LOSING Louisiana wetland to the Gulf as it subsides. Extra rungs: the Lena Delta, a frozen Arctic fan in Siberia; a cross-reference to the Okavango, a river that 'deltas' into a desert instead of a sea. Distractors: other named deltas and river landforms.
topics.source: Build-research (Grokipedia-first, corroborate Wikipedia): Nile Delta, Mississippi River Delta, Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta / Sundarbans, Danube Delta, Lena Delta, River delta.
topics.framing_note: Teach 'delta' and that its SHAPE depends on river mud vs. wave/tide power (fan vs. bird's-foot vs. tidal). Every answer is a named delta or its landform/shape. Invert on T3 (largest -> Ganges-Brahmaputra/Sundarbans). Dinner-test payoff: the bird's-foot delta and the disappearing-Louisiana rung. Lane border: the Sundarbans' tigers and wildlife are the animal bank; a delta city's cuisine is the cooking bank — keep every answer the delta landform. Distractors are other real deltas so all four stay live.

topics.name: The great caves — water's underground cathedrals
topics.scope: The record-holding voids that seeping water has dissolved out of solid rock. T1: under the hills of Kentucky, Mammoth Cave is the LONGEST cave system in the world — over 686 km (426 miles) of surveyed passages already mapped and still growing — all eaten out of limestone by percolating water. T2: Son Doong in Vietnam holds the largest cave passage on Earth — roomy enough for a Boeing 747; where its ceiling collapsed, sunlight pours in and a jungle grows underground, and the cave even brews its own drifting clouds. T3: in New Mexico, Lechuguilla Cave was carved the 'wrong' way — from the BOTTOM UP, by sulfuric acid rising from deep oil deposits — and it is hung with 6-meter gypsum chandeliers found almost nowhere else (invert: acid-from-below is the hook, Lechuguilla the answer). T4: the two deepest caves ever found both plunge more than 2 km straight down into the Arabika Massif in Abkhazia — Veryovkina and Krubera(-Voronya) — vertical labyrinths that take divers weeks and have cost lives to reach the bottom of. T5: teach the difference — most caves grow slowly downward as rainwater turns mildly acidic and dissolves limestone (Mammoth, Carlsbad), but Lechuguilla's acid rose UP from oil below ('hypogene' cave-making), which is why its crystals are so bizarre. Extra rungs: Carlsbad Caverns' Big Room (key the chamber, not the bats); a 'how a limestone cave and its dripstone form' rung anchored to a named cave. Distractors: other named caves and cave types (lava tube, sea cave, ice cave).
topics.source: Wikipedia (all fetched): Mammoth Cave National Park (>686 km / 426 mi, world's longest); Son Doong Cave (largest passage, 747-scale, dolines with jungle, own clouds, discovered by Ho Khanh 1990 / BCRA 2009, Phong Nha-Ke Bang); Lechuguilla Cave (hypogene sulfuric-acid formation from oil-derived H2S, gypsum chandeliers); Veryovkina Cave (>2 km deep, Arabika Massif, record vs. Krubera).
topics.framing_note: Teach how dissolved limestone makes caves; every stem names a real cave and the answer is that cave's superlative made knowable (longest / biggest passage / acid-carved / deepest). ACCURACY RAIL on the deepest rung: state Veryovkina and Krubera as the TWO deepest (both >2 km, Arabika Massif) rather than betting on which is #1 — the record has swapped on re-survey. Invert wonders (the 747 hook -> Son Doong; acid-from-below -> Lechuguilla). Dinner-test payoff: Son Doong's jungle-and-clouds inside a cave, and Lechuguilla carved by acid rising from oil. Lane border: Carlsbad's bats and cave-adapted animals are the animal bank — key the cave/chamber. Distractors keep all four live.

topics.name: The meander & the oxbow lake
topics.scope: How a river wanders across its own valley and then strangles its own bends. T1: on the lower Mississippi the river swings in giant S-curves called meanders — fast and biting on the outside of each bend, slow and depositing on the inside. T2: when a loop grows so tight that a flood cuts straight across its neck, the abandoned bend is left behind as a crescent 'oxbow lake' — the Mississippi valley is freckled with them (name the landform = the answer). T3: at the Goosenecks of the San Juan River in Utah the river coils back on itself in tight loops 300 m below the desert floor — 'entrenched (incised) meanders,' bends the river sawed DOWNWARD into solid rock as the whole land rose, so it could no longer wander free (invert: the 300 m depth is the hook). T4: Horseshoe Bend near Page, Arizona, is a single incised meander of the Colorado — the green river wrapped almost all the way around a lone sandstone butte. T5: 'The Rincon' on the Colorado is an ABANDONED incised meander: ages ago the river cut across the neck and walked away, leaving a dry, rock-walled loop stranded high above the new channel — a fossil oxbow carved in stone. Distractors: other river landforms (delta, canyon, waterfall, braided channel).
topics.source: Build-research (Grokipedia-first, corroborate Wikipedia): Meander, Oxbow lake, Goosenecks State Park / San Juan River, Horseshoe Bend (Arizona), Incised meander, The Rincon (Colorado River).
topics.framing_note: Teach 'meander,' 'oxbow lake,' and 'incised/entrenched meander' before testing; every answer is a named landform or a named place. Invert on T3 (the 300 m depth -> 'entrenched meander'). Dinner-test payoff: the oxbow lake (a river that strangles its own bend) and the Rincon (a canyon-loop the river abandoned). Pure geomorphology — no animal/food. Distractors are adjacent real river features so all four stay live.

topics.name: The world's great rivers
topics.scope: The planet's mightiest rivers, each keyed to a knowable named fact rather than a bare superlative. T1: the Nile (~6,650 km) runs the 'wrong' way — south to north, out of the heart of Africa to the Mediterranean — and its floods built ancient Egypt. T2: the Amazon carries about a FIFTH (20%) of all the water the world's rivers deliver to the oceans, more than the next several biggest rivers combined (the discharge is the hook, 'the Amazon' the answer). T3: the Blue Nile pours off the Ethiopian Highlands out of Lake Tana and delivers most of the Nile's flood, while the White Nile's remotest waters feed from the Lake Victoria region — a place-anchored 'where the Nile begins,' no bare date. T4: the Congo is the world's DEEPEST river, plunging to about 220 m in dark canyons where isolated fish evolved, and it is the only great river to cross the equator twice. T5: at the 'Meeting of the Waters' by Manaus the coffee-black Rio Negro and the sandy Solimoes run side by side for about 6 km WITHOUT mixing, because they differ in temperature, speed, and density. Extra rungs: the Yangtze (Asia's longest, the Three Gorges); the Danube (flows through more countries — about ten — than any other river); the Mississippi-Missouri (North America's great artery). Distractors: other great rivers.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Amazon River (fetched: 20% of global riverine discharge, largest basin, Nile length dispute, Meeting of the Waters at Manaus); Congo River (fetched: deepest ~220 m, crosses equator twice, 3rd by discharge, Livingstone Falls). Build-research (Grokipedia-first, corroborate Wikipedia): Nile, Blue Nile, Yangtze, Danube.
topics.framing_note: Invert every superlative (put the number in the stem, make the NAMED river the answer). Teach 'discharge/drainage' before testing. ACCURACY RAIL: the Congo is 3rd by discharge (behind the Amazon and Ganges-Brahmaputra) — word its rung as 'deepest,' never 'second-biggest.' Dinner-test payoff: the Meeting of the Waters (two rivers that refuse to blend) and the Congo's deep-canyon abyss. Distractors are other real rivers so all four stay live.
topics.history_overlap: Ancient Egypt on the Nile, and the Victorian search for the Nile's source (Speke/Burton), may appear as human-history episodes in the history bank; keep every answer here a river/landscape fact, not a dated human event.

topics.name: Tower karst — stone forests and drowned dragons
topics.scope: Limestone hills dissolved by rain into forests of stone, above water and below it. T1: along the Li River around Guilin and Yangshuo, hundreds of steep limestone hills rise straight out of the flat rice paddies like a forest of green thumbs — 'tower karst,' rock slowly eaten by rainwater over millions of years. T2: the most famous stretch of that scenery, the peaks near Xingping on the Li River, is the very view printed on China's 20-yuan banknote (which real place is on the money = the answer). T3: teach the terms — a 'peak forest' of separate towers standing on a plain is fenglin; clustered cones sharing one base are fengcong; both are carved DOWN by water, not pushed UP by tectonics. T4: Ha Long Bay in Vietnam is DROWNED tower karst — the same limestone towers, but the sea rose and flooded the valleys between them, leaving about 1,600 islands jutting from the Gulf of Tonkin (invert: the 1,600-island hook -> drowned karst). T5: in Yunnan's Stone Forest (Shilin), rain dissolved the limestone from the top down into a maze of tall grey blades and pinnacles you can walk between — karst at ground level instead of towering hills. Distractors: other karst/rock scenery (fjords, mesas, hoodoos, and the Zhangjiajie sandstone pillars).
topics.source: Wikipedia: Karst (fetched: definition, tower karst, dissolution). Build-research (Grokipedia-first, corroborate Wikipedia): Guilin / Li River, Yangshuo, Ha Long Bay, Stone Forest (Shilin), Tower karst (fenglin/fengcong).
topics.framing_note: Teach 'karst' and 'tower karst / fenglin / fengcong' before testing; every stem names a real place and every answer is that place's landform or the term for it. Invert where possible (Ha Long's 1,600 islands -> drowned karst). Dinner-test payoff: the 20-yuan-note view and Ha Long as a flooded stone forest. ACCURACY RAIL: Zhangjiajie's pillars are QUARTZ SANDSTONE, not karst — use them as a distractor, never label them karst. Pure landform — no animal/food. Distractors keep all four choices live.

topics.name: Waterfalls — the river's great leaps
topics.scope: Where a river meets a sudden drop, keyed to named places and the process behind them. T1: deep in Venezuela's Canaima wilderness, water falls 979 m off the edge of Auyan-tepui, a flat-topped 'table mountain' — so far that it drifts into mist before it lands: Angel Falls, the world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall (the Pemon call it Kerepakupai Vena). T2: on the Zambezi a curtain of water 1,708 m wide and about 108 m tall throws up spray visible for miles — locals named it Mosi-oa-Tunya, 'the smoke that thunders'; we call it Victoria Falls, the world's largest single SHEET of falling water. T3: Victoria Falls hides how it was made — the river carved a zigzag of deep gorges by tearing along cracks (fault lines) in the flat basalt, and the falls have marched slowly upstream, gorge by gorge, over the ages.
