topics.name: Krakatoa 1883: the loudest sound on Earth
topics.scope: The Indonesian island volcano whose 1883 eruption was the loudest event in recorded history. T1: Krakatoa (Krakatau) sat in the Sunda Strait between Java and Sumatra; in 1883 it blew itself apart in an eruption heard across a quarter of the planet. T2: invert the wonder -- the final explosion was heard 4,800 km away on Rodrigues Island near Mauritius (people there thought it was distant naval cannon fire), making it the LOUDEST sound in recorded history; sailors 64 km away had their eardrums ruptured. T3: the real killer was water -- the volcano's collapse sent tsunamis over 40 m high crashing into Java and Sumatra, killing about 36,000 people. T4: the pressure wave from the blast circled the ENTIRE Earth about three and a half times, recorded on barographs worldwide for days afterward. T5: so much ash reached the high atmosphere that sunsets turned blood-red across the globe for months -- fire brigades in New York were called out to 'fires' that were only the sky. Deeper: a new island, Anak Krakatau ('Child of Krakatoa'), rose from the same submarine crater in the late 1920s, and its flank collapse triggered a deadly tsunami in 2018.
topics.source: Wikipedia: '1883 eruption of Krakatoa' (fetched/verified: sound heard 4,800 km at Rodrigues Island, official death toll 36,417 mostly from tsunami, tsunami up to ~40+ m, pressure wave circled globe ~3.5 times, worldwide blood-red sunsets, Anak Krakatau emergence). Grokipedia to be checked first at build stage.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led; the PLACE (Sunda Strait / Krakatoa) is the anchor and every answer is a Krakatoa fact. Invert-the-wonder is the spine (loudest sound, globe-circling pressure wave, worldwide red skies). Accuracy rail: 4,800 km / Rodrigues Island for the sound; the ~36,000 dead were mostly from the TSUNAMI, not the blast itself -- keep cause-of-death correct. Dinner-test payoff = the sound heard nearly 5,000 km away (T2) and fire engines chasing a red sky in New York (T5). Distractors are other real 'loudest/biggest' claims and adjacent eruptions (Tambora, Pinatubo, Mount Pelee) so all four stay live. Any Munch 'The Scream' red-sky link is a labeled hypothesis, not a fact.

topics.name: Laki 1783: the fissure that starved a nation
topics.scope: Not a cone but a CRACK in Iceland that bled lava for eight months and caused a famine. T2: in 1783 the ground tore open along a 25-km fissure in southern Iceland called Lakagigar ('the craters of Laki'), and lava poured from a row of more than 130 vents -- a 'fissure eruption,' not a single mountain. T3: invert the wonder -- the eruption's gas, not its lava, was the killer: clouds of fluorine settled on the grass and poisoned Iceland's livestock (about 80% of the sheep died of it), and the famine that followed, the Modhardhindin or 'Mist Hardships,' killed roughly a fifth of everyone in Iceland. T4: the bluish sulfur haze drifted across Europe that summer -- in America, Benjamin Franklin noted a strange 'dry fog' that dimmed the sun -- and the crop failures it caused killed tens of thousands more (about 23,000 in Britain alone). T5: some historians argue that the misery Laki spread across France helped stoke the unrest that led toward the French Revolution six years later (a genuinely debated link).
topics.source: Wikipedia: 'Laki' (fetched/verified: 25-km fissure, 130+ vents, ~20-25% of Iceland's population died from famine, ~80% of sheep dead from fluorosis, Modhardhindin 'Mist Hardships', ~8 Mt fluorine and ~120 Mt SO2, ~23,000 British deaths, Franklin's 'dry fog'). Grokipedia first at build.
topics.framing_note: Earth-process wonder anchored to Iceland; teach 'fissure eruption' via the scene (a 25-km crack, a row of 130 vents) rather than defining it cold. Accuracy rail: the mass deaths were from FLUORINE-poisoned livestock and the resulting famine, not from lava burning people -- keep cause correct; ~20% of Iceland's population. Dinner-test payoff = a crack in the ground, not a mountain, starved a whole country (T3). The French Revolution link is flagged as a DEBATED hypothesis, never stated as fact. Distractors are other Icelandic volcanoes and other eruption styles so all four stay live.

topics.name: Lava lakes: the world's eternal fire pits
topics.scope: Only a handful of volcanoes on Earth hold a permanent, churning lake of molten lava -- here they are. T2: at Mount Nyiragongo in the Democratic Republic of Congo, a lake of liquid lava churns in the summit crater -- one of the largest lava lakes ever known, glowing above the lakeside city of Goma. T3: invert the wonder -- Nyiragongo's lava is unusually runny (very low in silica), so when its crater wall broke in 1977 the lava raced downhill at up to about 60 km/h, the fastest lava flow ever recorded -- most lava you could simply walk away from. T4: on the far side of the world, Mount Erebus in ANTARCTICA holds a lava lake too -- a pool of fire on a continent of ice, and the southernmost active volcano on Earth; and in Ethiopia's scorching Danakil Depression, Erta Ale ('the smoking mountain') has kept its lava lake for over a century. T5: strangest of all is Ol Doinyo Lengai in Tanzania, the only volcano on Earth that erupts 'natrocarbonatite' lava -- so cool (barely 500-600C) and runny that it pours out black like motor oil and then turns chalky WHITE within days; to the Maasai it is Ol Doinyo Lengai, the 'Mountain of God.'
topics.source: Wikipedia: 'Mount Nyiragongo' (fetched/verified: most voluminous known lava lake, very low-silica lava, 1977 flow up to ~60 km/h the fastest recorded, 2002/2021 eruptions and Goma), 'Mount Erebus' (Antarctic lava lake, southernmost active volcano), 'Erta Ale' (Danakil, long-lived lava lake), 'Ol Doinyo Lengai' (unique natrocarbonatite lava ~500-590C, black cooling to white, Maasai 'Mountain of God'). Grokipedia first at build.
topics.framing_note: EARTH-SYSTEM theme ladder: the spine is persistent LAVA LAKES and lava chemistry, deepened across named places (Nyiragongo, Erebus, Erta Ale, Ol Doinyo Lengai, with Kilauea's Halemaumau available). Every rung names a place; the answer is a place/lava fact. Accuracy rail: Nyiragongo's record speed (~60 km/h in 1977) comes from LOW-silica lava; Ol Doinyo Lengai's cool black-to-white carbonatite is genuine and unique -- keep the chemistry honest. Dinner-test payoff = the black lava that turns white / the only-in-the-world Mountain of God (T5) and a lava lake in Antarctica (T4). Respect the Maasai sacred name on its own terms -- present it plainly, neither advertise nor dismiss. Distractors: other lava-lake volcanoes and other lava types (pahoehoe, aa, basalt) so all four stay live. Lane border: geography owns the lava/landscape, not any creature living near these vents.

topics.name: Mount St Helens 1980: the sideways blast
topics.scope: The Washington State volcano that erupted SIDEWAYS. T1: Mount St Helens, a snow-capped cone in Washington State, USA, erupted on 18 May 1980 in the deadliest and most destructive eruption in United States history. T2: for weeks beforehand a huge 'bulge' swelled out of the mountain's north face, growing about 1.5 m per DAY as magma pushed underneath. T3: invert the wonder -- a morning earthquake shook the bulge loose in the LARGEST landslide in recorded history, and that avalanche uncorked the magma so the volcano exploded not upward but SIDEWAYS, a lateral blast that flattened forest across nearly 600 sq km. T4: geologist David Johnston, camped 10 km north, radioed 'Vancouver! Vancouver! This is it!' seconds before the blast reached him; 57 people died, including innkeeper Harry Truman, who had refused to leave his lodge on the mountain. T5: the mountain lost about 400 m of its summit in minutes (from 2,950 m down to about 2,550 m), leaving a mile-wide horseshoe crater where the peak had stood. Deeper: nearby Spirit Lake was buried under a raft of shattered logs that still floats on it today, and a new lava dome has slowly rebuilt inside the crater ever since.
topics.source: Wikipedia: '1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens' (fetched/verified: 18 May 1980, M5.1 quake triggering the largest subaerial landslide in recorded history, the lateral blast, bulge growth ~5-6 ft/day, 57 dead, summit 9,677 ft -> 8,363 ft, ~230 sq mi of flattened forest). David Johnston's final radio call is documented. Grokipedia first at build.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led drama anchored to the named mountain; every answer is a St Helens fact. Accuracy rail: the LATERAL (sideways) blast and the record landslide are the twin wonders -- keep the sequence right (quake -> record landslide -> uncorked lateral blast); 57 dead. Dinner-test payoff = a volcano that blew out sideways (T3) and Johnston's last radio call (T4). Distractors are other eruption styles and other Cascade volcanoes (Rainier, Hood, Shasta) so all four stay live.

topics.name: Pinatubo 1991: the eruption that cooled the planet
topics.scope: The Philippine volcano whose 1991 eruption measurably cooled the whole Earth -- and whose forecast saved tens of thousands of lives. T2: Mount Pinatubo, on the island of Luzon in the Philippines, roared back to life in 1991 after about 500 years of silence, in the second-largest eruption of the 20th century. T3: invert the wonder -- it injected about 17 million tonnes of sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere, and over the next two years global temperatures dropped by roughly half a degree Celsius -- a whole planet cooled by one mountain. T4: scientists from the Philippine institute PHIVOLCS and the U.S. Geological Survey read the warning signs and ordered a mass evacuation days before the blast, saving tens of thousands of lives; the giant U.S. Clark Air Base nearby was abandoned. T5: teach the term 'lahar' -- the danger did not end with the eruption; for years afterward, monsoon rains remobilized the loose ash into lahars, fast rivers of volcanic mud that buried whole towns downstream.
topics.source: Wikipedia: '1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo' (fetched/verified: global cooling ~0.4C / NH ~0.5-0.6C for ~1991-93, ~17 Mt SO2 largest ever measured, second-largest 20th-century eruption after Novarupta 1912, VEI 6, ~60,000 evacuated saving tens of thousands, Clark Air Base abandoned, multi-year lahars). Grokipedia first at build.
topics.framing_note: Earth-process + human-preparedness wonder anchored to Luzon. Accuracy rail: ~0.5C global cooling and ~17 Mt SO2 (the largest sulfur injection ever measured by instruments); the successful evacuation is the humane payoff -- credit PHIVOLCS + USGS honestly. Dinner-test payoff = 'one mountain cooled the whole planet half a degree' (T3). Teach 'lahar' via the T5 scene before naming it. Distractors are other real eruptions and other climate effects (the ozone hole, El Nino) so all four stay live. No alarmism -- settled earth science told with wonder.

topics.name: Santorini: the caldera behind the Atlantis legend
topics.scope: A crescent-shaped Greek island that is really the rim of a drowned volcano. T2: Santorini (ancient Thera) in the Aegean Sea is a ring of steep cliffs curving around a deep blue bay -- the whole island is the wall of a 'caldera,' the flooded crater left when a volcano collapsed into the sea. T3: around 1600 BC Thera erupted in one of the largest eruptions in human history (VEI 7); the center of the island collapsed, letting the sea rush in and forming the crescent shape visitors sail into today. T4: invert the wonder -- buried under the ash at Akrotiri lies a Bronze Age town so well preserved it's called the 'Minoan Pompeii,' with three-story houses and vivid frescoes -- but UNLIKE Pompeii, almost NO bodies have been found, so the townspeople seem to have fled in time. T5: because the eruption devastated the nearby Minoan civilization on Crete, some scholars have proposed Thera as the real place behind Plato's legend of Atlantis, the great island that vanished into the sea (a popular idea, but not accepted by most scholars).
topics.source: Wikipedia: 'Minoan eruption' (fetched/verified: ~1600 BC eruption, ice-core ~1628 BC and disputed dating, VEI 7, caldera collapse forming the crescent island, Akrotiri the 'Minoan Pompeii' with no human remains found, Marinatos's Atlantis hypothesis NOT supported by current scholarship). Grokipedia first at build.
topics.framing_note: PLACE-wonder anchored to Santorini/Thera; every answer is a Santorini fact. Teach 'caldera' via the scene (the cliff ring around a drowned crater). Accuracy rail: the Atlantis link is a labeled HYPOTHESIS (proposed by Marinatos, not supported by current scholarship) -- never state it as fact; the eruption is ~1600 BC (ice-core ~1628 BC, disputed). Dinner-test payoff = the 'Minoan Pompeii' at Akrotiri where no bodies were found (T4). Distractors: other calderas and other Aegean/Greek islands so all four stay live. Lane border: the Minoan civilization's DECLINE is history-bank territory -- keep answers on the island's landscape and the buried town, not Bronze Age politics.
topics.history_overlap: The Minoan civilization's collapse belongs to the history bank; keep this ladder's answers on the caldera/Akrotiri landscape and burial, not the Bronze Age political story.

topics.name: Tambora & the Year Without a Summer
topics.scope: The 1815 Indonesian eruption so vast it changed the world's weather for a year. T2: Mount Tambora on the island of Sumbawa, Indonesia, erupted in 1815 in the most powerful eruption in recorded history (VEI 7), blasting away the top third of the mountain and killing about 71,000 people. T3: invert the wonder -- the following year, 1816, became known worldwide as 'the Year Without a Summer': snow fell in New England in June and harvests failed across Europe and North America, all traced back to Tambora's dust. T4: trapped indoors by the gloomy, storm-dark summer of 1816 beside Lake Geneva, 18-year-old Mary Shelley began writing 'Frankenstein' -- a novel born from a volcanic winter half a world away. T5: the mechanism is the deep wonder -- Tambora flung sulfur gas high into the STRATOSPHERE, where it formed a haze of sulfate-droplet aerosols that reflected sunlight back to space and cooled the whole planet for over a year.
topics.source: Wikipedia: '1815 eruption of Mount Tambora' (fetched/verified: VEI 7, most powerful eruption in recorded history, Sumbawa, ~71,000 deaths, 1816 Year Without a Summer with June frosts/snow in New England, Turner's altered skies). Mary Shelley / Villa Diodati summer 1816 is widely documented. Grokipedia to be checked first at build.
topics.framing_note: Earth-process wonder anchored to Sumbawa; the answer is always a Tambora/1816 fact. Accuracy rail: Tambora 1815 is the LARGEST eruption in recorded history (bigger than Krakatoa); the cooling worked via sulfate aerosols in the stratosphere reflecting sunlight -- state the mechanism plainly, no climate alarmism. Dinner-test payoff = 'the Year Without a Summer' (T3) and Frankenstein born from it (T4). Distractors are other real eruptions and other historically cold years so all four stay live. Lane border: the novel is a one-rung cultural payoff BORN of the place's climate effect, not a literature ladder.

topics.name: The mystery eruptions: reading Earth's ash archive
topics.scope: Some giant eruptions marked the whole planet -- but the volcano that did it stayed a mystery for centuries. T2: ice cores drilled in Greenland and Antarctica showed that around the year 1257 SOMETHING erupted so violently it dusted BOTH poles with sulfur -- one of the biggest eruptions in 7,000 years -- yet for 750 years no one knew which volcano did it. T3: invert the wonder -- in 2013 scientists matched the ash chemistry to Mount Samalas on the island of Lombok, Indonesia; its collapse left the huge caldera that today holds the Segara Anak crater lake beside Mount Rinjani, and a medieval Javanese chronicle, the Babad Lombok, even describes a mountain that collapsed and buried a kingdom. T4: an older mystery -- in AD 536 a strange dust veil dimmed the sun for over a year across Europe and Asia (the Byzantine writer Procopius said the sun shone 'without brightness'); scientists now blame a huge volcanic eruption, though they still argue over WHERE (Iceland, or Ilopango in Central America). T5: the biggest of all is written near Lake Toba on Sumatra, Indonesia -- a caldera about 100 km long left by the largest eruption in roughly 2 million years, about 74,000 years ago; some scientists proposed it nearly wiped out early humans (the 'Toba bottleneck' -- a genuinely debated idea).
topics.source: Wikipedia: 'Mount Samalas' / '1257 Samalas eruption' (bipolar ice-core sulfur, 2013 attribution, Segara Anak caldera lake by Rinjani, Babad Lombok), 'Volcanic winter of 536' (Procopius's dimmed sun; disputed Iceland vs Ilopango source), 'Toba catastrophe theory' (~74 ka, ~100-km caldera, debated human-bottleneck hypothesis). Grokipedia first at build.
topics.framing_note: EARTH-SYSTEM theme ladder: the spine is DETECTIVE earth-science -- finding ancient eruptions by reading ice cores, chronicles, and calderas, anchored to named places (Samalas/Lombok, the 536 event, Lake Toba/Sumatra). Every rung names a place; the answer is a place fact. Accuracy rail: the 536 source is DISPUTED (Iceland vs Ilopango) and the Toba human-bottleneck is a DEBATED hypothesis -- flag both as such, never state as settled. Dinner-test payoff = a giant eruption whose volcano was a mystery for 750 years, cracked by ice cores (T2/T3). Distractors: other Indonesian volcanoes and other big eruptions (Tambora, Krakatoa) so all four stay live.

topics.name: Vesuvius & the burial of Pompeii
topics.scope: The volcano over the Bay of Naples that buried two Roman towns in a single afternoon in AD 79. T1: Mount Vesuvius rises behind Naples in southern Italy; in AD 79 it buried the town of Pompeii under meters of ash and pumice, freezing a whole Roman city in time. T2: the people of Pompeii were not killed by lava but by a pyroclastic surge -- a ~300C avalanche of superheated gas and ash that killed instantly. T3: a young man, Pliny the Younger, watched from Misenum across the bay and wrote the only eyewitness account, comparing the eruption cloud to an umbrella-pine tree -- which is why this towering-column eruption style is now called 'Plinian.' T4: his uncle, Pliny the Elder, sailed the Roman fleet TOWARD the eruption to rescue friends and died on the beach at Stabiae. T5: the famous body 'casts' of Pompeii are plaster -- archaeologist Giuseppe Fiorelli poured plaster into the hollow VOIDS left in the hardened ash where victims' bodies had decayed. Deeper rungs: nearby Herculaneum was buried by hotter flows that CARBONIZED a whole library of papyrus scrolls (the Villa of the Papyri), now being read unopened by X-ray scanning and AI (the Vesuvius Challenge); Vesuvius is a 'somma' volcano, a young cone growing inside the ring of an older collapsed crater; and ~3 million people now live in its shadow.
topics.source: Wikipedia: 'Eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79' (fetched/verified: Pliny the Younger's letters and 'Plinian' naming, ~300C pyroclastic surges, Fiorelli plaster casts poured into ash voids, Villa of the Papyri carbonized scrolls + Vesuvius Challenge, Pliny the Elder's death at Stabiae). Grokipedia to be checked first at build stage per policy.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led wonder about the PLACE and the earth-process that entombed it. Accuracy rail: 'Plinian' is named for Pliny the YOUNGER (the eyewitness), NOT the Elder (who died); the casts are plaster poured into body-shaped voids, NOT petrified bodies -- keep that exact. Dinner-test payoff = the plaster casts made from body-shaped holes in the ash (T5) and the AI-read carbonized scrolls. Invert the wonder at T3 (the 'umbrella-pine cloud' is the hook; 'Plinian' is the recalled answer, not restated in the stem). Distractors are other real eruption terms (Strombolian, Vulcanian, effusive) and other buried sites (Herculaneum, Stabiae, Oplontis) so all four stay live. Lane border: geography owns the burial and the site's archaeology -- do NOT drift into the political history of Rome.
topics.history_overlap: The AD 79 event and Pliny's account may appear in a Roman-history ladder; keep geography's answers anchored to the place and earth-process (pyroclastic burial, the plaster casts, Herculaneum's carbonized scrolls), not Roman political history.

topics.name: Volcanic lightning: the ash cloud's dirty thunderstorm
topics.scope: Some eruptions crackle with their own lightning, born inside the ash instead of a rain cloud. T2: when Iceland's Eyjafjallajokull erupted in 2010, photographers caught bolts of lightning flickering INSIDE the towering ash plume -- lightning made by a volcano, with no storm at all. T3: invert the wonder -- this 'volcanic lightning' (nicknamed a 'dirty thunderstorm') comes from the ash itself: countless jagged ash particles rub and collide as they blast upward, building up static electricity until it discharges as lightning. T4: at Sakurajima in Kagoshima Bay, Japan, one of the world's most active volcanoes, these lightning storms flash so often that scientists travel there to study them; volcanic lightning also lit up the 2020 eruption of Taal in the Philippines and the 2018 collapse of Anak Krakatau. T5: it is not new -- nearly 2,000 years ago Pliny the Younger, describing Vesuvius, wrote of a darkness lit by flashes, and today satellites detect these bursts to warn aircraft that an invisible ash cloud is aloft.
topics.source: Wikipedia: 'Volcanic lightning' (mechanism = static charge from colliding ash particles; documented at Eyjafjallajokull 2010, Sakurajima, Taal 2020, Anak Krakatau; Pliny the Younger's ancient description; satellite detection for aviation warning). Grokipedia first at build.
topics.framing_note: EARTH-SYSTEM theme ladder: the spine is VOLCANIC LIGHTNING, deepened across named volcanoes (Eyjafjallajokull, Sakurajima, Taal, Anak Krakatau). Every rung names a place. Accuracy rail: the mechanism is STATIC charge from colliding ash particles (not ordinary weather) -- teach it via the scene at T3, keep it correct. Dinner-test payoff = lightning made inside an ash cloud with no storm (T2/T3). Distractors: other eruption/atmospheric phenomena (St Elmo's fire, pyroclastic flow, ashfall) and other volcanoes so all four stay live. The Pliny reference is a real historical description, not embroidery.

topics.name: Yellowstone: the supervolcano under the park
topics.scope: America's first national park sits inside the crater of a sleeping supervolcano. T1: Yellowstone in Wyoming, USA, is famous for its geysers and rainbow-colored hot springs -- and the whole park sits on top of one of the world's largest volcanic systems. T2: invert the wonder -- the reason for all the geysers, the vast Grand Prismatic Spring, and Old Faithful is a giant chamber of molten rock a few kilometers down heating the groundwater; Yellowstone holds about HALF of all the geysers on Earth. T3: teach the term -- the park sits inside a 'caldera,' a basin roughly 55 by 72 km wide that formed when the ground collapsed into an emptied magma chamber after a colossal eruption. T4: Yellowstone has had three giant eruptions; the most recent, the Lava Creek event about 640,000 years ago, ejected around 1,000 cubic km of rock -- a 'supervolcano' eruption thousands of times larger than Mount St Helens. T5: the hotspot itself hasn't moved -- the North American Plate has DRIFTED southwest over it, leaving a 700-km trail of older calderas across the Snake River Plain of Idaho, like a scorch mark showing where the continent has slid.
topics.source: Wikipedia: 'Yellowstone Caldera' (fetched/verified: Lava Creek Tuff ~640,000 ya ~1,000 cubic km, Huckleberry Ridge ~2.08 Ma ~2,450 cubic km, Snake River Plain hotspot track). Caldera ~55x72 km and 'about half the world's geysers' are standard USGS/NPS figures. Grokipedia first at build.
topics.framing_note: Keystone place-ladder with the hotspot earth-process as its spine. Accuracy rail: teach 'caldera' before testing it; last supereruption ~640,000 years ago (Lava Creek) -- do NOT imply it is 'overdue' or frame it as alarm; the hotspot is fixed and the PLATE moved (same physics as Hawaii). Dinner-test payoff = the geysers are the surface sign of a supervolcano's magma (T2) and the Snake River Plain 'scorch mark' trail (T5). Distractors: other calderas/supervolcanoes (Long Valley, Toba, Campi Flegrei) and other geyser fields (Iceland, New Zealand) so all four stay live.

topics.name: Antarctica -- the Windiest, Coldest Place on Earth
topics.scope: The frozen continent that holds the planet's records for wind and cold, driven by air pouring off the ice. T1: at Commonwealth Bay in Antarctica the wind blows near gale force almost every day and has gusted past 300 km/h -- the windiest place at sea level on Earth; answer is Commonwealth Bay (the katabatic coast). T2: these are katabatic winds -- freezing, dense air sliding downhill off the high ice sheet under gravity, funneling and accelerating as it races to the coast; answer is katabatic (downhill) winds. T2: Douglas Mawson's 1911-14 team lived in that gale and he titled his account 'The Home of the Blizzard'; answer is 'The Home of the Blizzard'. T3: high on the inland plateau, Vostok Station recorded -89.2C (-128.6F) in 1983 -- the coldest air temperature ever measured on Earth; answer is Vostok Station. T3: two miles beneath Vostok lies a hidden liquid lake -- Lake Vostok -- sealed under the ice for millions of years; answer is Lake Vostok. T4: the wind-scoured McMurdo Dry Valleys may not have seen rain in two million years -- the closest thing on Earth to the surface of Mars; answer is the Dry Valleys. T4: Antarctica's ice holds around 90 percent of the planet's ice and most of its fresh water; answer is (most of Earth's) ice / fresh water.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Cape Denison / Commonwealth Bay (Mawson called it the windiest place on Earth; fierce katabatic winds; 'Home of the Blizzard'). Vostok Station -89.2C on 21 Jul 1983 (coldest surface air record); Lake Vostok subglacial lake; McMurdo Dry Valleys -- well-established, verify at build.
topics.framing_note: INVERT THE WONDER: the 300 km/h gusts are the hook, the PLACE the answer. Teach 'katabatic'. Dinner-test payoff = the Vostok cold record. ACCURACY RAIL: -89.2C (1983) is the coldest AIR temperature at a weather station -- satellites later found colder ICE-SURFACE spots on the plateau; say 'air temperature' so both stay true. LANE: penguins and seals are the animal bank -- keep every answer the PLACE (the wind, the cold, the dry valleys, the ice), never a creature's biology. Distractors = other extreme places (Death Valley hottest, Atacama driest non-polar, Commonwealth Bay windiest).
topics.history_overlap: Mawson's 1911-14 Australasian Antarctic Expedition is a light exploration-history touch -- keep geography's answer the place / the wind and defer the expedition narrative to history.

topics.name: El Nino & La Nina -- the Pacific That Shifts the World
topics.scope: The warming and cooling of the tropical Pacific that reshuffles weather across the planet. T1: off the coast of Peru, fishermen long ago named a warm current that arrived around Christmas 'El Nino' -- Spanish for 'the Christ Child'; answer is El Nino (the Christ Child). T2: normally the trade winds pile warm water in the western Pacific and let cold, nutrient-rich water well up off Peru; in an El Nino the winds slacken and the warm water slides BACK east, shutting the upwelling off; answer is the warm water sliding east / upwelling stops. T2: when the cold upwelling dies, Peru's anchovy fishery -- one of the largest on Earth -- collapses; answer is the anchovy-fishery collapse (a place-economy fact, not fish biology). T3: the opposite phase, La Nina ('the little girl'), brings extra-strong trades and an extra-cold eastern Pacific; answer is La Nina. T3: the see-saw of air pressure between Tahiti and Darwin that tracks it is the Southern Oscillation / Walker circulation; answer is the Walker circulation. T4: through 'teleconnections' one warm Pacific patch can dry out Indonesia and Australia (drought, bushfire, failed monsoon) while flooding Peru and the southern US; answer is the worldwide teleconnection/ripple. T4: El Nino years quiet Atlantic hurricanes (extra wind shear) but boost Pacific ones; answer is fewer Atlantic hurricanes. T5: coral and sediment records show ENSO running for thousands of years; a monster El Nino is tied to the catastrophic 1876-78 global famines; answer is the historical famine / the record in corals.
topics.source: Wikipedia: El Nino-Southern Oscillation (Peruvian sailors named warm Christmas current after the Christ Child; Carrillo 1892; anchovy collapses 1972-73/82-83/97-98/2015-16; Walker circulation; teleconnections). Cross-check Grokipedia at build.
topics.framing_note: The name-origin rung respects the religious naming on its own terms -- no smug aside. Dinner-test payoff = the teleconnection (a warm patch of Pacific water lights bushfires in Australia and floods in Peru). ACCURACY RAIL: El Nino = WARM eastern-Pacific phase, La Nina = COOL; do not conflate ENSO with long-term global warming. LANE: the anchoveta is a fish, but the FACT is the fishery/upwelling place-economy, never the fish's anatomy (animal bank). Distractors = other ocean-climate patterns (the monsoon, the Gulf Stream, the North Atlantic Oscillation) -- real but wrong.
topics.history_overlap: The 1876-78 Great Famine (Late Victorian Holocausts) rung could duplicate a history-bank episode on colonial-era famine -- keep geography's answer the El Nino/climate fact and defer the political-history narrative.

topics.name: Foehn & Chinook -- the Warm Wind Off the Mountains
topics.scope: The dry downslope wind that pours off a mountain's lee side and warms as it falls. T1: in Alberta a warm winter wind spills off the Rockies and can melt a foot of snow in hours -- locals call it the chinook, the 'snow-eater'; answer is the chinook (snow-eater). T2: in Spearfish, South Dakota a chinook once shot the temperature from -4F to 45F in TWO MINUTES -- the fastest temperature change ever recorded; answer is Spearfish (the two-minute jump). T2: why it warms -- air wrung dry going up the peak descends the far side and COMPRESSES, heating as it sinks (the foehn effect); answer is the descending air compresses and warms. T3: in the Alps the original 'foehn' melts the snow and (in folklore) frays people's nerves -- old Alpine courts once treated a foehn day as a mitigating factor; answer is the foehn (Alps), mood-effect labeled folklore. T3: in Southern California the Santa Ana winds are the same beast, and they fan wildfires downslope toward Los Angeles; answer is the Santa Ana winds. T4: Argentina's Zonda drops off the Andes onto Mendoza -- same wind, another name; answer is the Zonda. T4: foehn winds sweeping over Antarctica's ice shelves can melt the surface and help crack them apart; answer is (foehn over) Antarctic ice shelves.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Foehn wind (dry warm downslope lee wind; adiabatic warming; chinook 'snow-eater' Rockies/Alberta; Santa Ana CA; zonda Argentina; can raise temps ~14C in hours). Spearfish SD -4F to 45F in 2 min, Jan 22 1943 = world record -- well-established, verify at build.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led -- snow vanishing off an Alberta field in an afternoon. Dinner-test payoff = the Spearfish two-minute record (an accuracy rail: -4F to 45F, Jan 22 1943). ACCURACY RAIL: the mood/health effects of the foehn are FOLKLORE -- label them so, do not state as fact. Ties to the rain-shadow ladder (same compression-warming physics) but anchor each to a DIFFERENT named place. Distractors = COLD downslope/regional winds that are the opposite (mistral, bora) -- adjacent-but-wrong.

topics.name: Hurricane, Typhoon, Cyclone -- One Storm, Three Names
topics.scope: The single most powerful storm on Earth, wearing a different name in every ocean. T1: the exact same spinning storm is a 'hurricane' over the Caribbean, a 'typhoon' over the Philippines, and a 'cyclone' over India -- three names, one beast; answer is they are the same storm (named by region). T2: at its heart is the eye -- a calm, often sunny circle of still air -- ringed by the eyewall where the deadliest winds howl; answer is the eye. T2: the biggest killer is usually not the wind but the storm surge, a wall of seawater the storm shoves ashore; answer is the storm surge. T3: the deadliest on record was the 1970 Bhola cyclone in the Bay of Bengal -- up to half a million dead in what is now Bangladesh, because the funnel-shaped bay magnifies the surge; answer is the Bay of Bengal / Bhola. T3: they only spin up over ocean warmer than about 26.5C and never right on the equator (no Coriolis spin to start them turning); answer is warm water, not on the equator. T4: the Saffir-Simpson scale rates them 1 to 5 by wind; a Category 5 like Typhoon Haiyan (2013, Philippines) or the 1935 Labor Day hurricane (Florida Keys) erases everything in its path; answer is Category 5. T4: Typhoon Tip (1979, NW Pacific) was the largest ever measured -- about 2,220 km across, as wide as the western United States; answer is Typhoon Tip. T5: Hurricane Catarina (2004) was the first hurricane ever recorded in the South Atlantic, a basin where they 'should not' form; answer is the South Atlantic / Catarina.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Tropical cyclone (hurricane=Atlantic/NE Pacific, typhoon=NW Pacific, cyclone=Indian Ocean/S Pacific; eye 30-65 km calm, eyewall strongest; storm surge deadliest; needs Coriolis, rarely forms within 5 deg of equator). Bhola cyclone 1970 (deadliest, ~300k-500k), Typhoon Tip 1979 (~2,220 km), Hurricane Catarina 2004 (first S. Atlantic) -- well-established, verify figures at build.
topics.framing_note: The three-names fact is the spine; scene-led -- a satellite eye, a drowned coast -- never 'What is a hurricane?'. Dinner-test payoff = Typhoon Tip's continent-spanning size, or the one-storm-three-names reveal itself. ACCURACY RAILS: the Bhola death toll is an ESTIMATE/range (label it); ~26.5C and the ~5-degree-Coriolis limit are real thresholds; distinguish the Saffir-Simpson wind scale from actual damage. Distractors = other storm types (tornado, nor'easter, derecho) and other named storms -- keep all four live.
topics.history_overlap: The 1970 Bhola cyclone's role in triggering Bangladesh's independence could duplicate a history-bank episode -- keep geography's answer the storm / the Bay of Bengal and defer the political aftermath to history.

topics.name: Rain-Shadow Deserts -- the Dry Side of the Mountains
topics.scope: How a mountain wall wrings the rain out of the air and casts a desert behind it. T1: cross the Andes from the wet Chilean coast and the far side is bone-dry -- Argentine Patagonia is a cold desert sitting in the mountains' 'rain shadow'; answer is the rain shadow (or Patagonia). T2: the mechanism: moist ocean wind climbs the windward slope, cools, and dumps its rain there -- so it clears the crest already wrung dry; answer is the moisture squeezed out on the windward side. T2: behind the Himalaya and the Tibetan Plateau -- the world's highest wall -- lies the Gobi, cut off from the monsoon; answer is the Gobi (the Himalayan rain shadow). T3: in North America the Sierra Nevada casts the shadow that makes the Great Basin and Death Valley, the driest and lowest place on the continent; answer is Death Valley / the Great Basin. T3: on Kauai the windward flank of Mount Waialeale is among the wettest spots on Earth (~11,000 mm) while the leeward Kona-style coast stays sunny-dry -- a rain shadow only miles wide; answer is Mount Waialeale's dry lee. T4: New Zealand's Southern Alps: the West Coast drinks six to seven meters of rain while Central Otago just over the crest is the nation's driest land; answer is the Southern Alps rain shadow / Central Otago. T5: the Judaean Desert lies in the rain shadow of the Judaean hills only miles from the green Mediterranean coast -- a desert beside the sea; answer is the Judaean Desert.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Rain shadow (windward ascent/precipitation, leeward descent/foehn; Atacama & E. Patagonia rain-shadowed by Andes; Gobi/Taklamakan behind Himalayas; Death Valley & Great Basin behind Sierra Nevada/Cascades). Mount Waialeale ~11,500 mm and NZ Southern Alps contrast -- well-established, verify figures at build.
topics.framing_note: Teach 'rain shadow' and 'windward/leeward' before testing them; scene-led -- climb the wet green slope, cross the crest, drop into the dry lee. Dinner-test payoff = Death Valley, or the miles-wide Hawaiian shadow (wettest and driest almost touching). ACCURACY RAIL: the Sahara and Arabia are HADLEY deserts, not rain-shadow -- do not miscredit them; the Atacama gets only ONE passing mention here (its full multi-cause story is a separate ladder). Distractors = deserts formed by a DIFFERENT cause (Sahara=Hadley, Namib=cold current).

topics.name: The Atacama -- the Driest Place on Earth
topics.scope: A hyper-arid Chilean desert made bone-dry by three forces at once, yet full of wonders. T1: in northern Chile's Atacama, some weather stations have NEVER recorded a single drop of rain; answer is the Atacama (the never-rains desert). T2: it is dry for three reasons stacked together -- the Andes block Atlantic moisture (rain shadow), the cold Humboldt Current chills the coast so little water evaporates, and it sits under the sinking Hadley air; the reason people forget is the cold ocean current; answer is the cold Humboldt Current. T3: there is almost no rain but there IS fog -- the camanchaca rolls in off the cold sea, and coastal 'fog oases' (lomas) catch it; people string fog nets to harvest drinking water; answer is the camanchaca fog / fog-catching nets. T3: its soil is so Mars-like and lifeless that NASA tests Mars rovers and life-detection instruments there; answer is (a stand-in for) Mars. T4: once every few years a freak rain triggers the 'desierto florido' -- the desert erupts in a carpet of flowers from long-dormant seeds; answer is the flowering desert (desierto florido). T4: the skies are so clear and dry that some of the world's biggest telescopes -- ALMA and the VLT at Paranal -- are built there; answer is the great observatories / ALMA. T5: preserved by that aridity, the Chinchorro mummies of the Atacama coast are the oldest deliberately made mummies on Earth -- older than Egypt's; answer is the Chinchorro mummies.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Atacama Desert (two-sided rain shadow Andes + Coast Range; cold north-flowing Humboldt Current; South Pacific anticyclone/Hadley subsidence; stations never recorded rain; possibly no significant rain 1570-1971; camanchaca fog supports lichens/cacti; desierto florido Sep-Nov; ALMA/ESO Paranal & La Silla). Chinchorro mummies oldest deliberate mummification -- well-established, verify at build.
topics.framing_note: INVERT THE WONDER throughout -- the 'never rained on record' fact is the hook, the PLACE (and its causes) the answer. The three-causes rung teaches that a great desert can have STACKED drivers (Hadley + rain shadow + cold current) -- but keep it ONE coherent answer (the cold current is the missed piece), not a theory-stack. Dinner-test payoff = the camanchaca fog-nets, or the flowering desert. LANE: the flowering-desert PLANTS and any fog-drinking creature are botany/animal -- keep the answer the PLACE-fact (the bloom, the fog oasis), never species anatomy. Chinchorro rung: respect on its own terms. Distractors = other superlative deserts (Sahara largest, Death Valley hottest, Antarctica coldest/polar).
topics.history_overlap: The Chinchorro-mummies rung could touch a history/archaeology episode -- keep geography's answer the place-fact (aridity preserved the world's oldest mummies) and defer the culture-history detail.

topics.name: The Coriolis Effect -- Why the Storms Spin
topics.scope: How Earth's rotation bends every moving wind and sets the storms turning. T1: a hurricane in the Caribbean spins counterclockwise, but a cyclone off Australia spins clockwise -- a perfect mirror image; what flips them is Earth's own rotation; answer is Earth's rotation (the Coriolis effect). T2: named for Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis (1835), the effect nudges anything moving over the spinning globe -- to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, to the left in the Southern; answer is the Coriolis effect / deflection to the right (north). T2: it is why tropical storms almost never form within about 5 degrees of the equator -- there is too little spin there to get them turning; answer is (too little Coriolis) at the equator. T3: long-range gunners had to correct for it -- WWI's Paris Gun, firing 75 miles, drifted noticeably from the Coriolis bend; answer is the Coriolis drift on the shells. T3: the 'which way does the bathtub or toilet drain' story is a MYTH -- a basin is far too small for Coriolis to matter; drain shape and swirl decide it; answer is a myth (label). T4: winds do not flow straight from high to low pressure -- Coriolis bends them until they circle the pressure center (the geostrophic wind); answer is they spiral around the pressure center.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Coriolis force (deflection right in N. Hemisphere / left in S.; storms counterclockwise N / clockwise S; cyclones rarely form within 5 deg of equator; bathtub/toilet drain is a debunked myth; Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis 1835). Paris Gun Coriolis correction -- well-established, verify at build.
topics.framing_note: Teach the effect through scenes -- a storm seen from space, a becalmed equator -- never a bare definition. Dinner-test payoff = the toilet/bathtub-drain MYTH, which doubles as an accuracy rail: debunk it explicitly. ACCURACY RAIL: Coriolis is negligible at household scale; real at storm/artillery scale. Distractors = other real forces or drivers (gravity, magnetism, the jet stream, air pressure) -- keep all four live so the player must KNOW the answer.

topics.name: The Hadley Cell & the 30-Degree Deserts
topics.scope: The great overturning loop of tropical air that makes rainforests at the equator and deserts at 30 degrees. T1: over the Congo and the Amazon, steamy equatorial air rises and dumps daily rain -- which is why the great rainforests sit in a band right on the equator; answer is the rising equatorial air. T2: that risen air spreads toward the poles high up and comes back DOWN, dry, around 30 degrees latitude -- and that sinking air bakes the Sahara, Arabia, the Kalahari, and Australia's Outback into a belt of deserts; answer is the sinking/descending dry air. T2: the whole loop is the Hadley cell, worked out by George Hadley in 1735 to explain the trade winds; answer is the Hadley cell. T3: sailors called the calm-wind zone under the sinking air the 'horse latitudes' -- legend says becalmed ships threw horses overboard to save water; answer is the horse latitudes (label as legend). T3: where the trade winds of both hemispheres converge and lift, the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) marches north and south with the seasons, dragging the monsoon rains with it; answer is the ITCZ. T4: the descending branch parks semi-permanent high-pressure zones over the oceans -- the Azores High, the Pacific High -- that steer summer storms; answer is the subtropical highs. T5: the Hadley cell is WIDENING as the planet warms, pushing its dry edge poleward and threatening to dry the Mediterranean and California; answer is the expanding/widening dry belt.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Hadley cell (air rises at ITCZ, descends ~30 deg producing subtropical deserts incl. Sahara/Arabian; George Hadley 1735 explained trade winds; clear skies + evaporation surplus in the descending branch). Horse-latitudes etymology = disputed legend. Cross-check Grokipedia at build.
topics.framing_note: INVERT THE WONDER: the deserts-line-up-at-30-degrees pattern is the hook, the sinking Hadley air the answer. Teach 'Hadley cell' and 'ITCZ' before testing them. Dinner-test payoff = the horse latitudes (LABEL the horse-overboard story as legend, not fact -- an accuracy rail). ACCURACY RAIL: not every desert is a Hadley desert -- the Atacama and Gobi are rain-shadow/current deserts (own ladders); keep this ladder's answers the SUBTROPICAL-belt deserts under the descending branch. Distractors = rain-shadow or coastal deserts (real, but formed by a different cause).

topics.name: The Jet Stream -- the River of Wind That Steers the Storms
topics.scope: The fast, narrow ribbon of high wind that flows west-to-east and drives mid-latitude weather. T1: seven miles up over the North Atlantic a band of wind screams along at over 100 mph; a jet from New York to London rides it and lands an hour early, but fights it going the other way; answer is the jet stream. T2: a Japanese meteorologist, Wasaburo Ooishi, discovered it in the 1920s tracking pilot balloons near Mount Fuji -- but published in Esperanto and was ignored for decades; answer is (published in) Esperanto / near Mount Fuji. T2: in WWII Japan floated thousands of paper balloon bombs (fu-go) onto the jet stream to reach North America -- the only WWII attack to kill civilians on the US mainland (six, near Bly, Oregon); answer is the fu-go balloon bombs. T3: the jet forms along the polar front, where cold polar air meets warm subtropical air -- the sharper the temperature contrast, the faster it blows; answer is the polar front / the temperature boundary. T3: it does not run straight -- it snakes in giant Rossby waves, and a deep southward dip drags Arctic air far south (a cold snap); answer is the meander / Rossby-wave dip. T4: when the jet buckles and locks a pattern in place (a blocking high), you get stalled heat domes and week-long floods; answer is a blocking pattern. T5: the polar vortex is a ring of jet-stream wind bottling up Arctic cold; when it weakens, the cold spills south into North America and Europe; answer is the polar vortex.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Jet stream (near tropopause ~30,000 ft, >180 km/h, up to 400 km/h; Ooishi 1920s near Fuji, published in Esperanto and overlooked; Pan Am 1952 Tokyo-Honolulu cut 1/3; WWII fire balloons, six deaths). Fu-go: six killed near Bly, Oregon 1945 -- well-established, verify at build.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led -- a plane pushed early across the Atlantic, a balloon drifting over Oregon -- never 'What is the jet stream?'. Dinner-test payoff = the fu-go balloon bombs (or the Esperanto snub -- both retellable). ACCURACY RAIL: Ooishi published in Esperanto (real reason his 1920s work was ignored); fu-go killed six near Bly, Oregon, May 1945. Place-anchored in Fuji, Oregon, the North Atlantic. Distractors = other wind systems (the trade winds, the Gulf Stream as a WATER current, the Hadley cell).
topics.history_overlap: The WWII fu-go balloon-bomb rung could duplicate a WWII history-bank episode -- keep geography's answer the jet stream / the place, and defer the war narrative to history.

topics.name: The Monsoon Reversal & Meghalaya's Wettest Places
topics.scope: The seasonal wind flip that drowns South Asia, deepened across the wettest inhabited places on Earth. T1: in the hills of Meghalaya in northeast India, the village of Mawsynram catches about 11,800 mm of rain a year -- the wettest inhabited place on Earth (invert the wonder: the huge number is the hook, the PLACE is the answer). T2: neighboring Cherrapunji (Sohra) once collected about 26,470 mm in a single year, 1860-61 -- a genuine 12-month record; answer is Cherrapunji. T2: what soaks them is a WIND REVERSAL -- in summer the land heats faster than the Indian Ocean, air rises over the continent, and the winds swing around to pull wet ocean air onshore (the summer monsoon); answer is the reversing wind / summer monsoon. T3: Meghalaya specifically because the Khasi Hills form a wall that lifts moist air funneling up off the Bay of Bengal (orographic lift); answer is the hills forcing the Bay of Bengal air upward. T4: the Khasi people weave the living aerial roots of the rubber fig (Ficus elastica) into LIVING ROOT BRIDGES across flooded rivers -- bridges that grow stronger for centuries (the double-decker bridge at Nongriat); answer is living root bridges. T4: despite record rain, Cherrapunji suffers dry-season water SHORTAGES because the rain sheets off deforested slopes -- a paradox; answer is dry-season water scarcity. T5: the monsoon 'burst' arrives around June 1 at Kerala and sweeps north; a failed monsoon meant historic famine -- the rains are the heartbeat of a billion farmers; answer is the monsoon onset/burst.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Mawsynram (avg ~11,872 mm; wettest-inhabited claim contested by Colombian sites Lloro/Lopez de Micay); Wikipedia: Cherrapunji (26,470 mm 1860-61 record). Living root bridges of Meghalaya, Khasi Ficus elastica jingkieng jri -- well-established, verify Nongriat double-decker at build. Cross-check Grokipedia at build.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led -- a hillside vanishing behind a wall of rain -- never 'What is the wettest place on Earth?'; put the rainfall number in the stem and make the PLACE the answer. ACCURACY RAIL: 'wettest INHABITED place' is contested (Colombian rivers claim higher averages) -- say 'inhabited' carefully; the 26,470 mm Cherrapunji figure is a real single-year record. Dinner-test payoff = the living root bridges (a cultural creation born of the monsoon). STANCE RAIL (bake into that rung, no ladder-wide mandate): celebrate Khasi root-bridge engineering as sophisticated living architecture, never 'primitive'/'exotic'. LANE: rice paddies get at most a one-rung mention -- rice DISHES belong to the cooking bank. Distractors = other real superlative-rain places (Colombian Choco, Hawaii's Waialeale).

topics.name: The Named Winds -- Mistral, Sirocco, Harmattan, Khamsin
topics.scope: The famous regional winds that rule their coasts, each anchored to a named place. T1: in Provence a cold, dry wind roars down the Rhone valley to the Mediterranean so hard it bends the cypress trees and scrubs the sky brilliant blue -- the mistral; answer is the mistral. T2: the mistral shaped Provencal life -- farmhouses built with blank north walls and rows of cypress windbreaks, and Van Gogh painted lashed to his easel at Arles; answer is (blank north walls / cypress windbreaks). T2: from the south comes its opposite, the sirocco -- a hot wind off the Sahara that carries red dust across the sea and drops 'blood rain' on southern Europe and the Alps; answer is the sirocco (blood rain). T3: in West Africa the harmattan drives dry Saharan dust down to the Gulf of Guinea in a haze that grounds flights -- yet it is so refreshingly dry that locals call it 'the Doctor'; answer is the harmattan (the Doctor). T3: that same Saharan dust, much of it from a single spot -- Chad's Bodele Depression -- blows clear across the Atlantic and FERTILIZES the Amazon rainforest with phosphorus; answer is it fertilizes the Amazon. T4: in Egypt the khamsin ('fifty') is a scorching spring wind named for the roughly fifty days it can recur, burying roads and darkening Cairo's sky; answer is the khamsin. T4: the icy bora off Trieste and the summer meltemi of the Aegean round out the family -- each a named local wind that governs a shoreline; answer is the bora / meltemi.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Sirocco (Saharan hot wind, red 'blood rain' in S. Italy, up to ~100 km/h); Harmattan (dry dusty NE trade Nov-Mar, 'the Doctor', harmattan haze, RH <15%). Mistral (cold dry NW down Rhone, Provencal architecture) and khamsin (~50-day hot Egyptian wind); Saharan dust from Bodele Depression fertilizing Amazon with phosphorus -- all well-established, verify at build.
topics.framing_note: Each rung anchors to a NAMED place and its signature wind; distractors = OTHER named winds (adjacent-but-wrong, all real). The mistral-architecture / Van Gogh rung is a genuine cultural creation shaped by the wind. Dinner-test payoff = Saharan dust crossing the ocean to feed the Amazon (ACCURACY RAIL: verify the Bodele Depression as the dominant source and the phosphorus-fertilization link at build). LANE: no wine-of-Provence or food ladder (cooking bank). Keep hot vs cold winds correctly sorted -- an accuracy rail.

topics.name: The Trade Winds & the Doldrums -- the Highways of Sail
topics.scope: The steady tropical winds that carried the Age of Discovery, and the dead-calm belt between them. T1: for five centuries, sailing ships crossing the Atlantic from Europe to the Americas rode a reliable wind blowing steadily from the northeast -- the trade winds; answer is the trade winds. T2: 'trade' here first meant a steady 'track' or course, not commerce -- but the winds became so vital to merchant fleets that the money-meaning stuck; answer is 'a steady track/course' (etymology twist, label as such). T2: Columbus rode the trades WEST from the Canary Islands, then looped home on the higher-latitude westerlies -- the great clockwise wheel of Atlantic wind; answer is the westerlies (the road home). T3: right at the equator the two hemispheres' trade winds collide and cancel into a windless belt -- the doldrums, where sailing ships could sit becalmed for weeks; answer is the doldrums / ITCZ. T3: for 250 years Spanish galleons rode the trades and the Kuroshio from Manila to Acapulco -- the longest sustained trade route in history; answer is the Manila galleon route. T4: the Portuguese 'volta do mar' -- swinging far out toward Brazil to catch the westerlies home from Africa -- was the trick that unlocked ocean navigation; answer is the volta do mar. T5: the trades blow east-to-west because the Coriolis effect bends the equator-bound air; without Earth's spin they would blow straight toward the equator; answer is the Coriolis bend.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Trade winds (etymology 'track' -> later 'commerce'; NE/SE toward equator; doldrums/ITCZ; Portuguese volta do mar, cross to Brazil then east ~30S; enabled colonization of the Americas). Manila galleon route -- well-established, verify at build.
topics.framing_note: STANCE (vision_mandated): CELEBRATE the Age of Discovery and its seamanship honestly, and be honest BOTH WAYS about what the routes carried -- immense wealth and exchange AND colonization and slaving -- plainly, without warping the wind facts. Dinner-test payoff = the doldrums (becalmed for weeks) or the volta do mar counterintuitive detour. ACCURACY RAIL: the 'track not commerce' etymology is the real older meaning -- present it as an etymology twist. LANE: no spice/cargo-as-food ladder (cooking bank). Distractors = other named wind systems (westerlies, monsoon, roaring forties).
topics.history_overlap: The Columbus-westward and Manila-galleon rungs may duplicate Age-of-Discovery voyages in the history bank -- keep geography's answer the WIND / route, not the voyage's political narrative.

topics.name: Tornado Alley & the Supercell
topics.scope: The stretch of North America that breeds more tornadoes than anywhere on Earth, and why. T1: the central US Great Plains -- Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Nebraska -- see more tornadoes than any place on the planet; the belt is nicknamed 'Tornado Alley'; answer is Tornado Alley. T2: the recipe is a collision: cold, dry air spilling east off the Rockies rides OVER warm, wet air streaming up from the Gulf of Mexico, and the unstable layers erupt upward into rotating supercell thunderstorms; answer is the clash of Rockies-dry over Gulf-moist air. T2: the sharp boundary where dry desert air meets Gulf moisture -- the 'dryline,' often over the Texas Panhandle -- is where the storms fire; answer is the dryline. T3: the widest tornado ever measured struck El Reno, Oklahoma in 2013 -- about 2.6 miles (4.2 km) across; answer is El Reno. T3: Ted Fujita built the scale (F, now EF) that rates tornado damage from EF0 to EF5 -- only an EF5 peels pavement and levels a brick house; answer is the Fujita scale. T4: 'Dixie Alley' across the Deep South is often deadlier -- its tornadoes strike at night, hidden in rain and trees; answer is Dixie Alley.
topics.source: Well-established meteorology: Tornado Alley (Great Plains, US leads world in tornado count); supercell ingredients (Rocky Mtn dry air over Gulf moisture, the dryline); El Reno OK 31 May 2013 widest on record ~4.2 km; Ted Fujita / (Enhanced) Fujita scale; Dixie Alley nocturnal/rain-wrapped risk. Verify all figures against Wikipedia + Grokipedia at build.
topics.framing_note: Scene-led -- a green-black sky and a lowering wall cloud -- never 'What is a tornado?'. Dinner-test payoff = the El Reno widest-tornado record (ACCURACY RAIL: ~2.6 mi / 4.2 km wide, 31 May 2013 -- widest by radar; note it was rated EF3, not the strongest). ANIMAL/LANE: none. Distractors = other severe-weather features/places (derecho, haboob, hurricane, Dixie Alley) -- adjacent-but-wrong. Teach 'supercell' and 'dryline' before leaning on them.
